_childDocuments_.review: Even aside from the remaining bugs, I do feel this game is roundly a downgrade from the first, which was a game I wasn't expecting to like but ended up enjoying a LOT lot. And it's not like 2 is particularly worse than 1 in any major ways... just a lot of little ways that add up. And, don't get me wrong, it's still GOOD, quite good - but, it's like going from a 9/10 to an 8/10. The magic just isn't there this time.Specifics? Well, one, I'm just not thrilled about having three weapons. I think the weapons, individually, are all good, all have their uses, I bounced between them all fairly regularly, and the puzzles and platforming involved with each of them are pretty fun, too! But... none of them feel as versatile or as -good- as your standard blasphemous 1 sword. All the different moves that game had got doled out between the sword and the daggers in this one, with the mace kinda just being its own thing, so I always feel like I'm playing with an incomplete kit - and parrying, while, one, feeling nerfed in this game, also just doesn't feel as useful - I swear bosses have way more unblockable magic attacks than they used to, or attacks you can't really counter even if you can parry.I'm also not a fan of all the extra steps the game adds to powering up this time around - it was already true of some upgrades in the last game, true, but now even basic health and mana increases require you to drag quest items to NPCs, which are a lot more spread out than they were last time, too. And the game still has as many obtuse puzzles and quest items as before, though at the very least nothing truly missable this time. Rosary beads feel less useful, basically just existing as two or three tiers of the same few defensive capabilities and all the cool ones got doled out to the altarpieces instead, which, okay, fair, and those can be pretty fun to play around with - once you unlock the ability to change them from save points, anyways.Bosses do feel roundly harder in this game, and combat is generally faster-paced as a result of the higher level of movement you have, and I'm mixed about some of them - more aerial bosses than last time, I feel, which COMPLETELY nerfs the sword and its reliance on ground combos, and doesn't feel great with the daggers or mace, either, though the mace generally fares best in the air out of all three. Oh, by the way, the enemy bounce is just. Gone. Not even something you can eventually get back. I miss it so much. Was a cool, fun mechanic that had both platforming and combat applications. Anyways, so Odon is the worst boss across both games, easily. I just. Do not think mob fights are ever fun - dude would be fine on his own, but the addition of enemies, even relatively weak but numerous ones, suggests the devs thought the boss wasn't interesting enough on its own (it was - the pre-fight proved that imo). And the battle arenas, carried over from the first game, also feel like a mess this time - instead of themed areas with different arenas, you get one bare-bones arena and a random scattering of enemies, which are already more palette swap-y than they were in the first game, usually two or three different elemental varieties of the same enemy types.And, my least favorite change - the back half of the game is COMPLETELY linear. The first half? Very open, and very fun. The back half, new areas literally don't appear until you kill the boss of the previous one. And I really don't get why it had to be that way. The areas themselves are cool and fun, but being ghost train ridden through them all in what was originally a wide-open exploration game just feels baaad.I gripe but, again, I had a lot of fun with this game - the combat, when it works, and that's most of the time, is really fun and a fresh take on the first game's combat, and the introduction of new movement abilities, often integrated into the fights, goes a long way in facilitating that. And the platforming and puzzles are better than ever here - no instakill spikes or pits this time, for one, but the bigger toolset of moves just leads to more interesting platforming. Though I lament the loss of really clever stuff like falling in pits to go to lower areas and take shortcuts or get treasures you couldn't otherwise get but, ehh, the novelty of that would probably wear off if they repeated it. I still think this game is a good fun time, worth its asking price etc. but it doesn't feel as "special" as the first game did, or as unique - just another good metroidvania with the lightest of light souls-like elements.

_childDocuments_.review: The sequel jinx is real. There is no question about the high quality of art unique to the franchise, but it's clear as day that  is a significant downgrade from the original game in terms of storytelling and gameplay. Do not get me wrong;  is still a very well-made Metroidvania game. It's just that this sequel could not live up to the glorious reputation that the first  game set for the franchise.The big difference that you cannot help but notice when you start this game is that it uses fairly bright and mild animations for its cutscenes. This was a very un--like design decision. The first  game was all about dark and gothic, immersing players in the despair that fell onto the denizens of Cvstodia. However, the Penitent One's journey in this sequel feels very light, compared to the first game, thanks to the relatively peaceful animations. I just could not feel the similar level of urgency from the art style. Even after finishing the game, I still cannot figure out why they switched their art style, at the expense of the franchise brand they worked so hard to build up with the first game.Combined with the bright and mild animations, the relatively easy boss fights also contributes to ruin the immersion in the dark world unique to the franchise. Compared to the bosses from the first game, bosses from this sequel feel very... repetitive, to say the least. They do not feel like challenges as they should be, but feel like jobs you have to complete to move on. There was one really good boss: a very pleasant exception from the pattern. But it is still one boss out of about ten; not a good news to the general gameplay quality. I am expecting some updates later on to buff up the bosses, but who knows when?Overall, still a fine game to those new to the franchise in terms of art, but not quite there to satisfy the fans of the first  game. I am still planning to keep my eye on this game though, because I see a lot of potential for future DLCs. So maybe I made my judgment too quick. As a solid fan of the first game, I'm keeping my fingers crossed for the DLCs to eventually bring out -likeness from this game.

The art in game is great at a technical level but i often found its more muted washed out look far less interesting than the original, often finding most areas uninteresting. Way fewer finishing animations too, a lot of bland crushing with thorns.The new weapon system i think is a nice idea but in practise made most combat feel far worse and sloppy. I especially dint really enjoy the whole movement systems locked to certain weapons.The audio is fantastic again, same with the voice direction for both languages. Way fewer large interesting creatures to fight boss wise.By no means a bad game, but after my run of it i just came away thinking it was disappointing compared to my time with the original (that was spent before the multiple basically free dlc patches).

_childDocuments_.review: "Plasphemous 2" is a visually stunning masterpiece that continues to captivate players with its mesmerizing pixel art. The intricate details and hauntingly beautiful landscapes immerse players in a world of dark beauty and despair. The introduction of new weapon mechanics adds a refreshing layer of versatility to the gameplay, allowing players to experiment with different combat styles and strategies.The game's non-linear storytelling and the introduction of new mysteries create an enthralling sense of exploration and discovery. Players are constantly challenged to remember their steps and retrace their paths to uncover hidden secrets and unlock new areas. This non-linear approach adds depth and complexity to the gameplay, keeping players engaged and eager to explore every corner of the game world."Plasphemous 2" is a testament to the power of pixel art in conveying emotion and atmosphere. With its innovative weapon mechanics, non-linear storytelling, and captivating mysteries, it offers a gaming experience that is both haunting and unforgettable.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is everything that I ask for in a metroidvania.Some fans of Blasphemous 1 will hate it, due to how different it is at points. Three weapons, human-sized bosses, different art direction, lesser difficulty level, and so on. Other fans will love it for those same differences. Three weapons means more combat variety. Human-sized bosses will sport different movesets and feel faster-paced at times. Different art direction is a matter of taste. Lesser difficulty level is partly because spikes no longer 1-shot you like the cheap bastards they are.The game is different from Blasphemous 1, and I think whether or not you enjoy it is going to somewhat hinge on whether or not you're okay with something different. 2 isn't a perfect game. The enemies don't always feel as cool as they did in the first game. Some of the bosses feel easier, too. And sure, the art is different. But it also has things like greatly enhanced combat, cool levels with fun music, some neat lore, and some bosses which, thought not always the hardest, were genuinely cool, and a joy to fight.This game is different. If you're okay with that, and want a good metroidvania with some fun action and great music, you'll have a good time. If you're looking for Blasphemous 1 all over again, you won't get that here. Personally, I'm okay with that, but maybe you're not, and that's fine too. But me? I recommend it. Like, a lot.

_childDocuments_.review: This review was negative, but my friends convinced me to change it to positive since I liked the game. I hope you still take the time to read my criticisms.Ok, im lying. I do recommend this game. But, I have to leave a negative review. This is great game, but its such a downgrade compared to it's predecessor, I have to leave a negative review because it erks me that it has a high percentage of positive reviews. This game has a lot of what made the first game great. If you're like me and loved the first game, you'll enjoy this game. It's more of what you loved, and is a great metroidvania.But the first blasphemous is a masterpiece. Not acknowledging that this is a downgrade is a disservice to the love put into the first game. To get the least important complaint out of the way: this game is buggy. Twice I jumped while charging the flail attack and got stuck in the charge until i restarted the game. Sometimes the flail's little animation to start the fire doesn't play, and I just get stuck standing there. No spoilers, but a character who appears during some boss fights tanks the fps when they show up. Next, the art. The beautiful, gritty pixel art cut scenes of the first game gone and replaced by still, unmoving hand-drawn stills. While the art is good, and I'd have no complaints had I not played the first game, it PALES in comparison to the first games incredible cut scenes. The new art feels cartoony and really does not fit the majesty of the playable world. The animations of the enemies clearly have less love put in. Not focusing on the old crone who has a glitch in her animation so that sometimes two of her frames overlay each other, there's other places its clear less time was put in. Way less enemies have unique executions. Many just stay in their hitstun animation while you summon a cone of vines around them to crush them ( a copy, pasted animation).Lastly, this game reuses enemies way more than the first. It especially sucks because the devs insisted on reusing the giant brutes who tank damage like crazy. I never remember feeling like any enemies were sponges in the first game.This game is great. But these devs can do better than great. I started this game because recently a coworker asked me if I think any metroidvania is as good as Hollow Knight, and blasphemous was my answer. But I couldn't say the same about blasphemous II. They were clearly ambitious, and the weapon system is awesome. This game is so good, but it could have been better. My guess is that the devs had time constraints, since they licensed with much bigger companies for this game. I always worry, when games have less time put into stuff like animation, that devs will see that and think no one cared about animation. The first game is art. I hope the devs release an update revamping these flaws, so blasphemous II can stand with it's parent as two of the greatest metroidvanias ever made.

_childDocuments_.review: It was a good game until the Eviterno boss fight. Very frustrating and odd choice in significant difficulty spike vs. what the whole game prepared you for. I wouldn't say the boss is hard. Rather he is cheap, with small open windows, lighting fast movement, screen clutter, waiting through the dialogue, and just other tedious aspects to this. I really enjoyed my time otherwise, and would give it a thumbs up other than this one part. It is so frustrating that I just had  to put this down after so many attempts. Before you say git good, learn his mechanics, etc I get it. As a souls borne veteran this just doesn't work for me and I don't have the time or  the patience to do it. I've gotten close a few times and probably could get through it if I did nothing but concentrate on it for an hour but that is just not up my alley. Hopefully the devs realize there are some issues with this fight that could be addressed fairly (e.g. you get hit with a fire wall and on recovery you get hit again, there is no time to dodge or recover)Edit: I was finally able to beat Evitreno after concentrating for one hour. I still hold by that it was an odd choice in difficulty spike. You basically steamrolled through the entire game (Veridicto is OP). This boss fight would have been more palatable if the rest of the game was more challenging and getting you to dodge and parry more. I changed my review to thumbs up. The thumbs down was due to sheer frustration,

_childDocuments_.review: In some ways this improves over the first, but it falls short in others. Overall, there's a lot to love here. In terms of improvements: the movement and abilities are much more fleshed out and they are a lot of fun to use. Exploration, secrets, and quests are just the right amount of obscure, with a few of the possible quest lines being buried in item lore descriptions. Visually, it does not quite live up to the harrowing body horror of the first, but it is still successful in creating a feeling of a complete, strange, and grueling world with a handful of memorable NPCs and set piece encounters. Bottom line: it is a fun and engaging world to explore.The biggest negative is that the game is too easy, which makes my favorite boss in the game into a huge difficulty spike at the very end. Platforming is also much easier, and I missed the presence of insta-death spikes a la Castlevania. Also, I ran into a number of visual bugs, like enemies freezing mid-animation before dying and one of the weapons having some bugged animations. Also had a few deaths to bugged screen transitions where I died for no apparent reason. I've also read that some quest lines can bug out, but I did not experience that.In all, my complaints are minor and the experience of playing the game more than makes up for them. Strongly recommend for fans of the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: My first encounter with the work of The Game's Kitchen was with their point & click pixel art adventure: The Last Door, a game that to this day I still like very much. However, it doesn't end there, as I later played its sequel and was even more enchanted with the world they had created, and with the continuation of a very enigmatic but captivating story. So what does this have to do with Blasphemous 2? When the developers announced the first, I was excited thinking that perhaps it would be a new installment on The Last Door’s saga, and that it would delve deeper into the world behind the "veil" (I recommend playing The Last Door to understand this, sorry!), but I found myself with something quite different and that tried a new approach; a bloody and unforgiving world in which I immersed myself, and ended up amazed. Blasphemous exceeded my expectations and those of the general public, and even if it was of a completely different genre to what I knew from the team, I loved how they approached it. Now I find myself once again in this situation, with a sequel that proves once again that the developers have it clear when it comes to continuing their sagas. Blasphemous 2 far surpasses its predecessor, adding new mechanics and improvements that elevate the experience to a new level, and that left me very satisfied. This time, the story will take a different course; the miracle will give birth to a new event, and the Penitent one will wake up from his rest to once again put on his shoulders an arduous task. But standing in his way will be the Achicofradía, a group of penitents who were welcomed by the miracle as its defenders; an arduous and very fitting challenge for our character. If I can add anything, it is that without a doubt the religious setting is maintained and deepened, and it’s an aspect that really catches my attention.As in the first game, the  will be revealed to us little by little, with a lot of cryptic dialogue and at the hands of several new characters. On the other hand, we’ll also have some side quests, assignments and legends that we can follow if we want. In my case, I got quite lost in the world looking to complete these "quests", although some are easier to track than others. Overall, I really enjoyed this section, the narration is interesting and the fact that there is voice acting for the characters made me enjoy the experience so much more. On a side note, this sequel also features different endings; I'll leave it at that.The  remains fairly similar from the first game, being the classic metroidvania gameplay, with platforming, combat and exploration being the main focus. However, the character's movements felt more fluid and precise this time around, and there are several other new tidbits I'd like to comment on; by the way, we finally have a double jump! But what impressed me the most was that we now have three weapons at our disposal: the classic sword, dual blades, and a mace with a chain (my favorite). Each of them has its own characteristics, such as different attack speed or movements, and they have skill trees to improve their repertoire of techniques or increase the damage inflicted by them. But the most interesting thing about this is that they also have unique mechanics for exploration; an example would be the mace, with which we can ring huge bells that materialize surfaces or open certain doors. Having them interact both with combat and exploration left me ecstatic, truth be told.Beyond our arsenal of weapons, we’ll also have rosary beads; objects that will give us passive bonuses such as more defense against physical attacks, to give an example. We can also make use of prayers, divided between chants and verses; powerful spells and prayers, among which we’ll find from electric or blood attacks, to gigantic pillars of light that will rain judgment on our enemies. But something that stands out a lot, along with the new weaponry, is the Retablo de Favores and the carved sculptures that can be equipped on it to grant us powerful advantages, and which have special combinations depending on the ones they’re paired with. This addition, while quite similar to the rosary beads (as both are passive systems), I quite liked and it felt more interactive, letting me try out different statuettes to see if I could get those combos unlocked. In short, there are varied systems and mechanics that are very entertaining, and make the section feel robust and very complete.In terms of , the game returns to that beautiful pixel aesthetic, with muted and gloomy tones that create a very unique atmosphere. In addition, we’ll also be able to see animated cinematics, both in digital and pixel art, which are super neat and feel great from start to finish. The design of characters and bosses maintains that peculiarity that represented so much of the first game, the panoramas and environments are desolate and hopeless at times, and everything is very bloody, raw; I loved it. The   is excellent, just like in the first game. From suspenseful and calm melodies, to more lively ones between combat and dangerous areas; and in my opinion, those that make use of masterfully played guitars stand out a lot. The voice acting, both in Spanish and English, was impeccable and very immersive, and it is one of the few times where I have constantly changed the language of the voices to appreciate the differences. Both sections, visual and audio, left me fully satisfied, and absorbed in this particular world. In , Blasphemous 2 gives us a new and interesting story, improves practically all its aspects and mechanics, from exploration to combat, and even gives us at last a real double jump ability, which affirms it as a full-fledged metroidvania! I must admit that I had a couple of moments where I felt a bit bummed, like being hit in the middle of the getting up animation (which in "challenge" rooms, where many enemies spawn, can be a pain), and having to replay some cinematics several times when losing against the bosses they belonged to (although this is fixed by getting good haha!); but, all in all, I was delighted with the game, and I feel it was a marvelous sequel. Without any hesitation, I invite you to enter this religious world, and do your penance; whether you are a fan of the previous game or not, I think you can appreciate it either way.

_childDocuments_.review: Other than maybe the art style of the cutscenes, atmosphere and some of the boss designs, Blasphemous 2 is a straight upgrade on Blasphemous 1. - The controls are muuuch better, the platforming is more satisfying and there are no more instadeath spikes. - The two new weapons weren't as good as the sword for combat in my experience, but they at least had a function with some of the platforming. - The bosses in Blasphemous 2 are good, some are great, the only reason I give the edge to B1's bosses is because they were a little more creative. Most of the bosses in B2 are humanoids so it was missing that bit of weird monster killing that B1 had.- Music is always a matter of taste and I enjoyed the music in B1, but I would say the music in this game is more memorable.- Some of the collecting gets frustrating and tedious at times. There are a few collectables in this game that take far too long to achieve. The game needs some kind of system unlocked at the end of the game to let a player know when they have found everything in a room, otherwise you can spend literal hours backtracking and checking every room in the game for a small collectable. - There are also a few collectables that just require grinding and that's no fun. Nobody wants to grind in a metroidvania. But overall I really enjoyed Blasphemous 2, when I saw the change in art style I was initially put off, but as I played it more I realised how much Blasphemous 2 improves on the first game.

_childDocuments_.review: I must say, as a very big fan of MetroidVanias, and more of a fair-weather fan of the "souls-like" aspect, I was hesitant to try this one out. Boy, am I glad I did.I will start by saying I never played the first one (and I've since started playing it), so coming to this completely fresh and having watched a few reviews, I can definitely recommend this game.The controls are fluid, intuitive, and responsive. The difficulty is tough, but fair. The penalty for dying isn't as steep as it may seem, and there's a good deal of secrets and lore to uncover.I've read complaints from others about how this game changed the animation style for the cutscenes from the first to the second game, and for me personally, I didn't mind it. Some said it jars you away from the "pixelated" retro feel; but you can take this how you will, I didn't find it all that annoying or intrusive.The bosses are fun, just tough enough to keep you trying, but not so frustrating that you just have to give up. This game is all about learning enemy techniques and avoiding, countering, or outsmarting them. Each new area offers lots of stuff that's just out of reach (as is typical of the genre), and the map screen lets you add various markers so you can remember to come back later.The incentive for finding secrets is pretty nice too, makes going back for 100% completion much more approachable. This game also added 3 different weapons, as opposed to the main weapon used throughout the game. You start off by choosing one of the three, leaving you to progress through the game to find the others (and you will need all of them to fully progress, so don't fret).After having put in about 20 hours through this game and near 100% completion, I can say that this was one time I didn't mind picking up a game that was sure to kick my ass in spots. You should do the same, you won't regret it.Just don't drop your guilt...

_childDocuments_.review: [Disregard time played - much of it was spent AFK while I did other stuff] The art direction in this game is fantastic, but in full honestly, I can't say I'd recommend this game. Far too much of the game is based around finding hidden collectibles, and there are a TON of these things.First off, in the obligatory Metroidvania playstyle, there's a lot of unlockable mobility skills - dodges that let you go through certain walls, weapons that let you activate certain objects, and abilities that let you grab walls and hooks. Unfortunately, until you get those abilities, you have to just ignore every single one of these things you see, because you can't do anything with them until you unlock the ability. As a player, it's obnoxious to be exploring a new area and constantly run into passageways that you can't explore again and again and again because you haven't unlocked the necessary ability yet. It's almost Donkey Kong 64-esque.When you eventually unlock the ability, you'd better be prepared to do a lot of backtracking. For most of the game, you're only allowed to teleport between specific Gates and there aren't very many of them spread around, so you'll be legging it constantly through areas you've already explored. This becomes absolutely UNBEARABLE about midway through the game, when you hit a dead-end because you don't have a specific power-up unlocked yet, so you have to turn around and backtrack through every single area in the game, searching for the way towards unlocking that power-up. At one point, I spent almost 2 hours searching for the next area to go to, because it was actually ONE SINGLE UNMARKED corridor in a far-off part of the map that I was meant to go to.Keeping things spoiler-free, you will almost certainly receive Ending B upon finishing the game. To obtain Ending A, you have to collect ALL the collectibles in the game. Normally in a game with this many collectibles, the game will provide you with a map/radar of some sort after you've found MOST of the collectibles, to help nudge you towards the last remaining few - but not this game. The map is absolutely barebones and provides no hints about remaining collectibles, or even information about collectibles you've already found. The only thing the map provides are Pins, so if you haven't been manually marking every single collectible you've found since the start of the game, your only alternative is to look up an online guide and go re-check every single area to find the ones you missed - and some of them are EASILY missable.Lastly, from a lore standpoint, I never really felt engaged. So much of the games story is vague, as you travel around hearing about the Miracle and see all the weird NPCs affected by it, most of which will ask you to go find a bunch of collectibles for them. A dying woman laying in a bed, surrounded by mourners? Go find my 5 daughters. A mysterious, extremely tall nun-creature? Go find my 8 sisters. A gigantic man breastfeeding a baby? Go find 6 seeds of wax. A two-headed Jester with burning shoes? Go find me 12 boysenberries. I actually made up that last one, but it makes just as much sense as any of the other NPCs you'll come across. They're just there for the sake of being there, with very little plot relevance (if any). But don't forget: you HAVE to go collect all their thingamajigs if you want to see the REAL Ending,Also, as a minor gripe, the penultimate boss of the game comes with two unskippable cutscene segments that you have to sit through every single time you die to them. Upon completing the game, I pretty much just felt relieved that it was finally over.

_childDocuments_.review: My opinion on this game is a complicated mess which evens out to being better than lukewarm; this review is one bug-fix away from going positive. I handle metroidvanias and soulslikes very particularly, similarly too, the one major difference being in story progression. Dark Souls games have very volatile questlines which are extremely easy to fail if you progress too far, and metroidvanias, especially this one, have branching paths which should naturally funnel the player towards progression; past a certain point, the area boss is the only thing between you and the next. Blasphemous pulls from dark souls' open-ended design philosophy more-so than it likes to follow standard metroidvania conventions, and this combined with my vania-brained habits led to me completing ~40% of the map within 4 hours without fighting any mainline bosses at all; my first boss was optional, and was around 48%. The next 20 hours were extremely solid: I recognized that I was mistaken for not just sticking to a path early on, and the rest was pretty stellar right up until ~98% completion. One of the items that I'm supposed to collect---a cherub similar to those in the first game---undoubtedly failed to register, and I'm pretty sure that that means that all of my efforts have been effectively wasted, given that not collecting all of them almost certainly locks me into a run with the bad ending. Supposedly this has been a known bug for a few months now.One thing that I particularly disliked about this game was how disappointing the rewards for your efforts are; almost all of the prayer beads are tiered defense boosts, presuming that you're lucky enough to get those and not some other generic stand-in reward in the form of tears (souls) and marks (skillpoints), and while I know it's a bug, I'm still not okay with that trend of not keeping in lock-step with my efforts extending to my entire playthrough as a whole. This is my first negative review, and because it's for a game that I enjoyed enough to fixate on, I desperately hope that I'll have a reason to get rid of it.EDIT: THE AFOREMENTIONED BUG FIX IS FINALLY HERE; I've checked daily for almost a year, but they have now patched the cherub count bug. I'll go over and redo my review later on, but I'm upholding my promise and bumping it to positive, as I'd originally wanted to! :D

_childDocuments_.review: This is an incredible sequel over the terrible blasphemous 1. I purchased blasphemous 1 & 2 as a package deal, and I'm ultimately glad that I did. Blasphemous 1 was a chore, I think I hate that game. It was lacking in many aspects, forcing me to repeatedly question 'Why do people like it so much'.  I was lucky that I had already purchased this game, otherwise I likely would have overlooked it entirely.Blasphemous 2 is an absolute joy to play. The metroidvania style level design is superb, and a marked improvement over the 1st entry. Some real thought went into this one. Blasphemous 1 & 2 both allow the player to move in any direction they want, but the 1st simply required you beat 3 bosses to proceed to next area, then repeat. in the 2nd, movement abilities are required almost before every boss to unlock. On that topic, the movement in this game is also way more fluid and responsive. Perhaps not on the same level of fluidity as 'Ori: Of the blind forest' but it's a respectable improvement over the clunky control scheme of the 1st. Combat took a little getting used to; I was originally kind of opposed to the 3-weapon system. It grows on you, and while I never really strayed from my bread-n-butter mace, the other 2 weapons were fun to occasionally use depending on the situation.Story-wise is lacking a little, but honestly it just might be me not investing enough into the lore. It's presented in a very souls-type manner, which is to say you get as much out of it as you put into it.My only major complaint of this game is that achievements are largely, and knowingly, busted. They remain that way to this day. I'd play this game more if I thought I could actually 100% it. It's to the point where the community recommends you make backup saves prior to triggering certain achievements, in case you need to revert to try again. One post stated that the only achievement that failed to unlock was 'Complete all other achievements'. Like.... what?Anyways, despite that glaring issue, it's still an awesome game. I can wholeheartedly recommend this entry, while simultaneously condemning  blasphemous 1.

_childDocuments_.review: It hurts to not recommend this because Blasphemous 1 is one of my favourite games, but this needs some polish first. There is a very good game here but they need to fix it up a bit - when they do then I'll change this to positive.TL;DR This is lesser than the first game in several ways. It's still worth buying (the first game was so good so  good that even 'worse' is relative) but wait for a sale or for some balance / content updates first.Current complaints:1) The switch to anime-style cut scenes was a terrible idea, They're not bad animations in themselves but they clash badly with the overall style and are very jarring every time.2) The original game had many unique execution animations - here they are mostly just the same one over and over.3) There are too many enemies pasted from the first game and not enough unique ones.4) The whole concept of wave-style arena rooms is not something I enjoy generally, but some 'arena' rooms have ill-considered combinations of enemy type that can make it feel more random / unfair than challenging. One room in particular can be either fine or an absurd difficulty spike depending on how the enemy ai behaves on any given attempt. 5) The last area has basically no mid area saves, and multiple tedious 'arena rooms' forcing you to grind through the same ones repeatedly, which is seriously testing my patience to want to complete the game. There are a few elevators but not enough shortcuts to remove the tedium. Each individual 'screen' is not particularly hard and I'm sure I could get through it quite quickly but the tedium of repeating yourself if you die makes me not want to bother, after the first couple of deaths. Making me repeatedly complete challenges I have already passed is not challenging it is a chore. And then the boss has 3 stages with un-skippable slow transitions between them which is infuriating.There is a lot to love - the music is great, the pixel style art is great, and I adore the first game. It wouldn't take much to solve the issues. But this needs a bit of balancing, a couple more save points to reduce the tedium of repetition towards the end, plus a few more enemies and execution animations. And unskippable boss dialogue can kiss my butt.If you liked the first game, this is basically the same but somewhat lacking by comparison. Still good, but not up to the standards of the first. Wait for some updates. which will hopefully address the above

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a Blasphemous 1 fanatic I finished it through and through 4 times at 150% so here are my generic thoughts. These may or may not be positive it's up to you to decide if it's a pro or a con. The review may seem overly critical but you shouldn't be detracted from the fact that this is a good game that just missed the bar the older game made by 1 inch. I suggest waiting to get it at discount around 20-25$ USD.- Controls remain tight but move execution is too complex. I wish I could map Parry to a specific button or both types of prayers. I will have to fix this using Steam Input unfortunately.- Overly complex controls to accomodate XBOX style controllers. I have a 6 button controller and my 2 extra buttons are dead because its impossible to remap them. A lot of the in game flourishes youre allowed to perform with your weapons is just fluff and useless and never as good as just flailing your opponents to death.- Weapons offered are extremely unequal and imbalanced (Flail is best, Sword 2nd, Rapier dead last)- B1 had a specific path you followed and a clear goal, this one feels more freeform.- Game settings screen oversimplified (No resolution choice for example). Lacks depth.- Pixel cinematics replaced with cartoon FMVs, the quality of the cinematic is better but it detracts from the horror theme.- Severely toned down difficulty overall (Platforming the most, bosses also, teleport to town and around plentiful).- Soundtrack isn't worse quality, but the songs offered do not fit as well the theme of the world the first had. The best example is Mother of Mothers area. Overall the music is softer without tension and more ambiant.- Revisit of a lot of areas covered in the first game feels a bit lazy- Prayers are mostly just as useless as the first game and only there for eye candy if you get bored of flailing stuff- No wokeness in-game (We dodged a bullet there, Game Kitchen is severely woke)Play it and don't worry too much, but this isn't a clear step up from the previous one.EDIT: I'm so sorry I forgot to say this, just like my first review:"My great guilt"

_childDocuments_.review:
The second scripture in the Blasphemous series portends the return of The Penitent One, with a story that continues from the free Wounds of Eventide DLC for the original game, where The Heart in the sky heralded the return of The Miracle and foretold the birth of a new miracle child.

Awakened in a strange new land, and displaced from his final resting place, The Penitent One is thrust back into the endless cycle of life, death, and resurrection, with no other option than to explore this perilous new world and uncover its long-forgotten secrets.

Hordes of grotesque enemies stand in your way, awaiting final judgement by the brutal hand of the Penitent One, with titanic twisted bosses also lurking in the darkness, waiting for their chance to return you to the grave from whence you came.

name: Hollowbody
detailed_description: It's a Shipper's biggest fear. You're grounded in the exclusion zone, twenty miles of death and decay sealed off by the towering, suffocating walls erected after the collapse. Alone, stranded, and with limited resources at your disposal you'll have to push your way through the zone, solve environmental puzzles, manage resources and fight for your life as you try to find a way to escape beyond the wall. Play as Mica, an unlicensed black market shipper who will stop at nothing to find her missing partner. It’s been 12 days since Sasha left. You talked about it, you argued about it and you even laughed about it. Anybody in their right mind knew going to that place was a death wish, a one-way trip to the end of the line. But Sasha wasn’t one to scare easily, she wanted answers and there was only one place those answers held any truth. Her mind was already made up, you just didn’t expect her to do it without you. Twelve sleepless nights later and you finally get the call. Tax has found someone, A border security suit looking to make some extra credits on the down-low. He can get you clearance, a two hour window to fly into the zone, find Sasha and get the hell out of there. You make your way across the exclusion zone but something’s wrong. The nav's running in circles and you're losing altitude. Before you know it a blinding white fills the sky. The dash goes dark and your hover drops out of the air like a lead balloon, slamming into the paved streets below. You wake to the acrid smell of an electrical fire, rain pounding on the cracked windshield. You're surrounded by the crumbling remains of what were once considered homes. You need to find a way out. Call for evac, scale the walls. Something. Anything. Survive. FEATURES: Classic survival horror gameplay inspired by early 2000s horror titles. Cinematic blend of dynamic and fixed camera angles. Logic puzzles, resource management and limited combat with a focus on narrative and exploration. Full voice acting. An emphasis on strong world building set in a dystopian near-future. Carefully paced save points ensure tension is maintained whilst respecting the player's time. Difficulty options to aid players who prefer exploration over combat. Post-game unlocks and features.

short_description: A tech-noir survival horror short story, set in the urban decay of a long abandoned British city. Solve environmental puzzles, manage limited resources and fight for a way to escape beyond the wall.

_childDocuments_.review: Hollowbody is more than just a throwback to the survival horror greats of the PS2-era.It's an incredibly well-crafted game in its own right.Great worldbuilding, excellent atmosphere and ambience in its derelict, post-apocalyptic British suburbia setting.But ultimately it really is a classic, fixed camera survival horror game that feels often astoundingly accurate to how games like Silent Hill 2 and 3, Haunting Ground or Rule of Rose felt to play and control, down to the way camera and movement works, and largely to the visual aesthetic and graphical limitations to evoke the technical feel of a game of specifically the 6th console generation.Ah and: you can play with camera-relative controls (like it was common for many PS2 survival horror games) and with the classic tank-controls. AND -- it features a secret, unlockable first person mode that I only just recently discovered.Disclaimer: I received a review key for the game several weeks before launch. I also posted a video-review on YouTube which you can watch here if you're interested:
_childDocuments_.name: Hollowbody

_childDocuments_.review: One person designed this game. Yes there are flaws, yes there are bugs. But you know what's the crazy part about all of that? There are less flaws, less bugs, less glaring issues, than there is in Triple A games that have thousands of devs working on them over, and over; yet I'd take this game as a more finished product than the rest. This was worth my $16. Thank you for making this game for us.
_childDocuments_.name: Hollowbody

_childDocuments_.review: For a one man game, Hollowbody is a crazy achievement. It has a vibrant amount of soul, and a clear focus on being an unsettling, slow burner filling you with unease, instead of an intense or emotional ride. I cannot praise the audiovisual presentation enough, the game captures perfectly the vibe it's going for with these extremely well textured models and environments that have a narrow amount of polygons. The audio creeps up on you slowly and the general ambience is excellent to keep you on edge as the game world whispers environmental storytelling to you. As an atmospheric tour in a somehow more horrific England, this game excels. As a survival horror game, I am slightly wishing more. There is a limited enemy and weapons roster, and while the combat does the job, it nearly falls from the "intentionally bad" to "player killing handicap" at a specific stage later in the game. There is also some audio mixing issues with some dialogue, which can make some scenes difficult to understand. And on a personal note, I wish the game had harder and more varied puzzles.But ultimately, I do want more. I would love to see more of this bleak futuristic noir setting, and get a look into the bigger picture of the story. New Game Plus offers some replay value with a FPS mode and difficulties, so that will do for now however. Thumbs up, definitely pick it up if you are looking for a game to play with good headphones in the dark.
_childDocuments_.name: Hollowbody

_childDocuments_.review: Updating this review now that I've finished the game! Hollowbody is an excellent throwback to classic PS2-style survival horror. If you grew up with Silent Hill and Resident Evil, or enjoy more modern offerings like Signalis and are looking for a more restrained, understated take on the genre, I expect Hollowbody will be to your liking.Important to note that this is largely a solo dev project, and expectations should be set accordingly when making a purchasing decision. To that end, I'm going to begin with an enumeration of the game's flaws, as they are few, insubstantial, and easily remedied.First: menu feel is quite rough. Options may not always update correctly, or will update in-game but still display incorrectly in the menu; setting up keybinds is unwieldy; the default selection/cursor position can shift unexpectedly; and the presentation of the game controls in the options menu is a bit of an eyesore.Second: a general lack of polish. The "Seek" vs. "Pickup" labels on certain items randomly switch; footstep SFX are disabled when using tank controls; stomp attack SFX only play about half the time; background tracks may stop looping after a little while; tapping "back" in the prologue sequence with tank controls enabled will send your character backpedaling indefinitely; thumbnails for manual save files are all red boxes; the cursor is impossible to see in the Load Game menu when hovering over the Autosave slot; clicking "Resume Game" from the pause menu will unavoidably result in your character executing a stomp attack as the game resumes; certain ammo boxes can be stomped multiple times for indefinite amounts of ammo; skipping lines of dialogue during specific segments will often splice the next half-second of audio into the start of the next line of dialogue; etc. etc.As you can probably tell, these are minor bugs that come up naturally when playing a release hot off the presses. By my estimation the developer behind Hollowbody has proven nimble and reliable at squashing bugs of a similar caliber in the past, and I will not be at all surprised if most of the issues I have mentioned above are handled pretty quickly (I will be keeping an eye on these efforts, and will excise the whole above portion of the review if it is rendered irrelevant.)My third and final critique of Hollowbody regards enemy and environment diversity. This, as well, is kind of unavoidable when you don't have the resources of a large dev team and a fleet of designers at your fingertips, and I mention it here more as observation than condemnation. That said: you will quickly notice that 90% of the time, you're fighting the same type of creature. There are one or two others, but they appear only quite rarely. For some people this will be an immediate dealbreaker - for those of us more interested in atmosphere and worldbuilding, this is no great concern.Speaking of atmosphere, I now happily transition to Hollowbody's strengths, as they are numerous and well-appointed. All the weaknesses I have mentioned above are but passing irritants; I was rendered immune to their nipping by the immaculate vibes of Hollowbody, and the excellence with which its creator executed this loving homage.And the vibes here are truly immaculate. Hollowbody's music is evocative of Silent Hill: less a conventional soundtrack and more a collection of eerie, droning soundscapes that will burrow into your mind and follow you home at night. The creatures you directly observe will not terrify you, but what they represent for the protagonist, and the implications of their existence, are well-leveraged reminders that the most frightening things in this world are rarely seen.Broken-down mechs and darkened terminals litter the streets of a ruined tech-noir European city, their dying lights blearily cutting through an incessant twilit drizzle. The occasional fixed camera angles are striking and skillfully placed; this is a game world with many spots where a player might simply sit and steep in the unmoored desperation of a city that has suffered its own personal apocalypse.I completely adored the protagonist, Mica - she is competent without feeling arrogant, maintains a steady composure despite being genuinely disturbed by her grotesque surroundings. Her mission is straightforward: a friend has fallen into shadow, and must be rescued. I appreciated the forthright manner in which this plot unfolds, true to its "short-story" ambition: three acts, a final escalation, a compelling finale.Five other notable strong points are worth mentioning here. First: combat (read: melee combat) is precisely in line with the bizarre appetites of SH/RE fans. It is janky, and clearly not by accident; it has "the right kind" of jank, I think I would call it. Anyone who has swung a lead pipe as James Sunderland will certainly feel at home here.Second: a well-deserved hat tip to the developer for including both tank controls and more modern controls, and allowing players to easily toggle between the two. I myself found that the tank controls were well-suited to the claustrophobic indoor settings, handling nicely alongside static camera angles, whereas the modern controls handled better when roaming around outside with an over-the-shoulder camera. This is a nontrivial development task and is deeply, deeply appreciated by many genre fans. Third: this is a spoiler-free review, so all I will say here is this: a series of choices made early on in the game can have a pretty substantial effect on the entire mood/framework of your playthrough. I was surprised and delighted to find out about this after the fact, and will almost certainly go back to investigate this alternate route through the game.Fourth: the save system is, like most other things in Hollowbody, just right. Occasional save spots can be used at will; where they are absent, autosaves occur at intervals wide enough to discourage reckless death, but close enough that if you wish, you really can bull-rush from one to the next once you know what to do. (The one exception to this compliment is, I think, the final encounter. At present it's about a 3-minute run to get there each time, followed by around a minute of unskippable cutscenes. The encounter itself can be a bit tricky, so if you mess anything up, well...get used to running.)Fifth, and of considerable weight: I was pretty surprised to find that not only does Hollowbody feature full voice acting, but the cast is also extremely good! Difficult to overstate just how much life was breathed into the game world by this inclusion. Predictably, Mica's voice actress deserves special mention here, providing an exceptional performance right from line one. Bravo to all and I dearly hope this becomes more of a norm among indie horror titles.Excellent game. Will delight long-time genre fans and could serve as a gentle, smaller-scale entry ramp for curious or apprehensive newcomers. With a nice crisp ~5 hour playtime and positively dripping in its moody atmosphere, Hollowbody is the perfect autumn treat for a creepy, rainy weekend, an expertly portioned love letter from a talented creator, and an easy recommend from me.

_childDocuments_.review: Flawed, but...impressive for a game mostly made by one guy. Soundtrack included!From a spooky early sequence that closely emulates the visual approach of the original Silent Hill's prologue - i.e. highly cinematic "fixed" camera angles, combined with the added atmosphere of constant camera movement - it's clear this is going to be a trip down Memory Lane. A somewhat more  Memory Lane than either the Silent Hill or Resident Evil franchises - and a slightly more bleak and British one! - but a third-person survival horror game very much in the "old-school" style, nonetheless. (Read: heavy resource management, manual saves using a household item - a telephone, in this case - lots of spamming of perimeters to ensure you're searching each area as thoroughly as possible, no end of locked or otherwise barred doors, eerie radio noises when a monster is near, highly manipulative yet effective scare techniques...heck, there's even sections where you run through decrepit streets, avoiding monsters galore a la Silent Hill...albeit to the power of ten!)Graphics and sound are mostly very good - even if our heroine doesn't always look like her feet are firmly connecting with the ground! - and the maps are pretty excellent once you adjust to their especially sci-fi-ish nature (the same goes for Menu/Inventory screens, and the constant in-game pop-up displays). And while the game itself recommends, multiple times, that you use a controller...I personally had no issues with keyboard and mouse. And the weapons are definitely fun - road sign doubling as a "makeshift axe", anyone? - but a bit awkward and unpredictable to use at times, due to pedantic aiming and a surprising variety of "moves" (all just one button; yet your character rarely attacks the same way twice in a row, instead cycling through a few distinct approaches per item)!One regard in which traditional survival horror buffs might find this game slightly  generous: it's not necessarily clear which items can be picked up/interacted with until you're right on top of them (unlike, say, the blatantly glittering items we're used to in RE games). Not a huge problem indoors - see "spamming of perimeters", above! - but in wide open areas filled with enemies and no end of miscellaneous debris, you really do have a good chance of bypassing something useful unless you're patient enough to systematically fight everything in sight, search around...then, presumably, go back to your last save should you determine you just wasted a bunch of ammo or healing for no good reason! I lucked upon quite a few bonus finds - including ones that contribute to mere Achievement-scoring - yet can't help but wonder how many things I managed to miss...which probably doesn't sound like a biggie to survival horror -vets, but for those of us who like to explore every inch of a map, "just in case"...*And the story is nothing I'm gonna rave about, but it serves its purpose passably...for a game. (Though many may find the ending a tad abrupt, not least 'cause it lacks anything that proves - at least on "Intended Difficulty" - to be a significant final boss fight, provided you have a mere handful of shotgun shells remaining! And yes: there  a hidden climax that pays tribute to Silent Hill 2's infamous "dog" ending, as well as an unlockable first-person mode for future playthroughs...and another mode where you idiotically walk around with an oversized HEAD!!)I'm guessing, by now, that you're wondering about that thing so many gamers obsess about nowadays: the length. The good news is that - for people like me who don't want their horror games to drag - it's probably under five hours' long (unless you really take your time or get seriously stuck at some point). The bad news is that - for people who DO demand that the games they fork over even moderate amounts of cash for last at least ten or twenty hours - well, it . So for those in the latter category, sure: I would strongly recommend waiting on a sale. For peeps in the former category, or those with bags of money hanging off every inch of their belts...WHAT THE FLIP ARE YOU WAITING FOR?! (And there are, as I mentioned, multiple "modes" to replay through with, as well as multiple Difficulty levels. And more than one ending, depending on decisions made throughout the game. So there is, at the least, some definite replayability...though you'd still be hard-pressed to get more than fifteen, twenty hours out of it, total.) as good, overall, as 2022's Signalis: another recent game to bring a futuristic dystopian sci-fi setting to a mostly traditional "survival horror" approach. Oh: and if you think you've struck a bug, or somehow badly screwed up, in the sewer section? It seems people have all sorts of "different" experiences down there (based, it seems, on the undercutting of design expectations we gamers have grown to know and love)! My advice: just go with the flow, and see where you wind up...Verdict: 8/10.(* For what it's worth: on my first playthrough, I got 55% of Achievements. So I clearly missed a bit, but maybe not  much. Never did find a bow to go with that quiver of arrows, though!)(PS If you enjoyed this review, feel free to check out my two Curator pages: Cheers!)

_childDocuments_.review: Hollowbody is another one of those games that makes me wish Steam had a "maybe" option for the reviews.There's quite a few things to love in this game - but also so many that frustrate me.What has to be said is that this game, despite my complaints, is an achievement. This title is basically a 1-person-effort and that alone deserves commendation. The developer certainly deserves our support.With that said...The visual style of the game is great. It's not quite "lo-fi" but it is very much inspired by the aesthetics you'd see in PS2 games. It has some more modern bells and whistles, of course, but the details of the models, the texture quality and overall level design is pretty faithful to games of that era.However, what it  nail is, for example, the camera. Funnily enough, games from that PS2-era this game tries to pay homage to have better camera systems than this game. I'd go so far as to say that the camera in Hollowbody might very well be your biggest enemy. It is incredibly slow to respond, lagging behind constantly. This combined with lots of camera angle changes (the game going from an over-the-shoulder camera to a different camera angle) messes with the controls so much that I got turned around way too often. It makes playing this game rather frustrating at times.The camera is also buggy in a few areas. Sometimes it seems random but there are also multiple areas where the camera  doesn't switch angles correctly and I had to go back and forth a few times to make it switch.The actual gameplay is... alright. It obviously uses games like Silent Hill as inspiration, as even the overall structure of the game is reminiscient of those games - meaning you go from an outside city-like area to an inside area with puzzles and more, followed by another outside area but different from the previous one. And the way it plays is similar to those games, but......combat is quite underwhelming. The enemies aren't all that interesting. But the only "real" offender are the dogs, which don't telegraph their attacks properly. Anyway.Melee weapons feel nearly useless and way too dangerous as you have to hug enemies to use them most of the time. Also, their animations are slow - and it only takes three or four hits for an enemy to kill you. So the vast majority of the time, you want to stick to projectile weapons, which are pretty standard, in the form of a handgun and a shotgun. To be fair, there's also a bow and arrow, as well as a flamethrower - but I never used either. Didn't need them. Maybe it would've been more fun with those, but it's probably not a good sign that the two "main" weapons aren't all that enjoyable to use. There's enough ammo around so that you never really have to worry about it too much.Speaking of which, the item pickup zones - or rather, all interaction zones - are really strange and occasionally buggy? Sometimes you can stand  and hit the interact button... but nothing will happen, because the interaction zone hasn't activated. (The game will show a text in the bottom-left corner telling you to pick up, seek or what-have-you.) Then you have to go back and forth and try different angles to activate the interaction, and  hit the interact button again. And when there's multiple interactive objects close together, activating the correct one can get a finnicky affair. That occurrence is rather rare, though. Thankfully.The puzzles are unfortunately nothing to write home about. Most of them I wouldn't even categorize as "puzzles," to be honest. Putting  onto the  does not exactly require much thinking on my part. The way I see it, there's two puzzles in the game. The safe puzzle in the apartment building (which was... okay) and the electrical switch puzzle, also in the apartment building.And during a second playthrough using NG+, the game mostly skipped the events I put behind spoiler tags. It just let me continue without doing that and then removed the relevant items from my inventory when I moved on.When it comes to the story and the lore of Hollowbody - while it provides a refreshing locale and an interesting premise, it doesn't feel fully realized and just left me wanting.The story is a pretty standard "find and rescue this person" affair. Which is fine - but the way I see it, there's nothing of note in regards to story beats between the start of the game and the very end. Only then a few things unravel, but that's about it. There was potential for more but it wasn't used.World building, realized through documents and "signals," also left me undwerhelmed. The vast majority didn't really add too much. It was mostly fairly standard "things are not going well" bits and pieces. I never felt like I was really learning about the world and what happened.And if all this wasn't enough, some of the documents, signals and achievements are buggy. During my first playthrough, I was missing a signal - but was awarded the achievement for getting all of them at the end of the game.During my second playthrough, I got all the signals and all the documents - or so I thought.I counted 24 documents, but it should have been 25. So I counted again and again. 24. Afterwards, I opened a guide and checked what I was missing. The list of residents was not in my inventory, even though I was 100% certain that I had it. So I went all the way back to the apartment building, and... the list was not there, so I did pick it up. It just  And when I then went and finished the game anyway, the stat screen at the end said . Of course, I wasn't awarded the achievement for finding all documents. Great.All in all, it's a very  game that lives off of its vibes and elements taken from Silent Hill. It's alright for what it is - but I can't straight-up recommend it. If these kinds of games are  your thing, give it a go. If you just have a general interest in horror games... maybe you should wait for a sale or skip this game.Now, despite my complaints, I wouldn't hesitate to support another of their Kickstarter campaigns. I want indie devs to be able to follow their passion and do interesting things, even if the results sometimes miss the mark.

_childDocuments_.review: Hollowbody was one of my most anticipated horror games of this year and I was extremely excited about giving it a shot. Unfortunately however, I really did not have a great time with Hollowbody and that is a shame because the game does so much right. So even though I do not recommend this game, I still want to talk about everything it does well and even exceptionally.This is by far Hollowbodys biggest strength and it even dwarfs other games in its genre in this category. The visual aesthetic and art direction of this game is superb and is a large contributor why I finished the game in the first place. Nathan (the dev) managed to craft a world that feels perfectly aligned with the PS2 horror classics it is trying to emulate and makes you feel on edge, scared and tense. Walking through the ruined city streets of an abandoned Britain feels incredible and combined with the stellar sound design and foley work the world of Hollowbody is near perfect. This also extends to the character and enemy design. Every single thing in this game looks disgusting in the best possible way. Enemies are almost abstract in their design, with unclear proportions, strange tentacles wiggling around on their bodies and horrifying screams that are sure to make you tense up every time you hear them coming. And the characters you see are also just as messed up, with dried blood and stained clothing being a constant. It really feels like these people are holding on to their last string of life and makes them fit like a glove for this type of game.The voice acting too helps a lot in selling the depressing and heavy feeling of the world. The story itself isnt anything groundbreaking, but I really enjoyed how it is delivered and liked listening to the characters talk with each other, especially Mica and the Nameless Man you meet very early on. I enjoyed the ending I got too, even though I will not talk about it more because of spoilers.But sadly, praise is over now.Hollowbody really badly wants to be Silent Hill and you notice it everywhere. The ambient soundtrack (which is really good btw), the starting zone is an apartment building, the first weapon you find is a 2x4 with nails in them, your screen turns red when you save and a few more things that I am not going to list here. Now dont get me wrong here, other games have nods like these too and even one of my favorite games of all time SIGNALIS does the same thing. But while the inspirations in SIGNALIS enhance the end product, Hollowbody feels like it's a collection of Silent Hill moments stitched together. This sadly soured my enjoyment as the few original bones that Hollowbody does have are really good, but I can never shake the feeling that Nathan wanted to make a Silent Hill fan game rather than an original title. This sounds harsh I know, but that was tame in comparison how I feel about the combat because holy crap is it terrible. For starters, I appreciate the commitment to a fixed camera in order to be extra oldschool and it works great most of the time, but during combat it all falls apart. Shooting is not great but servicable, its a bit rigid and making sure you lock on to the correct enemy is annoying but other than that it's nothing too offensive. Melee combat however is the most painful thing I have experience in a survival horror game in a while. It is SO clunky and feels SO unfulfilling that even the OG SIlent Hill 2s melee combat is an improvement compared to Hollowbody. The biggest issue by far is how unreliable it is. Both melee weapons have different attacking animations that they cycle through which all have  and therefor  So it is very possible that you are fighting an enemy and miss your melee attack because Mica played the wrong animation and you end up getting hit, which is a big problem as health is pretty hard to come by and enemies do a lot of damage. I have no idea how you are supposed to play this game on Punishment difficulty without pulling your hair out, because my patience was already stressed in my playthrough on Intended.I wish that as the game went on my sentiment would improve, but overall I really did not like Hollowbody. At the same time however, I see how much love and care went into this game and Nathan should be incredibly proud of what he made. Doing this solo is a gigantic accomplishment and I see plenty of other people loving and praising the game. At the end of the day however, the most important part in a Survival Horror game for me is the gameplay and there are plenty of other titles that pull it off way better than Hollowbody did.

_childDocuments_.review: Strong recommendation. Things I liked:I really enjoyed this game, it was a short but enjoyable experience that wasn't too hard on my first playthrough and I like that there's a New Game+ with a first person mode, higher difficulty and some extra goodies.I liked the location of the game, set in the UK, England was an interesting choice and I think it was a good one. I was immersed throughout my playthrough so big win.The story was interesting but very vague, even with the notes & audio "logs" to find. I think expanding on that in the sequel (if there is one) will be cool to see.The puzzle's also were fair, as someone that isn't too great with them, this was appreciated but might be a downsides for others.The voice acting was good, there wasn't any performance that stood out as bad or that took me out of the immersion I was feeling. Really good in my opinion.The graphics & design of the game I really liked. The lighting is good, the style is just gritty, low-ish quality settings and I think it adds to the games strengths as sometimes less is more which I think this game nails. The price is also fair in my opinion, maybe a bit more things to find in the more open sections would have been cool to make exploration a bit more worth it but for a first try, really great overall package. Well done.Things I would like the dev(s) to look at:Floating props/trees, this is really noticeable in the park but I'd see geometry not aligning with trees or random floating gates that are easy to spot if you're just exploring. Just a bit of environmental polishing is needed to make things not look floaty.Audio mixing needs a little fine tuning, sometimes the dialogue would get drowned out with music/environmental audio. (Mainly when answering the phone outside.)The game's melee I really didn't like and maybe it's by design but there were times where I swung my weapon and felt like it should have connected only for it to NOT and I then get struck. Guns felt much nicer to use than melee because of this. (I did enjoy shooting the enemies though and appreciated the gore but just wished the melee wasn't as janky.)Sometimes in the more open areas, I wasn't sure where I was going and though I found it, maybe a few more pointers such as some lights just to give you an idea that you're headed in the right direction. (Maybe I missed this and I'm wrong.)Lastly, this might be an issue with me being on ultrawide (21:9) but sometimes when the camera was taken to another perspective, I'd see through a wall which was a bit immersion breaking. (Props for also fixing the ultrawide resolution issue within the day of it's release.)

_childDocuments_.review: Everyone praised the game's visuals and sound and I will too. Hollowbody really feels and looks like a PS2 horror and this is a massive achievement for, I suppose, solo dev and in the end we have something that has strong, creepy atmosphere due to very well done combo with sound (some of them are unnerving at worst and spawns sh1t in your pants at best) and visuals.But... Game take notes from Silent Hill 2 not only in terms of audiovisuals, but also from a gameplay point. What is very strange - Hollowbody ignores to look on a narrative parts from Konami's series.And I hate gameplay of Silent Hill 2. Empty locations and lackluster combat is what I have most of my playthrough of Hollowbody plus some kinda neat, but mostly filler puzzles. Played this on Intended Difficulty and at the end I filled my pockets with various ammo, have a bunch of melee weapons and pack of healing sprays, because melee combat is that easy. Yes, just like in Silent Hill. You just run around and bash the useless enemies on the head by stick. Or guitar. Or road sign. When I found guitar and equipped it as a melee weapon I start to realise that this game would have some problems, because this much of a comedic shift is just "WTF?!". There's so much trash that Mica can use as a weapon, but she decides to grab a guitar and a road sign? Few, again, Silent Hill knock-off enemies, but wich lacks originality. Just some grey, goofy baddies: normal sized, big sized with poison gas, big sized without poison gas. Also dogs (annoying af) and crawling bugs (I don't know what they can do to player). Normal sized spam enemies we just bonk on the head with melee weapon and other guys is just shooting targets. Ammo, as I said, is not a problem at all, so you can enjoy yourself here and blast near half of enemies.Again, there's a piles of VERY creepy dead bodies. Why not use them as an enemies? They are so unnerving that I was holding aim button every time when I walk past them, because I was AFRAID of them to raise and attack me with some scary as sh1t noises and animation like from Fatal Frame or Kuon. But no. Take your pack of goofy baddies and whack-a-mole them with your road sign. And okay, deliver a good gameplay is a colossal task and in survival horror it usually act like a glue to combine parts like atmsophere, sounds and plot, but here we have so minimalistic plot that dev can just delete it or change just to "you have amnesia, you don't know where are you and why and also there's some hallucinations and other supernatural sh1t. enjoy <3" and nothing will be worse in that department (or maybe even better, who knows).Most of the narrative is stuff from the past - countless notes and flashbacks that adds LITERALLY nothing to what we already can know by just listening to intro. All of this is just a waste of my time. Protagonist, her girlfriend and his friend Tax is uninteresting excuse to have some journey. I can hardly name them as a "characters", because they are lack any characteristic outside their relationship with each other (we try to save our girlfriend with a friend's help that calls us by the radio). I'm sorry, but this game really looks on Silent Hill 2? Because there we have a cast of, you know, developed characters? I don't know on what games from PS2 era devs was looking whole development cycle, but it was clearly not Siren, Silent Hill, Rule of Rose or, for god's sake, Obscure or Manhunt.Game is really HollowBody. We have a nice facade, but there's nothing interesting inside. If we have this game in a PS2 era it would be bashed by critics and gamers due to it's lack of originality, because this is just Blade Runner 2049 cyberpunk ~vibes~ and Silent Hill 2 mashed together. Just because "it's cool and everybody loves that two things", I suppose? "This two beloved things was inspired by something else too, so what's the difference?" you may want to ask me. If we take again, as prime example, SH2 then we can see dozens of sources of inspiration: from obvious Jacob's Ladder to something more subtle like Angel's Heart, Crime and Punishment, works of Stephen King, David Lynch, Dario Argento, Hitchcock, David Fincher, David Cronenberg, Francis Bacon, Andrew Wyeth, Rembrandt. Games? Alone in the Dark, Silent Hill 1 and even Tomb Raider (all of this and even more are mentioned by the Team Silent in various interviews).And my main question here - how much SH2 resembles any of this sources 1:1? Closest example is SH1, but if you played or watched it on youtube then you know that despite they are games from one series, they are very different in so many aspects... Team Silent research work was so massive and result is something that stands on it's own and what can be source of inspiration for other devs. And we have Hollowbody where dev took two hyped to death things, added reference to a giant face from SH: The Room, beaches from Shadows of the Colossus or Half-Life 2 and call it a day.  LOL.Sorry, but I just don't get the hype at all. Even considering that I was waiting for that game to be released.Gosh, even last boss is just random game mechanic (yeah, Pepsi-Man!) and not a test of player's game knowledge. But, on the other hand, it would be strange to test player's ability to mash up attack button to swing a guitar like Jimi Hendrix.

_childDocuments_.review: I do recommend this game for people that enjoy old survival horror games, but for me this was *very* mixed experience. Visuals and sound design are on point, most enjoyable part of the game for me. Atmosphere is ehh, could be better, there was only one moment when it legit felt spooky, the rest of the time i was just running around funny. And you'll have to do a lot of running because open areas are very open and big and the move speed is kind of slow. The camera is terrible. It rarely does fixed camera (but that part is decent) and mostly relies on follow cam, but you don't have control outside of just centering it all the time and it gets really annoying really fast when it starts affecting gameplay. Game is very linear and forward moving, the only level where's there's some semblance of nice backtracking and interesting level design and figuring out what to do is right at the start, the rest of the game is just move forward, find one item, find where to use it, progress, and a lot of the times you find the item before where to use it, so it loses the most interesting aspect of that whole formula. Combat is fine and so is the story. For something calling itself "tech-noir" there's very little actual tech in it, just papers with text and a few voice recordings, but the story and setting are enjoyable.Overall very mediocre game outside it's visuals and sound.

_childDocuments_.review: A competently made and solid indie survival horror. Great presentation and atmosphere, really nails what it was aiming for visually, loved wanting to just explore the small areas you have access to. I will say I do wish combat/movement/interactions were improved a bit more or at least polished up - the axe's swings felt INCREDIBLY jank, being forced to do the three hit combo but the second attack being a weird light jab of the hilt with a super short/small hitbox lead to me just getting hit as it'd consistently miss, club felt more consistent to use even with the lesser damage. Guns felt nice though.Movement/interactions - no matter which setting I used something felt *off* regarding movement. Mica would either just suddenly slide/float to the left/right when turning instead of turning slowly/more naturally, sprinting was a tad cumbersome with L1 being the default vs square/cross from other survival horrors. In terms of interactions - I always found myself having issues picking up ammo (mainly the revolvers) on the floor, I'd have to wriggle Mica around for a couple of seconds just for the game to let me pick them up, could never find the sweet spot. Did have a pretty nasty bug in the Subway near the end of the game, after obtaining the gold coins half the subway stopped loading and it persisted through my save, had to reload to an older one just to fix. Either way, decent game - hope the developer is able to stick with survival horrors and improve on future titles!
