_childDocuments_.review: I'll be honest. I never played a whole lot of the original Silent Hill 2, as I joined the series late. Most of my time was put into Silent Hill 4: The Room, Silent Hill: Homecoming, and Silent Hill: Downpour which I think are all great games. Except you, Homecoming, but that's irrelevant. This remake feels uncanny to a hybrid between Silent Hill: Downpour and Alan Wake 2. Now, my thoughts on what surprised us all: Blooper nailing it. The ONLY games I've ever heard of from Blooper were Layers of Fear 1 and 2 which I absolutely adored and fell in love with. Great atmosphere, and these games were based off of environmental storytelling, something many horror games could actually benefit from and is perfect for a Silent Hill game, especially when it's using mechanics that make it feel like a modern remake (hinting at RE4, RE3, RE2). We shouldn't have given Blooper as much skepticism when it came to killing it, but the combat is where my worries lied the most. A developer creating two games without any combat, to remaking a classic horror game where they actually upped the number of threats and made it so it's not so simple to just run away. But, thankfully, it does just fine. It's not an indepth combat system, there's no crafting, no weapon repairs, no currency, nothing. No crazy kill animations, no executions, just fun. A faithful remake to what gaming should always be and should always feel like.Also, not sure what everyone is talking about with the stuttering and poor performance. The game is capped at 60FPS with 30FPS cutscenes and there's plenty of chatter about stuttering and crashing. My specs:AMD Ryzen 7 7700GeForce RTX 4070 SUPER32GB RamI've got solid 60fps at 1080P, and never encountered a stutter or a crash. Not sure if people with underpowered PC's are looking at the specs and immediately trying to max it out? Or people just don't yet understand that UE5 isn't quite yet the most optimized engine just yet.Either way, a stellar job, Blooper. Let's talk about getting Silent Hill 3 and 4 on here next ;)

_childDocuments_.review: It's certainly not bad, but it wouldn't be my go-to version. Everything related to the performance and depiction of the main characters are all extremely well thought out and a great addition; Eddie's bossfight in particular is really phenomenal and a particular highlight, comparable to MGS3's The End. However, the pacing of the game has been hurt a good deal, with every section given 2-3 extra areas and puzzles that feel pretty unnecessary. The horror and atmosphere has been changed a good deal from the original's subtle and surrealist style, to something which is very recognizably Bloober Team's house style, with an emphasis on aggressive visual effects, "realistic" presentation and puzzle solutions, and superficial jump scares, which all feels extremely mid. Level design is a mixed bag, the prison and hotel are great improvements, but the hospital and labyrinth are considerably worse. A few downright unpleasant additions were added, like Last of Us style move-the-box puzzles, but these are only small and nitpicky issues.Some things are better, some things are worse. It shouldn't be your first playthough of SH2, but its not bad.

_childDocuments_.review: Some performance issues detract slightly from the experience but its not a deal breaker by any means. Still one of the best remakes alongside Dead Space and RE4. Akira Yamaoka somehow managed to improve on the music of the original which I didn't think was even possible. The audio team did a fantastic job with keeping you on edge throughout the game even when there's nothing trying to murder you. Voice acting is superb across the board too.Gameplay also got quite a revamp - the town offers so much more to explore this time round with shop windows etc. that you can break in order to get inside. Game progression has been tweaked to keep familiar players on their toes with events playing out slightly differently or in a different order. Combat is clunky but in a good way, adds to the intensity when in combat. Graphics are absolutely beautiful despite the frame rate issues at times, especially the fog. I cannot stop looking at the fog - it is so awesome how it engulfs everything and feels so menacing and claustrophobic. Easy recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: Played Resident Evil 1&2 when I was a kid but never got around to any of the Silent Hill series. I know, I'm a horrible person. So glad they remade this. This now sits at the top of my favorite horror games. The pacing is great and maintains the old classic horror vibe where there is a LOT of silence, exploration, and ambiance, peppered with small enemies, and then something reminds you of your place in this world. Nothing like the trend over the last decade or so - where there's a Big Bad /constantly/ chasing you and bursting through walls like the damned Kool-Aid Man. That isn't horror, that's just action. This, however, gives you just the right amount of peace, so that when it's taken away you are psychologically damaged a little bit every time. It's lovely. I'm so glad that Bloober didn't feel the need to turn the game into a 10-hour foot chase, as some other franchises have done.Speaking of ambiance, the sound design on this is absolutely top notch. I'm a sucker for audio atmospheres and this has the quality of audio atmosphere to match the absolutely gorgeous prop and world design. Definitely recommend some good headphones with this.

_childDocuments_.review: Before getting this game I was very sceptical. Konami, Bloober taking this on this massive game, Angela looking as she did...don’t get me wrong other things looked great like the environments but then I heard doubts about the combat and I was just not sure what to expect.I can confidently say that so far this has been a major win. No spoilers and I’m only up to meeting Laura outside the apartments. The three things I recall that are key to a successful remake are: stay true to the original, develop that with twists, like new locations, monsters like crimson heads in RE1R, and QOL updates. This game has it all.+ Echoes: locations in the remake that are a nod/thumbs up for OG fans. It’s such a small thing to add but it means a lot.+ Switching weapons and healing on the fly. You can even switch melee and ranged just by using a different button, no witching required.+ Exploring through smashing windows and checking drawers etc. Not ground breaking but just makes you work that bit harder inside of just having stuff lying out in the open.+ Puzzles are in many ways the same but evolved. I LOVED what they did with the coin puzzle in the apartment for example. The same, but with a twist.+ Combat is better that the OG. I love the OG but the combat was very wooden and static and it wasn’t the strongest trait of the game and it didn’t mean to be. This game has monsters hiding or running away and then suddenly coming to life. They’ll parry and counter you making combat much more intense. I’m having fun doing melee only so far. Is it the best combat? Hard to say but I hope the doubters feel their feedback has been listened to.+ Strange photos: picking up random photos with numbers on. Not sure what that’s about but it’s fun to explore and hunt them down.+ James and Eddie feel like they are different but within their character boundary so to speak. They may be subjectively better/worse but objectively they are different in their own way and that’s fine, I can believe they are who they are meant to be.+Environments look GORGEOUS. Sometimes I do feel there’s a bit of a bubble around me but it’s nothing like SHHD collection. The town feels more windy, leaves and rubbish blow through the town, it’s so much more alive. It seems that the rain goes through James, maybe there’s something I can do to address that but this seems kind of a minor issue.+ The settings is taken right out of RE4R. You can customise so much and see how it will look in game.+Achievements are always good and of those that aren’t hidden there look to be some standard ones and also ones for OG fans. Won’t spoil but if you like to explore and do things in the OG, try them in the remake.+ The camera. Some might not like that you can move the camera (not sure). I though love that you can move the camera. Being able to look up and see the trees towering above you or the apartment block looming high makes you feel like you’re in the town.And so on to the negatives:-Angela still feels like she could be so much better in her facial appearance (maybe modders can fix it on Steam). At first I felt her lines felt rushed but listening again I’d say no. She sounds like she lacking confidence and her body language is on form, but she just seems to not be the character she is in the OG. It’s not a massive problem, certainly not as bad as I feared and she is a relatively minor part, unlike say James. I don’t think that this is a VA issue, it’s a director issue.- Laura came across somewhat aggressive in the trailer and I’ve yet to see this in game but she has yet to win me over with her performance.- The frame rate. Sounds like I’m not the only one and it’s not unplayable, my pc was fairly high end 5-6 years ago but maybe I’m pushing it that bit too hard. I’ve tried a few setting recommendations from reddit but my pc can run in the high 50’s and then every now and then take a giant dump and run as low as 7 fps. I’m confident that tweaks to settings or a patch can address this. Again, this is a hiccup but not something I’d say was obnoxious.If I had to give this a rating I’d say probably 9 out of 10. Will update this if I deem it necessary.

_childDocuments_.review: The Silent Hill 2 remake was always going to be "good". It was going to be decent, playable, maybe even pretty good, a great game in it's own right. It was never going to be Silent Hill 2 again. That's an impossible task - you simply can't replicate the same team, the same environment, and the same artistry that went into the original. We all knew that since first reveal - I still have nightmares about James's stupid grimace in the noose and mirror scenes originally shown. But hey, what else can you expect from Bloober Team, right? Especially when under the control of modern Konami. Divorced from the original, I assumed it would still be a decent horror game, even if it could never capture the original's lightning in a bottle miracle existence. I was wrong. The Silent Hill 2 Remake is not just a good game, it's an excellent game. It's not just an excellent game on it's own merits - though it is that - it is an absolutely fantastic remake of Silent Hill 2. It's a modernization, yes, and one that is subtly different in many, many ways. No, it's not exactly the same. How could it be? Knowing that, Bloober team doesn't even try. It's not Silent Hill 2, again - it's *their* Silent Hill 2, and it's much stronger for it. Take performances, as an example. The OG Silent Hill 2 performances are lauded and for good reason. Cutting edge mocap and animation technology 20 years ahead of it's time paired with an uncanny/unnerving vocal performance from the cast resulted in characters that were grounded and felt real, but also felt subtly off in a way that communicated to the player that none of these characters were what you would call "mentally stable." How do you replicate that early 2000's era video game voice delivery in 2024? You don't - you can't, so Bloober doesn't even try to. The performances are quiet, grounded, and realistic, and instead the emphasis is now placed on body language and facial cues.  The OG's facial animation is still unmatched by any other game in existence, this isn't to say that the remake's facial animation is necessarily better, but it IS more detailed. James looks away uncomfortably when talking to Maria, refusing to meet her eyes. Eddie's eyes are glazed over with self-loathing and insanity. Maria has a strange, uncomfortable, unnerving smile on the entire game. Let me sum it up for you. Silent Hill 2 Remake, by BLOOBER TEAM, correctly identifies the core elements that contributed to Silent Hill 2's original success (character performances, atmosphere, narrative) and modernizes them in subtle ways without compromising the original vision, and then on top of that makes elements of the original game that were lacking even better (combat, level design, gameplay in general). The fact that this game both has amazing renditions of the Silent Hill 2 character performances AND modern 3rd person shooter combat that is both more responsive than the original and yet still horror game clunky is an incredible achievement. You should play it.

_childDocuments_.review: I've never played a Silent Hill game before as it came out just a couple years before I was even born. I have heard a lot about this series, how it is one of the best in the horror game genre. This made me wanna play one of the games at some point, but never came around to doing it and eventually kind of forgot that this series existed. Until I saw the announcement of this remake. I bit the bullet and bought the game even though it costed me around almost $100 in my local currency. Let me tell you it was worth every penny, like this seriously makes me wonder how I managed to evade playing such a masterpiece for this long. Never been a huge fan of either horror movies or games. As to me it feels like they all use cheap jumpscares to make you feel scared, and they never manage to captivate me. But this? Never has a game made me feel this geniunely terrified before. Team Bloober has managed to create an amazingly oppressive and terrifying atmosphere. The obscured and foggy townscape of Silent Hill paired with the amazingly detailed sound design made me experience a new level of discomfort and suspense that I've ever experienced from playing a game. The amount of detail they've put into the environment in general is absolutely insane. They've managed to make Silent Hill look lived in even though it's seemingly desolate. You can pretty much go to any nook and cranny and still see the same amount of detail as anywhere else. As for the sound design, there is such a big variety of sounds and the amount of detail in the sound scape in general is insane. It just makes me wonder how big their sound library for this project is. The sound design by itself gives me a level of unease and discomfort that shouldn't be possible by sounds alone. Just try to stand completely still ingame, and close your eyes and take a listen. I haven't written about the music yet, and I can simply boil it down to this. I listen to it in my spare time, it's that good. One of my favorite aspects of the soundtrack is it's use of this sort of industrial sound, as if there is metal clanking around. And it fits so perfectly when you progress through the game and end up in a more distorted reality. My favorite track is "Blank Fairy", it fits so well and improves the experience of the sequence this track is tied to.The actors and animation team have done an amazing job. From the detail in the facial expressions of the actors, stellar voice acting and their expressive body language. It really enhances the experience to another level. Luke Roberts' performance as the main protagonist James Sunderland is simply amazing. For it being his first performance in acting for a video game he really blew it out of the park. This is especially apparent in one of the endings for this game. This is definitely GOTY for me, and it has been one of the best experiences I've had when playing a game. To everyone involved in the making of this game. Thank you for the amount of talent, dedication and passion that you've all poured into this game, it really shows.

_childDocuments_.review: From what I've played, it's pretty good. The original is my favorite game and this should be an easy recommend, but wow this PC port is bad. Unreal Engine 5 continues to prove itself as the worst optimized modern graphics engine. There are frequent traversal stutters, but they become increasingly, and significantly more annoyingly, common in Silent Hill itself (particularly around Neely's Bar for some reason). The traversal stutters are up there with Star Wars Jedi: Survivor as some of the worst I've seen in a PC release. It is incessantly common to experience multiple stutters within a few seconds of one another. There are occasional white banding artifacts from heavy occlusion-culling that can break immersion. There is also very noticeable ghosting that made me wonder if the QA testers even had eyes. Floating leaves, shoes, entire characters, whatever moves can and WILL cause ghosting artifacts on the ground and puddles that use Lumen reflections. It's very easy to see this when looking at the falling leaves to the right of the car in the opening cinematic. The fog looks great, pooling toward the ground in thick patches, but the ghosting is especially bad there. Whenever a character moves when the fog is in the background, they leave a very noticeable trail that is a very common issue with temporal anti-aliasing, but it also happens with DLSS. This fog ghosting also happens whenever you move the camera, making it impossible for me to get immersed. This visual bug is also present on the PS5 release. I guess some people are blind to it and think it's intentional, but it's a common enough issue with UE5 that it's disappointing to see. It's a real shame because I love Silent Hill and was really looking forward to this one, but I simply can't recommend this game in its current state.REVISION: I'm running on a 4090 and a i7-13700k. I didn't mention that because framerates are about what you'd expect from a UE5 game (running in DirectX 11 through "-dx11" in the launch options helps greatly). Traversal stutter occurs when an influx of assets are loaded onto the GPU at once, typically measurable through a sudden increase in VRAM usage. If traversal stutter exists (in this case it does), then it will ALWAYS happen at the same locations in-game on EVERY PC regardless of your PC configuration; you can't brute force through it with more powerful hardware. Unreal Engine has had this issue for decades; I remember it being an issue with the original Gears of War. Anyone saying, "it runs fine on my PC" is either used to poor PC versions of UE5 games or are blind to inconsistent frame pacing and stutters. Not calling anyone out, I wish I could also enjoy games regardless of technical issues. As an update after completing the game, the game is great but performance really sours it for me. Would definitely recommend once the PC version is in better shape.

_childDocuments_.review: I have been trapped and my only possession is an egg. Without prior knowledge of its progenitor, I have intuited the egg will engender a neonate viper. I place it at a distance. Venomous even in its infancy, I ignore the hatchling. Repulsed and afeared, I move as far away as I can from the snakelet. Sometimes, from the corner of my eye I espy its writhing form: it grows, it slithers, it hisses, its scales black like the walls of my prison, its speckles menacing, its gaze abyssal — I am overtaken by dread and shun all contact with the beast, risking nary a stray glimpse. I am unable to face it.Unable to face it until I feel the tickle of the beast's uncouth forked tongue on my nape, followed by a feeling of suffocation from the weight of its gigantic reptilian mass coiling about my being. Utterly disgusted by this slithering serpentine form that has immured me in its embrace, I, now am forced to face it as it locks its accusatory eyes with mine. And it is now that I realise I had no need to know the parent of this entity to know of its nature, for it was I who birthed and nurtured it, for it was a part of me and the repulsion I felt was born of my own inability to face myself, my deeds and the inevitable consequences.Guilt, regret, fear, pain, resentment, hatred and emotions that consume and eat away at one's soul must all be acknowledged, made peace with, and resolved when yet inchoate and then eliminated, lest they fester past their nascence. Fleeing these fledgling emotions and denying their existence is to give Silent consent to their growth. And when these fledglings mature into venomous beasts, they come to collect their due — to be granted acceptance, now though, through no choice of our own.

_childDocuments_.review: Silent Hill 2 remake is absolutely amazing; however, the original still stands triumphant due to two design changes. The music, atmosphere, cutscenes, enemies, puzzles, and sound design are all present and extremely well-executed, but some liberties were taken with how combat is approached and how the characters are portrayed. New additions are pretty neat, such as upgraded enemies and fitting new flavor text, which fleshes out minor details in the town. The new Mannequins are now one of my all time favorite enemies from any horror game.In the original, the characters seem almost shell-shocked and disconnected from reality, with monotone speech and carefree reactions to everything. The remake takes a more realistic approach with more profound facial expressions, reactions, and dialogue, making them feel more human. Comparing any cutscene to the original shows a big difference in tone. It’s not bad by any means, but it detracts from the original's mysterious atmosphere. This change probably aims to make the game more coherent on the first playthrough.My second critique is with the combat. It feels meaty and well-crafted, but Silent Hill isn't about combat. The original James was a frail, clumsy man who could barely swing a metal pipe. In the remake, James is doing weakspot takedowns while i-frame dodging against multiple enemies. I defeated the big half-scissor-wielding baddy on hard difficulty with almost just melee, which felt pretty wrong. There's a lot of enemies and some sections have you fighting them like it's the corridor from Oldboy. Enemies pursue you for a long time, and without loading screens when traversing through doors, running isn't much of an option. You want to be beating up nearly every enemy in order to explore. As a result, James killing monsters left and right diminishes some of the dread and the feeling of playing a really weak protagonist. The new combat system doesn’t ruin the horror, just lessens it slightly compared to the original. It’s still very creepy, and the sound design really puts you on edge at times.That said, the game is amazing, and I highly recommend playing it. Even though I still prefer the original, I had a blast playing the remake. I had little hope for this project, but they truly did the game justice.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who is a big fan of the original and not so much of a fan of Bloober Team, I approached this game with some apprehension. I ended up buying the game on the off chance that it was at least entertainingly bad. On the contrary, the game is a perfectly fine remake and nothing more. It borrows heavily from the Resident Evil 2 school of game remaking for better and for worse. The town of Silent Hill itself is impressively rendered in high resolution and fog as dense as ever. On the other hand, there is more renovation than a fresh coat of paint. Voice acting is a lot less awkward, combat is more fluid, etc. etc. Ordinarily, these would be welcome changes for nearly any other game. However, with Silent Hill 2, I find that the original is a game strongly characterized by the ways it is, whether intentional notwithstanding, contains flaws in the experience. I know that we had practically no chance of getting a big budget horror game in 2024 with tank controls and fixed cameras. I know that some of the original SH2 cast are weirdos and probably not worth bringing back to reprise their roles. Nonetheless, I wish that Bloober Team had sought out more interesting creative compromises than just largely copying the homework of Capcom's RE remakes. This game is not as bad as it could have been. Far from it, in fact. However, it still resides in the shadow of both its own potential and the original game.

_childDocuments_.review: The Silent Hill series set the bar quite high for me when it came to horror games.  I’ve never been too inclined to play the genre and I think it’s because a lot of horror games are missing something that Silent Hill did so well - a story rich with complex characters, emotion and symbolism.With that being said, this is a phenomenal remake.  The developers seriously exceeded my expectations.  Not only does it look good but combat has greatly improved and feels so much more rewarding than it did in the original games.  The atmosphere is the best part and is what really makes this game unsettling.  It had me on high alert at all times - random rustling in the background as I’m walking, unknown whispers as I enter a room, screaming coming from behind a door I could not access.  The creepy ambiance really adds to the anxiety that you feel as you lurk through the hellish environment of Silent Hill.  Each setting feels so eerily familiar yet they’re all unique, not to mention they change up again as you enter into the Otherworld.  The player controls James Sunderland as he makes his journey through Silent Hill in search of his late wife, Mary, who wrote to him from beyond the grave.  As the player makes their way through the town, fighting monsters and solving puzzles, they’ll find tons of clues, metaphors and symbolism that link to James’ past and the reasoning for why he was lured there.  We watch as James is forced to face his grief, his guilt and his punishments.While some changes have been implemented that help make it a fresh and exciting playthrough for OG fans, the story still remains the same so it doesn’t feel like someone new to the game is missing out on too much.  Even the characters and their backstories feel more fleshed out and intricate - more human.  And the voice actors did a good job at conveying the emotions that the characters were going through during each phase of the game.  Silent Hill 2 is simply one of a kind and I’m excited for the remake’s success.  I’m hoping it’ll lead to another game within the series being modernized as well.

_childDocuments_.review: Fans of the original Silent Hill 2 should have a glorious time with the remake, and newcomers will find a highly competent third-person survival horror game with tremendous narrative intrigue. The remake preserves the original’s story practically verbatim, and it is probably the game’s biggest strength. New and decent adventure tasks help to make the game substantially longer, and combat alterations bring it closer to that popular series from Capcom. Unfortunately the action is a little plain given the lack of weapons and limited enemy types. And the performance stutters are a shame given the high quality visuals and captivating atmosphere. We have seen a few strong remakes already, each taking their own route, so it will be interesting to see what comes out of the fog next.

_childDocuments_.review: If you enjoyed the original, you'll like this one. Controls like the RE remakes do, enemies are smarter and vary their attacks more, and while you'll recognize familiar landmarks, they have been reworked, so you can't trust the path you used to take. Any concern over the look of the characters should go by the wayside. They look just fine and the rest of the graphics are just the right kind of dark and grimy to fit the Silent Hill theme. The sound is fantastic and the recommendation to use a headset is one I side with as it put the atmosphere right there in your ears. It doesn't appear that Bloober Team will disappoint here. Give this one a go.

_childDocuments_.review: After waiting 2 years for this game and cautiously eyeing all the trailers and pre release reveals, on top of playing the original in 2023, it feels nice to finally play it and for lack of a better word feel at easeWhen it comes to remakes people have a lot of different ideas of what they want, some people want something as "faithful" (whatever that means) to the original and some people want it to be far different to it's source material to go above it, there are benefits to both but either way you're going to upset some people and please others. With a game like silent hill 2 that's legendary for its use of ludonarrative in a survival horror game as well as it's iconography you ideally want to preserve that, and for the aspects of the game people remember for being so good you have to pay close attention to whether it's worth preserving or changing depending on how it might be received, but overall I think they've done a good job I want to start with the combat because this is the aspect I have the biggest bone to pick with. A lot of people defend the originals combat by saying that it was of its time, no I am not going to accept that excuse because it's neither a good excuse nor true, the originals combat was not rewarding and not satisfying, some parts had tension but that tension would more often than not go into frustration, silent hill 1 featured a backstep dodge and silent hill 3 featured a parry, both moves that require timing and dexterity on the players end, sh2 did not have either of that making it the least interactive, enemies could also be stunlocked into melee whilst on the other hand bosses were practically game over if you ran out of ammunition. So how does the remake approach it? Well the combat is over the shoulder opposed to switching between the mixed fixed camera/shoulder the og had, that won't mean it's better just more palatable to new players. The remake adds a dodge in which you can dodge in any direction away from the enemy, enemies also cannot be stunlocked with melee anymore, so melee interactions require you to see the telegraphed attacks and dodge accordingly, far more interactive!, however there's no cooldown or limit to the dodge which makes it a get out of jail free card when you're cornered by enemies which can at times feel cheesy especially when you have autosave removing the tension from these moments. The combat for lack of a better word (again) is a lot more fluid but a lot less snappy that it was or should be, you can make a comparison to re4 and the do or don't dynamic of shooting or moving, by not having this you remove a bit of agency from the player and make the combat slightly sluggish. On the fly weapon switching and having a follow up melee attack to finish enemies is much appreciated. Is the combat overall improved? I'm not sure if I can say with confidence, it's much better than the og but to me it's more like it's moved into the status quo of the genre only to be superseded in X amount of time till people say "wow wasnt sh2r combat pretty bad its in need of a remake" of to which my review will look silly but who knows. I'll talk about the rest of the game in one go because otherwise this review would be stupidly big. The atmosphere and level design is top notch, its nice to see stuff you're familiar with but flipped and reshaped to give you an almost dream like feeling or déjà vu, some of the environments are ripe with detail too, I was also surprised seeing the rusty blood metallic visual design seen before in the series,  . When it comes to boss fights the ante is upped far more than I expected  . The puzzles are great and there's lot's from the original but with modified riddles and objectives or split between new puzzles, like I said a familiar world changed. In terms of the story it's silent hill 2 left as it was, and it's good, as for story presentation . Overall the game is an awesome satisfying journey with lots of atmosphere to discover and soak up, it has its weaknesses and where the original might triumph but it feels like a worthy remake, not a successor I don't want that, and thankfully I don't have that, I like both games, and I'm glad I can finally put my thoughts to rest after waiting for so long

_childDocuments_.review: Wow. I can't believe this game turned out the way it did. I really enjoyed how much more fleshed out Angela and Eddie's character presentations are. The biggest improvement in this game over the original is definitely the boss fights. Even EDDIE's is super tense where in the original his was almost comical. All of them have been tweaked and I really love what Bloober did with them. The environments are absolutely stunning, especially the Otherworld's rusted hellscape. The puzzles have been expanded and and are more engaging. The only downside I can think of are that some voice line deliveries felt off, especially when they tried to stick too closely to the original script for what I can only assume was for the sake of fan service. I was a huge skeptic of Bloober Team when they were announced as the developers, but they’ve truly earned my respect with this remake, and I’m happy to say I’m now a fan.

_childDocuments_.review: I am a 48 year old father, probably one of the oldest people on steam. I am a single father to my son, who is now 15. My son downloaded steam and in less than a week, he had already played games for over 20 hours. This was terrible for me, as it was already hard enough for me to spend time with my son, as he is always out with his friends or just watching videos on Tiktok. So I decided to make a Steam account to see if I could maybe play alongside him. I loaded into a few games, did some tutorials but I was stuck on what you where supposed to do. I asked my Son for help and he bought a game for me to play with him. I loved it as it was the best time I had spent with my Son since my wife had died. Steam has ever since brought my son and I closer again and now we actually spend time together outside the house as well. This game reminded me that there's fun to be had in everything, and it has brought both me and my Son many happy memories

_childDocuments_.review: well i'll be damned.....they really pulled it off. I had every intention of writing this remake off due to my love for the original and my distrust of Bloober Team, but honestly I'm glad I was wrong because instead of a cheap cash grab, we got an honest love letter to the original game. Boss battles are improved big time (particularly the fights with the Abstract Daddy and with Eddie) the charafter performances do a great job of making the dialogue more serious while still keeping that dreamy/uncany tone, the sound design and music still delivers....almost every aspect of this game delivered. The only big mark against it is the performance which is admittedly a pretty big black eye on an otherwise solid remake. Definitely play this one, but maybe wait for a couple performance patches first.

_childDocuments_.review: It was almost perfect. The gameplay and level design was perfect, but the “small” changes they made to the story and the characters designs is holding back the game. One example I’ll give is Remake Maria’s design. In the original she was designed to be more enticing and playful because she is supposed to be the version of Mary James wishes he could be with. But in the remake the redesign is more reserved and she comes off more like some woman who just happens to look like Mary rather than a manifestation of what James wished Mary could be for him.
_childDocuments_.name: SILENT HILL 2

_childDocuments_.review: The best thing about this remake is that, even if you played the original, you're in for so many hours of new places to explore, puzzles, encounters, etc. They also somehow managed to make an already scary game into a terrifying experience, the sound design, music (still composed by akira) the combat that actually feels good and has a level of skill to it despite looking clunky in the trailers, it seems that even when you now have shoulder view camera and no tank controls, it still retains that difficulty that the original had. Oh and the acting of the characters is amazing, they kept the same personalities and stories obviously, but added so much more depth to them, which is more possible now as videogame voice acting wasn't taken too serious when Silent Hill 2 first came out in 2001. There is some issues though, I feel like they really need to release a day 1 patch for perfomance, there is a lot of stuttering sometimes when you enter new rooms along with fps drops. I also feel like the 70 dollar price tag is a bit too much, even if this is a remake on par with the Resident Evil 2 and 4 remakes, lowering it back to 60 will encourage more people to try it.

_childDocuments_.review: Cutscenes rendered in real-time and locked at 30 FPS, transitioning into gameplay at 120 FPS, is jarring. It's 2024, and they still haven't learned... There are plenty of cutscenes, and some transitions visually feel like they're lagging due to the drastic drop in frame rates from 120 to 30. Nope, it's a negative review until this gets fixed. I was so baffled by it that I spent ten minutes combing through the options, convinced there had to be a toggle for it. There is already a mod to remove this lock, and using it makes a night-and-day positive difference. To make matters worse, even cloth animations, like curtains, are locked at 30 FPS—it's just painful to watch. The last time I saw something like this was in the Horizon Zero Dawn port, but thankfully, that got patched after several updates.I just finished Until Dawn (2024), and aside from a few pre-rendered cutscenes, everything ran at 120 FPS. It was simply amazing. You might think it’s an unfair comparison, but I would argue otherwise. Both games are horror. Both are remakes. Both originally had fixed-camera setups, and their remasters do not. Both use Unreal Engine 5. And finally, both were released in the same month. Yes, Until Dawn is mostly an interactive movie, but the remaster allows for a lot of exploration. The levels are pretty big, and they look stunning. Visually, Until Dawn looks better to my eyes. Silent Hill 2 remake looks good, but nothing about it is particularly impressive. What makes it worse is that, despite not looking extraordinary, the game has performance issues. Even with Ray Tracing off, the frame rate fluctuates in simple scenarios—and let’s not forget the occasional stutter. Meanwhile, Until Dawn ran at a locked 120 FPS on my machine with everything maxed out. Oh, and Until Dawn didn’t lock its cutscenes to 30 FPS while looking perfectly cinematic and in-line with the gameplay.If you want a better comparison, let’s look at Alan Wake 2. I’m pretty sure the Silent Hill series was one of the many inspirations for that game. It was released a whole year ago—it looks several times better than Silent Hill 2 and runs at a locked 120 FPS on the same machine, with everything maxed out. Not only do the cutscenes run at 120 FPS, but Alan Wake 2 also has an incredible Ray Tracing implementation, including reflections. For instance, in Silent Hill 2, with everything maxed out, you still can’t see your character’s reflection in random mirrors around the world (I’m not talking about the intro mirror—there’s one, for example, in Wood Side Apartments). I mean, with RT, you do see some dark shape in a mirror, but I wouldn’t call it a reflection. Furthermore, Alan Wake 2 has far superior writing, while Silent Hill 2 stuck to the original script from 2001—back when professional-level writing in games was rare.Here’s how I see it: As of today, Silent Hill 2 costs EUR 69.99, has ugly locked cutscenes, and only OK visuals—but it does have replayability. Until Dawn remake also costs EUR 69.99. It looks and performs better, and it has replayability. Then there’s Alan Wake 2. It looks better than both, has much better writing and story, decent length, and replayability (a second playthrough is almost a must to advance the story)—and it costs EUR 49.99. You do the math.And yes, I understand nostalgia. I played Silent Hill 2 back in 2002. It was an amazing game that terrified me and stood out among others at the time. But today? Honestly, I expect better performance and visuals—and, most importantly, more engaging writing.

_childDocuments_.review: This remake of  deserves to go down in history as a shining example of why you should never judge a game’s book by its perceived cover. It feels like for the last year, all the impressions I’ve ever heard or read about this game has been how it was destined to fail, how it was going to disrespect the source material, and it would likely dumb things down for idiot casuals.Lo and behold, those of us who have experienced the game in its entirety have seen the light, or rather the absolute darkness that Bloober Team had surprised us all with.I want to start with the source material breakdown, because as someone who has been actively listening to SH2’s OST for the last 23 years, as well as revisiting James Sunderland’s sad journey at least two dozen times over the course of that time, I found myself smiling like a teenager in 2001 all over again, because not only did the game bring out the big-guns when it came to paying attention to most of the iconic moments (yes, I know, there was ice cream instead of pizza), but it elevated a lot of weaker aspects of the original. Exploration of the town is expanded in the best way possible, combat has been drastically improved, and every boss has been turned into a glorious horrifying recreation that tests your mettle and ammo supply in a way that feels truly survival horror.James’ journey has never felt more dreary and exciting.Immersion has reached an all-time high, and I genuinely hope that Bloober Team is going to be behind any future Silent Hill releases, as they just . I HIGHLY advise you use a Dual Sense controller (add gyro bound to L2 if you want some smooth aiming while you’re at it), because the way the vibration has been utilized made my skin crawl in several subtle ways. Yamaoka’s legendary audio has been preserved and simultaneously bolstered by so many new, exciting ear-gasms that I hope you won’t spoil for yourself before jumping into this, blind. Even the subtle changes like the way Mannequins don’t instantly trigger your radio leads to so many great sweat-inducing moments throughout.Combat is a colossal win, here, and I want to qualify that statement by saying: This game should, in my opinion, end the conversation about whether good combat makes a game less scary. The answer is: It doesn’t. I don’t know how it plays on normal mode, but Hard mode (IMO the way this game deserves to be played) absolutely makes the combat a joyful time. Fighting enemies never felt boring to me thanks to the variety of maneuvers the monsters can do, along with giving you fun dodge mechanics, but I also made a habit of avoiding fights as much as I could, simply because the slightest error in dodging instantly costs you precious consumable heals. There were several instances where I thought I had the combat down, with “Welp, I’ve got XXX bullets and xx healing now, what could go wrong?” Only for later boss encounters to eat three quarters of those resources, leaving me sweating over my imminent predicament. The best attribute to combat is: Your guns are not toys to have fun with, they are constant, dwindling compromises. Do you spend a rifle round head-shot on a knife-nurse? Or risk missing handgun bullets as she twitches toward you? Or risk lots of damage going full-melee? These are the choices you are constantly making, and it feels great.Seeing SH2 in this new blaze of glory feels like the happy ending we deserved, as fans. You owe it to yourself to dive into this one if you want a genuinely superb survival horror experience. I have zero regrets paying the full price, and as much as I cherish my time with the original, I believe we now have a superior version, and I loved every moment of it. Enjoy!

Having received a letter from his deceased wife, James heads to where they shared so many memories, in the hope of seeing her one more time: Silent Hill. There, by the lake, he finds a woman eerily similar to her...

"My name...is Maria," the woman smiles. Her face, her voice... She's just like her.

Experience a master-class in psychological survival horror - lauded as the best in the series - on the latest hardware with chilling visuals and visceral sounds.

name: Loop8: Summer of Gods
detailed_description: Loop8: Summer of Gods Digital Deluxe Edition Loop8: Summer of Gods 'Digital Deluxe Edition' Contents: Loop8: Summer of Gods game Digital soundtrack with 23 songs Digital artbook "Ashihara Town Guide" (English) About the Game Your choices shape the world in this coming-of-age RPG set in 1980s rural Japan. Step into the life of Nini, a newly earthbound teen who arrives in the quaint Japanese town of Ashihara in August 1983. Explore the town, befriend its people, and face off against the Kegai in turn-based battles where the outcomes depend on the relationships you’ve built and the decisions you’ve made. Use Nini’s special connection to the gods to reset the world, with each loop allowing Nini and his allies to relive the 8th month over and over until they get it right...or the Kegai overcome them entirely. With one month until the world ends, how will you spend each day? Live an Ordinary Life, Fight Extraordinary Enemies Build bonds with Ashihara's residents while protecting the town from the ever-present threat of the Kegai, repeating the cycle to uncover how your everyday actions impact your battles in the Underworld, and vice versa. A Picturesque View of Rural Japan Your adventure takes place in a nostalgic and beautifully recreated snapshot of a rural Japanese townscape. Head downtown to recharge at a local restaurant, or hang out at the shops to strengthen your bonds with other characters. Relive the Past to Alter the Future Though the deadline for humanity's extinction draws ever closer, Ashihara's fate remains in your hands. Repeatedly return to the start of August, alter your actions, and see how they turn the tides of destiny across multiple endings. Choices That Can Change the World Loop8’s emotion-driven AI system responds to every action you take and decision you make. Characters’ emotions and stories will vary greatly based on your choices, making each playthrough wholly unique.

short_description: Your choices shape the world in this coming-of-age RPG. As a new arrival in a 1980s rural Japanese town with a mysterious ability to loop time, your every decision and relationship will affect the outcome of battles against the invading Kegai.

_childDocuments_.review: Loop8: Summer of Gods animated intro actually starts off promising. This is also the first introduction of the Kegai. They are monsters that resemble natural disasters and threaten to destroy mankind. The Space Station, where our protagonist Nini grew up, even served as a place to retreat to in the intervening years. Now that the station has fallen apart, the part-time astronaut is forced to return to Earth, or more precisely, to the tranquil village of Ashihara.There, you'll meet villagers, who, due to the complete lack of other NPCs, seem to be the only ones going about their lives here. They stand out mainly because of their strange backstories. For example, there's the protagonist's grandmother, who not only completely ignores her relatives, but also looks and talks like a woman in her mid-20s. Or the teacher, who tries to replace his dead sister with a homemade robot who looks like a middle-schooler and also attends Nini's class.There are also various references to the mysteries surrounding Kegai and Nini's family, as well as the character's claim to be a godfighter or god himself. Unfortunately, none of this is ever explained in the context of the narrative. The plot, which lasts for roughly 17 hours, doesn't change this at all. As a result, the superficial conflict between good and evil persists, drawing Nini in as an apparent outsider and driving him to fight for humanity's survival. The locals of Ashihara don't talk much, but you can invite the characters to different places, like a café, for example.The majority of the time, you'll hear pointless phrases before being forced to pick between a number of options like "get to know them better" or even the brave "tease them," which results in a courteous word of gratitude and increased friendship, affection, or hate. As a result, the game more closely resembles a dull status simulator than a visual novel because the interactions with the various people are purely about improving your relationship values rather than engaging in meaningful conversations.So you must choose one of the three aforementioned social values with which to carry out your attack in battle. However, the differences are too small to talk about tactics here. So the actually interesting concept can't push the combat system beyond monotonous button-pressing. In addition, you do not have any control over your party members in a fight. They will just do what they want, and this can quickly lead to game over. The few battles Loop8 has to offer also take far too long—an odd contrast given the lack of complexity and depth. Also, be prepared to have the same enemy in normal battles throughout the whole game without any variation.On the other side, you can enhance combat-specific qualities like strength, agility, or intelligence when you aren't clicking through uninteresting cliché structures to raise your social stats. You do this by interacting with selected locations throughout Ashihara. The rest of the town, however, is nothing more than beautiful scenery. On the main street, you can find a restaurant and a café where you can regenerate your energy and stamina. Otherwise, there is not a single spark of a living game world in the entire village.A bigger issue with Loop8: Summer of Gods than the characters meaningless dialogue, the lack of variation, and the repetitive action is the game's fundamental idea. You are forced to repeatedly experience the month of August because you are caught in a time loop. Once game over and you go back to August 1st, where you encounter Ashihara's residents again.When a loop is completed, not only is your progress reset, but your relationships, emotional states, and character values will be reset as well. The only exception are the so-called blessings, which can be found at certain locations in Ashihara and permanently increase your stats, so it's worth visiting these places again and again just to read the same text phrases over and over again. On the other hand, regular conversations with other characters or interaction with such a location, while a character is on your team, will grant character-specific blessings that will then strengthen your team members.At least the presentation of Loop8: Summer of Gods doesn't have to hide behind the wooden animations of the characters in battle and everyday life. The backgrounds are picturesque and capture the atmosphere of a small Japanese village in the hot midsummer splendidly. A few flower petals sailing through the air also brighten up the static images. A soft soundtrack also accompanies your walks through Ashihara. All that's missing for the perfect summer feeling are the chirping birds and the pleasant sound of the waves. Additional flair is provided by the dubbing, which is available in Japanese as well as English and is performed by talented voice actors. It's a double pity that only some of the texts were dubbed.Loop8: Summer of Gods was something I was actually looking forward to. On paper, the digital short vacation in Ashihara read like an entertaining title for in-between times, with its gameplay mix of turn-based battles and dialog-heavy cast of characters reminiscent of Persona. However, an extremely boring gameplay loop is hidden behind the picturesque facade: A Kegai sneaks into Ashihara, you have five days to prepare by boringly increasing your stats and deepening your relationships with the townspeople with meaningless dialog, and finally you have to slog through a dark parallel world and a turn-based slideshow before the threat starts all over again. The context of the time loop only adds to the monotony. The 17 hours it took me to complete the game were one of the toughest experiences I've had in a long time. The well-done summer atmosphere of the village, the visually impressive art style, and your decisions about the number of available characters are unfortunately not enough to pull you out of the vortex of monotony.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is not fun. Don't buy it. Don't play it. It is EXTREMELY slow. Loading screens happen every 5 seconds. 85% of the gameplay is waiting for the game to let you press the A button to advance a dialogue. It takes 15 seconds -- literally, fifteen seconds -- to complete ONE of the mood-boosting dialogues. You have to do this hundreds of times. There is no gameplay except waiting to press the A button.Oh, I almost forgot: Your dialogues are RNG. They have a substantial chance of failure. In that case you just wasted 15 seconds of your life, and then an additional 15 seconds required to do a successful dialogue to push their stats back to where they were before the failure. With Loop8 you are sucking your life away for no gain.Your character moves extremely slowly. In regular gameplay you have fast travel to alleviate this. But once you get to the dungeons, you have no choice but to walk on foot, and your slowness makes itself known. The combat system is very simple, there is almost no brainpower required to succeed. If you fail it's because your stat numbers were too low, not because you could have strategized better.If you lose, the game world resets and prestiges.  The problem is you still have to suffer through every character's mandatory dialogue, which takes literally 15+ minutes per character, because each dialogue takes 15 seconds and they have dozens of lines and need dozens of prep talks.When other reviews talked about grinding, I assumed it would be like doing a lot of battles. That's not it. I don't know who thought this was fun. It's awful. And it's overpriced.Don't buy it. Don't play it.

_childDocuments_.review: Loop8 is an awe-inspiring anomaly when it comes to game design and execution. You have a neat idea: come live in a cozy town for the summer whilst navigating relationships and saving the world. If you thought "isn't that just Persona 4 but only one month?" then you'd technically be right in your assumption, but Loop8 is at an astronomically lower depth than simply "Persona at home". No, it commits the one fatal sin of any media: being mind-numbingly boring.The main character, Novus Nemo... or, Nini for short, is blander than un-toasted toast. He's a shell of what an AI imagines a real human behaves like, with non-dialogue and an expression that screams "I'm trying to imitate life, is it working?" He came to Ashihara to live with his cousin (once-removed, very important) after his parents... uh, died? I guess? I don't actually think it's mentioned why he's even there in the first place. The fact of the matter is, the only actual plot occurs in the first few minutes and it all goes downhill from there. What strikes me the most is that the opening cutscene music video is probably the best part of the game. The visuals look good and it almost feels like it's going to be interesting. They even show locations that you never see in the game itself! But, soon enough... you realize, that it's all smoke and mirrors, and the actual content of the game is shallower than a puppy's piss puddle. So Nini arrives in Ashihara and meets his cousin, Konoha, and she gets him acquainted with the town. Standard stuff, and the music and backgrounds are very pleasant. After day one of Konoha giving you the tour, your second day is spent giving you a bit of freedom to check out the town's various activities. Unfortunately, here's where the trouble begins, because this game runs on a time system, not unlike Persona, but instead of time only passing when you do an activity, it also ticks by every second you're in the overworld at all, and this can lead to some complications. What, you thought they'd pause the timer during your second day to get acquainted with where everything is? HAH! NO! On day 2, you're dumped in front of the schoolyard and told to attend supplementary lessons, but the game doesn't tell you AT ALL where that is inside the building. So you run across the schoolyard and... oh no, is that really Nini's top speed? A comfortable jog? It takes about 6 agonizing seconds for him to walk from the school entrance to the building. And no, despite him blazing around on foot in the intro, he never does that here. Not even in the combat zones! A ♥♥♥♥♥♥, comfortable jog like he just dumped ass for the entire. Game. The lessons are on the second floor in class 1-A, the first of only two enterable classrooms. I actually took too long to get there and the game gave up and warped me to the room. Absolutely amazing. You get some more cutscenes and it all seems fine. The tutorial that comes next is to play around on the iron bars in the schoolyard, and thankfully that one's easy to follow! Mostly because there's nothing else in the schoolyard. It's just a big, empty space that you cross on foot every time you enter the school. Awesome. After the tutorial to receive a blessing at the shrine, you rendezvous with Konoha to learn about the relationship mechanic. Your only option for her is "Get to know better", with Nini thinking to himself "I just know this'll work", so you select it, and Konoha just says "Thank you!". And that's it. Then a screen pops up that shows the relationship between the two characters. Afterwards, the game tells you to try eating at the restaurant. But again, they don't show you where it is, it doesn't stand out, and time continues to tick on by. You are left to flounder around while being forced to run at the slowest speed imaginable. It's AGONIZING. That night, Nini sees a vision of a Kegai (the mythical monsters), breaking through the barrier and entering Ashihara. When you wake up the next day, the game deadass says "An entrance to Yomotsu Hirasaka (the shadow version of Ashihara) has appeared in the shrine. Nini can somehow sense this." Even the game has NO EXPLANATION as to how Nini is even a protagonist. You go there and meet up with Beni and Ichika, two girls from your class who have experience fighting the Kegai. And this is just a big tease because the game makes it out to be like they're going to be easily accessible to fight with, but no, not at all. Then, you get a battle tutorial, and if you thought that the framerate wasn't distracting before, then it kicks into overdrive here, especially with Beni. While the devs call it "artistic choice", I'm inclined to call it "we don't know how to fix this and we're all out of ideas, so just call it artistic." If you're photosensitive enough, it'll give you a headache.Anyway, the tutorial battle makes it seem like the game has depth. But no, there is no depth, it's all useless. Battles in this game all boil down to numbers. If your numbers are high enough, you win. Though I should mention that the only REAL "depth" of the combat is that attacking with friendship is neutral damage, affection is weaker but lowers the enemy's attack, and hate is the strongest but builds up to make your enemies stronger. So most of the time, you'll be using friendship, MAYBE affection if the boss you happen to be fighting goes higher than threat level 1. Also, you can't control your party members, and outside of this tutorial, if anyone dies in battle, they CANNOT be revived and you will be locked out of the true ending. So... you know... better to just run the game solo. Bringing others along will just slow you down. So much for the power of friendship!The tutorial fight ends with a boss you can't defeat, so you wipe and get a soft game over, or a loop. You might think, "oh, so the loop will tie into the narrative now and get the ball rolling?" Hahaha, no. No, silly child. The only thing looping is good for is to go back to the beginning of the month. And to also get to read all the dialogue you read before, see all the scenes you saw before, and relive all that ♥♥♥♥ you just went through. NO ONE remembers the loops. Not the other characters, not Nini, no one. Mercifully, your stats DO carry over, so really the only point of looping is to get strong enough to defeat a boss if you couldn't before. Your relationship with the characters doesn't either, but it DOES get put on steroids so it will get to its former value in half the time. It's a juiced up NG+. But uh... that's it. That's the flow of the game. It's broken into 5-day cycles. On the second or third day of the 5-day cycle, a non-combatant character will be kidnapped by the Kegai, and it's up to you to boost Nini's stats and go rescue them. (There's 5 of these, and then the final boss.) I just hope you accurately predicted who is getting kidnapped first, because without enough friendship with them, Nini simply kills them and they die, so you'll be forced to loop. So really, the beginning of the game is where you'll loop the most, trial-and-erroring until you get high enough friendship with the first victim to avoid killing them. Also, if you need to bring a companion in to pass a friendship/affection trial to reach the boss, you should probably avoid bringing someone who has a poor relationship with the kidnapped, because that strengthens the boss and your companion will likely die. That is THE ONLY level of strategy that really exists going into boss fights. Your main focus is just buffing your stats, boosting your relationship with the upcoming victim, and mingling with the characters that fight on the side. Actually, I just saved after each successful boss and then slept for 2-3 days in a row to see the future of who would be kidnapped and then reload and focus on them, lol.All the girls are thirsty for Nini too, despite being his cousin and even his Grandmother. Yep. I hit the character limit. The game sucks. Do not waste your money.

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr: The game is a time management sim where you take your best friends into the underworld to beat up the people you didn't make friends with. In-game, every week presents an underworld encounter with one boss. In the 8 hours I've got logged as of writing, I've actually entered combat fewer than 5 times.Very little by way of unique dialogue, animations are nonexistent for character interactions (even during cutscene events!)They went with a "true" groundhog day scenario type deal.By "true," I'm referring to the fact that you, the player, experience everything again. Every intro cutscene [there are 6 on your first day], every exposition dump [there are 50+ dialogue boxes associated with repeated information that you'll be skipping over with every loop], and every character interaction.Despite dumping hours of lore to the player, they decided to leave the combat system ambiguous. As previously stated, most of the game is boosting relationship and stat points, so while this issue isn't high impact, I'd like to know why it is I'm mashing "A" to "get to know" somebody.Stat increases and character interactions are the focus of the game. As for why they neglected even a minimal amount of polish for these activities is beyond me. They did an OK job with the aesthetics of the combat. The music for the overworld is determined by the "mood," which is largely determined by time of day, activities available, and the characters present (and their relationships with one another). The music is NOT synced to anything that's actually happening in game, so there are some jarring tonal shifts where the peppy "normal mood" music kicks in after the protag shoots a 1 minute monologue about how he got one of his friends killed.

_childDocuments_.review: This is absolutely not a finished product, it's a concept pitch for a game that has a price tag.The idea of the game is simply this: You move into a Japanese town and you have the power to see yokai and people's inner thoughts. Time loops during the month of August and a yokai occassionally breaches the town and possesses someone who is stressed and sad about something. Some of the civilians can fight and some are aware of the time loops. You have to talk to people to increase friendship affection and hate parameters which each have different affinities in battle and increase your own stats to fight in the underworld when someone gets possessed.Almost none of the story elements in the game has a scenario that plays out. You are from a space colony that orbits Earth and 80% of the population is secluded to small areas that are protected by barriers from the yokai that destroyed the world. All that is not relevant, you just ride a train to town and all the civilians comment occasionally that you're from space and that everyone is trapped. You increase parameters by picking dialogue options with people that show favorable odds of success and all of them (Greet, Flirt, whatever) that don't raise hate just have them thank you unless it's an event where you take them somewhere. When you go to save someone, it's just a bunch of stat checks and few encounters walking through an inverted version of town to gain access to the boss and when you defeat them, depending on if you have the right friendship levels with the person you battled, if you get the option to not kill them. During all of that there's small scenes where they talk about their feelings and everyone mostly doesn't acknowledge what happened, nobody panics when someone disappears and aren't very sad if someone dies. There are very little cutscenes in the game.I completed a playthrough by just spamming favorable dialogue with the party members I wanted, kept going across town each day to all the hidden blessing locations that permanently increase stats for the save file, and focused on 2 choices of the potential 5 party members that would make the battles easiest and beat the last boss in 2 or 3 loops.I see what the game is supposed to be but it's just skipping through generic dialogue responses for 80% of the playthrough and I'm disappointed that I didn't get to have sex with the teacher.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop8: Summer of Gods

_childDocuments_.review: This game is fascinating in that it presents interesting ideas for how the "social life" part of RPGs that is kind of typical to the contemporary setting JRPG but unfortunately the execution is so baffling that I can't imagine some of this stuff is even working right let alone working to how it was envisioned on paper.like you talk to a girl for 10 minutes and she decides you are now dating and then you get a blessing every time you talk to her for the next 20 minutes of clicking through dialogue after which she has become God's Strongest Warrior. It's hilarious, but also *completely* baffling.if it kept up that kind of baffling energy all the time it'd be at least funny but the moments where the social system produces really bizarre interactions are spread over hours of just clicking on the same menus over and over again to make numbers go up in probably the most insipid way possible. You can occasionally see a spark of an interesting idea sometimes but it always manages to tragically end up being the most boring version of itself possible. this review is kind of a mess but the short version is that Loop8 is bad, but like, Fascinating Bad and a bit Boring Bad rather than like Evil Bad. An attempt was made and sometimes it's hard to even see what was being attempted, but at any rate, it really doesn't work at all.

_childDocuments_.review: Hard to recommend. Definitely wait till it's on sale for around $30 or less. Now I haven't beaten the game yet, but if anything changes from the 7 hours I've played if it so far in the future I'll change the review accordingly.The game has a lot of interesting ideas, soundtrack is good, environment is gorgeous, voice acting is great, and the characters are memorable for the most part. However, while it has a good concept going for it with the relationship and stats systems it fails to really do much with it other than stat boosts. So the game quickly becomes a stat grinder.The characters, while they will comment on your progress with other characters; the town feels pretty dead since these are the only characters that exist there, no background characters or even silhouettes indicating there are other people living there and they don't interact very often in big ways. No group activities, get togethers, or festivals. It all feels self contained between you and that character.While playing I did find myself really wanting a sprint button of some kind since the casual jog was a bit too slow for me.I'm not sure if it was a stylistic choice or not but the low framerate animations on the models bugged me. It didn't bother me too much in the "overworld" but the animations look really bad in battle. Largely just makes the animations look like the game is lagging during the fights.All in all, what I'd say is I'd like to see more relationship content and more reactive content with the characters.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop8: Summer of Gods

_childDocuments_.review: The map/battle animations are kind of choppy in a netflix anime kind of way, and there's some obvious jank that could leave a bad first impression. But I'm having a pretty good time just grinding stats in a comfy anime town, feels nice.Edit: A few more notes on what to expect, the JRPG combat isn't much of a focus outside of specifically boss fights and is pretty much just a stat/relationship check. Improving relationships and stats unlocks more powerful skills and increases max HP/MP.Party members act on their own, but their battle AI works well.Since the bosses (at least the ones i've seen so far) are all possessed characters, a big part of preparing for them is social manipulation tactics and making sure you have party members that are:1. strong enough to survive the fight,2. Good enough friends/rivals that they will use support skills on each other and,3.  don't hate the possessed character too much. Hatred can give a power boost to the boss and can get out of hand pretty fast.Because of this, the game mostly revolves around stalking friends with your magic eyes to take advantage of their moods for mad stat/relationship gains, hunting down blessings for stat buffs that carry across loops (fixed interaction points on maps alone or with a friend, bonuses from viewing special character interactions, and as rewards for earning a talisman (keys to the boss room.)The tension from having to keep pushing back doomsday as more characters are possessed, and playing around the moods and schedules of the AI keep things hectic and engaging, and between  that, seeing numbers go up, and pretty enjoyable character interactions, its a pretty enjoyable experience for the main meat of the game.There are a lot of rough points and a lack of some quality of life features. The protagonist doesn't really keep memories between loops, and you'll have to sit through a lot of repeated dialogue and the default window size cropped out the key prompts showing that there actually has been a fast forward toggle the whole time. The keyboard controls for the menus are strange and take some getting used to, And the way events work in order to accommodate the AI world/character simulation the game revolves around can make for some strange interactions.On the other hand you get double stat gains as a catch up bonus on new loops until you reach your personal best, and the permanent blessings mean you can maintain a pretty good baseline for any character you invest time in.All and all I would say this is a very unique and interesting game that can reward someone willing to explore it and play a bit past the tutorial, and the bad first impression they'll probably have.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop8: Summer of Gods

_childDocuments_.review: Loop8 might be the funniest game I've ever played. Is it good? No. Is it fun? Sometimes, but never for the right reasons. But I can't deny that while playing it, the strange mixture of how the game handles how it tells you it's story, along with the baffling combat system didn't make me laugh. You should play it, but not to enjoy it traditionally. After all, hay is for horses.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop8: Summer of Gods

_childDocuments_.review: I thought that this game would be a good contender against the Persona franchise. And boy how wrong I was for thinking this. The game is not horrible, but gameplay is mediocre. The relationship system is just another by number system, the story is non existing and visuals are nothing to write about. The time loop system only existe to waist your time and create a false sense of depth.  This game would be a 6/10 even if it was at a lower price, but as it is I would say that is a 4/10. I don’t recommend this game until it drops down to $15-$20 dollars.

_childDocuments_.review: Unfortunately, while I did get some enjoyment out of this game, it's going to be a tough sell for most people. If you are still interested in this title, I would recommend waiting for a sale instead of picking it up at full price. The game suffers too much from questionable design choices and bad balancing issues. I really wanted this game to be great, but it just isn't. Fortunately, there are still some redeeming factors for those who are still interested. The game can be a genuinely relaxing experience when it isn't a tedious slog. The sense of atmosphere is truly great. If you are a Steam Deck user, you don't have to worry about how this game will run. _childDocuments_.review: Not the greatest JRPG, but still a nice game. It's very relaxing increasing relationships stats, trying to improve from your previous "loop", and a battle system where your relationship stats are key. If you fail, you can do it all again in another "loop." Not worth the $50 price tag, but if it goes on sale for around $30 I'd definitely recommend getting. Pros: Great relationship system that consists of friendship, affection, and hate. You might feel friendly towards someone and the other doesn't like you at all and will treat you as such. Excellent voice acting in both the Japanese and English dubs.Good soundtrack that I enjoy listening to.Cons: Can be repetitive having to relive the same month.Battle system a tad boring with the other two in your party acting on their own.In the English dub, the mouth still moves considerably after the line had finished. Very noticeable and slightly jarring. Overall I'll give it a 7/10 for now. I'm enjoying it so far and am looking forward to playing it more. Definitely not for everyone though.
_childDocuments_.name: Loop8: Summer of Gods

_childDocuments_.review: As a fan of SteinsGate and Tokyo Revengers, Loop 8: Summer of Gods manages to hit the time loop trope perfectly; even when you think you have all the answers, there is potentially another factor that you might have missed that throws a wrench into your plans. The game does not hold back the punches by having the player find out the game's mechanics on their own rather than having their handheld. The game's combat system and friendship system can take a while to get used to and the game's AI can be a headache. On one hand, it is nice not having to control everything in battle, but on the other, some of the choices that are made can be infuriating.When it comes to each character in the game, they all have their own unique personalities and emotions. Each character has their own likes and dislikes that impact their relationship with you and other characters. Losing a character due to death in the underworld can be heartbreaking, but makes you want to do a new loop in order to save them. Each character has so many reactions based on their bond with the player creating a variety of responses. This makes it so that you will want to replay the game in order to learn more about a character.Our biggest complaint comes down to the inability to adjust the game's settings outside of visuals. Honestly, it would have been nice to turn off certain character voice lines or make it so every character has fully voiced lines. The voice acting within the game was enjoyable, but after you heard it once, it is fine to skip it on the next go around.Loop 8: Summer of Gods is an enjoyable game but it is not for everyone. If you are a fan of strong narratives, then I recommend picking it up. If you are a fan of traditional JRPGs then it might be better to watch some gameplay first. Full Review:

_childDocuments_.review:
Eight months after hope for humanity was destroyed...

Nini, the protagonist who lost his home and family to the ancient calamity known as the "Kegai," arrives at the peaceful countryside town of Ashiharanakatsu to stay with his mother's relatives.

In this town where everyday life and the extraordinary intertwine, Nini's radiant and stressful summer begins.

LOOP8 is a juvenile RPG in which you live your "everyday life" and fight "the extraordinary." Live a summer all your own while forging relationships with the people around you, while fighting calamities known as "Kegai."

The game's unique emotional artificial intelligence, the "Maturity System," controls all aspects of the game's progress, and the character's emotions and stories are constantly shifting. Each "choice" you make influences the game's world, offering a different experience every time you play.

detailed_description: Join Our Discord About the Game The Land Beneath Us is a turn-based rogue-lite action dungeon crawler. Use powerful skill combos and stylish weaponry to battle your way through the Underworld known as Annwn. Enjoy challenging dynamic encounters and discover the mysteries of this mythological world. BATTLE THROUGH THE UNDERWORLD! Forged by The Creator, the Ultimate Soul Harvester (U.S.H) is crafted to gather Souls. Now armed with Soul-Technology, its mission is one of redemption. Explore The Underworld, engage, barter, or confront characters. Learn from their tales to shape your unique path. MASTER THE COMBOS! Overcome enemies with powerful abilities, executing customizable movement combinations. Plan strategically through short, action-packed levels to maximize hits on creatures! VARIED ARSENAL Strategize and wield a diverse array of weapons, from Blood Axes to Longinus Spears and Lazer Pistols. Equip different weapons in each slot for a dynamic hack 'n' slash journey through the Underworld. REPLAYABILITY FACTOR Enhance stats and abilities by collecting souls from defeated enemies as you explore each world. Enjoy direct combat? Boost your Weapon skill tree. Prefer a strategic approach? Unlock potent Combo Abilities to hit enemies from a distance.
