_childDocuments_.review: So, the game was played, the credits rolled, time to speak on what this game got right, and what it did not: Fast, pulse-pounding, diverse sets of enemies mixed generously in almost every encounter to make you dance on your toes, as it should've done. Tower feels much more hostile, rampant and chaotic by that margin, since there is no single powerhouse of the Keymaster to hold everyone else in check. Fights are crowded, busy, hectic, and everything else that was Hel's fights in her DLC in the first game, so it's more of what's amazing in the first game.Platforming took a bit of a punch, with less walls being as free to reign and run over, and stamina bar added limitation that was not present in the first game, which might irritate you, but it is not bad in itself, I would argue, as otherwise you would not be adequatly challenged, especially if you are a seasoned player of the first game. The incorporation of your abilities into platforming is great, as platforming is half a gameplay, and that incorporation added depth to thing that we know and love. Once again, it is a good thing, because it gives us new situations to pull through and a new high of excellence to achieve while replaying or participating in speedruns. Would not say that I got enough appreciation for it on my first playthrough, as I have a tendency to go bare bones in games until games serve me my hubris on a silver plate. More of a me problem. Nontheless, the upgrades provided aim at enchancing certain ways of playing and solving tasks presented by the game, and they are diverse enough to give replayability value, as you might mess around them to find some nasty combos. I know I will definetly get into that later. Wast, expansive, greatly contrasted from region to region, levels are a testament to the megastructure built by the Architect, of which we only have had a small glimpse in the scope of the first game, which now feels more like an anthill through which we run up and down in a hurry, rather than a strictly controlled web of locks and shahts through which you can try to squeeze to get to the top. That sells  out the feeling of the Tower being a place where many conflicting groups do things for themselves and not being united with one another, as it would be in anarchy that followed after the fall of Keymaster. While dialogues and RP elements were definetly not the main focus of the development, with character's faces being rather static, the dialogue conveys emotions and points it needs to, builds up characters and deepens their relationships, and sometimes provides comic relief. With how straight to the point and focused everyone were in the first game, where every action of everyone was dictated by concrete goal, which promoted urgency, there we have more flood in communications, when situations allow it, or even when it would not be adviseable, giving off the perspective and deepening the images of the characters, who become more than a plot contrivances utilized only to focus player's attention at the task at hand, which is great for the worldbuilding and for the game. The score of this game is bombastic, for lack of a better word. It builds up when needed to, it explodes, where needed to, chills out, when it don't have to blast. The music is catchy, pleasant to ears, and setting the mood just right, in, I would say, all of the levels, and I have had no seconds thoughts buying it right after the first session of playing the game. Favorite track: We are Magonia - God run.OMG JACK HAS LEGS TEN OUTA TEN. On more serious note, I no joke love everything about design of characters and enviroments. Jack borrowed Hel's swordgrip, which is good, because the first game had really hard time convincing me even a cyborg can slice a person in half with 1-handed strike with a sword, holding said sword on chest level with a bent elbow. Old enemies has had a rehash which freshed their looks up while leaving them recognizeable enough, new enemies and variations from different factions are distinct putting emphasis on who's lands you're treading and who opposes you. Locations look marvelous and memorable, Cybervoid finally does not look like you're playing on TV with out-of-touch cables so that your entire picture is filled with white noise, walls are clogged and show signs of wear and the fact that they are not made soly for the purpose of Ghostrunners running them up and down from one headed that needs to be rolled from shoulders to another. There is more of them, than there was in original, which is to be expected, they are more complex, more nuianced, their pace differ from one another greatly, while all of them manage to still be blood-pumping-fast, and the combat mechanics greatly reward excellence. A) Invisible walls, and the fact that there are far too many of them in places where they are least warranted. You might find a small dent in the wall that houses a vent fan behind a bar, and find yourself unable to touch said bar, because for some misterious reason there is an invisible wall that is far enough so that you can step into the wall, but just a step or two from what would be natural wall that is rendered, with nothing but questions about why that invisible wall even exists there. And some more glaring examples, of which I shall not speak there for reasons of keeping review as spoiler-free as I can.B) The bike. Or, more concretely, the fact that level from the demo that showcased bike, was much more adapted to it, than what came after. While  you may well find that bike can easily stuck in the simpliest obstacles, like small rocks, or even stuck completely while trying to ride up a hill that was deemed one degree too steep to ride up against, which can lead to you having fair bit of frustration around randomly bonking from 180 km/h to 0 in a snap of fingers, exploding hillariously, or in getting stuck on some particularly rocky terrain, and it's not like you can just ignore bike there, because distances needed to traverse are enourmous for foot travel, and some places can't be reached without usage of a bike. Word of advise from experience: if you reached those levels in one go from "New Game" button, take a break, and take them on when your mind and body are well-rested and clear. That might not remedy issues with those levels, but reduce chances of you stubbornly trying to reach places that were not the right place to go, spending more time than I am willing to admit on that, all the while getting stuck on all of the pesky terrain.A) Hell mode, because why wouldn't there be a Hell mode, if it is present in the first game.B) Endless Roguerunner.EXE with a scoreboard.C) Possible prequel DLC involving Ashura's run-in with Mara and Adam?Should you buy and play?Yes.Do I have regrets in buying BE?No. Loved the first game, loved Project Hel, loved the second game.Is the game perfect?No.Is the game better than the first one?Depending on whom you're asking.Is the game holding up to the first one?Most definetly.Personal score: 9/10.

_childDocuments_.review: running cyborg ascends tower the sequelA pretty great sequel, with some very minor caveats. I'd recommend Ghostrunner 2 for everyone who enjoyed the first.*STORY:*The story is way better in this one. Because of this players will have to spend more time talking and focusing on dialogue than in the first, which may be a downside to some. It definitely slows down the pacing for repeat playthroughs/speedruns, though thankfully, you can skip through all dialogue if you really do not care enough. The characters are better written, especially your machine companions AND antagonists. The character interactions in the newly introduced hub are however a bit less great. It's comparable to Starfield where you just stand there and they stare back while dialogue plays with some VERY awkward silences. Thankfully most of the dialogue is optional.*GAMEPLAY:*The gameplay is improved, but not nearly as much as some people say it is. There are a few more enemy types, some of which are great additions such as a Roller found later in the game, forcing you to think outside of the box sometimes. But most of the new enemy types are very weak and uninteresting, providing either an alternative to already existing enemies or just offering nothing new. There were also a few enemy types from the last game that did not get introduced until the late game, which left me wondering if the developers intended to have more unique enemy types but couldn't do it, or if the overall difficulty for this one was supposed to be lower than the first. Which ever answer it is, it does feel quite anticlimactic seeing the same enemies pop up in the late game, while in the first game they were there quite a bit earlier.That is not to say that the gameplay is worse, because the game flows a lot smoother. There are quite a bit more parkour sections that often take up more time than the combat sections, usually it works quite well. The only problem I found with it is the little platforms you can grapple to your location, I simply do not understand why they appeared so late into the game while they work way worse than a simple grapple point. Some levels are a bit long compared to the first, but when the combat really works, it shines. More abilities, and a currency to buy them with and the motherboard system makes the possibilities in this game way more interesting.*SOUNDTRACK:*The soundtrack to this game was a little less up my alley than the soundtrack to the first. Dan Terminus uses an upbeat, more classic synthwave approach that feels more like enjoying some good times, while having less punchy sound design. Arkadius Rejkowski composed the tracks that play during some of the more desolate segments of the game, and they work quite well, although they are sometimes a little too minimalistic for my taste. The style was bound to change with the fact that Daniel Deluxe only made two tracks in the entire game, but some of the tracks composed by the other composers work very well. A few standouts are "Mind as Universe", "The Temple", "Road Zero", "Already Dead" and "Protocol Overload".*PERFORMANCE:*Sadly (and this is probably just early days issues) some people seem to have quite bad performance, including myself. There is quite a bit of stuttering involved in this game, even when your overall framerate is very high the game sometimes just stops for about half a second to a second, usually resulting in suddenly seeing a "Critical Failure" on your screen. Hopefully the stutters can be worked out for the people who have it.Overall, Ghostrunner 2 builds upon the story of the first quite well, while giving you way more to parkour with. The combat is a step up, when you actually get to fight lots of enemies, use all your abilities, and slowly figure out an encounter using every death, just like the first game. The soundtrack is great for the most part, although the unique style of Daniel Deluxe is pushed to the background in favor of mixed styles.And hopefully this one will be just as fun to pour many hours into, optimizing speedrunning into oblivion just as the first.

_childDocuments_.review: A bit slow and tedious in many areas compared to the first game, with fewer/simpler combat puzzles, and far fewer examples of the game mixing enemies into the linear traversal sections between arenas, from what I can remember. The pacing is especially thrown off in the exterior bike level where you're just riding through barren, post-apocalyptic hellscape for 30 minutes, but almost all the levels reflect this change to greater or lesser degrees. Compare that to the first game where each level is a tightly honed string of set-piece arenas connected with some light platforming, basic puzzles, and parkour combat. Hopefully the devs can release a new mode, as they did with the prior game, that remixes the encounters in each level to provide a more intense experience that aligns closer to what they already achieved.I also don't understand why they felt the need to change the skill and upgrade system. I thought it was perfectly elegant the way it was, where you had to balance your upgrades spatially with the tetris grid and also your upgrade complexity vs. energy regen for your skills. The rows and columns system of this game just seem like an unnecessary over-complication. Why does blink require so many button presses now? I guess the capability to precisely select enemies to target over a wide area is interesting, but it felt more intuitive when you just took out everything in a straight line in front of you in two keystrokes.I will say that there's a ton of variety in the mechanics and enemy units that you encounter, so that will mix things up when there IS something to do. That is, when you're not autopiloting through the long stretches of empty environments listening to VO.Plus, why did they feel the need to add a dialogue system to Ghostrunner? Truly baffling.Some significant performance issues, but what do you expect. Modern gaming, right? The days of getting a working product on launch day are long gone.There's still no other game quite like it, if you like the first, it's still worth checking out. Hopefully in the future it can be made better by adding more enemy encounters and hazards throughout the levels, à la Hardcore mode from 1, because the game has good bones.

_childDocuments_.review: I feel like they took everything about the first game and made it bigger and better.I love having the hub.  Roguerunner.exe is great if you just feel like doing a run.One of the things that I find particularly exceptional about the design of the boss events, is the seamless inclusion of Parkour and Platforming in a way that feels like combat.It can be frustrating, and I die often,  but it's incredibly rewarding, and visually breathtaking.I was a huge fan of the first game, and 7 or so hours of gameplay and, I love this one even more.My one complaint, would be the implementation of the checkpoint system, I made it three to four checkpoints into a boss fight, and then I had a system issue, when I finally got my computer restarted, all that hard fought progress was lost, I really wish that was not the case.It didn't take me here to make it back to the point where I had shut down, but it did diminish The experience slightly.Also, for those worried about the one hit death scenario, I was skeptical about it before the first game, but it really does work for this formula, if you had a highly durable character, I feel like it would diminish the experience, and make all the mobility mechanics last meaningful.This isn't a game where you want a tank through a level, you are an incredibly nimble, incredibly dangerous character with many tools that your disposal to annihilate everything you come across, the trade-off is being a glass Cannon.Every level has a pattern or several, you don't want to run into a crowd, you want to run, around the crowd, over under and past the crowd... The developers give you the tools to make the environment is much of a weapon as anything else.  Highly recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're looking for an incredible, top tier gameplay experience from this game, you can't get any better than this. Vastly outperforms even the original in that regard. You're introduced to an impressive amount of new mechanics throughout the game at a perfect pace, the devs never let you get bored of a mechanic before introducing a new toy. Each mechanic feels incredible to utilize, leading to even more satisfying moments throughout the game as you get more and more mechanics to string together.While the story might not win any awards, it's much more engaging than the previous title. You're much more involved with a tangible threat that, when coupled with the gameplay innovations on offer, creates a great sense of progression throughout.There's a few aspects in particular that Ghostrunner 2's expanded scope does not stick the landing with. Luckily, every single one of these aspects is contained to a single, separate instance that only occurs for around 5 minutes periodically after certain levels. Nothing about the Hub worked for me. The animations were quite stiff here, and there's an attempt at dialogue options that never feel natural. Abrupt tonal shifts and pacing problems are constant. It's very jarring to go from the beautifly animated, perfectly paced package that is the rest of this game, to the EXACT opposite. It feels tacked on in the truest sense of the phrase. The developers exceeded even my highest expectations with the aspects that mattered the most. Gameplay is some of the best I've ever played in any video game, and the story is a step up from the original. The aspects that don't work for me, while they  dont work, are all self contained within the Hub world, which you never spend more than 5 minutes in at a time. 99% of your experience will be spent with an extremely fluid, satisfying gameplay formula that evolves meaningfully throughout

_childDocuments_.review: Ghostrunner is one of my favorite games, so I really hate to give its sequel a thumbs down, but I was pretty disappointed by this game—not because it was bland or dull, but because it ended up taking many steps backwards from the original. For what it is, Ghostrunner 2 is certainly not terrible, still a pretty exciting platformer with incredible visuals, but it somehow manages to screw up a lot of things the first game did really well. Firstly, however, here are some of the things I think it DOES do a good job of:-As mentioned before, the visuals are absolutely fantastic. This game is even more stunning than GR1, and it features a wider range of environments, all of which look beautiful. I’ve seen people complain about the performance, and while I had a couple small issues, I was consistently getting >100fps on max settings with a fairly mid-tier GPU, so I don’t think that’s a huge problem here.-Naturally, the movement is still decently fun, even if it’s a big step down from its predecessor.-Personally, I really liked the upgrade chip system in this game. The “Tetris block” system in GR1 was fine, but unlocking different chips and arranging them in the motherboard felt a lot more personalizable and interesting to me.-The soundtrack is once again a banger.-The  introduced in the last level is absolutely incredible, it’s without a doubt the best part of the game and I really wish there was more of it.With that being said, there are two massive issues, as well as a few other small ones, that really ruined this game for me.Firstly, the level design is extremely unpolished. To me, GR1 is the pinnacle of great level design. It does such an amazing job of using subtle color patterns and aspects of the environment to lead the player around without them even realizing it. Everything feels super smooth and intentional, and it’s what makes the platforming gameplay so much fun. I’ve even published a video essay on why GR1 is a masterclass in great level design. GR2, on the other hand, very much lacks intentionality. Many of the environments in GR2 are more muted and bleak than the neon-lit parts of Dharma Tower in GR1, which isn’t inherently bad, but when the first game leaned so heavily on using the environment to prevent the player from getting lost, eliminating those patterns with nothing in their stead creates a problem for GR2. I found myself constantly getting lost in this game, finding little visual indication of what I was supposed to do next and frequently running around in circles or aimlessly going to areas I wasn’t supposed to. This was especially a problem with the motorbike levels, which I’ll elaborate on later. But the bottom line is, getting stuck and lost is completely antithetical to fast-paced and fluid gameplay, and it was really frustrating to be constantly losing my momentum because of unclear level design.In addition to its opaqueness, this game’s level design is also poorly implemented and could’ve benefited from significantly more QA/playtesting. I encountered many instances where the gap-jammer (grappling hook) didn’t pull me quite far enough to land where I was supposed to, or it flung me directly at a wall I was supposed to be landing on top of. There are several points where swinging on bars didn’t get me far enough to land where I was supposed to go either. These issues, among many others, indicate a lack of polishing and consistency with the level design. I also quite experienced many geometry/physics bugs where the game would make me start wall-running on something that wasn’t even a wall, or conversely, I would be unable to wall-run on a wall that was supposed to be run on (sometimes there was also a bug where I ended up partly inside of a wall and could only run very slowly on it). The launching air vents sometimes just didn’t do anything when I walked over them. Once again, these issues feel like they could have been prevented or at least recognized before releasing the game, and they drastically decreased my enjoyment of GR2.My other main problem with this game is that it appears to take a design approach of prioritizing quantity over quality of new features. Nearly every single level was throwing some new mechanic at me that would rarely be used again in any level thereafter, and most of these mechanics came out half-baked because there are simply too many of them. It doesn’t seem like the devs took the time to deeply craft any of these features, instead just coming up with something to add for one level and then moving onto the next one. There can be potential for some really interesting combinations when you start to mix mechanics together, but unfortunately, that didn’t really happen here. This leads to GR2 almost feeling like playing with fifty different mods installed that aren’t meant to go together and sometimes actively conflict with one another.As I alluded to earlier in my review, one of the most glaring instances where this flawed design philosophy crops up is with the motorbike. This addition definitely had potential, but it ended up making the middle portion that implements it the worst part of the game by far. This is because, in addition to the motorbike controlling horrendously, having very glitchy physics, and it being extremely difficult to “read” levels while driving it, the motorbike plays into GR2’s identity crisis that so many modern games are having because it wants to be every genre at once. The first level involving the motorbike still feels like a Ghostrunner level, because it’s relatively fluid and fast-paced—it would almost be fun, if not for all the other motorbike issues I already pointed out. But after this, GR2 basically pretends to be an open-world game for the next 3 levels, making you use the motorbike to traverse a world that has almost no visual indications of where to go whatsoever. One level in this open-world section of the game took over an hour for my first completion, because I just kept driving around aimlessly on the motorbike, extremely confused where the game wanted me to go. This is the EXACT opposite of what Ghostrunner gameplay is supposed to feel like! The fact that people complain about the game’s hub world interrupting the flow but then praise the motorbike is absolutely bewildering to me—trying (and failing) to be an open-world game is the single worst thing the devs could have done for the flow of GR2’s gameplay. And I won’t even start on its “roguelike mode” that apparently every game needs to have now… it took about twenty minutes to see everything there was to be seen, and it was even shallower than Ghostwire: Tokyo’s “roguelike mode” which is really saying something.In addition to these two glaring fundamental flaws the game exhibits, many other small issues hampered my enjoyment of GR2 as well. For one, I’m still extremely puzzled who thought that having FEWER control layouts than the first game was a good idea. Having to play GR2 with a different control layout than GR1, like I did, is absurd, and there is absolutely zero reason for this. Also, some of the achievements have very misleading descriptions. For example, the most difficult achievement Godrunner, says that it requires you to “finish any 5 levels without dying,” but as it turns out, boss levels do not count for this. I could maybe understand if the achievement had simply said “finish 5 levels without dying,” but the use of the word ANY is incredibly misleading for an achievement where it cannot actually be any arbitrary five levels. Other achievements have similar problems.Overall, while Ghostrunner 2 delivers some of the same thrill as its predecessor, this sequel ends up shooting itself in the foot as a result of its poorly-intentioned level design and cramming in of far too many shallow new features. It’s a shame to say this, but if you loved the original game, don’t come into this one with high hopes—it butchers a lot of what made the first one so good.

_childDocuments_.review: Meh, Ghostrunner 2 disappointed me. It bored me and was weak on gameplay. I thought about giving this a thumbs down, but it does all the basics of a mainstream casual game right. It's not outstanding in any way but casually enjoyable. The graphics are awesome, the bike ride is a cool new addition (but super basic) and the dark synthwave soundtrack is heating up the action really good. The gameplay though is lacking in my opinion. You've got a melee sword attack only, so you first need to get near the enemies by using your parkour movement. The movement options need to be used in the same patterns repeatedly and don't offer enough to make moving varied. So you avoid getting hit by their projectiles while running towards the enemies and then slice one or several up with a single sword swing. Pretty boring. Most of the times you don't even need to get there, because when you parry an enemy's projectile it flies back to the sender and eliminates your gameplay goal before you started the fun part. Talking about parrying: when standing still the projectiles' distance can badly be seen, because the first person camera is directly in line with the trajectory, no angle between to see a shot coming. There are a lot of projectiles and attacks coming in and sometimes I didn't know what hit me. Sadly there is no kill-cam-like feature to know what happened.Level design doesn't even care to look like a real world, but puts floating wallrun panels and narrow corridors  everywhere and in a way so that you feel like in a devs level and not like in a cyberpunk world.The characters and their talk is so wannabe cool like what kids think is cool how to talk. It was rather awkward for me so I rolled my eyes quite a lot. Also there is unlogical talk like "Uhh I hate all those clans. Why are they pushing everyone down? I just want to survive. We will come through. Even if that means pushing everyone down..." where the character isn't aware that if you are the one pushing others down means you're in the exact same boat of the ones you're complaining about, but it's presented as the right path we're stepping on.Further cons:- Doesn't save key binding. You have to rebind the controls on every startup- Getting stuck in fences, ropes and terrain on foot or with the bike- More bugs like the boss stopped working all of a sudden, doesn't move and is invulnerable and have to restart- A challenge run repeatedly started with the bike turned in the wrong direction- Restarting from checkpoint didn't respawn me near the bike so I had to run a minute to get there- Can't put the Rooting chip upgrade into the motherboard when it's not the same category even though it enables every chip to be put whereever wanted. You first need to remove a column, put the Rooting chip first and then put the others in again which is the same layout as before but it needed to be put in this order.- Some "puzzles" require you as in the first Ghostrunner to go past the visible wanted item, drop down a random chasm and go a secret passage back to the item.- Weird attack hitboxes which hit you after the boss had already swung his sword when you're going in for the whiff punish.Didn't really convince me. Only recommended for casual playstyle. I rather recommend SPRAWL and Armless Samurai!

_childDocuments_.review: From the hub area to the more open and spread out arenas, I think they slowed the game down significantly as well as made it much easier. I'm disappointed because I absolutely adored the first game. In the first game, the combat felt more like a dance, while in this one, it feels more like a checklist. Rather than dodging and weaving my way through enemy attacks, this one - due to the openness of the area - feels like I'm just killing a guy, walking over to the next guy, killing him, rinse and repeat. Also, the new openness makes it easier to get lost, and the added hub area between missions slows down the pacing significantly. For a series built upon fast movement and quick thinking, they slowed it down to a crawl in this game.

_childDocuments_.review: 9/10 Very good game. Some of the best gameplay in a modern game. Movement feels incredible and the level design lets you use the full use of your mechanics and feels great while doing it. The boss fights are the only let down, they where never a strong suit in the first game and this game is no different. The ai and boss mechanics don't mesh well with the tools you're given and most bosses can be resolved by simply dashing at the boss and swiping mouse 1 over and over. Hardcore mode if a great addition to the game, being able to play a remix of the game with much more complicated platforming sections and much more difficult combat scenarios is like a love letter to fans who really enjoy the game. The best way to do a new game + for sure. The rougelike mode is fine but wears thin after the first few winning runs. Not a huge amount of run diversity and can be beaten by simply hitting every platforming node. But given this mode simply didn't exist in the first game and could have easily be packaged as a DLC nowadays the fact its there at all is only an addition to the game its just gravy.
_childDocuments_.name: Ghostrunner 2

_childDocuments_.review: The game takes the good things from the first game and brings a few new mechanics. However the Level design seems like to be worse than in the first game and it feels kind of slower at all.While you just have in the first game mostly people with who you talk about the Communicator and that was the story. Here you have a HQ where you come back after every mission where you can upgrade your skills and talk to old and new friends. Even though I appreciate the bigger Focus on Story and that you have after every mission some time to relax it kind of takes the speed away and the excitement.The fact that you got thrown in one level after another and had few till no time to chill was what made the game so cool. Don't get me wrong Ghostrunner 2 is really great but for example I played the first game 3 times. (The first two runs just for fun and the last one was a no hit run.) But Ghostrunner 2 feels like the games you play one time and then you are done with it and carry on to the next game.This what makes Ghostrunner so special seems to be missing here at least partly.Anyway this sounds much more negative than I meant to be. Like I said it is still a good game and a clear recommendation for those who loved the first game like me. For all the others they would be good with only the first game since it has a complete and satisfying ending.EDIT: The Levels with the motorbike are really cool though.
_childDocuments_.name: Ghostrunner 2

_childDocuments_.review: Very good, combat is way more enjoyable than the first game. Movement feels pretty good, especially the bike and other other movement option you unlock later in the game. The "open world" aspect of some of the biking section was interesting, but I am not sure how to feel about it just yet. The new upgrade system I feel was a good change of pace compared to the original, but I feel some abilities and ultimates greatly outshine the rest. The worst part about the game was having to return to the hub area and interact with the NPCs. It completely broke the flow of the game, and really dampened the ending of the game, since the final boss fight was followed by clunky dialogue with the other characters. Overall a very enjoyable experience, and I will be replaying it a few times to explore everything and get all the collectibles. 8/10

_childDocuments_.review: Just great.Its basically GR1 but more in every way. More skills, lvls, enemy's, challenges, mechanics, puzzles.They even kept DSJs, Grappling cancel and the original parry mechanic (+ added the new parry mechanic) and added a skip cut scene option. This makes transitioning from GR1 to GR2 very pleasant. Also they reworked the skill balance in a nice way and made different skills/mechanics synergies in interesting ways.The new puzzles are great and the parkour between fights is nice too. I kept my wording vague to not spoil some of the new features.I was really excited when i encountered some new mechanics so i don't want to spoil them.Its (almost) everything i hoped for in the sequel.

_childDocuments_.review: So far it's alright, the first one was really good and I played it first (and if you haven't played it yet go do so), but the level designs for this one are pretty good. I will say there are some issues with it though, such as some mechanics being over-explained. For instance, within just the first few levels I have already experienced TWO TUTORIALS on parrying (only one was necessary) and the second is only validated by a dodge roll tutorial. Other instances so far include: Knocking down signs with the grappling hook tutorial being explained for way longer than necessary, grappling onto stunned enemies, exploding barrels using shurikens, stunning power boxes using shurikens, and more that I probably do not remember.Game feels like it was designed for game journalists over all else, way too much hand-holding. In the other I could turn off all combat assists, never use the time slow, and play an actually difficult game where I needed reaction time and could theory-craft ideas on how to deal with specific rooms. Tons of bugs as well, I sniped some enemies from afar on one of the levels, and it tricked the game into thinking i was further into the level. A fun speedrun skip in concept but horrible game design in the eyes of anyone who wants to just kill a bunch of enemies they see.Will make full review later when I finish the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Ghostrunner 2 is sad to play through after GR 1.I'll start with my highlights of the game before getting into why the game is a sad sequel. Beginning with the visuals, same as GR1 they're beautiful, the designer NAILED the look of Dharma (minus bad textures) and the cybercity aesthetic. The first level is a visual treat and so much fun to replay through.The soundtrack too, incredible and also nails the vibe that they were going for. High energy, lots of synths and a tempo that makes you want to play through the game as fast as possible.However, the design feels way off in comparison to its predecessor and the jank is inexcusable, throughout my first playthrough I managed to get out of bounds 3 times and on repeat playthroughs that number just goes up. (Made even worse by the players need to go back for collectables and look around)  Collision is horrible throughout every level and getting inside bits of geometry is so easy it feels like the game wasn't playtested at all. Not to mention the horrible movement system and the way the game tries to take control away from you only to kill you by doing so, making for a frustrating experience. The amount of times I've climbed on a dead body is laughable because how does that happen? You can turn down the assistance in the options menu but there's no off setting, just low assistance. The story is okay, if not a bit hard to follow at first. Little bit forgettable if you ask me. The only really interesting parts were the sections with rahu but I won't spoil them here but they were my highlight of the game, he calls out a lot of stuff regarding morality and the origins of the GR's The mechanics that differ from GR 1 are fine on their own but they don't stop shoving new stuff in your face throughout the game. The last level includes new mechanics and it makes you feel like you've never actually learnt to play the game to begin improving. You're never testing your skills as much as you're just trying to understand what the ♥♥♥♥ the new thing they've given you is The bike was a nice idea, and it can be addicting when you get it right but also feels like it wasn't tested at all. You have 0 camera control while riding it and when moving at high speeds and riding on walls, that makes it impossible to react to obstacles. When you died in GR 1, it felt like you deserved it because you made a wrong move that you COULD see coming. GR 2 breaks this by becoming a throwing ♥♥♥♥ at the wall simulator until you remember whats coming up.The new abilities are okay, the shuriken and its upgrades make for a nice change of pace (when they work and don't switch up the mechanics seemingly at random) but they mostly feel bloated and tend to do the same thing that GR 1 abilities did.The game is also so unoptimised it made me laugh and it has nothing to do with hardware. The game runs at the exact same FPS with max settings to low settings and Im still struggling to figure out how because the game looks almost identical to GR 1 which runs perfectly fine. GR 2's difficulty doesn't really come from new exciting enemies with new ways to kill them, (while there are a few new ones that are fun like the whip dudes)  it comes from the sheer number of projectile enemies they throw at you at once which again forces you into this trial and error gameplay loop instead of improving your skill. You can remember the entire arena your fighting in and still die because the enemy halfway across the arena you ran past at the start is still trying to snipe you. Leading nicely into enemy AI, it's broken a lot of the time. Half the time an enemy will just stop, for no reason and then once you go to kill them the game will suddenly realise that its broken and the enemy will kill youIf you played GR 1, don't ruin your impression of the franchise with this one. The game needed way more time in the oven and it's honestly just upsetting to see this game release in the state that it's in.*side note, the GR1 re-cap is in the extras menu and there's no prompt to have said re-cap play before starting the game so anyone who plays GR 2 first or hasn't played GR 1 for a while will find it even harder to follow the story*

_childDocuments_.review: I bought and played the first game on that store that should't be named. So, I'm glad that I bought the sequel and the better game in Steam this time.While the first game seems like a good proof of concept, this sequel improved on the first one in so many ways that I could confidently say that if ever you only want to buy one of the two, buy this one instead.I think my only complaint is that at times it gets really really tough especially for me whose reaction time is diminishing with age. Almost all missions took me an hour and 100+ deaths to clear so I think the "6-8 hours to finish the campaign and 16 hours for completionist" is a complete lie in my experience.Anyways, if you're up for the challenge and have the patience to keep on dying and trying, I highly recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I am a huge fan of ghostrunners 1, I mean HUGE. Recommended it to all my friends had it as my desktop for ages. Then I seen that the 2nd one was coming out and it was great news, I thought to myself, "I mean, all they can do is make it better right? they have the formula down so I wonder what they will do differently?". Well they definitely did do some stuff differently. Parkour elementThe parkour on each story mission I've played so far is so painfully slow for what ghost RUNNERS should be. They have got to capitalise on the golden game mechanic that is dashing then jumping. It would make the parkour much more interactive and fast. I find myself having a slow walk in between some of the parkour elements, and sometimes when I hit a wall run even from a very fast momentum I will end up sort of dragging along the wall like a snail. There is a lack of the dopamine hits that GR 1 provided with its much more unique and planned out environment. They use the grapple as a heavy crutch during most of the sequences and I really don't feel like I have to think about what I'm doing or where I'm going. The parkour in the simulation is much better, way more challenging and thought provoking. It's a shame it's hidden in some weird mini-game. World-buildingThe environments are awesome, perfect mix between urban slum and neon district. The parkour is semi blended in well, as much as you could expect from a game centred around it. The characters introduced in this sequel are incredibly 2D. I never usually skip dialogue, even ones that I feel drag out, but with GR 2. I found myself skipping more that I would listen. Their designs (on direct 11) are painful to the eyes. Very little features and sometimes so incredibly bright and glossy I can only see their eyes. Even the main enemy and their motives aren't really fleshed out.CombatThe combat is alright. It requires you to note your surroundings, look for approaches and utilise mechanics. There is an good variety of enemy types that keep you on your toes, for about the first 3 missions. The shinobi is a great example. After I encountered him once, it became incredibly easy to just parry for an easy window of invincibility and a kill. One of the enemies abilities is just making an electric line on the floor, very boring and all he does. Sometimes they are located over holes so they will just sorta stare at you and perform their move with no success. The game will just spawn gun enemies near a wall run or many melee enemies on a flat plane. Very repetitive.Overall not utterly terrible but lacking in comparison to the first one. I don't mean this review out of spite, genuinely just what I found disappointing about the game and giving my piece on what would make a instant hit for any other games from this dev. I can tell that there is sparks of passion there but I feel as if it has faded from the burning blaze of it present in GR 1, feels a little like a cash grab, and the reason I bought this game for 9 pounds.

_childDocuments_.review: Look, if you want more Ghost-Runner slicing and dicing go for it, it's fun. But I don't want to recommend this because of a few things. Optimisation is lacking, there is stuttering in the game when doing certain actions and its really annoying considering I have a pretty beefy PC. THE HUB WORLD is just bad. like I appreciate the effort to expand the characters and the world but no one asked for it.   it slows down gameplay to a slog where you are forced to talk with NPC's when facial animation is pretty bad and the writing is even worse(not like cringe or anything, just bland and monotone. not all of them, i liked some characters) dialogue doesn't flow you can tell when a line starts and one ends and you have dialogue options for more exposition. Most likely just a skill issue but the movement is inconsistent and clunky. THE BIKE. I am mixed on this. It is fun but ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ is it buggy , you can get stuck with it which forces you to restart from a checkpoint which isn't the biggest deal. hit-box feels a little bigger than it actually is and the camera is fixed which means it does some dumb things sometimes.The final boss Overall I am a little disappointed . I liked the first game a lot and this sequel just feels rushed,  like it tried to be cool and hip like most popular AAA games with the hub world and characters.

_childDocuments_.review: Update: Fun enough you get used to these things. The game offers enough to ignore them. Still, would be nice to not have to deal with them. You get a motorcycle and can ride it vertically down the tower. You get a wingsuit and can skydive enemies. The level design is great and the boss designs are far better than the previous game. Worth.As for the controls, Gap Jammer being mapped to X took getting used to, but it is manageable. L3 to block, however, I'm sure was murdering my stick.Old: Fun but glitchy. I won't not recommend it, but this game needs serious bugfixes from vanishing enemies to incorrect player behaviors from ability interactions.For controllers, the control scheme is WAY too bloated. The previous installment had smooth controls for controller, but this game realistically needs 6 shoulder buttons rather than the 4 that are standard.Block comes with its own button and functionality, which contributes to this problem, and was completely unnecessary as it worked perfectly fine in the previous game mapped to the attack button, you just needed good timing.There's way more use of skills, like shuriken, in this one. This also contributes to the problem. It's not really viable to slap this onto a face button because the precision you need at the speed you need just isn't there if you're not aiming as you fire.This leaves, attack, gap jammer, jump, and dash for your shoulders--which is the GR1 BJ layout. I ended up mapping block to L3 which feels awful and gap jammer to X/square which doesn't feel right.

_childDocuments_.review: When i played ghostrunner, i cried tears of joy at a game that did not lack in visual aesthetic, interesting narrative, tight game play and mechanics, AND an all banger soundtrack. it was and is a beautiful and near perfect gem that will stand for an extremely long time. Ghostrunner 2 is the same, plus more. As a game with no scaleable difficulty, this translates for some to simply being harder. In some ways this may be true, but what good sequel hasnt added new mechanics and environments? These new mechanics and environments may present new challenges but they are not shortcomings of the game. That was to address one complaint i have seen that i found rather invalid. That said, there is an area of valid complaint. The NPCs are...pretty lifeless. Granted it is a rather extreme change of pace from the first game, having casual and candid conversations with ambient characters between levels, and it shows. The voice acting is still fine, cutscenes are orchestrated well, but alot of the dialog and smalltalk between jack and the other characters has alot of awkward pauses and lines delivered by swaying manequins. It is worth noting that these lacking points are the smallest and least notable part of the game and are most certainly not meant to be the focus but are simply meant to offer some more spoon fed background lore on the world and its workings. To me the effort and inclusion of an option to get these voiced lines giving me background is a nice inclusion that i can forgive the oblivion npc style of delivery.TLDR parkour cyborg ninja simulator with banger tracks nonstop

_childDocuments_.review: Transcend flesh, become speedThe game itself isn't that bad as it is good at what it was made for. Allowing the player to go to high speeds and cut enemies into meat loafs in a split second. But it feels like the 2nd game is not as fulfilling as the 1st one. The level designs are built so that it restrains the free movement of the player, which is what originally made the game so fun and special. I have a feeling that the levels are designed to just be harder without regarding the fun aspects.This in result restrains the player's ability to freely create their own route to beat a wave of enemies, as the level design almost requires the player to beat the enemies in a pre-determined way. On the other hand, the game does add some fun mechanics that weren't present in the 1st one, such as the new skill building system where you can try out various different builds.I'd recommend the game, only if you're a fan of the 1st game and really want more.

_childDocuments_.review: Ghost runner 2 is a good game that with a few things that I found annoying.Combat and is the same as the first and is very fun. There are skills or perks you can buy with points and make a build that fits your play style.Where I think the game falls short compared to it's first is level design. Where the first game focused on a more linear and close quarters style of combat that allowed you to run across walls more often the second game moves towards a more open battle arena with more grapple hook opportunities and jump fans which made me feel that I was in less control of my character.I did like these mechanics when traversing the map as it felt less like just holding W. The motorbike section of the game was also fun but suffers from QOL with the ability to free look. This is most obvious when riding up / down walls as you can't see what you're riding towards.This review sounds pretty negative, but if you've played the first game you know what to expect as it's more of the same which is is great. But the points made here are what made me enjoy the game less.Would recommend especially if you can get it on sale!

_childDocuments_.review: 7/10 Wish there was a mixed-review button. The game still is good, but it isn't SOLID great like the first game.The first Ghostrunner was 10/10, soundtrack hit, levels were short 10-20 minute bursts of high energy with a great soundtrack and a movement system that rewarded you for learning it. Not just for speeding through levels, but getting better at combat. The build system had a unique Tetris way of balancing it. Loved it, one of my few 100% games because it was enjoyable the entire way through.The second game moves away from a lot of that. Levels are lengthier, including an open-world one where you drive around in a generic, very buggy post-apocalyptic desert that lasts just about an hour (without getting lost, which was a common complaint). The build system is gone. Base movement speed is nerfed (there are upgrades for traversal now but they're fairly conditional). There's a hub world now, where you talk to a vast range of characters (with a short range in personalities) that you don't care about as you wait to get to the next level because there's too many to really flesh out, even the villains.The first game had a cast of three main characters, with one being absent for half of it, and they still managed to cultivate a somewhat compelling story in the background with the conversations they had and the levels you went through, with little fluff. The second game expands upon that, but it feels Ocean-wide, yet pond-deep. And yet ,you still feel like you're wasting your time listening to these characters talk. Too many characters to flesh out any of them, including the many villains. The Good Guys' range in personality is dark and broody Jack, the Tech girl who's overly fascinated with everything for the sake of exposition, and Zoey, who seems downgraded from the first game.Let alone bugs and performance issues: "Shader Compilation..."I'd still recommend, its got some great moments and is overall pretty fun. Its good, just not great.

_childDocuments_.review: Ghostrunner was very much a surprise hit for me and others. And I'm happy to say that Ghostrunner 2 is a worthy sequel. It's a breath of fresh air to finally get a game that is very much about the game and not so concerned about being a boring movie walking simulator that seems to be everywhere now. Not only that, but it's also nice to have a game that is finished??? No way! It's like, what should be the standard and it isn't! That being said, I've had one fatal crash and frames would dip below 20 frames but only during cutscenes was this issue prominent. Let it be known however that yes, this is just more Ghostrunner albeit fine-tuned with its combat and some new ways to play. It is still super fun. The biggest complaint I have with this game though is a new character named Kira. And no, it's not because she is a "black female character" although I see it as no coincidence she's there for those sweet ESG points. She's insufferable, incompetent, and down right annoying because of course she has that "MCU" effect and the annoying pop culture references with her. Wouldn't be a thing to complain about if she wasn't such an invasive presence and you always hear her dialogue especially during the outside missions. Remove Kira and this game would be a 10/10.

_childDocuments_.review: The first Ghostrunner is my favorite game of all time, so I've been patiently waiting for what feels like an eternity for Ghostrunner 2. After completing the campaign, I can say that they definitely improved on a LOT of the core mechanics. I will say what others have said before, that the motorbike is a good addition but sometimes the execution is not entirely up to par. (For me it was the lack of clarity on where to go and the camera movement being to slow for vertical movement)One thing I haven't seen anyone else mention is, WHERE IS NEW GAME+??? I was willing to accept the fact that GR2 is easier than GR1 when I was still expecting to finish the campaign and have a hard mode to go through. Now I'm feeling like 30 dollars was too steep a price. I got 9 hours of gameplay before I lost any reason to play any more (unless I want to go find every collectable, which is not my preferred tasks when theres baddies to kill).TL:DR Game needs new game+, without it the gameplay is way too short.

_childDocuments_.review: Side note after going back and playing 1:1 just does feel better. I like the things they've added here but the combat in 1 feels more focused and pure. I thought it was a lack of difficulty here, but it's not. This is often harder than 1 in certain spots. But 1 still just feels better... except boss fights. Those are hugely improved here.Original review:Right off the bat, the design decisions that they've made for this game give it that feel of a real sequel. Gameplay feels a little smoother than before. They've added a block mechanic, but you trade blocking for stamina... so it gives you something new that takes the same old resource, so it's not actually making anything easier while giving the player more options of approach. I like the addition of allies and actual speaking characters. And I _really_ like how the new boss fights aren't the perfecting of a repetitive gimmick but instead lean into the risk-reward trades that you'd make in regular combat.I've only beat the first level, but I definitely like what they've done here. I do get the frustration of players from the original that they've made it easier. I don't know if I think that's true yet, but if you just came off of the hardcore mode from the original, then of course it's easier. Hardcore mode was the hardest game I've ever played and beaten. The sequel shouldn't continue up-scaling the difficulty from there, it should only aim to approach and maybe surpass it at the very end of the game but also probably not until the sequel gets its own hardcore mode (it might have it already, I don't know).After completion:I definitely feel the same way... though I can definitely see the complaints about it feeling easier. The main campaign is far more accessible but the difficulty definitely exists in the side content. Can't wait for hardcore mode.

_childDocuments_.review: Pricey and disappointing.I'll start with the positives. The combat is good like before and it has kept it's difficulty (a little easier, 90% of the enemies you fight are ranged because melee combat is so easy) the techs such as the shuriken, ghost and the other one are pretty cool and let you fight in different ways which i like. And of course the graphics are very good (a little laggy at times).Now for the negatives. I'll start with the characters. Jack is an insufferable MC, shows no emotional care and has the "monotone badass cyber ninja" voice throughout the whole game. The other characters are so forgettable except for Kira and Zoe. I'm glad that they killed Connor in the beginning since all he did was make unfunny jerking off jokes and be a satirical ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Kira seemed to actually show interest in Jack throughout the whole 3 towers mission but Jack always shrugged her off which was so annoying, like let me get to know the MC better. Zoe is fine as a character since she was in the first game Jack was actually kinda warm to her. Bakunin was such a confusing character, like he just randomly showed up, Connor just trusts him out of nowhere and he does nothing until the city gets raided. The main bosses were pretty cool and Rahu had a good twist, though never really did anything with him. The boss fights were MOSTLY enjoyable, only issues I had were the two last bosses. 2nd game and they ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up the last boss again. It was just so boring, at least they tried. The skill tree also sucked, I never used it and had no desire to get like 90% of the tree since most of the skills had a side effect that wasn't worth. The bike was soooo sensitive, if i hit the smallest sign it would explode. The whole 3 tower mission was just so long for no reason, nothing to do between towers just ride and listen to Jack be an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ to Kira for 5 minutes until you reached the next tower, super boring.Wish there was a neutral button for reviews since some people might just care about the combat and not care about the story like I do but overall I can't recommend anyone to play this game, especially at that price. 40 dollars for a 6.5 hours snooze fest is not something I enjoy.

_childDocuments_.review: Ghostrunner 2 is essentially OG ghostrunner improved in every possible way. Cleaner presentation, better/clearer upgrade progression, improved abilities overall, slick motorcycle segments, more open exploration and puzzles, really just took the base mechanics of Ghostrunner and expanded upon them universally. The rogue like/lite (I never know which is which) mode that is included in this also adds a awesome level of replayability, without the same "trial and error" safety net that the main game has, which adds a nice extra level of tension/excitement. If riding a cyber motorcycle, gunning a dude down from it, hopping off to clear some lasers, slicing another guy in half mid flight, then grapple hooking back to your motorcycle to continue on seems even remotely interesting to you, you'll be right at home here.

_childDocuments_.review: Ghostrunner 2 handles some aspects of its predecessor better, and some worse. One thing I've noticed in GR2 that differs from GR1 is the way the movement and camera flow together. GR1 had more static, snappier movement, which created a better feeling of control over your character. GR2 does the opposite. The camera and movement are more fluid and shaky. The fluidity adds to the game in some ways, but can create some rather disorienting situations. GR2 really expands onto GR1's setting and story, and creates a better understanding of it. GR2's boss fights are absolutely outstanding though, compared to GR1. Some boss fights are more than just a "hit-dodge-hit" system, with some bosses having parkour sections and traversal sections in their levels. To conclude, I would give Ghostrunner 2 a 10/10, same as GR1. The graphics, gameplay, lore, and soundtrack all stand out when compared to other games, and helps create a more unique experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Ghostrunner was easily one of the most unique games I’d played in a while. You can find my jumbled thoughts on that one . In summary, it was a really fun, reasonably challenging time, albeit one with a few inconsistencies and odd decisions that prevented it from being a home run. The sky was the limit for the potential of its follow-up though, and I think they nearly fully realized it. Ghostrunner 2 is the prime example of how to do a sequel, expanding on everything great about the first game, fixing what didn’t work, whilst retaining its identity as a challenging one-hit one-kill experience that is unlike anything else.Taking place one year after the original, the Ghostrunner, now fully adopting the name ‘Jack’, is working with the rebel faction dubbed The Climbers to keep order within Dharma Tower. When a group of rogue Ghostrunners named the Asura arise and threaten the power balance against the Climbers’ favour, Jack journeys to eliminate these threats and return some semblance of peace to the remainder of humanity. The writing and plot are much improved from the original; while this post-apocalyptic world was always interesting, the monotone exposition delivered by characters I didn’t care for made me forget much about what was going on. Here though, its presentation is more interesting, largely due to engaging voice performances delivered by the whole cast. You also have more opportunities to learn about its world and characters via between-level hub sections, where you can converse with actual character models of the cast this time around as opposed to their disembodied voices. Nevertheless, the additional worldbuilding is largely optional and can be ignored if you want to get back into the action quicker.Ghostrunner’s unique gameplay is better than ever in this sequel. Levels are split into platforming segments and combat arenas, though your parkour skills will be paramount to finishing all of these without getting hit. The core gameplay loop of dodging enemies and grappling about the environment to close the gap, slice them down and repeat for the whole room is largely unchanged, but it is refined to have greater consistency and offer up more options to outsmart your enemies. While you could only parry bullets in the original, Ghostrunner 2 gives you a short block meter, offering an additional window to slice your attacker down. The abilities system has been reworked to provide you with three options you can consistently use, and one ultimate ability which should result in a few easy kills. The shuriken can insta-kill some enemies, but it can also be used to open up grapple points on the environment and certain foes. Shadow provides you with temporary invisibility, and Tempest acts as a small force push which can dispatch a group of foes if used carefully. As for the ultimate ability options, they all have their uses; Blink and Overlord are back to help you eliminate a few key targets, whilst new additions like Flux give you a beam to disintegrate a bunch of foes instantly, and my favourite, Motoric Overload, temporarily buffs mobility whilst also allowing you to survive a single hit. All of your abilities and movement options can be upgraded by slotting in modules, unlockable with a currency obtained by killing enemies. Easier parrying, longer dodges, more precise shurikens, and bonuses tied to your combo meter are just some of the options on offer here. There are enough viable choices to ensure that many unique builds are possible through this system, it’s just about finding what playstyle you want to lean into.In terms of difficulty, I’d say it’s about as challenging as the original. New enemies such as the Priest, which unleashes a gigantic wave attack, and a killer wheel enemy, which can close the gap on your position really fast, are great additions to the already diverse enemy roster and can easily shut you down. Put these enemies into some of the largest arenas in the series so far, and there are so many areas where you could be caught off guard and need to restart the sequence. For the bosses, while they are certainly more interactive than the ones in the first game, they are low points in the difficulty. Outside of this game’s parkour boss, they are really straightforward, and ultimately feel a bit underwhelming compared to the standard levels. The game’s strongest asset is easily its level design. While most levels in the first game felt similar in structure and visual identity, the levels here are incredibly distinct, consistently offering up new mechanics and locations to keep things fresh throughout the campaign. One standard level locks you into a large environment until you dispatch a certain number of foes, and another adopts a non-linear design to its objectives. Variation is further increased with the motorcycle levels, resulting in new level structures and traversal options, whilst also not overstaying its welcome to overshadow the core gameplay. My absolute favourite level is the second to last one, as it introduces a one-off mechanic which completely changes how you approach that environment. The unprecedented sense of euphoria this mechanic provided me with resulted in the very best sequence I've played this year.A further improvement comes in the form of the reworked Cybervoid sections, which killed the pacing of the original upon level replays. Ghostrunner 2 instead turns these sections into unique traversal puzzles, typically requiring you to hit a series of objects in a limited time window, and these are infinitely more fun to re-experience. My only criticism relates to the coherency of this campaign; some levels begin by teleporting you to the starting point with no animation to speak of, making it feel a bit more disjointed compared to the original. Separately, I’d like to quickly highlight the great soundtrack; each level has a unique theme, and outside of some of the motorbike levels where the soundscape is a lot more subdued, there is plenty of good material to be found here.Once you wrap up the campaign, Ghostrunner 2 also offers a roguelike mode, an addition that feels perfectly suited to this experience. You start with the bare minimum abilities, and work your way through four visually distinct, increasingly difficult stages, selecting between combat and parkour challenges whilst earning upgrades and lives along the way. I hope this mode receives further updates though, as there is not much reason to replay it outside of earning all four rewards, and some level layouts repeated more often than I expected. Overall, it took me 11 hours to roll credits on Ghostrunner 2, earning every collectable along the way. It then took me an additional 5 hours to clear the roguelike mode and unlock every achievement. This makes the sequel a longer game than the original on Day 1, making it easier to recommend even before content updates.I knew Ghostrunner 2 was going to be great, but I was honestly caught off guard by how much of an improvement it ended up being. Almost every issue I had about the original is ironed out, cementing this franchise as one of the pillars of its subgenre. Its gameplay is challenging but always satisfying, its world is more interesting both visually and narratively, and a few of its levels are easily some of the best content I’ve experienced all year. Ghostrunner 2 is an easy GOTY contender, and I cannot wait to see what One More Level has in store for the future.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who endured the first Ghostrunner, I had hoped the sequel would address its predecessor's shortcomings. Unfortunately, Ghostrunner 2 not only retains the original's flaws but manages to surpass them.The game is undeniably longer and introduces a slew of new mechanics. However, nearly every new feature feels imperfect and cumbersome. Checkpoints are frequently unfair and oddly placed, making progression more frustrating than challenging. The platforming is clunky, and the behavior of enemies often seems random, making strategic planning a near impossibility. The motorcycle sequences, meant to add variety, can occasionally be pleasant, but the controls are buggy and junky, leading to frequent frustration.Once again, I’m left with the impression that the game wasn’t properly tested. The sheer number of issues suggests a lack of thorough quality assurance, and I have little faith that the developers will address these problems in future patches.Overall, Ghostrunner 2 is a disappointing follow-up that fails to improve on the original and instead amplifies its flaws.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR:  Just play the first Ghostrunner!The good:Wingsuit is cool and the 2nd to last parkour tower level was actually fantastic.The bad:Fixes some of the issues of the first Ghostrunner ie: wallrun inconsistencies, in-game performance, in exchange for boring level design, repetitious encounters, and some awful enemy changes. Arena diversity was heinous, much of Ghostrunner 1s charm came from different enemy combos in different gameplay spaces. Rarely were you in a large, flat, multi-platform arena with hitscans and yet every encounter in Ghostrunner 2 is this exact setup! The story and dialog of the first game was lean but decent for the first two-thirds of the game before it became convoluted, I muted the dialog for Ghostrunner 2 because it was so intrusive and nonsensical. Props to the conversations between the Cybervoid AI and Jack though, they're at least slightly interesting. Onto the enemy changes: rifle and pistol enemies now look identical, they have different sound FX and projectile colors but this makes it difficult to order-of-operations who you need to kill first in a fight. Why did they change this from the first game?? New enemies are non-starters and don't meaningfully change the formula. Enemy variety and combinations are also down, most arenas are 2x pistols, 1x rifle, 3x melee, with a rare loader or laser enemy (useless) thrown in. Reduced movement speed of Jack and increased projectile speed of enemies means you spend most of your time abusing time-slow dashing to avoid projectiles in flat spaces. Spending two-thirds of the game in the brown and gray wasteland is exactly what I want in my cyberpunk sword game /sI'll be going through hardcore mode on this as well, but I'm concerned the aforementioned arena design is gonna make this a time-slow slog

_childDocuments_.review: Ghostrunner 2 feels weird. It's a bigger game in practically every way. Most levels are bigger, almost every level introduces some new enemy or mechanic, with some of them not appearing anywhere else, so gameplay is never stale, almost all old enemies make an appearance (the only one I can't remember coming back is the sniper) with new ones added in as well. Gameplay is as fun as its always been, with the new upgrade system being much easier to use and allowing you make Jack far stronger and faster than his GR1 iteration. And yet, despite all of that, I can't help but feel like the game is worse. I've encountered many more bugs than in the first game, it's shorter than the first one despite having bigger levels, one of which can last for nearly an hour on your first playthrough, game is also less challenging, which being one of the main selling points is certainly a questionable decision. Graphics don't feel like much of an improvement, mainly it's the character models that got the most touches, and yet the game runs worse than the original. I'm running the game on SSD and I often get stutters between combat arenas, though this seems to happen only in specific levels. The last 2 levels (not counting the very last boss one) also had some framerate issues which didn't feel justified at all.Bosses are also a mixed bag. On one hand, they're actual bosses now instead of puzzles. They have proper healthbars you can whittle down with your attacks or special abilities, and overall allow for a much more aggressive style of play. On the other hand, the first and last boss feel very similar to each other, with third boss being forgettable outside of his appearance. The only really interesting boss is the worm you fight on a bike, but that one has issues I'll explain when I get to the bike itself. Overall while bosses overall play like actual boss- now, I can't help but feel like the first game had more memorable fights even though it had less of them and they were glorified puzzles or rhythm game sections.Level design is also questionable. The first game is full of non-stop action, any time you're not fighting you're listening to the story dialogue or doing some light platforming puzzles. The second game did add many more platforming puzzles and platforming overall is a more important part of the game, with the player being forced to use their special abilities a few times instead of simply jumping around, however, there's also a lot of downtime. While levels are bigger on average, nearly half of your playtime on some of the levels will be spent simply traversing the environment or solving simple puzzles with no challenge or threat to you. Bike sections in particular suffer from this. I must say that Cybervoid is an improvement though. It flows much better and is much more varied than the cybervoid in the first game. Speaking of the bike. Its introduction is certainly impressive. You move fast, it handles very well and you can slash and fire on top of it. However, bike sections often don't communicate very well where you're supposed to go, so you might have to go  through a lot of trial and error just to memorize the correct route. Compounding the issue is the absolutely  FOV on the bike when moving upwards. Any time Jack is riding up, be it on a wall or inside the aforementioned worm boss, more than half of the screen is taken up by the bike itself. It can be hard or nearly impossible to see where you're actually going, so situations where the moment camera realigns itself you're suddenly staring at a wall or a moving obstacle are not rare at all. The game's description also boasts about "nonlinear levels with complex motorbike sections", but really, the only truly nonlinear level is the one where you're thrown in a big deserted city environment and have to go to 3 towers to activate them. Almost the entire time you're there the only threat is accidentally hitting a wall from going too fast. On my first run of this level it took me approximately 14 deaths to beat it, and that run took me nearly 40 minutes. Even if we cut out the time I spent looking for hidden collectables, which include upgrade points that you need to get new skills, I'm still confident that I wouldn't be lying if I said that half of that time, if not more, was spent on moving through empty, barren environments. That level is boring, tedious, and feels like it exists to justify the bike's existence and to boast that the game has "nonlinear levels".Platforming also feels strange. A lot of the time it felt like the game wanted me to use various techniques that aren't really taught by the game to progress, such as using the slowdown mid-air to strafe closer to my target or using dash-slide technique before jumping. Otherwise a lot of the time it felt like my character would fail to make it to the other platform or wall and would plummet to his death. Though maybe it's just me.The soundtrack is overall good, but not really much better or worse than the original.The game also introduced the "roguerunner" mode, a semi-roguelike where you go through 4 stages, each of which consists of different routes you can take, including nodes like parkour challenges, arenas, shops to get upgrades, etc. You have a limited number of lives, and if you run out of them, you lose the progress and start again with nothing carrying over. Levels aren't randomly generated, so after some time you will start seeing similar stages, but it's a fine distraction. I do hope they add the survival mode from the first game at some point (though I'd prefer it not to be part of the season pass).The story is alright, I'm not a fan of the new supporting character you spend most of the game with, and there are some weird story points that I'm unsure about , but overall story is fine for pushing the player forward. I did like it more in the first game, but neither of them is really about the story, it's just there to keep the player going.Overall I certainly do like Ghostrunner 2, it's a fun game that I will continue playing for a while trying to get better results in missions, however, it didn't leave as much of an impression on me as the first game did, and I feel like developers tried too hard to make their next game "bigger and better" and didn't quite stick the landing.

_childDocuments_.review: In general it's not a bad game but I stand on mixed feelings for this one, when it's more true to the original it's great, when it tries to be bigger and better it results in a worse experience.The main problems I have with this game are the open areas , often arenas feel too big with enemies too far from each other to actually worry about (in the first game there were more tight spaces where you had to be either more creative with Jack's skills or with you skills as a player), the open spaces also feel a lot easier to deal with because of the block button which feels a bit too powerful.My main complaints are in the level design but there are other small issues like the hub that feels a bit dead without a background music or some kind of environmental effect (apart from the radio) and talking to the npcs kinda slows down a lot the pace of the game, other than this I don't really like the ultimate skills especially the blink which feels clunky to control while the others are not really that useful, also another negative is the bike that often gets stuck  (otherwise I did really enjoy the bike).Enough with the negatives tho, let's list some great things starting with the cybervoid levels, they feel a lot better to navigate and show a general improvement in level design, the music is great (especially the first time you get in the bike) and the voice acting is spot on like the prior game, I also liked the kind of aesthetic change when  and to end this section: when the game tries to have the tight level design, like the original, it's really great.Overall is not a bad game but I expected something different, I feel like Project Hel did a better job at following the original game's vibe, speed and level design quality but this is more ghostrunner and I like it.

_childDocuments_.review: I am incredibly sad to write this review. 2 things to say before the review: 1, I haven't finished the game yet (I absolutely plan to) 2, Ghostrunner 1 is my favorite game of all time.TL;DR: Amazing music and visuals, more story than GR1, Rougerunner mode is awesome. Movement feels clunky (when compared to GR1), bad platforming sections, and gameplay feels slow at times.Some of the positives of GR2 is that the story is somewhat interesting and is much more engaging, I have enjoyed Rougerunner alot so far, as it feels much faster paced than the main game. I played the demo before pre-ordering the brutal edition and I was SO excited for GR2 as the demo felt good, like the original and fast. But then on day 1 of being able to play it I boot up the game it it just fell short. Even of the demo. It felt clunky and unpolished, the levels where not good and felt like they had no direction to them, and most of all, the platforming sections where disappointing. But even these super fun things dont make up for the downsides that are the clunky movement, bad level design, and bad platforming sections. Overall, I don't regret paying $70 for this game as the studio more than deserves it as GR1 is an absolute masterpiece and they have put so much effort into GR2.
