_childDocuments_.review: If it weren't for the fact that the first game's story was integral to most of the circumstances and motivations of everything that goes on here, then I'd say you could just disregard the first game entirely and just play this, because this is better than the original in every way and the writing and worldbuilding are still as token and bland as ever. I do not understand how you have an awesome cyborg ninja character classified as a Ghostrunner and decide to name him "Jack" of all things.But you're not here for the story.  no one is here for the story. If there's one thing I respect about the  games, it's that they did what I wish more games did at the development stage and took a style of play and built an entire game around it.  is *the* cyborg ninja game.  is the game that Genji Shimada looks at and feels inadequate over. Then you have , which took everything that was good about the first game and made it better while still keeping all its flaws, including the crappy boss fights that somehow only get worse after the mediocre first one and the fact that first-person melee combat and parkour just doesn't bloody work because you can't see yourself in relation to the environment.There are a couple other issues, too; as well as the motorcycle controls, it's not fun when you keep bumping into things and coming to a complete stop, necessitating you slowly reversing out and changing direction. Would be nice if the motorcycle reversed on its own. I also encountered a terrible issue where my bike got caught in the environment and there was no way for me to free it so I had to walk to finish the level. Also, devs, I get that you want us to care about the characters, and I admire that; the games could definitely use stronger context. But making us walk slowly around a small hub area and talk to everyone one by one is not how you fix that; you need better writing. And why do we even have a sprint mode in the hub area? We don't even have a sprint in the actual gameplay. I feel like you're trying to replicate something that was successful without understanding why it was successful. Also also... Also also also, what happened to the -style upgrade system? That was so fun. These chips are nothing by comparison. I miss that upgrade system so much.I recommend  for the gameplay; it is very fun and I enjoy it a lot, flaws notwithstanding. The motorcycle levels are amazing; the penultimate level introduces a *really* fun mechanic that, while it's been done for about twelve years now, is still just as good as it was then; and the usual slicing and dicing is better than ever. The roguelike mode has also been expounded on with many more upgrades and cool features. Just be mindful that 's always had some fundamental issues that don't go away with time.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't like comparing games so I'll try to keep ghostrunner out of the question, but just to say it ghostrunner is better than it's sequel. Now that I've said that lemme just say that I recommend this game not because I enjoyed it but because I know that it can be enjoyable with certain specifications. This game tried it's hardest to be different and unique from it's original form but completely missed it's mark. The gameplay is nearly the same with some exceptions coming to the end. speaking of the end, some people didn't enjoy the end, stating it was boring, but the end to me personally was actually enjoyable This was because throughout almost all of the beginning it was the same reused mechanics of the first game, but near the end they introduced an open world, a dope motorcycle, and a surprisingly very functional wingsuit. the open world was admittedly empty, but then again it wasn't very big so it didn't take long to get to the action. The game was short as you can see it did only take me 9 hours to complete the game and a lot shorter for most but I bought it on sale so rating for the price I got it at, which was $12.50 with the deluxe edition, it was worth it's price. Here is where we get to the specifications. The game has good graphics IF, and I mean a STRONG IF, you can run them. I don't have a great computer, but don't have a terrible one at that, and I cannot stress enough how frustrating it was to play on 30 fps in some locations and then 100 fps in another. I checked task manager on multiple occasions and none of my hardware was overloading, or even close of doing so at that, and I would look back at the game and I would be watching a powerpoint presentation. On the occasions it did work the game was enjoyable in fact I would say it's enough to want to play it again, but just the thought of having to go through 30 fps in those areas again burdens me. Another topic I wanna touch is on whether the game has self optimization or not because when I started, everything had choppy animation and bad lighting. In fact the game had turned off shadow quality completely making characters who are next to light very reflective because there is no shadow to be casted. To have a visual of what that looks like one of the characters right next to a light source became the embodiment of light right in front me. I did end up fixing this by going into the settings and changing them to make the game look better but if it self optimization that's ok but if this is their choice that definitely is messed up.Surprisingly the game only crashed once, don't know what caused it, so it could be my fault but there's no telling. Other than that though I didn't run into any fundamental issues which surprised me because I was fully expecting some to be honest.To sum it up, it is a good game looking at it as it is. The game mechanics were similar to the first but the first was an enjoyable game, so them just adding on to that, is disappointing, but I just can't say it's not fun. The graphics are good, but the optimization isn't, so having a high end computer would make your experience more enjoyable but it sucks to say that you're outa luck if you don't. I don't really like 1/10 ratings but just for people who do

_childDocuments_.review: A Brief Review of Ghostrunner 2, Released on October 26, 2023.Strengths:1. Enhanced Gameplay: Ghostrunner 2 maintains its tradition of being fast, precise, and deadly, delivering an intense experience. The addition of new elements to the arsenal, such as the shuriken for environmental interactions, expands strategic options, making combat more dynamic and challenging.2. Improved Exploration: The game extends exploration beyond the Dharma Tower, offering a more diverse environment. Levels featuring the futuristic motorcycle introduce a welcomed variety, providing relief after moments of tension and difficulty.3. Improved Accessibility: Ghostrunner 2 is less punitive, offering a larger window for decision-making. This makes the game more accessible, allowing a broader range of players to enjoy the adrenaline and speed of the title. Enhanced subtitles also contribute to a more inclusive experience.4. Variety of Enemies and Abilities: The game presents an expanded range of enemies, each with unique reactions. New unlockable abilities add dynamism to the gameplay, encouraging strategic and stylish approaches to defeating adversaries.Weaknesses:1. Shallow Story: The narrative remains a weak point, with the plot still lacking depth and explanations. The potential of a post-apocalyptic cyberpunk universe remains underutilized, with the story taking a backseat compared to the quality of the gameplay.2. Repetitiveness in Motorcycle Sections: While motorcycle sections provide relief, the repetitiveness in these segments may diminish the impact of the frenetic action. Variation in the mechanics of these phases could have been more extensively explored.3. Larger Action Window may Challenge Veterans: Expanding the action window may make the game more accessible, but some series veterans may feel that the reduced challenge detracts from the experience, removing some of the characteristic tension of the franchise.In summary, Ghostrunner 2 continues to offer an exhilarating experience, with notable improvements in gameplay, exploration, and accessibility. While the narrative remains a weak point, the diversity of enemies and enhancements to mechanics compensate, making the game an appealing choice for lovers of fast-paced and strategic action.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who adored the first game (and it's OST), I wanted to pick this game up to try. There will be a lot of comparisons to the first game in this review.I waited for a bit, as I heard that the performance was really bad (comparative to running the original Ghost Runner w/ Ray Tracing levels of bad). ♥ Overall, I enjoyed the game, and it was certainly longer than the first one. It took me 8 ish hours to complete the story while partially looking for the collectables (part of that was due to performance issues, which is covered later on). ♥ I quite enjoyed the story actually, It's a direct sequel to the original Ghost Runner.♥ The soundtrack. If you liked the first game's OST, I'm confident you'll fall in love w/ this game's OST just as much. It's fantastic. Most of the songs are done by We Are Magonia, with some appearances from Gost, Dan Terminus, Arkadiusz Reikowski, and Danial Deluxe (The OG Ghost Runners composer/writer). Songs are uploaded on Spotify by 505 Games themselves, if you wanted to take a listen there.♥ Controls wise, it's slightly more clunky than the first game in my opinion, but generally the mechanics are on par with the last game. Later on in the game a mechanic completely breaks ledge boosts though, so keep that in mind if you intend to speed run/like that movement tech.I'm gonna start this off w/ the performance. It's ATROCIOUS. There is constant VRAM and DRAM memory leaks, meaning restarting the game every now and then will drastically improve your performance (in my experience). ♥ I originally downloaded this onto my 1TB HDD (although to One More Level's credit, they did recommend that an SSD is to be used), and the stuttering made the game entirely unplayable. I'd be going from 140+ FPS to 10 FPS every half second. ♥ Moving the game to my NVMe M.2 SSD resolved only some of the stuttering, and improved my overall average FPS to around 180 FPS ish inside the Dharma Tower. ♥ As I progressed through the game, the performance got astronomically worse. It was so bad to the point where one of the last few boss areas dropped my overall average FPS to 20... I had to drop my render resolution to 25% in order to achieve 60 FPS in this area.♥ The stuttering is constant, and random. To my knowledge there is no fix for it (at least I'm aware of). DX11 and DX12 mode both stutter just as bad in my testing, and it also really, really hampers the game. I hear that the console versions are also EXTREMELY poor in performance too, so I don't think it's just an issue w/ the PC version.These are my personal opinions, so keep that in mind*♥ Story -> 10/10I really enjoyed the story. Jack has a LOT more voice lines, is more vocal, and seems to be significantly more free thinking. His interactions w/ the climbers are also a lot more personal, and more human rather than his original self in the start of the original Ghost Runner. ♥ Performance -> 1/10 When the game isn't stuttering it runs actually reasonably well. But w/ significantly lower frame rates than the original game. Highly, highly recommend to install this on an SSD if you have one. Otherwise it'll likely be unplayable. ().Starting the game off, I averaged roughly 140-180 FPS @ 1080p max settings w/ my setup. However, after the first 2 levels that quickly tanked to low 90's. So I tweaked some settings, and that only brought it to 100-110 or so. Halfway through the game I was struggling to maintain 60 FPS min settings, and towards the last quarter of the game I barely maintained 30-40 FPS consistently.♥ Mechanics -> 7/10 Some of the controls were moved around to make room for new mechanics (), and dashing in this game feels a lot more janky than in the original. DSJs and Ledge boosts are extremely inconsistent from a mechanical standpoint. Fine for normal gameplay, but for someone looking for an OG Ghost Runner experience w/ movement tech, it's a bit lacking.♥ Speed-running? -> I'm not sure what to rate this tbh. A lot of the OG's mechanics were tweaked or changed partially from what I can tell (), I would love to give this game an 8.5/10 or higher, as at the core of it all it's good. But the performance issues actually made it nearly unplayable. I had to take frequent breaks due to the constant stuttering causing motion sickness/rage. Also the stutters would often lead me to die right before a checkpoint, so I'd have to do ALL of a room again in order to progress.

_childDocuments_.review: The game's good, and it improves on the first game in certain areas like level design (in its linear areas) and enemy variety (even if a good number of the new enemies are absolutely not fun). But it has a number of issues that show that the devs (or whoever was resposible for these decisions) didn't fully undesrtand what made the first game great.The first game was a tight experience focused on its movement system. The second game tries to do too many things, and ends up feeling messy in certain areas. From the unnecessary HUB and the annoying NPCs to the open area levels, it just feels like the devs thought that the first game wasn't enough. Instead of trying to build on the great systems that they already had, they decided to build around it. As an example, there's a rogue-like mode that's fun the first time you go through it, but it quickly becomes stale. They could have easily removed that mode from the game and nothing would have changed. And, imo, if something doesn't make the game better, then it should not be in the game at all.It's also sad to see that, just like in the first game, the levels were designed exclusively for newer players, and apparently tried to discourage the use of any movement tech that goes beyond the most basic movement (by placing rubble in annoying places or with the introduction of certain level design elements that make the game feel like an autoscroller, like the rails or the moving platforms later on). Now, I'm not saying that the game should be designed around speedrunners, but rather that they should have embraced at least some basic movement tech and made it a core part of the game, as that movement tech makes the game way more fun to play and the higher skill ceiling makes the game a lot more replayable. Maybe they could have taught the player how to slide-dash-jump at some point and start designing later levels around it, or at least build some alternative harder parts to rewards layers that learn it. Celeste did this very same thing, teaching players how to hyper dash and designing optional levels around that mechanic, as well as other movement tech for that game. Ghostrunner has nothing like that, and so it always feels like playing a tutorial of a game that you've already completed. Solving a puzzle to unlock a grapple point to access a platform that you could have easily reached before just by climbing a wall or ledge-boosting is constant through the whole game. But that's only an issue if you already learnt movement tech in the previous game or if you wanted more depth out of its movement system.I mentioned rubble before. Rubble and barrels and other random objects were already an issue in the first game, but it's worse here. It's just really annoying to try to move around a level quickly to kill an enemy at the other side just for the player character to stop on his tracks because a random object was in the way and the character decided to cault over it, which kills all of your momentum. These kind of annoying obstacles are everywhere and they are just frustrating. I don't see any point to them. Even in combat, you don't ever need cover from enemies since you can dodge everything by just moving. So these obstacles will just get you killed whenever you try to dodge a bullet and you end up not moving at all because there was a barely visible barrel on the ground next to you. I get it that the game would look empty otherwise, but I'd rather compromise visuals than gameplay fluidity in a game centered around quick movement. If they wanted to add so many enviromental objects, then they should just be destructible and not affect movement at all, tho I doubt that would be a good idea, game performance-wise.Overwall, it's still a good game, and I'd argue that at it's best it's better than the first one. But it spends too much time in its more mediocre parts. Some remarkable positives to the game are its visual design and setpieces, as well as the bosses which are a massive improvement for the most part. And the movement is still really fun, even if it's slower. Bike has a few really cool sections. Also, one of my favorite new ideas is the inclusion of challenges in the middle of the levels (but these challenges just reinforced my previous point about the game being designed ignoring movement tech. All of the time based challenged are just way too easy and the later ones are just annoying. An optional challenge should be the place to raise the difficulty and require more knowledge about the game's movement system, but alas, you can just run normally through the course and get the gold time reward). It's just frustrating to think that a game could be so much better if it had less stuff. It's a 7/10 for me, but it could have been a strong 9/10

_childDocuments_.review: Coming from an addict of the first game, the sequel is a massive disappointment. Everything feels like a downgrade from the first game. Combat and abilities: Clunkier. The basic loop is fine, but everything else feels worse. Blink has been completely ruined, now you have to manually mark targets before activating it (which often gets you killed because it does not stop time), shinobi's atttacks land before the attack animation finishes, and the deflect animation stops the flow of combat for the sake of a  mildly cool execution. Movement and parkour: Movement is largely unchanged, which is fine, but for some reason the rails that you slide on pull you in like a black hole whenever you get near them, often leading to death. The wingsuit and motorcycle are neat gimmicks in normal mode, but their terrible controls and handling become obvious in hardcore where pinpoint precision is required. The motorcycle especially has inaccurate hitboxes (you will often barely miss an obstacle, only for it to kill you anyway), a camera angle that makes seeing where you're going an issue sometimes, and a unique affinity for getting stuck absolutely everywhere, forcing a restart. Everything else: They got rid of the unique Tetris-like upgrade system from the first game in favor of a more typical tree in which you place upgrade nodes. The problem is that several upgrades and perks make certain sections of the game literally impossible, leading one to wonder why they were ever added in the first place. The mid-section of the game is an absolute slog, where the game turns into a pseudo-open world that doesn't service the gameplay nearly as well as the indoor sections. The boss fights are fun, except for the Dismantler, who has a move that kills you the second he starts his animation and is also not telegraphed, so if you're right up on him when he uses it (which you probably will be), there is absolutely no way to prevent a death. There are still annoying puzzle sections that kill the pacing, but they are usually paired with some platforming that makes them not quite as obnoxious.Hardcore mode is also really lazy and feels like the devs didn't even play test it with how most encounters are either trivialized by cheese or made almost impossible due to clunky controls and hitboxes.Idk man it's fine but really disappointing after the first game. 6/10

_childDocuments_.review: The game is good, dont get me wrong, but there are a lot of flaws that i just cannot ignore. The bike was cool at first but all it really serves after leaving the tower is just to get you from point a to point b without much cool stuff in between. Cybervoid that was previously a fun puzzle parkour in Ghostrunner is now just a glorified retexture of the normal world, just without enemies. The levels feel more repetetive with seemingly the same 3/4 mission types just repeting over and over, The Winds of the Desolate level is the worst of these with you getting on the bike, getting off to open a gate and doing it like 4 times. The upgrade system from the original Ghostrunner was very fun and intrigueging in my opinion although i understand it has its problems, what i dont understand is that they replaced it with a form of collectibles, so now if your struggling and want to get more upgrades, you need to go on a wild goose chase with a guide to find them all and god forbid you accedentally go to far, you will have to restart the WHOLE LEVEL just to get the one missing collectible you need. Overall i think that the game would have been better if it was shorter and tried to stay more in theme with some of the unique quirks of the original Ghostrunner

_childDocuments_.review: I really liked this game. Compared to the first game, the combat and abilities feel more refined and overall much more balanced, the story is a lot more fleshed out here, although it feels slightly cut short, almost like there were supposed to be 2-3 more levels that were cut late in development. The bike is absolutely amazing. If you're expecting another game exactly like the first one, you will be disappointed, but in general I think this game is better than the original in almost every way.

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely enjoyed Ghostrunner 2.  For the most part the game ran very smoothly and reignited the same adrenaline fueled joy that the first one gave me.  There were a couple bugs here and there but nothing game breaking.  It did seem to be a fair bit easier than the first Ghostrunner but perhaps, had I not played the first iteration, it may not have seemed as easy?  The cybervoid sections weren't anywhere near as tedious this time around and that was definitely a welcomed change.  While I did enjoy the soundtrack, I still think the first one was definitely better.  I'm also a little bummed that there isn't a "hard core" mode just yet but hopefully that will change later on.

_childDocuments_.review: THE GAME IS GOOD. I really 'd like to give this game a thumbs up, cause it is NOT a bad game at all. But compared to the first one - which I adore to this day - its such a huge downgrade, so I have to give it the red thumb. How u fight the enemies doesn't have the flow as the first one had. They are placed so far away from each other, u'r not getting into any flow. The only time I had this awesome feeling was during an optional enemy challenge, where u had those flying drones and a specific way to fight the enemies and it was awesome. But its so rare. Overall the levels are way too flashed out here. And im not even outside the tower rn.And while the story in the first game wasn't anything special, at least it wasn't annoying. Now the story IS annoying. All the segments where u have to talk with ur "crew" are blatantly boring and the dialogues are frankly trash (but not in a good way). Additionally there are more bugs and level loading stutters in this game, raytracing or nvidia reflex don't even work in the first place and the game didn't get a single fix to this day.The gameplay itself and most of the platforming passages are still good, thats why I still like and play the game. And while I still have to get to the part with the motorbike in this playthrough, it felt awesome in the demo. The bike is the only addition I think is really cool.

_childDocuments_.review: A great (but not flawless) sequel to the fast paced, blood pumping game play of the first installment. I can't help but feel OML could have gone a /little/ further with the game, as it was quite short. I finished the game in under 10 hours, with having spent a lot of time chasing down collectibles. Hopefully the developer will have put a fairly priced DLC out for the game by the end of the year. Otherwise, this is a visually stunning game, well optimized (steady 1440/60fps, high settings, on a 2060 max Q!) with a decent story. It certainly made me feel like a Ghostrunner again. Enjoy!

_childDocuments_.review: [~] Ghostrunner 1 is the better entry of the two.[+] Gameplay is tight as it was in the first game[+] New gameplay and upgrade mechanics are a welcome addition[+] Soundtrack does well at setting the mood[-] Level design can be hit or miss, mostly miss outside Dharma tower[-] Story is largely uninterestingOverall: Decent game on its own, but not a good Ghostunner sequel. Worth playing if you're really itching for more after Ghostrunner 1.----- The Rant'y Portion Below -----Ghostrunner 2 is a conflicting game to review. Overall, I would describe the game as "okay", but dive into the details, and it becomes a balancing act of a lot of good versus a lot of bad for a sequel that didn't fully live up to the expectations of Ghostrunners 1.One area this game did very well in was its gameplay mechanics. To sum it up nice and quick:The level design is a mixed bag. Many of the opening segments were fantastic and had a good mix of parkour and combat to keep things fresh and satisfying to play. Other segments felt a drawn out where it was just some light traversal put to dialogue. Then some segments are just outside Dharma tower.This part of the game was by far its weakest portion and felt like a major departure from the level design that made Ghostrunner good. The vivid cyberpunk colour palette of Dharma tower was traded out for a drab wasteland colour palette, which made all these levels feel the same. While not initially bad, this portion of the game carried on for far too long and I found it to have the least interesting combat and parkour. Thankfully, the end sequence for this chapter redeemded itself a little with a killer bike obstacle course.That said, where the game was its strongest was when it stuck to its roots in Dharma tower. When the game did that, it meshed very well. Using the environment to efficiently parkour around, slash enemies, and dodge attacks to clear through rooms is where this game thrives. They are the kind of levels you want to go back to and replay to see if you can beat your time or reduce your death count. The majority of levels outside of Dharma tower did not offer that feeling, which made those levels feel a little alienating.Part of what made Ghostrunner 1 mesh so well was the synthwave soundtrack it was all set to. Ghostrunner 2 continues that trend and does a good job at setting the vibe in its levels. Nothing beats entering a room full of enemies just as the beat drops to get you in the zone.Ghostrunner 2 puts a much greater emphasis on story than its predacessor. While not necessarily a bad thing, its execution unfortunately fumbles pretty quickly. World building is rushed and what is there is monologued to you from a character. Despite big story moments between running missions and returning to the hub, there is not a very strong sense of impact or urgency. You do a mission, get some story, return to the hub (sometimes) and get some more 1-1 dialogue with characters then repeat.The characters themselves pull from standard architypes, which did not make hearing their backstory particularly rivotting. The one exception I found to that was Kira -- her personality, backstory, and voice actor's delivery easily made her the most interesting character of the crew.The game also tries to flesh out Jack's character, which I thought was just okay -- if not contrived. I can tell they were going for a "machine tries to become human" angle, but unfortunately most dialogue sequences where Jack shows his human side felt stiff and awkward.If I could give this game a neutral rating, I would. When this game hits the right notes, it can be a superior experience to the original game. However, a significant portion of the game strays away from a proven good forumla, which ultimately hampers the overall experience -- especially when compared to the original. I applaud the game for trying new things, but I think it is best to remember what got people hooked in the first place: a cyberpunk-themed fast paced hack and slash parkour game set to synthwave. Is this game worth playing? Yes, but only if you've played Ghostrunners 1 and are itching for more to play.

_childDocuments_.review: Ghostrunner 2 is a fantastic sequel to the original Ghostrunner that builds upon and improves upon the original's blueprint. It's unfortunately plagued by an uninteresting first act that uses a somewhat clunky hub word and empty feeling open level locations, but once you're past the first 2 hours or so, the game gets really amazing. I won't spoil why it gets so much better, but trust, me, stick this one out for a while. The combat is improved and far less frustrating than the first game, parkour feels smooth yet challenging, the level design is more open, there's more secrets to find, and the game overall just feels like an improvement from the already great first game. The scale is far larger too, and my biggest complaint with the first game, its cyberspace segments and bossfights, are much better in this game. If you can stick through the game's pretty short first act, there's a fantastic game waiting for you that I highly recommend playing after the first game.

_childDocuments_.review: Play Ghostrunner 1Edit 1: You should DEFINTELY play Ghostrunner 1 over the 2, it has a simpler story and is way more polished than the second installment in every single detail.Let's start with the graphics, in a lot of occasions when changing zone making the old one deload and load the new one you will experience a serious framerate issue, even if you cap the graphic settings at low, 60 fps and V sync on there are certain point where the game will just reach 2 fps. The gameplay is fine, I still liked more the version of the first game. one thing that I didn't like at all where the bosses. without going into spoilers, in the first game you had to do one hit with the sword to remove a whole bar, making it more of a precision game; in the second one you have to keep hitting the bosses with your sword, like its Devil may Cry. This would be a fine change if the whole game was not based around a "you are oneshot but you will also oneshot everyone". Basically the bosses in Ghostrunner 1 seems like they had higher stakes than the 2nd.The hub, where do I even start, you get meaningless dialogues with NPCs which don't even have their face properly animated. also after you end every level you are teleported inside of it instead of continuing the previous level where you left off. In Ghostrunner 1 you had a feeling of continuity even if basic: you end the level in an elevator, you start the level in an elevator, its basic but also effective. in Ghostrunner 2 you are just teleported at the start of the level, even if by chance you end the level on an elevator, that's because of, you guessed it, THE HUB.The writing, the story of the first one ended . in the second game you don't get an explanation as to why you are alive, you just are there. now its time for the elephant in the room, this game seems to be written by millenials. their sense of humor is plastered everywhere making you cringe and (almost) work for the enemy. also whoever created KIRA is the worst writer i have ever seen. She is a character which just doesn't know when to shut the ♥♥♥♥ up, she always has a cringe joke and she has to comment on every single thing that happen. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ whoever can created this NPC is a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ monster.The bike, which was also one of the most hyped new feature, is actually pretty cool. The problem is its tied to stupid open world levels which are just awful.TL;DRPlay the first game if you are new to the series, it will be hard because the game actually require skills, but it will be more satisfying to complete. the second game is fine in itself, where it suffer the most is that this sequel is not at the level of the first game, making it look like a cheap cashgrab. If you really want to play this game take it when its on a deep discount.

_childDocuments_.review: I wish this was as simple as "if you like Ghostrunner, buy Ghostrunner 2" because this game is difficult to talk about.  It has improved combat and enemy variety, but a confusing-ass story with inconsistent level design and diabolic pacing at times.  When this game is acting as a follow up to the first game, it absolutely sings providing some incredible highs.  When it's trying to be a semi open-world game like seemingly all action-adventure games nowadays, it falls flat on its face.  Do I recommend this?  Ehhh, I don't know.  Do I enjoy this game?  For the most of it, hell yes.  Also for the love of god, please get shader compilation under control for the third installment, both this game and Ghostrunner stutter horribly thanks to shaders not being precompiled.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm leaving this as a Negative review in hopes that more feedback on the game will help the developers in the future.There is the core of what could be good game mechanics and lore in Ghostrunner, and in the hands of either a more experienced developer/creative team or if the current team had more skills, this could be a worthwhile double A title/franchise.Sadly, the game is not there yet. The mechanics need more refining.1) More responsive controls. 2) Better telegraphic of hazards when platforming.3) A better FOV and camera system for multilevel threat assessment.4) More variety in combat than the bare system that is currently in the franchise.5) A bigger budget for the story that barely had any cinematography or worthwhile world building.P.S. The bike section of the game dragged on longer than was necessary. If that section was cut into a third of what it was, it would have been memorable but instead it made the game become a chore. The game drags on way longer than it should. This is a good 4 hour experience that has been stretched over 10 hours. Hence it just overstays its welcome by the time you reach the third quarter of the game.Devs, if this game didn't bankrupt you, please try again, there's a chance you could strike gold with this franchise.For anyone else, please get this game only if it interests you and only at a very big discount. 80% or more. I got this in a Humble Choice.

_childDocuments_.review: Solid game to get while it's on sale. I can appreciate that the developers decided to take some risks, but they honestly didn't quite pay off. The first time you get access to the bike is extremely well done, despite the controls for it being a bit jank, it's a fun puzzle to play though. The mission immediately following it is incredibly painful to get through though. The open world level was entirely unnecessary in a game thats core gameplay loop is killing enemies while exploiting movement mechanics. It was a chore to get through and felt like a weird way to artificially extend the time it takes to play the game. The other risk they took was redesigning the movement mechanics from the original Ghostrunner. I don't honestly like the way momentum works in this game at all, and many mechanics felt jank and out of place. Dashing while mid air for some reason cancels all your forward momentum, so rather than getting a boost to the momentum you already have, you might just miss a jump because of dashing. On top of that, many areas feel oddly inconsistent with how momentum works. You can do the same exact thing several times and get a different result each time. Some times you fall short on a jump and then for some reason you make it the next time despite fundamentally changing nothing in what you did. Story is meh just like GR1, not really much to note, it's quick and basically all the characters are forgettable. If you liked GR1, you'll probably like GR2 as well. Despite feeling like it needed more time in development, it's still as fun as the last, just a bit less fluid feeling. If you haven't played GR1 yet, I would play that first before playing this one, since it is the objectively better ghostrunner.

_childDocuments_.review: Jack is back and One More Level does it again!Almost everything about Ghostrunner 2 exceeded my already high expectations. The combat is fluid as ever bosses feel more challenging and exciting and the story and environments feel more rich and fleshed out. Top it off with an awesome soundtrack I could listen to for hours and the recipe is *chef's kiss".As nearly perfect this game feels there are few drawbacks some more glaring than others.If you played the first Ghostrunner no doubt you know how mind numbly hard some areas can be with the fast movement and one-hit death system, well for good or for bad Ghostrunner 2 feels somewhat easier mostly due to the fact new abilities such as the ninja star make dealing with enemies much easier tacked on with environmental interaction to assist in your slaughter this can make things feel easier than the first game.If you saw the trailer no doubt the motorcycle clips caught your attention, well unfortunately the bike sections were some of my least favorite (Minus one part in particular). Controls feel hard to figure out and the insane speed make the camera go bonkers sometimes. Once you get a grip on the controls it's not that bad but still I found myself wanting to simply return to Jack on foot not to mention once I really had a grip on the bike I was already back to being on foot anyways.Finally performance, probably the only real negative thing that isn't me nitpicking. Near later half of the game you will leave the tower and enter an apocalyptic wasteland there is one particular worm enemy here that spits acid, perhaps this is just me but once the acid landed and the deadly green cloud lingered my performance TANKED, some points even to 10-15 FPS. This is such a small section of the game where these enemies create the issue but dang if it doesn't just kill the experience when it hit me hard the game was near unplayable. Such a terrible smudge on this near perfect work of art and I'm holding out OML with patch this soon.All in all even with these issues my overall experience with GR2 was fantastic and recommend this to old and new players of the series. 8/10

_childDocuments_.review: While i enjoyed this game, I do prefer the first installment. GR2 doesn't have the same "grip," and the open world aspect was mediocre at best, this kind of game does *not* lend itself well to this format.Enemy variety is okay, the parry mechanic doesn't feel like it adds much compared to the previous game. If you haven't played GR1 yet: do so if this kind of game interests you, but don't but GR2 at full price, it isn't worth it. Maybe at a 40% discount. GR1 had me coming back: GR2 gets left behind after it's campaign. If you plan on finishing the storyline and leaving the game afterwards, expect ~6 hours of gameplay time.I don't think this game is bad, but it definitely feels worse than GR1. DLC swords are cool but generally not worth it unless you plan onm replaying the game a lot, because there is a decent roster of "free" swords you can find throughout the game.TLDR: if you value your time and money, get GR1. If you really want to play this game? Don't spend more than 15 bucks on it.

_childDocuments_.review: So... Ghostrunner 2. I really liked the first game and I really like this one, too.When you check what's on paper, all the features added to this sequel are reasonable.So why do I still think the first one is the better game?Because I feel that the simplicity of the first one made it more straight to the point. Now we have a base where we can walk around and a lot of story stuff with characters nobody cares about, more puzzles and more open levels. That is all fine by itself, but I feel like Ghostrunner simply did not need a sequel with more features and lore. It does not have to grow into an overblown IP. It is fine as it is. Because of the gameplay.And it's the gameplay that felt a bit more precise in the first one.Still. Ghostrunner 2 is an excellent game. The gameplay still keeps you on your toes. The visual design of every level is peak. The music is even better than in the first game.If you never played any Ghostrunner, I recommend playing the first game first and then playing the second, if you want just more. If not, that's also fine.It's up to you, but I recommend playing both.Would I be happy to see more Ghostrunner in the future, even with more features? As long as it's good and not turning into a completely different game, sure.Because if we gamers demand something, it's quite simple: Just a good game.And Ghostrunner 2 is exactly that.

_childDocuments_.review: On one hand the sequel had added a lot of features to the original formula, such as bosses, a hub, actual 3D characters to interact with, new weapons/ abilities, new parkour elements.On the other hand the game feels very rushed with a feeling of there being way less effort put into actual presentation it.The gameplay feels way more janky and unfinished than the previous game The lighting is way worse than the last game, the dialogues are terrible with unfunny jokes and stupid characters, the 3D models of pretty much everything look worse and are animated marginally worse than the previous game.The character models, animation and dialogue almost feel like the're from Hunt down the Freeman or something Overall this game feels closer  to something like a copy paste Ubisoft game rather than a proper sequel to the original ghost runner.

_childDocuments_.review: I agree with what most others have said about the general game experience. Overall this is a fun game that for the most part improves on the original game. I think overall everyone will have fun with this. However I personally found one massive negative that turned me off to the game and I don't see many reviews discussing it and I think if you played the first one you should know because it changes the game pretty drastically.And that's the hub. I think the inclusion of a hub for this game was a near-sighted decision. I think above and beyond what made the first Ghostrunner game so successful was how well it was paced. You were constantly rushing forward with as much speed as you could muster, and the entire storyline of the game took place while you charged forward. It was so well presented, and so well done the story felt like an actual piece of your character.Now they've added a hub? So when you rushing through a level, jumping obstacles, grappling to a wall and wall running across, jump over that gap, slice that dude's head off and then... STOP. STOP and talk to these NPCs. Listen to all the nothing they have to offer you. Expanding a story is great, making the world feel bigger, more alive and real is great. But a hub for this game was the incorrect decision.It completely breaks that pacing of the first game, you complete a level and you STOP and talk. Stop and talk. Stop and talk. I don't want to stop? I want to keep running and murdering with my sword. It's awesome. That's the fun part of the game, don't make me stop the fun part of the game.Idk how my stats turn out because I was in the testing for this game before it launched, but I do just want to reiterate. I think the game is great and I think most people will enjoy it thuroughly, especially if you loved the first. I just wish the hub wasn't included in this, and I think the game would be 10/10. I do still recommend it though.

_childDocuments_.review: A decent sequel to the original. You can tell the developers were being more ambitious with this one with more complex boss fights, a free-form objective system in one of the later levels, a more fleshed out skill tree system, and a roguelike mode. Generally the combat balance changes, the enemy AI and movesets, and the level design don't do too much more to push the needle. Fans of the first game will most likely find this game fairly enjoyable and probably won't be too put off by some of the differences in this one.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR Easy recommendation. It improves on the first game in many ways, but also falls short in others.Longer explanation, I really REALLY like this game, but I don't love it like I loved the first one. It has more interesting abilities, more interesting enemies (although they are easier), and a far more ambitious story and scope. However, this leads to the feeling that it's unpolished in some areas. There's a thousand reviews that mention the "open-world" level, which let me just be clear it is not open world. Instead of just one objective at a time, there's 3 different objectives that you can do in any order but it's very contained in how you actually get there, there's only one way there and back to each objective. Now, I think that it is certainly the weakest section of the game, but I also don't think that it's inherently bad. I see people complaining that it exists at all, but I don't think having an open-world in a parkour style game is a bad idea at all, and I don't think people should write off the idea entirely. It just wasn't implemented very well and ends up being a little...boring. However, I commend the developers for trying new things, and taking the chance on some new ideas. Sometimes ideas work, and sometimes they don't. I just hope they take it as a learning experience, don't get disheartened, and approach the idea again from some new angles.I think the most frustrating part of the game is definitely bugs. Compared to the first, it feels...janky. Like sometimes I wouldn't stick to the wall when wallrunning and just fall off. Or I'd get stuck, or I'd dash in a direction and go hurtling way farther than I should have, or I'll dash in a direction and go straight up in the air for no reason. Or I would parry an enemy's attack, it would travel back and hit them and then I'd drop dead at the same time. It's just a little buggy, but it's not a AAA studio so I expect there to be a few bugs. I didn't have anything game-breaking, just annoying little things.The story is much more ambitious than the first game, and I don't know if I like it more? I like parts of it more, the characters especially are much more fleshed out than the first game, but I also feel like it was a less focused, less tight story. I think this is going to be a personal preference thing, but again, I'm glad they're trying new things.Overall the game is really very good, and if the first game was a 9/10, this one was an easy 8/10. It's a little short, I finished in only 7 hours, and I also was messing around collecting the purple memory slot things, but I would still say it's worth full price, and if you ever see it on sale absolutely buy it. If you've already beaten the first one.

name: Baten Kaitos I & II HD Remaster
detailed_description: Supported Text Languages: - Baten Kaitos: Eternal Wings and the Lost Ocean - English, French, Italian, German, Spanish, Japanese, Korean, Simplified Chinese, Traditional Chinese - Baten Kaitos Origins - English, Japanese, Korean, Simplified Chinese, Traditional Chinese (Voice overs are in Japanese only.) About the Game Wings of the Heart Take Flight Once More Baten Kaitos: Eternal Wings and the Lost Ocean and Baten Kaitos Origins are now on Steam with improved graphics and new features to aid game progression, making them even easier to play! Delve into the world of Baten Kaitos as you strategize with the unique card-based battle system in these two immersive RPG masterpieces. Play as a guardian spirit who guides the colorful cast as they struggle against destiny itself. A long time ago, there was a great conflict between the evil god and the people. After a fierce battle, the people managed to seal off the evil god, but what was left behind was only a desolate land. The people thus chose to abandon the land and live in the sky. Such fairy tales were passed down as legends. At this time, people had wings called Wings of the Heart and lived a peaceful life. It was an era of long-lasting tranquility. ...But the collapse had quietly begun. When a young man calls your name, the name of the spirit, the story begins to unfold. A story set on a floating continent in the sky, where thoughts and prayers intersect. • Unique Magnus Battle System In the world of Baten Kaitos, the true essences of all manner of things, including equipment and items, can be extracted and stored inside cards called magnus. A magnus' contents can be released at any time, returning the magna essence sealed inside to its original form. These magnus form the basis of the Baten Kaitos battle system. Battles run in real time, so you'll need to employ quick thinking to select the right magnus for the situation. Strategize against enemies of various elements using elemental magnus of your own, and experiment with mixing and matching different magnus to discover and unlock powerful combo attacks! • Vivid Graphics Remastered in HD The two titles have been fully remastered in HD, including retouched battle backgrounds, character graphics, and UI. Enjoy Baten Kaitos with even more vibrant visuals. ・ Aspect ratio expanded from 4:3 to 16:9 for play on wider screens! ・ Main character and boss graphics have been completely renewed in vivid detail! ・ All-new menu screens! Enjoy smoother gameplay with refreshed menu layouts, newly added sorting features, and more. Pre-existing graphics have been used for in-game maps as well as some screens and character models. • New Features for Better Gameplay Along with improved graphics, the features below have been added to make game progression much smoother! ・ Auto-save feature ・ Help menu containing terminology and hints for progressing through the game ・ New Game+ mode, unlocked after clearing the game once, which starts a new game while retaining all magnus, levels, and ranks ・ New Game- mode, a mode with level restrictions for an extra thrilling challenge Six new game system options have now been added, including adjustable game speeds and no-encounter mode. Save your settings as a Custom Set and turn them on or off at any time.

_childDocuments_.review: I see a lot of reviews referring to nostalgia of childhood. Well, in 2004, when Baten Kaitos was released in North America, I was in high school; I guess that’s part of childhood. But I didn’t get to play it back then. I didn’t even have a GameCube. My nostalgia of these games comes from them being the first games I played after breaking up with my ex who took all the video games and consoles we collectively had, in 2012. I sat on a folding chair (because he took the couch) and played them on a cheaply bought Wii, on the inferior of the two TVs my ex and I had. It was a depressing time for me and Baten Kaitos/Origins were successfully a great distraction. I remember spending so many days doing nothing but playing these wonderful games with amazing stories that fully captured my attention that I completely forgot about my dreary reality. Upon the floating landmasses of the world, there objects known as End Magnus: powerful magnus once part of the evil god Malpercio. There are those who seek to resurrect Malpercio for their own gain and those who intend to restore the world to its original state, with the forsaken earth and the forgotten ocean.You, the player, are a guardian spirit who speaks to the protagonist Kalas throughout his journey. He occasionally seeks your advice and how you respond affects the bond between you.    • When Kalas speaks to the player, the guardian spirit, he talks directly to the screen, giving the feeling of “breaking the fourth wall.”      • While the game utilizes cards in battle, it is  a “card game.” The main focus is creating combinations, which could be done without use of cards; that’s merely the form they chose. (I feel the need to mention this because so many people are put off by the cards.) (Same for Origins.)    • Taking pictures of enemies during battle and selling them is how money is earned in the game. Bosses are worth the most, of course.    • Collections other than magnus: Star Map fragments, signatures for a  family tree, and animals from all over the world.    • It’s recommended to , as many players have complained about keyboard controls. My PS5 (DualSense) controller worked perfectly. (Same for Origins.)    • HD Remaster Additions: disable random battles option, auto-battle function, 1-hit kill option, simplified post-battle results, and New Game+ options that allow the player to retain items or alter gameplay to make a second playthrough more challenging. For more specific info:  (Same for Origins)    • Amazing story and worldbuilding. (Same for Origins.)    • The plot twist is one of the best I’ve ever seen in storytelling.     • Super fun battle system, because, , it’s  a card game. You put together combos, which is done in several other JRPGs, just not in card form like this one. (Same for Origins.)    • Unique, detailed character design. (Take a look at the artbook images online, if you come across them.) (Same for Origins.)    • For an older game, everything is so pretty and detailed. The HD remaster helped highlight that. (Same for Origins.)    • Enchanting and beautiful Motoi Sakuraba music. (Probably my favorite of his.)    • Non-binary rep. Yes, I mean Mizuti. Minor spoiler:     • No English dub. I genuinely had no issue with the original English dub other than the audio quality could’ve been better. (Same for Origins.)    • Awful romance execution.     • Several achievements require a second playthrough. (More so for Origins.)This is a prequel to , taking place twenty years prior.Once again, you, the player, are a guardian spirit who accompanies the protagonist. The story follows Sagi, who gets framed for assassinating the Emperor of the Alfard Empire, begins a journey to investigate why he was framed, and discovers other sinister plots. Sagi also, quite mysteriously, experiences visions of the past every time creatures known as “umbra” are slain in his presence; such visions predate the landmasses ascending to the sky, over 1,000 years ago.    • Money is acquired through winning battles, like most games. No pictures this time.    • You can pause at anytime during battles.    • Items can be traded to NPCs rather than sold.     • Collections other than magnus: pieces of the magnus town of Sedna, field guide entries (bestiary), letters (as in, correspondence from NPCs), and magnus mix recipes.    • Other side stuff: Coliseum and greythorne quests     • The flow of battle is better and it is much easier to create combos.    • Menu actually keeps track of sidequests (or “subquests”) this time.    • The ridiculous “You win!” after battles is funny. It’s like … thanks for letting me know, mysterious announcer guy.    • Non-binary rep. Guillo is a non-human character with a voice that’s simultaneously masculine and feminine. (They avoid using pronouns though.)    • Overall, the character development is better because there are only three main characters.    • The back-and-forth between past and present keeps the story interesting, as it takes a while before it’s revealed how they’re connected.     • It’s neat to see some side characters from the first game when they were younger.     • No pictures is boring and less lucrative. I had plenty of money in the first game. In Origins, you have to “grind” if you lack enough to get equipment and items.    • While you’re in the “Build Deck” menu, to get rid of things you no longer need, you have to move them to “junk” then sell them at shops, which adds an unnecessary extra step, whereas, you could just sell things directly from your inventory in the first game.    • A few rather notoriously difficult bosses that make players want to pull their hair out.     • Wiseman is kind of a “meh” villain. He’s just this … uh, once a dude? Who is obsessed with heart energy. He’s just not that interesting to me.    • While the romance is slightly better than the first game,  If you care about amazing stories and less about gameplay, you  play the game with “one-hit kill” on if you’re so appalled by the battle system. Though, you could save money and watch a Let’s Play instead. But for real, the battle system is not a card game. It’s just about making combos. It’s not confusing or complicated, and definitely not boring. It just makes me sad that so many people don’t play these games because they see cards and get uninterested, when they’re such good JRPGs.

_childDocuments_.review: TL,DR: The Baten Kaitos games are both very interesting and unique 6th gen JRPGs that are well worth your time *if* you're an avid fan of the genre and are willing to overlook some game design quirks (OK, less "quirks" and more just straight-up flaws...) The collection is good and runs fine, but at essentially 50 bucks for two cult classics that are perhaps a bit more "cult" than "classic" it is a touch steep. I absolutely do not regret paying near full-price, but I am a Baten Kaitos 1 diehard, so I am already damaged... If you want to see what TENS of people have been going on about for 20 years, I do recommend both games, but I also suggest waiting for a discount. Baten Kaitos 1 is a strange and wonderful old-school JRPG from the GameCube, which together with Tales of Symphonia is near and dear to the hearts of all aging weebs who didn't have the foresight to ask their parents for a PS2 instead.Taking place in a psychedelic and lushly-realised world of floating continents and ancient secrets, your party of misfits has to foil the plans of an Evil Empire to collect all the Exodia cards and take over the world. The story and characters are both pretty good, although as the game goes on, there's a strong sense that some aspects had to be cut. It does all work out to an effective and memorable narrative in the end, but it definitely feels like some important details were just glossed over.The game is truly a feast for the eyes and ears. Baten Kaitos is both the pinnacle and last hurrah of pre-rendered 2D backgrounds. We never did see anything like it after... It also features hands-down the best soundtrack that Motoi Sakuraba (of Star Ocean and Dark Souls fame) has ever and probably will ever write, with a mix of epic orchestral and operatic songs, rocking prog-tunes and melancholy plin-plin-plonular piano melodies.Combat features an interesting and frankly rather half-baked card-based system that has a decent bit of hidden depth, but which is also badly in need of iteration and polish, on top of being very poorly tutorialized. If you master the combo system (a kind of poker-based damage multiplier), elemental resistances and special card fusions, you can get a lot out of battles. Combat is enjoyable, opportunistic, hectic and potentially quite strategic, but also frustratingly slow.Since basically everything in the game is all done with cards, there are a lot of unique items to find, which makes exploring the world and absorbing all the little bits of world-building scattered throughout towns rewarding and satisfying. There are also a number of large, game-long sidequests to complete as well as a number of smaller optional quests. There's a lot to get out of Baten Kaitos, if you're willing.Aside from the flaws present in the original game, the biggest complaints I have about the remake are some iffy changes to the script, the most egregious of which is that almost all references to alcohol have been scrubbed from the game, seemingly due to changes in Japanese ratings standards. Having barkeepers tell you they're keeping "Fruit Juice" in barrels in their BAR is just primo 4Kids-era cringe.Another unfortunate thing is that they removed the very crap, but very charming English voice acting from the game. I realize that the Japanese voice track is much better in basically every way, but I have such fond memories of Lyude going "THIS WILL CLEANSE THE EVIL OUT OF YOU!" before viciously beating on a tiny frog until it is mulch, that it still feels like a loss... Never releasing in Europe, this was the game I was most curious to play, and I must say that BK2 is a case of two steps forward, two steps back across the board.Taking place about 20 years before the first game, Origins tells the story of Sagi, a friendly young man who is roped into a tale of Imperial intrigue, industrial revolution and giant monsters along with his bickering sidekicks Guillo and Milly. The story is a mixed bag. It pulls a couple of strange and not wholly convincing retcons regarding the lore of the setting, which might upset diehard fans, but it also does some very cool stuff that will pleasantly surprise those same old fans. The party is also much better-characterized than in the first game. With only three playable characters, there is an abundance of charming moments between the three heroes.Gameplay-wise, BKO does a lot to fix and polish the flaws of the original, but in the process adds a number of new ones. Combat is snappier and less clunky, but also extremely confusing and samey. It also makes exploration and sidequesting MUCH less rewarding. You'll have your deck finalized by about halfway through the game and once you dig how the system works, almost every battle will feel identical. Combat is also much more challenging and consequently RNG-based, which can be quite frustrating. They have replaced a unique, but unpolished system with an equally unique, equally unpolished one...Overall, Baten Kaitos Origins is a more polished game in almost every way, but also less charming, psychedelic and memorable. Where BK1 was a strange, mythic tale of gods and secrets, BKO is a fairly normal, medicated JRPG with a quirky battle system. I'm glad I got to play it, but unlike the first game, I really don't see myself ever replaying this prequel.
_childDocuments_.name: Baten Kaitos I & II HD Remaster

_childDocuments_.review: I am biased. Baten Kaitos Eternal Wings and the Lost Ocean was the first game I remember purchasing for full price with my own money I had earned from mowing yards back in 2004. :D I bought it entirely based off the cover art knowing absolutely nothing about it. So, it was a big gamble, but man did it pay off. I love these games.The backgrounds/settings are beautiful. The music is beautiful. The story is really good too, and has some major plot twists I did not see coming my first time playing, but maybe I was too just young to see them coming. :D I would not consider the combat to be a amazing, but the combat in each game is very unique, and with so many similar games being released nowadays uniqueness goes a long way.This version of the game does not include the English voice acting, and that is a shame. I really miss the English voice acting. :( They only re-dubbed the opening cinematic, but in my opinion the opening cinematic is much worse than the version in the original version of the game due to the translation change.It is probably just nostalgia bias, but these games are probably my favorite turn based JRPGs of all time.
_childDocuments_.name: Baten Kaitos I & II HD Remaster

_childDocuments_.review: I loved the first game on the GameCube, but never got to experience the sequel. After well over a decade, I finally get the chance, and I can't be grateful enough.These are some great RPGs with unique card-based battle systems (each game's battle system is different), great stories with some amazing plot twists, and some of the best soundtracks I've ever heard.Now, there is one big problem with this release: the voice-overs are Japanese-only, with no option for an English dub. Sure, the English voices sucked (at least for the first game), but many players have a soft spot for the cheesy dub and miss it. Thankfully, there's a solution: if you look it up, you'll find an easy-to-install mod that restores the English voices. There are a few spots where the wording was changed, so the voice-over may occasionally differ from the text, but it's not a big deal and doesn't happen too often. This mod allows me to forgive this problem.Oh, and do be aware that these games may occasionally be very hard, even frustrating, but that's part of the charm. You have to master the unique mechanics like opposing elements, spirit numbers, and EX combos to succeed. There are options to skip combat by making all your attacks do a guaranteed one-hit kill, if a certain encounter is proving to be too much, and you can also disable normal enemy encounters if you find them annoying. I haven't had to use the one-shot mode yet (though I've been tempted, damn you Holoholobird), but I will turn on the no encounters option when I just want to make it through the dungeon without being interrupted.Oh, and cutscenes are skippable! This makes things way less annoying when you're fighting a difficult boss.
_childDocuments_.name: Baten Kaitos I & II HD Remaster

_childDocuments_.review: First of all, it's amazing to see these games available on Steam in 2024.At the time of this review, I've only played the first game. My focus will be on the technical presentation since I haven't progressed far into the game yet and didn't play much of the original on GameCube either. Despite its age, the game has aged beautifully, thanks to its stunning background art and unique world design. The only aspect showing its age is the slow-paced combat, but some quality of life options have been added to mitigate this. More on that later.I'm playing it at a stable 90 fps on the Steam Deck OLED, and I haven't encountered the combat stuttering issues reported by some PC players. To completely stabilize the framerate, you can limit it to 60, lower your TDP to 8, and enjoy many hours of smooth gameplay before the battery runs out.Playing it on the Steam Deck is ideal, as the game fully utilizes the 16:10 aspect ratio, and the AI-upscaled backgrounds look fantastic on the OLED screen. While I would have preferred a different method to AI upscaling, it still looks good. Despite all of this, the game does not show up as Steam Deck verified and that is something I expect Bandai Namco to take care of before release, not after.Several quality of life options have been added and are much appreciated. You can speed up gameplay for dungeons and battle scenes (up to 300% for the latter), and you can also disable the battle intermission screens that appear after every turn, which made the original release feel slow. There are also options to remove any challenge from the combat, but I haven't tried those. It's great that they're available for those who just want to experience the story.One minor complaint is that the map screen for the first region doesn't fully utilize the 16:10 aspect ratio. Instead of adding simple black borders to the left and right, they opted for a dropshadow effect displayed on top of the background, which doesn't look great. This is nitpicking, though. I also wish you could switch between the two releases from within the game itself. Unfortunately, you have to use Steam's launcher option, which defaults to your last selection and might confuse some people about how to access the other game. It would have been better to have two separate Steam apps so we could display them in our library individually and only download the one we want to play.
_childDocuments_.name: Baten Kaitos I & II HD Remaster

_childDocuments_.review: I've been waiting for this day, that Baten Kaitos Origins would be released on Steam. I was hesitant at first as it was only in Japanese audio, but there's a true legend in the discussions that linked to a fix, so that you can use the original English VAs. It's not 100% perfect, but, I'm still loving the game, and the nostalgia is strong.
_childDocuments_.name: Baten Kaitos I & II HD Remaster

_childDocuments_.review: I own this remaster on the Switch and when I saw it appear on Steam I bought it again instantly.If you're a fan of JRPGs and Card Battlers, you definitely should try these games!True hidden gems from the GameCube created by Monolithsoft and Tri-Crescendo.These two games feature an amazingly fun and unique Turn-based battle system (Baten Kaitos) and ATB-style system (Origins) combined with a card battler, have an amazing soundtrack composed by Motoi Sakuraba (also known for doing soundtracks for the "Tales of" games and "Dark Souls"), and beautiful pre-rendered backgrounds.The PC Port runs amazingly at a 120FPS cap, with no hiccups or crashes experienced so far. It also looks beautiful in 4K.I don't own a SteamDeck but according to others it runs flawlessly on it at 90FPS and supports the 16:10 aspect ratio.It would have been nice to see more graphical settings but these games aren't too graphically intensive, considering all the environments outside of battle and certain scenes being pre-rendered.
_childDocuments_.name: Baten Kaitos I & II HD Remaster

_childDocuments_.review: First of all my review is only for Baten Kaitos I. So for all the Steamdeck users, even tho it says unsupported, it runs without any problems or tweeking on the Steamdeck. Keep in mind this is a japanese game so confirm is on B and cancel on A.I really enjoyed the game, the battle system is weird and unique, the story is solid and the fights arent that easy. There are alot of neet ideas with the aging process about you cards and combos.The ending was abit weird and for my liking to many cutscenes.Overall great experience playing on the Deck
_childDocuments_.name: Baten Kaitos I & II HD Remaster

This port is good and adds a lot of texture to the atmospheres in the game. The most optimal way to play Baten Kaitos due to some of the extra features and QOL changes.
