_childDocuments_.review: Port works fine.  Looks like you need a controller.  Mouse control for combat would have been amazing but they probably couldn't modify the engine that much.  These are some of my favorite RPG's. Especially Origins has one of the best combat systems ever.  I hope the word gets out that they are on PC now.
_childDocuments_.name: Baten Kaitos I & II HD Remaster

_childDocuments_.review: More of a mixed review than a thumbs down.On an Xbox controller, A =  cancel and B = accept. You can change the bindings, but it doesn't change the button shown in game. So once you change it, you will forever need to remember that B = A and A = B.There are very few graphics options, but the game performs well.Also, the English VO is gone. Understandable for the first game (which sounds like a $5 microphone in a tunnel), but the second game was fine.I appreciate that JRPGs are being brought to PC... I just wish they would put more effort into the remaster/port.
_childDocuments_.name: Baten Kaitos I & II HD Remaster

_childDocuments_.review: So when I saw this released, I was both shocked and excited... mainly because I had no idea it was in the works lol. But I loved the OG game on gamecube, so I pretty much immediately picked it up. For a remaster, it's pretty freaking good (Except those shopkeepers, stuff of nightmares lmao). Though my first impressions were a bit sour, not being able to display the PC hotkeys on screen when interacting with something or making an action, and perhaps most of all, we are unable to have the English voice-acting in this game. Initially, I felt regret, as I never played the original with the Japanese VA, so on a nostalgia level it really took the wind out of my sails.  The Japanese VA is good, no issues with it, it just wasn't what I expected.  It's my understanding they removed it since they made some changes that made the English VA not line up or something, and I'm sure thats a fine reason... but it's just odd lol.  English VA wasn't even the best, but it was nostalgia. After digesting those couple sour grapes, I still dove in. The original game is obviously a bit dated in general, but the remaster gives it a breath of new life, everything is still fluid (PC controls can be a bit hard to adjust to since you can't click things), we already know it has a great story, and now we can go through it without the grueling process of either finding a crappy port or finding a gamecube and going through the OG graphics in 2024 lol. All in all, I definitely recommend. Just keep in mind that there is no english VA, and if you play with mouse/kb, you won't be able to see the hotkeys on screen in-game; and I definitely recommend re-mapping them to whatever makes most sense to you. I did:-A=M2  -B=M1   -X=R   -Y=F   LB=Q   -RB=E   -LT=T   -RT=G   -Left stick=Z   -Right stick = Cand it feels more natural to me. Great Mizuti is still awesome, Lyude is still my favorite lol.
_childDocuments_.name: Baten Kaitos I & II HD Remaster

_childDocuments_.review: The best JRPG ever is finally on PC and it looks better than ever, big Yes must buy. Best gameplay in a JRPG ever, Baten Kaitos origins is the slightly better game overall but both are amazing. The music is one of the best if not the best music I've ever heard in any video game ever. I know there is a lot of nostalgia goggles with these games but still I played them for the first time very late on an emulator on the Wii and it still blew me away. Anyone should give these games a try, from Balatro player or FF enjoyer anyone can find something amazing in these.
_childDocuments_.name: Baten Kaitos I & II HD Remaster

_childDocuments_.review: Just like the old games but it has some graphical updates that make a lot of graphics more clear looking and there is no english voice acting, which isn't really that bad to be honest. The old releases had bad way bad english voice acting. It also has a little 'cheat' menu that lets you increase game speed to 300% without increasing combat speed (which is important) and that's pretty great.It also actually tells you what the bonus for bulk leveling is which is great too, because most people didn't know what that was about before and it wasn't clear. I've seen some people mad about this remake but it's pretty nice.
_childDocuments_.name: Baten Kaitos I & II HD Remaster

_childDocuments_.review: Worth the price of admission for BK Origins alone - a true GOAT from the GameCube era that still holds up today.  The first game is nothing amazing but it still has enough plot twists and pretty music to keep you engaged.  The removal of the English dub and minor script changes are a little annoying but nothing that detracts from the overall goodness here.  Runs buttery smooth on the steam deck as well.BK 1 - solid 7 / 10+Amazing music and art direction+Interesting (if unrefined) mechanics+/- Story and characters waffle between being engaging and rote+/- Original dub that is missing was frankly not that good, but cut content is not good either.-Babysitting decks for all the characters can get a little tedious.-Battles tend to be incredibly slow; turning up the speed isn't useful because then it becomes difficult to choose cards in the time allotted.-You need a great memory or personal notes to keep up with side quests and possibly story related progression if you take significant breaks.BK Origins - 10 / 10+Even better soundtrack, still solid visuals.+Improvements across the board to deck building, battles, side quests, in-game journal(s), etc.+Significantly less (but also way more useful) cards.+Fantastic story and characters; benefits from a smaller core cast.+Nice balance of difficulty - regular battles are breezy, bosses will test your skills and deck.-Loss of dub sucks for this one.-Takes place in same world as first game, so you see a lot of the same areas again.The additions of NG+ for BK and NG- for both games are welcome surprises.  There is enough content and QOL changes in each game to warrant the price, which is a steal for two niche JRPGs.  Hopefully this means we'll get Xenoblade eventually!
_childDocuments_.name: Baten Kaitos I & II HD Remaster

_childDocuments_.review: These are possibly my favourite games of all time. I don't have much to add that hasn't been said in the reviews already, but as an artist- this game was and continues to be one of my all time biggest inspirations. Everything is lovingly rendered from top to bottom, from the character portraits bursting with color, texture and emotion, to the lovingly hand-painted backgrounds on every new screen. The remaster does an excellent job bringing these elements back to life- I've caught myself staring at little details and brushstrokes in the scenery that I never noticed before- and the character models look a lot better now too. I've been thoroughly enjoying a long overdue replay of these games. Thank you to all the developers, artists, voice actors, musicians and other creatives that put their heart and soul into these games- your efforts have not gone unnoticed. <3
_childDocuments_.name: Baten Kaitos I & II HD Remaster

_childDocuments_.review: Two of my favorite JRPGs, played them back on the Gamecube and finished the first one again on Switch last year. PC port is pretty basic but works perfectly so far. Just like the switch version, the Remaster only has japanese voices, which, at least in case of Origins, is unfortunate. Graphic options only include Resolution, V sync and Anti-aliasing, but just playing this at higher resolutions and frame rates is great. I didn't encounter any bugs or crashes, but of course 6-ish hours is not nearly enough to give a final opinion on this. Controller Icons are for XBOX, mouse and keyboard are supported, but there are no icons unfortunately.The Switch Version of BK 1 had a few broken animations for two of the characters, not sure if they are fixed in this port, but I almost doubt it. BK 2 looks fine in that regard, I played 20 hours on Switch and didn't see any Problems like in the first game, but again, there might be some later. If I encounter some, I will update this review.So far I can recommend the Collection, even if it is a basic one. The combat alone makes these two games pretty unique, and combined with the fantastic music and great story, the collection is a very easy recommendation for Fans of JRPGs (even if the price seems a bit high for the basic nature of the port), especially since these two games are pretty niche.
_childDocuments_.name: Baten Kaitos I & II HD Remaster

_childDocuments_.review: An absolute treasure of a GameCube title. I skipped out on Switch mostly hoping for a PC port as well as other improvements but I decided to just pull the trigger and get the Steam version once it showed up in my recommendations I had no idea it was released a week ago. The main drawbacks to these HD Remasters is lack of dub and some strange choices when it comes to button prompts (A to cancel, B to confirm). Hoping they patch that or include an a builtin mapping option. Some QoL improvements are nice and this appears be the same game I played back in 2004 with no real added content. The draw of this game is of course the deck building and a unique twist to your usual JRPG mechanics. Not many turn bases games give you the opportunity to react to your opponents attacks - the few that come to mind are the Mario RPGs, the recent Sea of Stars and Baten Kaitos. If you're into deck building games like Slay the Spire, you might end up liking this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Baten Kaitos I & II HD Remaster

_childDocuments_.review: Only have played Baten Kaitos 1 so far when I did this review, but if you remember the original GameCube version like I do this is the exact same game but in HD so it looks fantastic. Only other real change is the voices are only in Japanese (originally they were only in English), slight complaint is controls when selecting cards in battle is sometimes sluggish and unresponsive, but you also have to learn to be very fast. Also takes a little time to learn the deck building and attacking/defending systems.The original game was fantastic once you got into this and this is the same as before. Will update when I get into Baten Kaitos 2.
_childDocuments_.name: Baten Kaitos I & II HD Remaster

_childDocuments_.review: so happy to see this on steam and remastered! i played this game years ago on gamecube and it ended up being one of my favorites on that console the card combat is great and there are lots of cards to collect and unlock this is a beautiful looking game with an interesting story. the sound track and art style are 10/10remastered look is amazingIts aged pretty decent if turn based combat is your thing. what they added in the remaster is a nice addition. there is a feature to finish battles in one hit,turn the game and battle speed up to 300% and turn off wild encounters. If you are worried it might be to slow this is a nice feature but this is a relaxing game so the pacing is fitting. I haven't finished this one yet and i will update the review when i have but so far no bugs or issues. the added achievements is a huge plus. 10/10 1&2if you like card battlers or old school turn based rpgs try it outit has a casual feel to it. there is deck building. collecting. secrets to find. Lots of npcs to interact with. interesting story
_childDocuments_.name: Baten Kaitos I & II HD Remaster

_childDocuments_.review: If you like classic JRPGs (ala Final Fantasy I through IX, Chrono Trigger, Legend of Mana, etc.), you'll likely very much enjoy BK1 at least.  I first played BK1 when it came out on the GameCube in the States in late 2004.  I had forgotten much of the story, so it's been great to revisit this world.  I wasn't aware there was a sequel until this remaster came out, so I'm very much looking forward to delving into BK2 soon. Can't go wrong with two games for the price of one! :)Don't let the battle system scare you, either. It's a bit strange at first, and similar to card games like Magic, RNG can totally screw you over occasionally.  However, save points are plentiful, and I find it much more engaging to work with the cards I've been dealt (literally) versus digging through menus to take the "perfect" action.  I appreciate it more now that I'm older and have figured out that "close enough" is often just fine.
_childDocuments_.name: Baten Kaitos I & II HD Remaster

_childDocuments_.review: BRING BACK THE ORIGINAL ENGLISH VOICE ACTING PLEASE! It seriously sounded hella cool and I can't for the life of me understand why they took it out. That's really my only gripe about this game. There should have been an option to choose what language you wanted. I played this game back on Gamecube when I was a teenager and really enjoyed it and still do. It's a very unique RPG with gorgeous graphics and music. Highly recommend it if you have never played this game before.
_childDocuments_.name: Baten Kaitos I & II HD Remaster

_childDocuments_.review: Just finished the first game, even though it has many flaws, its worth playing it at least once.The card system is actually very easy to learn, just focus on doing pairs or upwards or downwards straight without canceling the elements.I dont understand the hate for the magnus aging mechanic, sure it spoils many healing items, but improves other cards, also you get more than enough cards to ever make this an issue.The added gameplay options save time by skipping much of the grind and occasional backtrack.It feels like a smaller, learning project by Monolith Soft before making 4 straight masterpieces (Xenoblade 1, X, 2, 3).Story 8/10 - another world ending story but with some interesting twistsCharacters 9/10 - i liked the whole party, no one is annoying and all have interesting stories.Music 8/10 - very good music but very few tracks, they get re used a lotGameplay 6/10 - the combat is good, but keeping track of quest, quest items and quest magnus is a mess.Ending 10/10 - very satisfying, no loose ends, very lovely.Bought it on sale and already feel satisfied with the money spent and the first game.Going to play the second game and maybe add more thoughts after finishing it.
_childDocuments_.name: Baten Kaitos I & II HD Remaster

_childDocuments_.review: First few games I had a tear roll at the end of the game in forever. Enjoyed the story of both games and the concept of what I'll call artificiality in BK 1 and BK 2 with the addition of machina vs magic. Never beat BK2 as a kid on my gamecube and glad it somehow ended up on steam.The gameplay, combat and puzzles can be pretty jank but I am glad I never played anything like it, check it out if you're into jrpgs.PS: If you want to have an english dub google it and swap the audio files. Modern translators changed up some terms which I did not care for as the game is a remaster not a remake.
_childDocuments_.name: Baten Kaitos I & II HD Remaster

_childDocuments_.review: The game runs quite well on steam deck. i should add that i have only played the first, of the two games. another thing is that both games are missing the english voice over. in my opinion this shouldn't be a deal breaker. like a film from a non english speaking, i think the original voice over is all you need.get past the things above and this duo of games should scratch a jrpg itch i know some people have
_childDocuments_.name: Baten Kaitos I & II HD Remaster

_childDocuments_.review: Baten Kaitos I & II HD remaster is a masterpieceExtremely well ported to the PC, Baten Kaitos has arrived to steam!This is by far one of the most exquisites yet beautiful JRPG ever made with a unique battle system based on deck cardsBaten kaitos 1 is such an amazing experience from the delicate art and music score to the characters that follow your adventures through the entire game, nothing is a waste here, countless hours or rich story and fun, truly a masterpiece.Baten Kaitos 2 or Origins, follows the same amazing experience than the first BK (with less characters and the deck cards summarized) but the battle system have been improved to provide amazing battle experiences and combos between your toons allowing you to eliminate everything in your path, the music score still being best of the best and offers amazing tracks like the Valedictory elegy. Follow Sagi, Guillo (The best Paramachina ever created) and Milly and discover the Origins of this amazing saga.The music score is by Motoi Sakuraba, famous by games like Tales of series, Star Ocean, Valkyrie profile, Dark souls and much more.I highly recommend this port is very well done. go Buy and support developers !
_childDocuments_.name: Baten Kaitos I & II HD Remaster

_childDocuments_.review: For those complaining the layout of their controllers does not work when mapping the A and B buttons, you can easily use a switch controller, the actual controller (not joycons) that plugs in USB they are pretty cheap, luckily I have a switch and have plenty. _childDocuments_.review: Not for me.To be fair, the game does have some nice qualities e.g. environment are beautiful, music is nice, and you can change game's speed, but:* not a fan of the card battle system - too much RNG that can results in huge difference in the outcome of battles* no way to skip skill animations in battle, and you can't speed up battle too much since the cards need to chained in real time* story didn't grab me in the first 2 hours (usually not that important)* no English voice acting* not a fan of the character art style, especially the 2D character portraits look awful

_childDocuments_.name: Baten Kaitos I & II HD Remaster

_childDocuments_.review: Both games are some of my favorite JRPGs from my middle school days. _childDocuments_.name: Baten Kaitos I & II HD Remaster

_childDocuments_.review:
A long time ago, there was a great conflict between the evil god and the people. After a fierce battle, the people managed to seal off the evil god, but what was left behind was only a desolate land. The people thus chose to abandon the land and live in the sky.

Such fairy tales were passed down as legends. At this time, people had wings called Wings of the Heart and lived a peaceful life. It was an era of long-lasting tranquility. ...But the collapse had quietly begun.

When a young man calls your name, the name of the spirit, the story begins to unfold. A story set on a floating continent in the sky, where thoughts and prayers intersect.

Two JRPG masterpieces return. Baten Kaitos: Eternal Wings and the Lost Ocean and Baten Kaitos Origins are back with improved graphics and new features to aid game progression, making them even easier to play!
_childDocuments_.name: Baten Kaitos I & II HD Remaster

name: RKGK / Rakugaki
detailed_description: The city is your canvas. Join the rebellious Valah and her RKGK crew to free the neo-brutalist Cap City from evil B Corp’s control. Collect secret treasures, find hidden paths, and light up the cold and grey concrete with your graffiti. How fast can you go? Chain together jumps, dashes, glides, and grinds. Reach the perfect flow state in Defacer mode – where Valah’s world becomes her animated wonderland. Master routes and speed through levels as you take down Mr. Buff’s cronies with style. Break through enemies, overload your senses, and take back control. Use Valah’s paint abilities for stylish traversal, chaotic mayhem, and leaving your vibrant mark on every corner of Cap City. Channel your power through art and resist Mr. Buff’s mind-controlling technology. Restore freedom to the citizens of Cap City and test your abilities against the B Corp minions. Valah’s creativity and imagination is the spark to guide you through a dark, controlling world. Color is power. Graffiti is resistance. Use art as the ultimate expression to speak for the underdog and light up the world. With plenty of paint and cosmetic customization options, Valah can reclaim her city and look great doing it. RKGK / Rakugaki and Wabisabi are proud to be a part of Riot Games' Underrepresented Founders program, working together to help increase diversity in game development.
about_the_game: The city is your canvas. Join the rebellious Valah and her RKGK crew to free the neo-brutalist Cap City from evil B Corp’s control. Collect secret treasures, find hidden paths, and light up the cold and grey concrete with your graffiti. How fast can you go? Chain together jumps, dashes, glides, and grinds. Reach the perfect flow state in Defacer mode – where Valah’s world becomes her animated wonderland. Master routes and speed through levels as you take down Mr. Buff’s cronies with style. Break through enemies, overload your senses, and take back control. Use Valah’s paint abilities for stylish traversal, chaotic mayhem, and leaving your vibrant mark on every corner of Cap City. Channel your power through art and resist Mr. Buff’s mind-controlling technology. Restore freedom to the citizens of Cap City and test your abilities against the B Corp minions. Valah’s creativity and imagination is the spark to guide you through a dark, controlling world. Color is power. Graffiti is resistance. Use art as the ultimate expression to speak for the underdog and light up the world. With plenty of paint and cosmetic customization options, Valah can reclaim her city and look great doing it. RKGK / Rakugaki and Wabisabi are proud to be a part of Riot Games' Underrepresented Founders program, working together to help increase diversity in game development.
short_description: Turn heads. Drop jaws. Be bright. In this single-player 3D platformer, you’re the only one who can take down Mr. Buff and his lackies to restore color and life to the citizens of Cap City. Accompany Valah and the RKGK crew on their journey to take down the oppressive B Corp.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm digging this game so far, and I'll try to explain why in relation to some of the criticism it's been getting (because I think that will be more useful for prospective buyers).It is fairly slow-paced, but I don't mind this because I prefer slower-paced platformers over the ones where you go ultra fast anyway. If you're expecting something like Sonic Adventure then this is not your game, but if you want something closer to Super Mario Galaxy 2 or the Crash Bandicoot games (in terms of speed and momentum) then this is a lot closer to those.There is some momentum loss when you jump, but the faster you're going the less you lose (which I noticed during the boss battle) so it didn't really bother me. I think they did it this way so that you're not constantly overshooting the small platforms and objects (which would have been far worse IMO). They also mitigated this with an Air Dash which helps you maintain your speed if you're trying to go faster, so you have that choice between air dashing for speed or jumping normally for accuracy.I feel like the movement mechanics in this game have a high skill ceiling (if you want to go at top speed) and honestly, isn't that what we've been crying out for for years now? More games with high skill ceilings that don't just hold your hand? If you want to go fast and maintain your speed in this game then that requires a very specific playstyle, which obviously won't gel with everyone but I don't think it's an inherently bad thing either.I personally loved the visual design, music and story. The dialogue is a bit cringe but not enough to be a deal-breaker for me.The game is really polished so far, with no noticeable bugs or frame drops (I set the max frame rate to 60fps).Clearly this game isn't for everyone, and that's fine, but if you like 3D platformers and you want something that's a little bit different from the others then I would recommend this game (especially since it has a low asking price).
_childDocuments_.name: RKGK / Rakugaki

_childDocuments_.review: This is a solid, simple albeit slightly conflicted game that unfortunately fell on misunderstanding ears. Not only did RKGK not sell well, it currently also sits at a wholly undeserved "mixed" reviews. It currently goes for 15 EUR, which is a very fair pricepoint for what it offers.RKGK is a very casually oriented movement platformer designed around speedrunning. It is very easy to play and tough to master. Some of the gold medal times this game demands for the levels are absolutely absurd. Unfortunately this was misinterpret by many people as "boring" - which almost certainly means they did not play the game as was intended. The latter is a bit of a consequence in how it presents itself; you can technically make your way through levels by not graffiti-gliding (the core mechanic of the game) and the game even seems to reward this to odd degrees - with many interactable object placed outside the fastest path to the goal. In reality this is not what the game wants you to do - it wants you to be as efficient as possible with your movement. And the game does feel quite good when things click together.The graffiti-gliding mechanic allows the player to generate momentum as if they were on ice. To compensate for the drag the player is also equipped with an immediate dash, allowing you to reset the orientation of your velocity. It's simple and it works. The game feels good when you go fast. Some levels have brilliant mechanics to compliment this movement - I especially enjoyed the level where parts of the geometry glow red before damaging the player - forcing them to skate in a tense weaving pattern.On the other hand the game has this very weird conflicting design, where it wants to reward both mastery of the mechanics as well exploration. The latter should have been pruned to maintain the integrity of the vision, and clearly the game paid the price for this by having these confused negative reviews. RKGK loves to place "collectables" outside the fastest path, contradicting its incentivizing of speed. It also has completely pointless meta-progression in the form of outfits. Just... why? Focus on making a good game instead of this tangential nonsense. If anything reward it for people playing well, as opposed to the opposite.Cool aesthetic, with nice mixed art, animated graffiti works. Soundtrack is very fitting if not a little generic for my taste. Sound design is servicable across the board.Just a solid game that unfortunately didn't quite play its cards perfectly. Absolutely deserves some love. Do not be deterred by the particularly badly uninformed negative reviews on this one.More reviews at .

_childDocuments_.review: It's decent, but could be better. 5/10.A 3D platformer that has emphasis on going fast with some of the challenges want you to clear the level in under 2 minutes, but the movement is not satisfying to make me want to go fast. You don't keep your momentum when jumping. No new mechanics to make you go fast other than hold L2 for 90% of the time. The platforming sections can be fun, with later areas gets more difficult, although you don't get introduced with new platforming mechanics to give each area some specialty. Your buddies do absolutely nothing other than offering cosmetics and an in-game OST player. Your hideout where your buddies reside is nothing more than a place to get new customization options (character, paint job, graffiti). It feels like the devs had the idea to put the hideout in the game very late in the game's development cycle, which would explain why the hideout is just so underwhelming. And your buddies, they have zero presence in the main story. Literally zero. It's just you versus one crooked bald man in lab coat for the entire story. As such, I feel that the game doesn't want you to care for your buddies at all. There's some light talk, but not enough to give enough character to your buddies.The story is okay I suppose. It's short, and I guess the devs already knew it's not going to be the game's strongest suit. You only get new dialogues when you face the area's boss, and a cutscene after defeating them. That's about it.Maybe get this game if you're a fan of old-school platformers which I guess is what this game is trying to appeal to. There's even a difficulty setting that caps your health to 3 and puts you back to last saved checkpoint if you fall off the ground to emulate the old platformers difficulty.

_childDocuments_.review: I see a lot of comments about the movement being slow, in a game meant to go fast, which I originally agreed on. But after clocking in 85 hours in the game so far, this is actually an issue of a higher than normal skill floor.RKGK is not a very beginner friendly game. Not in the sense that it's too hard, you can of course get through it if you try. But in the sense that if you actually wish to get gold medals on levels, and/or move fast, you can't just think the game is going to do it for you while holding forward.There are secret movement techniques that are not really explained in the game, but seems to be intentional, which both grants higher jumps, faster movement and ability to keep momentum when jumping (although you move the quickest while grounded).This game is probably not for everyone, but if you like 3D platforming with cool jump mechanics and you have the patience to learn, you will certainly enjoy it.

_childDocuments_.review: I was having a conversation with some friends recently about games that you could potentially dump hours into and defend from the influx of digital pitchforks of the internet, but there was a catch: the game had to be considered “not great.”  It’s easy to defend your Halo 3’s or your favorite Final Fantasy, but it’s a much more interesting conversation when you have a game like Syphon Filter: The Omega Strain that was critically panned as average and honestly doesn’t play well, but dammit, I love the game and I will fight people who seek to slander its name.  These games are always a weird anomaly, especially for reviewers, as how do you punch down on a game you are for the most part enjoying?  After putting around 10 hours into it, RKGK is taking me down this very interesting road.RKGK at its core is a collect-a-thon platformer with speed-infused techniques and combat.  Each level has a whole bunch of collectibles, objectives, and enemies to set up your next few minutes however you want to spin it.  Your main objectives are to find Mr. Buff’s, the evil B Corp’s head honcho, controlling screens and slathering your graffiti of choice to rid Cap City’s citizens of the mind-controlling schemes keeping them in check.  Valah’s movement and weapon of choice is the same paint used to deface the drab and deterring environment, as you’ll slide, slice, and dice through terrain and enemies alike to reach Mr. Buff and end his reign of terror.Cap City is broken down into 6 areas, with around 5 levels and a boss fight in each.  Levels are packed with things to collect: mainly graffiti cans to spend on murals and coins to increase your points and to spend on customizable items.  The couple dozen graffiti pieces that you’ll tag through Cap City are such a visual treat.  The different styles and ideas that come to life with the 3D-tooled pieces are eye-popping in their visual aspect and are sure to wow in a few places.  Tagging screens throughout the stages net you necessary progress to grant you access to boss arenas, and completing level objectives nets you Ghosts, which are a special currency that can also be found in secret areas within levels.  These are used alongside coins to unlock a multitude of items like outfits, graffiti pieces, different spray colors, and much more.  I really enjoyed the little easter egg nods to popular pop-culture pieces within the different colorways for Valah’s outfits and the fact you can mix and match “premium” Ghost-bought outfits with color-changed coin-bought outfits: something that should be doable in more games.Levels start small to grasp the basic mechanics and grow to some pretty hefty stages in regards to verticality and specificity.  Combat is simple, revolving around hitting with ground or air attacks, but enemies will restrict the moves you can do against them to avoid button-mashing every enemy.  Combo-ing multiple moves together, collecting items and defeating enemies, will put Valah in Defacer Mode: a special mode that allows you to move faster and can also truck any enemy that stands in your way so long as you don’t take any damage.  Defacer is key for the speedier objectives which we’ll go over later.The issue with platformers that introduce a quality of speed within their repertoire is that their game can feel awfully slow when not always in 4th gear, and RKGK suffers from this.  The initial run of the game’s levels is more focused on spraying graffiti, collecting coins, and finding the hidden secrets throughout, and this style of traversing the levels can feel molasses-like in its pace, making 6-8 minute levels feel like full-length episodes.  Combining this with a rather forgettable plot, the short campaign, which can be completed in around a movie’s time if done expeditiously, absolutely drags throughout the first run and is a tough sell to drudge through.This hits even harder with some of the later levels and bosses.  The interesting mechanics of some levels get drowned out with the need for absolute traffic jams of enemy placement.  There are objectives necessary to defeat a certain number of enemies or to collect every coin in a level but you’ll run into a few spots where your initial thought is, “Nuh uh,” and proceed to go back to it later.  With enemies that become invincible if not dealt with within a certain amount of time to constantly shooting enemies to adding in the normal grunt work and slapping them all together is not a test of skill but more of patience as the death tolls will get higher when the odds are just mercilessly stacked on you.  The final boss is guilty on a grand scale of this and is not a boss that I’m wanting to go back multiple times to master.But once you get through the initial campaign, learn all of RKGK’s movement tech, and toss aside the need to see the game through to its ending: there are points where this game absolutely clicks.  The time trials provided on each level are intensely gratifying when you hit the near-perfect lines needed to obtain the gold ranking, and putting together a top-of-the-line run to achieve an S rank is a breath of fresh air knowing you did everything needed on the level at a blistering pace.  Just taking each level in, learning a good path, and just nailing it makes you wonder why RKGK added the collectibles to begin with when the sense of speed when doing everything right is up and beyond better than its initial approach.  This second level of gameplay almost, almost makes the first part worth it, but it’s also immensely frustrating that this amount of quality in terms of mechanics and pace is buried behind what’s at surface level.In my opinion, RKGK is not great.  There’s a problematic line between adding many things and doing them all okay when you could shave off the edges and polish what could be great, and the game as a whole carries a heavy burden with the stuffing of genre staples.  But I can’t shake the urge to learn another level and try to high-tail it as fast as my fingers can allow me because getting S Ranks is a drug I didn’t know I needed.  Come to think of it: those small, fleeting, colorful moments surrounded by the melancholic mediocrity enveloping it all is very on the nose if you ask Valah and her time in Cap City.

_childDocuments_.review: Game's fun. A mix of a lot of different platformers like Solar Ash, Jak and Daxter, Super Mario Sunshine. What it ISN'T is like Jet Set Radio. At all. Yes, you paint graffiti... but you don't really. Not like in those games. Even simpler than JSRF which removed any directional input. Graffiti is simply an art style choice and an objective; You will collect spray cans throughout each level and if you have enough cans to "complete" that particular graffiti it is one button press and you move on. Regardless, it's still fun, still has cool art and all that. I'd say boss fights and anything where combat is forced really bogs it down though. You spend most of your time avoiding enemies and just navigating around them to spray graffiti which usually destroys all the enemies in an area. Boss fight sections often have waves of enemies you need to get through and they're just increasingly annoying as you go. I understand their inclusion for a change of pace but it's still just more annoying than anything to deal with. Main game is fun. Boss fights are not.Interested in this as a speed game but wondering what tech will be found for movement because the "fast" movement the game wants you to do (surfing and spamming paint) isn't fun.There's also tons of content here as far as completionists go. Every level has speed, enemy, coin, graffiti, ghosts, deathless, and S rank goals. It will take dedication I probably don't have to complete the game with S rank on every level.Customization is cool but I wish there was more of it. As it is, most of the customization is palette swaps of the default gear or joke costumes which just aren't my style. I typically don't play games for their story and this was no different. Nothing really pulling me in. Don't feel bad if you wanna skip all the cutscenes.the important bit is that the moment to moment gameplay is fun and addictive and it plays great on a keyboard. Don't let the man tell you to use a controller. You'll do great. I spent a lot of time in this review talking about what I don't like, and the easiest way to put it is that I liked almost everything about the game except for this stuff. Had a blast. Constantly wanted to keep going. 3D platformers are my favorite genre and this didn't disappoint.

_childDocuments_.review: It's kinda like the 3D Sonic games, and yes, I do mean that in a bad way.When you can get into a flow, it feels pretty good, but the level design far too frequently throws momentum killers in your path that really put a damper on things. There are also a lot of hidden items in the levels which require you to slow down and explore, but again, this feels like it's in opposition to the fun part of the game. I'm sure they'd like for you to play each level several times to find all of the hidden bits and improve your score/time, but the levels and mechanics just aren't engaging enough for me to want to do that.I feel a bit bad about giving this the thumbs down as it's not awful by any means, but I think most people will end up feeling disappointed. _childDocuments_.review: So this may be more of a neutral review but steam doesn't have that. I just beat the last boss and wanted to talks about some of this games strengths and flaws. Generally the game feels alright. The running, jumping, dashing, and sliding are all in a pretty good spot. I think some of their level designers did a really good job as well as most of the levels are pretty well crafted. They stretch the content well by having 3 general objectives for each level. Collect everything (this is strict, getting 999/1000 coins is a failure), time trial, and S ranks which is a combo of the previous 2 (but much less strict, for example a level with a 1m gold time trial can still give you full time score bonus for a 5m time. You also generally get 99% of the points for getting 99% of the coins.) Now for the flaws of which I think the biggest one is enemy design and hit boxes. Engaging with enemies feels terrible. Your dash attack come outs late, so its not uncommon to swipe through an enemy, get hit and take damage, and not kill the enemy. The spray paint swipe feels like it has a nebulous range as well. There is an enemy that looks like a little bomb, and if you try to ground swipe it you end up getting hurt (somehow, I guess your spray paint cloud is part of your body). So you have to use your downwards aerial attack against them, which btw doesn't work against the enemies with top shields that they are next to sometimes. I think if every instance of these two enemies was replaced with the default enemies the game would be better for it. Another annoying example is the enemy with damage bubble around them. When you get near them they pull it in then do an big aoe burst, after which they are left vulnerable. This is super slow and feels awful. You can try and kill them while the bubble is pulled in, but that feels like your dancing around invisible hit boxes and also feels terrible. It would be great if instead of this slow dance with the bubble they just charged up an aoe when you get near them encouraging you to deal with them fast. I could keep complaining about other enemies but I wanna move on to a few other minor points. One is grinding on rails... its slow and boring. Sometimes they have you do stuff like jump and grapple to another rail or attack a box on the path, but other times you just get to put the controller down and take a sip of water as you wait for it to go through a little spiral at a set speed with no way to speed it up. Another thing is finding all the collectibles can be a drag. Sometimes you get to the end of a level and its just like oh you missed 3 coins go do the whole level again or possible backtrack for a few mins (tbh I haven't tried backtracking really). Alright I've complained enough. Don't let this prevent you from getting the game if you think you'll like it cause its not like there is really an overabundance of 3d platformers. Just know that its not super special. I might actually go S rank a few more of the early levels, and if they fix up the enemies I'd actually make this a positive review.

_childDocuments_.review: While its presentation is overall stylish, and the colours are bright and dopamine inducing, I was really disappointed in the gameplay. While the Graffiti bombs are gorgeous, actually bombing it requires only a left trigger, and is an afterthought to the rest of the platforming gameplay. Which leads me to my other complaint, the movement needs polish. Traversal and motion feel like they're from 2002, where the player character can face only 8 hard locked directions. It feels okay at best, and there's no sense of flow that these kinds of games generally thrive on. I love the look of this game, but overall, the game feels shallow and I can't see myself coming back to it.

_childDocuments_.review: What do you get when you mix the aesthetics of Jet Set Radio and mix it with the bonus stages of Super Mario Sunshine? Rakugaki is what you get!  In the game you play as a teenage girl named "Valah." She is part of a group called "Rakugaki" who goes against an authoritarian by the name of Mr. Buff. Valah's objective is to traverse throughout the city and restore the livelihood by tagging sections with graffiti. The story is about as deep as a puddle of mud. It's not entirely original. The story is fairly similar to games such as Jet Set Radio and De Blob. Also, some of the dialogue was pretty cringe at times. The story is probably the weakest element of this game. It exists, but it clearly serves as an explanation for the game and nothing more.While the story won't grab, the presentation of this game absolutely will. The art style is reminiscent of Jet Set Radio. The game conveys a bleak oppressive cyberpunk setting, while Valah must paint bomb the city with color. The colors are loud and vibrant. It's truly visually a feast for the eyes and the artwork the first thing about the game that caught my eyes. While the music wasn't as memorable as the artwork, the techno beats did keep my adrenaline pumping throughout each level. As much as I like the art and music of the game. What good is all of that fluff if the game itself can't match in quality?Fortunately, I think Rakugaki mostly delivers on the game play side. While Valah would fit in to the Jet Set Radio universe, she controls very differently. In the game, Valah can jump, double jump, dash, and slide. When you press down the shoulder button, Valah can use her spray paint to glide across the floor. This helps with traversing the stages quicker. When jumping, she can use her spray paint to float across the air. This helps when clearing large gaps in between platforms. Think of it like using the jet pack like in Mario Sunshine. Controlling Valah is intuitive and easy to do. If you were expecting something similar to Jet Set Radio, you may be disappointed, as this game plays as its own thing. Throughout the game, you traverse multiple sections of the city. Each section of the city is broken up into roughly 5 stages each followed by a boss fight. The levels are structured fairly linearly. The point of each level is to get from point A to point B while tagging TV monitors, collecting coins, and defeating enemies along the way. At the end of each stage you will be graded on how well you did. The time and amount of deaths generally calculate the outcome of this score. At first, I thought this game started off easy for me, but steadily the game ramps in difficulty. Throughout the game, you can choose between "modern" or "retro" difficulties. I am not sure what those difficulties mean, but "retro" is the correct choice. So I played on retro mode. The first handful of stages started off easy enough. It helped me understand the controls and levels themselves were simple to navigate. Valah's move sets almost make the game too easy at times since you can correct a jump a few times in the air. I was almost getting bored that is until I hit the later sections of the game. By the later sections of the game, this game tests your platforming skills considerably. Before you know it, you will be jumping over shifting platforms, dodging lasers, and fighting enemies all at the same time. While the difficulty felt fair for the most part, there were certain times where I felt the game amped up to BS levels. Maybe I just suck at the game, but I swear the camera doesn't always keep track of everything that's happening. In the game the camera doesn't automatically adjust the players perspective at times and for the most part I would have to adjust the camera manually. This usually wouldn't be a problem, however, there were moments where an unseen enemy or bullet attacks me out of the blue to know fault of my own. Also I felt the depth perception was a little off. There were times where I swear that I could clear, but for whatever reason I just did not. Maybe I just need to get my eyes checked. Thankfully these cheap death moments are brief, and when I died it mostly felt like it was my fault. If you play this game, you may rip your hair out in frustration.Another criticism I have with this game is it feels like it's trying to be a type of game to speed through, however the level design seems antithetical to that premise. As I stated before, the levels are structure fairly linear, however the levels do branch out to alternative pathways. In order to complete the levels 100%, you must paint bomb several TV monitors throughout the stages. Some of these TV monitors will be hidden. This wouldn't be too much of a problem, but you really must go out of your way and explore these stages. Also these branching pathways confused me at times. There were certain points in the level where I scratched my head and asked myself "where do I go?" Another issue, there will be times where you will find yourself screeching to a halt only to wait for a foot hold to appear. It's similar to Crash Bandicoot in that regard. For the most part, these are minor gripes and do not happen often, but they do break the flow of the game at times. Overall I enjoyed my time with Rakugaki. I don't think it's going to set the standard for all 3D platformers to follow, but if you are craving for another 3D platformer with kickass artwork and a bopping techno soundtrack, you should give this one a shot.

_childDocuments_.review: This game was not at all what I expected, and it was a nice surprise.It's a classic platformer with the mechanics suited to the theme and story, but also demanding effort, especially for the time trials.Something to note; others are coming in thinking it would be a constant flow or momentum-based game (including me), and it can be, but it takes effort. If that's something you want, timing your jumps/attack/dashing in the air and on the ground as button combos gives you a sense of fast flow.It's tricky, but once you get it down through practice, it feels like a challenge to overcome, especially with the time trials.I'd assume it was the developer's intent to do it this way, considering the time trials seem very difficult to achieve just using the base mechanics. It's vibrant and it pops, with beautiful aesthetics in the graffiti and themes surrounding it, while existing in an industrial dystopian world. It's pretty cool and I dig it.Stunning and top tier; running smooth on my machine and very polished.It's a straight forward story; simple and fun with it's theme.The story scenes aren't animated, which is something that I would have liked, but they are fully voiced, which is great.In-between level dialogue is text, though I would have liked voice dialogue here as well, this is a common element in games for not main story scenes.For the previously mentioned, I understand potential development constraints. I like the game enough to enjoy and keep playing.It's good and it fits the theme. It's a consistent theme suited to the world and style of the game. It's very well done.All in all, I like it, and for what it is, I'd say 4/5 ✌

_childDocuments_.review: This game is incredibly underwhelming and, frankly, half-baked. The menu designs are BARE BONES, like done in two hours BARE, although I will say the level select getting splotched with paint after being completed is a cool touch. It's sort of just clear where their focus was in regard to non-gameplay areas, which I can't fault the devs for doing too much.I am exhausted by the theme of "corporate evil person is making the world evil; let's protest with flashy, funny art!" If you've played Mirror's Edge, De Blob, or even Splatoon, you most likely know where the story is going. A Rebellious young adult fighting the system through self-expression it's just overdone at this point. Gameplay is also incredibly boring. Many reviewers, such as myself, figured this game would be much more fast-paced with some real stakes and speed to each level. It's not that at all. If that's what you like, I'd say go for it, but just based on the ads and content pre-release, I expected more.I'd say give it a try if you're new to 3D platformers and like the game's aesthetics. _childDocuments_.review: Overall I'm going to recommend it since it's pretty fun for what it costs and what it is, but it has some issues that prevent it from being anything  than "pretty fun". Before I get into it, full disclosure; I have a 13% Clear save file and have just beaten Boss 2.: I have completed the game with a note below.Positives first, the visuals are bold and vibrant. The 3D animated graffiti effects are brilliant and feature a ton of really cool looks. They're probably the best aspect of the game.The music is also quite nice and contributes to an appropriately frantic feeling that pervades certain areas.The lead character is cute and has a few outfits to unlock. The movement is precise enough to allow for tighter platforming moments; I feel like difficulty scaling is often difficult to design for faster platformers so allowing multiple modes of travel allows them to simply switch to the tighter, but slower options to navigate these sections.The plot is light and goofy, which is definitely a positive since it allows more time to be spent on the core gameplay.The flow mechanic they introduce is a great idea because it rewards skilled play and encourages the player to do a little more than the bare minimum at least. The characters attacks don't require the character to stop completely to do which is definitely a plus and enemies shields stand out from their reddish designs from far away allowing the player to plan out the most optimal ways to dispatch them while spending the least amount of time.A TL;DR for the Negatives is, the game really lacks that feeling of "Deep" design that (in more polished games) creates a feeling of interconnectivity that brings the entire experience together, and some aspects of the presentation are weak (both understandably and not-so-much).The weakest aspect of the game is probably (unfortunately) the character controller. There's a level of tightness to the movement that feels pretty inappropriate. Dashes, slides and (to some extent) jumps all have fairly fixed values that are very rarely affected by things like environmental elements (like slopes), prior speed or additional inputs. The player is also locked into things like rails and certain other sequences until they end. This is another thing that harms player expression a little. The ability to pick up a bunch of speed by sliding downhill, and to keep more speed when you jump (possibly by holding or not holding the slide button?) really would have helped. Most games in this subgenre give the character some kind of skating mechanic for this reason.: After completing the game, it's pretty clear why the controls are so tight as it becomes super precision-based later. I feel like people probably won't expect that from this game, but I think that's fine actually.The graffiti walls are also a strange design element, since typically in platformers this is the sort of element that would have:A) Required a movement challenge (even only if very slight) to unlock instead of just pressing a trigger button. Imagine if there was a mechanic you had to perform and like, different kinds of walls that required you to clear a kind of micro puzzle to access while moving.B) Would have a bit more prominence in the design of the game overall since it's a core aspect of the character, possibly tied to some kind of progression.As far as the presentation goes, the voice acting is serviceable and the cutscenes are told via VN style portraits. This is fine, since its a smaller title. What's weirder though is the menus ( and other secondary and tertiary elements) have very few animations and supporting sound effects. Hitting a checkpoint just kind of plops some plain text onto the screen, for example. The levels also have the limiting factor of having to exist in a relatively set location and draw from a pool of similar-looking assets. The city streets, entrance to a facility, and the innards of said facility all look uncannily similar. Although, given its a smaller title it probably wouldn't have been possible to have a ton of discrete level assets.It's a decent game with some issues. Despite everything I still think fans of the subgenre will like it. It's cute and I plan on finishing it. Even though I haven't beaten it yet, it's not difficult to imagine a sequel or another similar title which has more focused design.It's pretty fun, and it's a shame more people aren't talking about it.

_childDocuments_.review: I went into this being sold by a friend as more of a “jak and daxter”-like platformer instead of some high flying momentum adhd one(as the description would make you think), so I got in thinking “okay sure.”If I had to relate this game to anything, it’s like being told Yooka-Laylee is a good successor. Yeah, remember that one?Jumps will slow down to accommodate more precise platforming, sure that’s fine, works in jak because he has a usual jogging speed and it’s designed around that. This game is designed around using your constant drift button to move faster than that jog, which *still* brings you to a screeching halt when you jump. The slide and air dash are also a fixed speed/distance unaffected by how much you lifted off the ground. So sure, just play it like a classic platformer and take more time until you learn where to optimally drift. Unfortunately the bonus goals of the game tell you otherwise, that you *can* do the first level in less than a minute. It wants to be jak and also be ultrakill at the same time. Every movement option just feels yanked from something else like a mismatched jigsaw puzzle. I was still fine with putting up with it, so I gave it until the first boss to start selling the ante, maybe teach how I should be moving better. First boss is a waiting game until he summons towers that he runs into three times. Five minutes or so of waiting in the so-called high speed platform game. You barely have to do ♥♥♥♥. So that’s where this review ends.

_childDocuments_.review: I found "Rakugaki" to be just plain cringeworthy and uninteresting. The environments are a drab repetitive cyberpunk-ish slop. Painting them over with graffiti is such a tired metaphor it's just pitiful. The main character is what a crusty 60-year old conservative would consider "hip" and "quirky". The writing is criminally bad. The main villain is perhaps the only thing about this game's world that I'd found tolerable in a better game, but he's still nothing to write home about. The gameplay is tolerable but too easy at first; and by the time it's gotten a bit harder in the fifth set of levels, I was so checked out I wished it would have just ended already. With all that, "Rakugaki" just feels desperate to me: desperate for our attention, our affection, and most of all, our money. I don't know about Wabisabi Design, they might be good people for all I know, but that sneaky Gearbox logo was a red flag. Really, nothing like a corpo mandated reactionary game about teenagers rebeling against the machine. Not that it's impossible to make good art while working for a corporation; but a "Hi Fi Rush" this ain't.

_childDocuments_.review: There's a trend emerging of indie devs trying to do their own take on a fast paced 3D platformer. While a certain Blue Blur stands as the obvious prototype for this sort of game, we've increasingly seen developers trying to create titles that are still fast, but have a very unique playstyle and moveset to them. Rolling Rascal, Penny's Big Breakaway... and here, Rakugaki - coming in with some punk appropriate flare and style.This game is a dream to speed through. Between jets, hovering and a rapid ground charge, it's been a while since I've seen a platformer feel this fluid and fast. The difficulty comes from trying to balance that with precision - you've got all the tools to control your movement, but it's easy to get overhyped and make a mistake. Still, it's a blast to play - jetting through levels, doing crazy acrobatics and dispatching enemy bots with barely a thought.The world's fun. They really go in on the graffiti and colour as a theme as you go - watching the level change is a delight. Valah’s a damn solid protag- cool to be around and gives every boss fight a feeling of 'I can do this'. I kiiiinda wish we'd seen a bit more love given to the enemies - only having Mr Buff as a named, voiced opponent means they can't really bring too much menace to things. But that's a nitpick. If you're in the mood for a 3D platformer, RKGK is worth a try.Also note - the game's got a strong suite of accessibility options if that's helpful to you.

_childDocuments_.review: So far I would recommend this, especially for people who like the gameplay of the older 3D Sonic games. This game really reminds me of them in a good way. You collect coins, grind rails, double jump, slide and so on. It also has it's own mechanics like gliding using the spray bot and the fact that you leave paint everywhere you go for example.It can feel slow in the first couple of levels before an additional power is unlocked. That power basically is a meter that fills up when you paint graffiti (quick one button press when you are near a spot for them) and as you glide through the level without getting hit. As it builds up you glide faster and at full power destroy enemies by just running them over. If you get hit it resets back to 0.I believe the idea here is to replay levels to gather all special items and get the highest rank, each level has objectives regarding this as well bonus scores if you hit specific times for completing the level fast. In that way beating the level while going slow can be easy and a bit boring, if you try to go fast and hit all the objectives you'll have more fun.Graphics are good but not amazing while the art style itself is great. The soundtrack fits with the theme and pace of the game.If I find something strange later I'll edit this, however from what I’ve seen I think the game is fun enough to get at full price.

name: Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons Remake
detailed_description: CRIME BOSS Buzz JOIN THE COMMUNITY ON THE 505 GAMES DISCORD About the Game Guide two brothers on an epic fairy tale filled with discovery, loss, adventure, and mystery. With their father suffering from a deadly illness, two brothers must bravely set out to find the “Water of Life,” the one cure that can save him. With no option for failure the brothers must rely on each other using their individual skills to protect one another and overcome the obstacles ahead in this unforgettable journey. A TIMELESS CLASSIC REMADE Hailed by critics when it was originally released, Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons is back! Faithful to the gameplay and touching story from 2013, Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons Remake features rebuilt characters and landscapes based on the original and has been updated to the latest generation of graphics, performance, and gameplay. Paired with a re-recorded soundtrack with a live orchestra, prepare for an emotional experience that will take your adventure to all new heights. EMBARK ON A FANTASTICAL EPIC Solve puzzles, discover hidden stories, traverse dangerous locations, and fight deadly bosses. In single-player mode, navigate this story as both brothers in tandem or play in local co-op with a friend, each controlling one of the brothers as you play together. GET IMMERSED IN THE EMOTIONAL WORLD OF BROTHERS Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons is full of hidden details that reward those who seek them out. In addition to the original hidden treats and rich storyline, the remake has added new secrets to be discovered. Please note: When playing the game in local multiplayer, at least one controller is required.
about_the_game: Guide two brothers on an epic fairy tale filled with discovery, loss, adventure, and mystery. With their father suffering from a deadly illness, two brothers must bravely set out to find the “Water of Life,” the one cure that can save him. With no option for failure the brothers must rely on each other using their individual skills to protect one another and overcome the obstacles ahead in this unforgettable journey. A TIMELESS CLASSIC REMADE Hailed by critics when it was originally released, Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons is back! Faithful to the gameplay and touching story from 2013, Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons Remake features rebuilt characters and landscapes based on the original and has been updated to the latest generation of graphics, performance, and gameplay. Paired with a re-recorded soundtrack with a live orchestra, prepare for an emotional experience that will take your adventure to all new heights. EMBARK ON A FANTASTICAL EPIC Solve puzzles, discover hidden stories, traverse dangerous locations, and fight deadly bosses. In single-player mode, navigate this story as both brothers in tandem or play in local co-op with a friend, each controlling one of the brothers as you play together. GET IMMERSED IN THE EMOTIONAL WORLD OF BROTHERS Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons is full of hidden details that reward those who seek them out. In addition to the original hidden treats and rich storyline, the remake has added new secrets to be discovered. Please note: When playing the game in local multiplayer, at least one controller is required.

_childDocuments_.review: Originally released in 2013, Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons was the first game helmed by the now legendary Josef Fares, who would go on to make the fantastic  and the even more prestigious It Takes Two. Before Fares and company formed the studio that made those titles, they ended up making Brothers, which is widely regarded as a significant release for the early mainstream indie scene. I played the original for the first time last year on the Steam Deck, and loved the evening I spent with it. Its visuals, gameplay and narrative held up perfectly ten years later, and its simplistic yet brief nature ensured no moment outstayed its welcome. While I never reviewed that version, I’ll link you the brilliant writeup my curator colleague  completed for that last year. Reviewing this remake in isolation of the original is tricky. The core experience is essentially the same game, with increased graphical fidelity and quality-of-life features headlining the differences for this version. And while that means it is equally as enjoyable to experience as it was in 2013, it equally doesn’t do much to justify its existence.The remake has the same narrative as the original. Two brothers head on a journey to save their father from a deadly illness by collecting water from the Tree of Life, and encounter various friendly faces, hostile threats, and traumatising hardships along the way. The beauty of Brothers is that its story can be universally resonated with, as it is delivered largely wordlessly. You can feel the joy and pain of the Brothers just by their facial expressions and body movements, and these are areas that the remake’s improved animations really help to spotlight. I thought much about my own brother and family whilst experiencing this narrative, and those thoughts really hit deeply when you see how the game wraps up.While the original release was built on Unreal Engine 3, this remake used Unreal Engine 5, and so the leap in visual fidelity between the two is quite dramatic. Many environments are far lusher and more life-like, character models, even for those with a minor role, are packed with neat details and personality, and certain areas, especially Chapters 3 and 7, have visual additions resulting in a much improved presentation compared with what was seen before. There are plenty of cool changes that fans of the original are likely to greatly appreciate.Unfortunately, this fidelity comes at the cost of worsened performance. Despite exceeding the recommended system requirements and lowering the graphical settings to High, my frame rate was very inconsistent; some areas ran at a perfect 60fps, but it would drop to as low as 35fps in places that appeared equally as demanding, and cutscenes were strangely locked to 30fps which was not the case for the original. This isn’t a dealbreaker since Brothers is a slow-paced game, but further optimization is certainly needed.Furthermore, I don’t consider these visuals to be a blanket improvement on the original. I feel the fairy-tale nature of the experience fits the more cartoony art style better, and there are many areas where the subdued colour choices make some backgrounds appear blander than they previously did. As it stands, this is one of the first renowned indie games to receive the remake treatment, and I can’t help but feel that going down this route in the first place misses the point of a core pillar of the indie scene. Few would argue that early successful indie games like Journey or Limbo need the remake treatment because their strong art direction makes their visuals truly timeless. I never took issue with the original’s art design, so seeing it remade in this manner feels deeply unnecessary. Ultimately, I’d recommend watching a side-by-side comparison so you can make your own judgement, as they both contain aspects that set themselves apart.The unique ‘single-player co-operative’ gameplay of Brothers is fully retained in this remake. Through the simultaneous control of the two Brothers, you’ll solve various puzzles, complete platforming challenges, and defeat or avoid the occasional foe or two. It uses its short runtime to its full advantage, consistently delivering interesting gameplay scenarios like the hang-glider sequence and boat traversal, before tossing them away for other equally compelling ideas like getting to ride a mountain goat and climbing up a cliff with the help of a troll. The controls do require some getting used to, but shouldn’t take that long as each Brother only requires inputs from the sticks and a single trigger. Nonetheless, if you still find this tricky, one nice addition is the ability to play Brothers in co-op either locally or via Remote Play. While this wasn’t the intended way to experience Brothers and will certainly change how certain segments of the game feel, it is a welcome option to have. The remake also advertised improved gameplay and boss fights alongside better enemy AI, but I feel that these changes were drastically oversold, as I couldn’t notice a difference in how any sequence played out. The same applies to the rerecorded soundtrack, which at first glance, did not have any perceptible differences from the original score. I also question what the developers meant by ‘new secrets to be uncovered’, as I found no interactions or easter eggs that weren’t already present in the original. The only ‘additions’ I identified were two achievements which are nothing but extensions of existing ones in the base game. Finally, there are some neat extras that you unlock after completing the story, namely an art gallery showcasing the character and environment redesigns, and the original’s developer commentary. Overall, fans looking for new gameplay reasons to re-experience Brothers will not find much on offer here.It would be disingenuous of me to rate the Brothers remake negatively because of the existence of the original. A lot of effort and polish went into recreating this classic indie title, and I found it equally enjoyable to re-experience on my beefy main computer as it was to play the original for the first time on the humble Steam Deck. Yet, it would be equally disingenuous of me to recommend it simply because it is shinier and newer. Personally, I am baffled that this remake exists in the first place. At least a couple of years of effort was put into rebuilding a 3–4-hour game in a new engine, completely redoing all of its assets, rerecording its soundtrack, and advertising its release. Meanwhile, the original exists on essentially every platform known to man including mobile, and still looks good and plays well to this day; why couldn’t they have pushed and advertised updates for that version in a similar vein to what Valve did to Half-Life last year?Ultimately, I could only recommend this remake if you meet at least two of the following criteria: A – You haven’t played the original, B – You prefer how this version approaches its visuals, and/or C – You want to play the game in co-op. Outside of that, the remake is just not worth it unless via a deep sale. While there are some neat changes, nothing is substantially improved to the point where I’d say this is the definitive way to play Brothers. I have no hesitation in saying it is the most unnecessary video game remake ever made, and I don’t think much would have been lost if the original was the only version that existed.

_childDocuments_.review: I played the original back when it came out and this remake still holds up the magic from the first. The game is beautiful, as well as the story. This game is still just as short as the original, not really adding much of anything "new" to the gameplay and story itself. Although the story is beautiful and moving, it didn't create as much emotional turmoil for my () playthrough of the game. I purchased it for the nostalgia and beautiful graphics. Like my title suggests, if you are like me, save your money. If you are new to the game, please buy it as it will be worth your time.While this game is definitely playable by yourself, it does not come without its frustrations. The gameplay is fairly unique in that you are controlling each brother with a different joystick and trigger buttons for their actions. Some of the solutions aren't outright apparent, but for me personally it didn't take too long to figure out the puzzle. The game will definitely be easier when played with a friend, which I would recommend if you are not confident in your skills with difficult puzzle-like gameplay. As stated in some other reviews, if you are not adept at figuring out those puzzles it will become frustrating for you very quickly.The gameplay is very short. While Steam says I played  for 4 hours, about 20-30 minutes of that was spent on a combination of chore break or snack break or phone call. I purchased this game on release day with it being on sale for $16; it has a regular price tag of $20. With the original version of the game being $20 as well, I think it is a fair price tag for the graphics upgrade it received. I also only managed to complete 7/14 of the achievements available on a "blind" playthrough. The rest of the missed achievements seem easy enough to go back and accomplish on another playthrough.

_childDocuments_.review: This remake is inferior to the original for a couple of reasons. 1: this is a single player game. adding co-op is misguided. i would advise against playing co-op, because the controls are part of the narrative, and it doesn't have the same impact if you would play it in co-op.2: the new visuals are a little uncanny. it looks technically higher quality, but the charm of astyle of the original is lost. kind of like how the Halo CE anniversary update kind of fails to replicate the original artistically.3: the cinematics i think ruin it. it was better without the cinematic cutscenes. it feels like they were trying to improve something that didn't need to be improved.Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons is one of my favorite examples of video games as an art form. the remake does not capture the brilliance of the original. just play the original version.

_childDocuments_.review: Nah.  The original is stylized and still looks amazing.  This just lacks much in the way of an individual personality, and I find it tough to look at in motion with all the artifacting or whatever's going on with the graphics.  Also the paths don't stand out as clearly during gameplay.  Won't spoil, but there were also unnecessary changes to the way a key npc was introduced that make the environmental storytelling a bit weaker.  But most crucially they changed the bittersweet, subtle, yearning background music to something happy and cinematic and oblivious.  It feels much less immersive and iconic to me, it's a tone killer.My opinions are from playing this level by level alternating with the original.  I didn't get past two before I really started to dread playing the remake's levels, which is why I'm writing this.  I'm still going to play the whole thing through because this is one of my favorite games of all time and I want to see what else is different, so I'll update if my opinion changes, but for now I'm disappointed overall and can't recommend the remake period. Edit: Ok I finished it.  Cons:-More missing atmosphere, replaced with music (the music gets better).-Glitchy animals messed with the vibe of two different sequences for me, and it was so hard to see the warning to avoid a certain hostile that I just assumed there wasn't one until I got to the same spot in the original.-Multiple puzzles were made longer and/or harder to do.  I found this engaging in some cases and frustrating in others; it's a con for me because one of them adds a whole cutscene to explain how to avoid messing up.  No.  Let me be careless, kill me, and restart the puzzle instantly please, it's just as effective as a lesson and doesn't make me watch the cutscene again.-Glitchy shadows and models.  I think they updated it to be a little easier to look at on Steam Deck but I still have a LOT of weird graphics nonsense. -Further confusing layouts (why is everything so dark??).  I am convinced the environments in the original just look better period, the visuals are more cohesive and appealing and particularly the water is much prettier.  Whatever corners they cut work within their limitations; the remake just tends to look like hi def textures got slapped on for the sake of hi def (with the exception of a location at the very end which I found very impressive).-Some minor to major changes that seem to be in the vein of "let's make it more realistic," overlooking the fact that this is clearly a fairytale world with unrealistic logic at every turn, there's no need to shoehorn in realism.  -There's this very specific conflict towards the end that may take you a few tries to figure out (unlike me, who is definitely very good at video games and didn't forget how to play this part).  In the remake, you are aided in this effort by a long, unskippable cutscene that wasn't in the original, which is there to tell you something the original didn't take nearly this long to convey (because the remake makes it deliberately more confusing for the sake of drama, thanks, I hate it; it does not have the desired effect my fourth time watching).-Co op mode is a neat gimmick, but if you play it that way the first time, then (unless they've managed to account for this in some way I'm having difficulty imagining) I think you'll miss out on the game's most iconic moment.Pros:-Some extra voice bits got added in a spot where they were lacking in the original, I thought that was nice.  There are some other little attentions to detail that prove some passion went into this.-Extra animations in the cinematics with more dynamic angles.  I found these mostly unnecessary and a little melodramatic at times, but they don't radically change anything and the ending applies them really effectively. -The ending was easily the best part of the whole thing, I had exactly one minor gripe because of course I did, but there was also an altered sequence I liked so much I wish it was in the original.-Still can't recommend it, but I don't regret buying for the fun of playing them both side by side and getting into my emotions about the story again. tl;dr: Letdown.  Play the original if you haven't.  If you already have, play the original anyway, it's the superior experience.

_childDocuments_.review: The remake of Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons offers a visually upgraded experience without altering the core gameplay or narrative elements that made the original memorable. While the gameplay remains unchanged from the original, the remake introduces the option to use a second controller for cooperative play. This feature can enhance the experience for those who wish to share the journey with a friend, reflecting the game's themes of teamwork in a more interactive way.Visually, the remake is a feast for the eyes. The environment design has been significantly enhanced, with improved lighting, models, better hair physics, and more detailed facial expressions. These upgrades breathe new life into the game’s world, making it even more immersive and engaging. For newcomers to the game, this graphical overhaul provides a more polished and visually stunning experience, allowing them to fully appreciate the game’s richly crafted environments.However, if you’re already familiar with the original or have a less powerful computer, the remake’s enhancements might not be as critical. The original game still delivers the same emotional impact and narrative depth with a lighter system requirement, making it a viable option for those who prioritize performance over visuals.
