_childDocuments_.review: I just completed my playthrough of Brothers, and I have to say: I really do think people have been a little too unfair on this one.  The art style is indeed a little bit changed from the original vision, but I still believe it's close enough that you really understand and get the idea. The gameplay itself too is perfectly preserved - clearly the game logic is the same, and that's how it should be in my opinion.The game also does add co-op with multiple controllers. This is a little odd how for some reason one controller is one analogue stick, and the other is the other stick, and honestly I hope they fix this in a patch (you can also fix this with a bit of Steam input tweaking), but apart from that it plays solidly enough and is really enjoyable in a couch co-op setting. That's exactly how I enjoyed it this time. Is the game originally designed for that? No. Does it really matter? Not really. Just enjoy the game SP or co-op, whichever way you personally prefer.I really enjoyed Brothers, and I'm a big Josef Fares fan. It's honestly a breath of fresh air to play his games: they're full of quality narrative moments and atmosphere, and not about the typical collection of pickups or collectables that most modern games are about.If you enjoy this, make sure you also check out the mighty A Way Out, and the even more (almost perfect) It Takes Two. Enjoy!

_childDocuments_.review: My most recent playthrough of the original Brothers was back in late 2021 and it still felt like an enjoyable game that has aged well. Yet here we are in 2024 having a remake of the game on our hands. A remake that primarily focuses on the graphics. A remake that - in all honesty - does not make the game any better. Thing is, the visuals in the original game, with their bleaker palette, created the otherwordly, magical and at the same time unsettling atmosphere that made me love the game in the first place. This is something that is completely amiss in the remake with its colorful and somewhat cinematic graphics. The remake feels modern, yes... and at the same it just feels mundane. Whatever little gameplay there was, now feels simpler as well, resulting in an oddly unsatisfying experience.So if you haven't played Brothers before - I strongly suggest you start with the classic version. If you are a fan of the original game (or - in a broader sense - of all games by Josef Fares), you'll probably want to have this in your collection, but definitely not at a full price.

_childDocuments_.review: Let's start with some positive stuff:-The original game is still on sale, this is an amazing move by everyone involved and in this day and age where original games get delisted all the time when a remaster comes out I can only praise this situation.-Game was sold at a huge discount for owners of the original, and even without this discount the game is only 5 more dollars (excluding sales of course, in sales the original is usually sold at around a 2 dollar price)-The game has finally received a patch that lets you change graphics setings! This doesn't change the new art direction that much but now you can optimize if you don't have a beast PC and you can remove a lot of visual blur with those new settings.-It includes the director commentary of the original game, which is an amazing watch on the original vision.Now I do not recommend this Graphical Remaster because the only thing this version adds is a "coop mode" that supports a second controller, you could always play coop with one controller if you wanted but coop was never the intended way to play (something the game even states when you pick coop which I find strange).And the new graphics, while they can look good in some very specific moments, have completely messed up the character design, art direction and for some reason they also changed the cutscene direction as well. (I find all those 3 changes inferior to the original vision).So now what would make this game a recommend then? _childDocuments_.review: for everyone out there saying this remake is a soulless cash-grab; the remake’s going for $16 with it’s current introductory offer, practically the same price you would currently get the original for. the remake’s a carbon copy of the original with a much more vibrant and visually astounding look harnessing the capabilities of unreal engine 5. a faithful remake everyone was hoping for. the original had a unmatched aesthetic with a low saturated colour palette meanwhile the remake makes every every colour pop out more and make everything simply more mesmerising to look at. I for one found myself appreciating the meticulous environments of this game more significantly than I ever did with the original. I say this as a player for whom the nostalgia plays a big part while comparing both sides.I remember playing the original on my iPad when I was around 10 ten years old and recently revisiting it in the past year. the unorthodox nature of the game just fascinated me, controlling two characters at a single time while each character having an almost equally significant role. me, and players alike of the original have always wondered what it would be like for the game to have strict co-op features similar to joseph fares’s other titles such as “a way out” and “it takes two”. the remake delivers, the game marketed a co-op mode and it’s here. a fully functioning co-op mode, the game’s designed to be played by a single player but players do have the choice of either playing it single player or co-op. I can’t help but notice that the clunkiness of controlling two players as a single player is still somewhat evident. meanwhile, the co-op mode feels way smoother. remote play, I wish it was present but it isn’t. I feel like there was definitely room to implement something similar to “friend’s pass” from it takes two or remote play in general via two players owning the game. granted, there’s the difference of different studios working on these games. however, surely the technology to implement this feature isn’t that complicated. there’s also the argument of not enabling remote play as a choice since the game’s not designed to be played that way since co-op mode’s an additional feature granted on the behalf of the community. I can’t support this argument since this is a remake we’re talking about, I don’t think it’s unjust to say that these demands could have been met in 10 years. again, the base price of this game is $20; $5 pricier than the original which is a very reasonable price to sell the remake at. I anticipated a much higher price, the developers had a clear opportunity to rip the audience but they didn’t. I strongly recommend brothers ‘24 to new players and players of the original alike. I wasn’t bereft of the impactful feeling the original notioned while playing the remake.

_childDocuments_.review: Back in 2013 Starbreeze Studios was in a weird position. They had lost several key team members in the years prior and in 2012 released Syndicate, a game that wasn’t well received. Releasing a small downloadable only cinematic platformer title was not something people expected of them at the time, but Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons was a success that made people trust the studio once again. Pitched and directed by Josef Fares, who has since worked on purely cooperative titles A Way Out and It Takes Two, it was a very curious attempt to create a “single-player coop” kind of game. That used its simple yet inventive controls to tell a wonderful fairy tale (in the classic dark but hopeful way) story that evoked emotions through basic interactions.The game has been re-released and ported numerous times since then and now, over 10 years since release, it got an almost shot for shot remake of the game, similarly to Like a Dragon: Ishin! from last year. This remake aims to be a new definitive version of the game and while it doesn’t quite succeed to be that at the moment, the game at the core remains amazing.This game is a very simple, but very well told story of a journey two brothers undertake in order to find magic healing water to save their father. Being a cinematic platformer at core, you could expect the controls to be quite simple. And you’re right, but they do have a twist – you directly control both brothers, with each of them having a dedicated analogue stick and action button to perform the necessary contextual action. Which, of course, means that it plays best on a controller. The game is balanced around this idea and while you should expect moments where your characters start running into walls because your brain starts mixing up which stick controls which character on screen, it usually works really well. The obstacles brothers face and the solutions they must come up with remain fresh throughout the whole (relatively short) game. And from time to time you also get completely optional little interactions you may engage with.Remake changes almost nothing about how the game works and how the levels are laid out. There are a couple of minor changes and you’ll probably notice them only in a side by side comparison, but as far as the gameplay goes, it’s basically the exact same game. Sadly, this means that the final big action sequence has a chance of being as finnicky as it used to be before, while having as poorly placed checkpointing as before. But since the game played really well originally, it makes sense to not change anything about it.What has been updated is the visual side of things. Moving from a small downloadable 2013 Unreal Engine 3 game to a modern and seemingly slightly higher budgeted Unreal Engine 5 title, the visuals get a huge boost. Not that the original game looked bad – due to its art style most of it still looks wonderful today. But a lot of the scenes in the Remake looks absolutely incredible while retaining the original visual intent. In fact, the new version is visually far more varied, with every chapter having a more distinct look to it. Due to all this added fidelity, cutscenes have been reedited to feature more close ups and dramatic camera movement than there were in the original. It’s not a question of “higher fidelity means better”, of course, but it is nice to see that none of the intent and emotion has been changed, while taking full advantage of the updated look of the game. Though, it must be said that a few of the late game cutscenes, and even one character, have been redesigned, but in a way that I found welcome.The move to the cutting edge and also still somewhat rough UE5, however, also means a lot of potential issues that the original version doesn’t have. People with older hardware, for example, will most likely have performance issues. But even on newest hardware you will notice problems. The picture often looks over-sharpened and noisy, depth of field occasionally misfires, the selected shutter speed for motion blur in cutscenes makes the scenes look laggy… There are also occasional bugs – for example, I once completed a chapter only to somehow die (I think) during the ending cutscene and after the cutscene finished, to be reloaded back to the last checkpoint.Luckily, any and all issues I’ve seen with the Remake are fixable, as long as the publishers are ready to support and improve game. While the updated look and feel of Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons is, in my opinion, worthy of becoming a definitive version of the game. Especially since now it also has developer’s commentary and coop, just like some of the later re-releases of the original game. Granted, I don’t think playing this game in coop is a particularly good idea, but it’s nice that the option is there. If you have the original game and considered replaying it – you won’t miss much if you replay the original again, especially if you have an older system. But if you have not played Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons before, Remake is probably a better option to go with, if your system can handle it. Whatever your choice will be, the game itself is still wonderful.

_childDocuments_.review: My wife and I played co-op with Xbox controllers. It was a considerably short game over all, but we thought it was fantastic, albeit a bit heart wrenching. In truth, I never played the original game myself, but I don't particularly get all the negative reviews about the Remake. Concerning the objections to co-op play, I personally feel like it was an amazing addition! Otherwise, I'd have likely never played it or come across it. I don't play solo games often. My preference of game play is either with my wife or our small group of friend that game together. My wife and I looked over the bonus content for the game after completion (In truth I'm not sure it was available prior to completing the game or not - if so I wouldn't view it unless you are up for some serious spoilers), and watched the entire commentary video from Josef Fares. We noted we missed quite a few things and achievements in our play through. We had one crash in our play through. Otherwise everything ran great and it was a beautiful and touching story. There isn't a lot in the way of combat, but my wife and I have played through quite a few puzzle games, and we don't mind that ourselves. If I had to compare it to a game, I'd say it is a lot like a 'choose your own adventure to some extent. There are puzzles you have to make use of both brothers to complete, along with challenges, and a few bosses, but ultimately you don't attack the bosses directly per se. You work together as a family would to over come the obstacles in front of you. The game is unique like many of the other games Josef Fares is involved in. My wife and I were ecstatic to add another game of this caliber to our collection. So long as you are fine with the fact that it is a short adventure, and you enjoy games similar too it, I suspect you'll love Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons Remake.

_childDocuments_.review: Don't be fooled by the title this is not a remake. It may say that in the title but it isn't. The only difference this has from the original is "better graphics," cinematic cut scenes, and a new coop feature so you can play it with two controllers instead of huddling around the keyboard. Also I've heard from other negative reviews that there are many bugs and glitches although I personally haven't experienced any so far. If you have the original or the original is cheaper don't buy this game. The only reason I'm gonna be playing it is so I can play it with my wife.

_childDocuments_.review: Refunded as it doesn't support ultrawide in 2024.It's literally a setting in Unreal Engine "AspectRatioAxisConstraint=AspectRatio_MaintainYFOV" and yet the game doesn't support it nor allow changing it through the config. The aspect ratio is locked at 16:9 with pillar boxed black bars at all times, and it even has letter boxed black bars during cutscenes (Vert- FOV), so double black bars.The game started in fullscreen exclusive and forced 1920x1080 and started an infinite loop of resolution changes on my monitor. I couldn't get out of it if not by pressing ALT+F4.Additionally, the game has a lot of graphical glitches (green pixels), though it's seemengly fixed by toggling HDR off and on? I don't know.

_childDocuments_.review: i cried 11 years ago and i cried again after playing this little emotional roller coaster of a game. its shows just how important music is to a game when there's no real "language" but you can still feel it through the music and emotions of the characters the games controls can take a few minutes to understand but once you do it just clicks really nicely. the game features a nice section of puzzles that aren't hard and offer a nice mild level of difficulty as does the whole journey there's nothing that really stumps you so you can just progress through it at a nice relaxing pace. as for the remake i find the new graphics pretty darn beautiful sure its a totally different take on the original art style but it works in its own way (imo) unreal engine shines nicely on this game and the new added details make the the game come to life kinda like a stop animation style. the game is a nice length at around 3-4 hrs depending if you explore the areas and interact with people and objects so for the low price the game is i highly recommend it. only gripe i have is the game can have some very minor stutters and performance could be better. but man in 4k maxed out on an oled with hdr on it totally shines and is a beautiful experience and with that said i rate this game a 9 out of 10

_childDocuments_.review: The remake is the same great game you remember, but rebuilt in Unreal Engine 5.  Aside from a few quirks, such as brief texture pop-in and a few stutters, it looks great and plays well.  The quirks only showed up in the beginning and seemed to sort itself out as the game went on.The updated visuals enhance the game, and the re-worked cutscenes help sell the great story even more.  Some cutscenes are 60fps while others are 30fps; a bit jarring, but maybe a patch can fix it along with the quirks.I don't think you need to run out and buy it; playing the original still holds up and will work for most people.  The remake is mainly for higher end PCs with NVIDIA 3000 series graphics cards or later (or AMD equivalent).  I have an RTX 4070 and a 12th gen Intel i7 CPU, and at 1440p with high settings and DLSS set to Quality, the ran smooth at a locked 60 fps.  I would also highly recommend using HDR if your monitor/TV supports it as the game looks noticeably better with it on.The remake is nice to have, and if you own the original you get a discount.  Whether you play this or the original, it's terrific and the story will stick with you long after playing.If you're interested, you can check out my video review of the original:

_childDocuments_.review: Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons Remake was great not only for those wanting to revisit the now eleven year old game, but for people like me who never had the pleasure. Sure, the original is still available to this day, but it never came to mind until news of the remake, so why not start there? It was beautiful in terms of visuals and mixed the fantastical with darker themes, sometimes at whiplash speed. It was easy to fall into the wholesome trap only to be reminded of tragedy seconds later. For this reason I didn’t entirely like the ending, “bittersweet” didn’t even begin to cover it. I still feel bummed out.For solo play the controls took some getting used to, but moving the characters individually yet simultaneously with each having their own unique interactions was pretty good—I also appreciated the other little details, such as the little brother being slower.

_childDocuments_.review: Unfortunately I cannot reccomend the game at the current state it is in. No UltraWide screen support and there are several issues with various graphical artefacts on water surfaces and hair textures when the camera is zoomed in up close. Also quite a lot of other bugs, not just graphical rainbow like artefacts and flickering. Performance is not that good aswell, needs a bit of work on the optimization side..It has a nice initial introduction launch price, on top of  -20% sale launch price, they even give you an additional 3.20 € discount for owning the original.But for reasons I described earlier, I cannot reccomend it. The original also looks quite nice, even after a decade. The remake has this weird brownish and yellowish tint/filter.*Edit 3.3.2024curently there is a temporal fix for those that want to play the game in an Ultrawide resolution made by RoseTheFlower Works fine, but you have to run the game in a borderless window.*Edit 28.11.2024even after 8 months after release, they still haven't added the Ultrawide support, but they fixed the various graphical bugs and artifacts . However the game is incredibly taxing to run, even with RTX 4090 and 4K resoluition its unplayable without DLSS on, I think this is a pattern with all the games running on UE5 unfortunately. Without DLSS the game barely is able to reach 60 fps. With DLSS set to quality the game runs from 80 - 140 fps, it fluctuates quite a lot. It's mind boggling considering how the game looks and what is on display here.I love the original, it was one of those games that was personally one of the best games in 2013, but that year some really legendary cult games came out (The Last of Us, GTA V, Tomb Raider, Metro Last light, FC3 BLood Dragon),so it had a really tough time among these games, but to me it still holds a special place in my heart after all these years and I prefer it to this soulless remake, which I haven't played through yet for various particular reasons.

_childDocuments_.review: edit: 7/24/2024 I got a brand new high spec PC and was able to finish the game, thankfully this time it didn't crash after the sequence of rescuing the girl. I would still recommend the original game over this new one, as pretty as it is.as of right now i physically can not complete the game, it refuses to load into the next area after i rescue the girl. i was looking forward to the release of this game as i've played the original (exact same game, just updated onto unreal engine 5) i wish we could take slightly different paths in the game, change a small part of a story and give us two different endings at least with the choices we make as the player, instead of being forced to go down one line.i wish i could not be disappointed in this game, it's visually stunning and the soundtrack is beautiful, both accompanied by a grabbing story that forces you to continue playing with anticipation and curiosity of what happens next. though controlling the two brothers takes some getting used to, which may deter people from playing with how weird it feels to play as both. _childDocuments_.review: Ignore the naysayers, this is a great game, and those who haven't played the original should at least play this. If you played the original and don't like the new look, why even buy it again?I discovered the original game a couple of years ago but never played it because a lot of time had passed already since the release and there was always something more recent in my backlog to play.Now I have played the remake twice or maybe even 2.5 times. I first played it in co-op mode with a friend and then played it in single-player mode. Purists might say that it should be played only in single-player, but I think it's better to share the experience. Both modes have different challenges, one is about trying to control two characters simultaneously, and the other is about communicating your intentions with the other player. After 2 playthroughs, I watched the included "making of" video and then hunted down all the remaining achievements.What has changed over the original? It no longer looks like a cartoon, the textures and levels are more detailed, the lighting is more realistic and the cutscenes are more professional movie-like.

_childDocuments_.review: This version looks gorgeous. Areas and characters look better than ever, new design elements were added to them, and some unvoiced characters have received one. Some scenes were remade, and those are a huge improvement!...but there were some missing voice clips, slight graphical errors and the game even hitches above recommended hardware specs. Music is radically different, some hit a lot less hard during the most important scenes.Would say that the final ~30 minutes of the original are much better, but the first ~2.5 hours are vastly better in the remake. The remake also added a few new cinematic events which I quite liked. These are only a few seconds long at most, and you most likely wouldn't notice unless you played both back-to-back. A lot of them are an improvement to the game.If you have the hardware, play the remake. If not, the original is also arguably just as good. And again, the last two areas are much better there.

_childDocuments_.review: What a gorgeous game this is.It's like entering a potpourri of a classic brother Grimm adventure. The visuals here are... Stunning, because it so perfectly fits the setting. Great animations, fun challenges, touching moments... It's one of those small games that stands as a strong reminder of "AAA addicts" like me to also keep a keen eye on the indie scene.This is why we need that scene, really.I played this game in coop with my daughter, and it works totally fine. However I gotta say that the dual controller implementation is a bit lazy. In single player left side of the controller controls one brother while the right controls the other. And in coop, controller A still has the left side working while controller B has the right side. It just feels weird, they could have made both controllers more natural (move with left stick, right trigger for actions etc).But that's really all I have to say of negative sides of this game.It's a must-buy within their genre.

_childDocuments_.review: I honestly don't get why there are so many complaints here.I managed to finish the whole game in 1080p at 60fps without any frame drop except for the cutscenes (haven't tried 1440p yet). _childDocuments_.review: This Game is awesome! I mean, like if you have played the original; This remake hasn't changed besides the graphics. If you wanted new content; don't buy it. The storyline is an absolute gem—I've lost count of how many times I've immersed myself in it, whether solo or with friends. Sure, it's a bummer that online co-op isn't included, but fear not! With a solid internet connection, you can still share the experience through remote play. Plus, even if you embark on this adventure alone, it's guaranteed to keep you entertained.And let's talk about that soundtrack and storyline—they're simply breathtaking! I absolutely adored the old player models, but let's talk about the landscapes—wow, they're absolutely breathtaking!  And those controls? Sure, they're a tad unconventional at first, but once you get the hang of them, they add a whole new layer of immersion. It's exhilarating to navigate the journey controlling both brothers with such finesse.The controls are unusual because you play the big brother with the right controller side and the little brother with the left. But this isn't quite bad. It's just unusual and sometimes a little bit hard to focus on 2 characters and 2 controller sides. I found myself tearing up nearly every time I played this game.So please, do yourself a favor and give this game the chance it deserves. It might not be the longest experience, but trust me, the beauty of its story will stay with you long after the credits roll. If you crave an adventure that's equal parts thrilling and emotionally resonant, look no further—this game is an absolute must-buy!

_childDocuments_.review: I never played the original so there was no nostalgia or bias toward the more cartoony style. The remake looks fantastic. _childDocuments_.review: Targeting modern PC’s and current consoles, Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons Remake was rebuilt using Unreal 5 to offer striking visual upgrades as well as a newly recorded soundtrack with a live orchestra that elevates the emotions of this game to new heights.  Characters have more complex and emotive faces with moving lips, and environments have been rebuilt with Nanite for increased complex geometry and rendered with stunning new textures.  Animations have been enhanced, specifically character turning, and everything runs silky smooth at 60fps.  At times, the game can easily be confused with a feature animated film when the light and shadows are working just right.  The new Lumen lighting makes the dark forest level even more sinister as you chase off hungry wolves with your torch.  The only critique I have for graphics is that the cutscenes are 30fps and contrast sharply with the gameplay visuals.The developers did a fantastic job of preserving the original material while adding nice flourishes to the overall experience and even a couple of new achievements.  One of the more controversial decisions was to add a true co-op feature which, in my opinion, negates the core design philosophy of the game and totally impacts that “one emotional moment” at the end of the game.  Apparently, a lot of people were playing the original Brothers by both using a single controller, so the devs just added a true co-op mode and thanks to Remote Play Together you can now play this couch co-op game remotely.  I can certainly see the appeal, and playing co-op will definitely shift the focus from manual dexterity to cooperative conversation.Simply put, if you enjoyed the original then you are going to love this masterfully crafted remake that takes all the heart and soul from an already amazing adventure and turns it up to eleven.Read the full review at More Steam reviews on our Curator page -

_childDocuments_.review: Breathtaking Revival of a Classic TaleThe remake of Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons stands not only as a testament to the original's heartfelt storytelling but also as a beautiful homage that builds on its legacy with modernized graphics and gameplay. This re-imagined adventure, deeply rooted in Nordic folklore, unfolds with a fresh coat of visual beauty that breathes new life into the enchanting world. The art direction is nothing short of magical, capturing the essence of a fairy tale that deserves to be retold. I can't help but bring up the delightful encounter with an oddly charming 'punk rocker looking' troll early in the game—an addition that is both whimsical and touching. Connecting with such characters enriches the experience, making it feel like a living storybook that's unfolding right before your eyes.The puzzles within this world are cleverly designed, providing the right balance of challenge and ingenuity without creating a sense of urgency that detracts from the narrative. It's this pacing that allows you to truly absorb every element, from the rustling leaves in the mythical forests, the eerily beautiful ruins of long-forgotten civilizations, to the countless individual and environment encounters you can engage with. One such encounter unlocks an achievement by picking up a sheep and spinning around with it in your arms until it barfs!For sure the harmony of the controls truly sets the game apart; the innovative mechanics have you maneuver two brothers simultaneously, forging a connection between player and characters that is rare and profound. (AND IT'S CO-OP!) It's a game that knows the power of its story and the strength of its silent moments of bonding, grief, and triumph."Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons" is a masterfully crafted story experience. Whether you're returning to relive the adventure or stepping into the shoes of the brothers for the first time, this remake is an invitation to an odyssey that will tug at your heartstrings and ignite your imagination.

_childDocuments_.review: Check out my full review on YouTube! Please note I refunded the game on Steam and completed the rest of the game on PS5. Full details explained in the video :)Let me first agree with the litany of steam reviews saying if you have already played the original, there is not much more here for you. But if you are fresh to the game, then you need to work out what kind of experience you are after. If you are prepared to go through boring chore work and traversing for some not new, but touching ideas and concepts, then this might be for you. But it gets complicated when you add in that 2nd player.I believe when you add in the second player, whilst it improves the gameplay, it may impact how you receive the story. I will admit when I was playing this game with my brother, we were cracking jokes, laughing and at some points not really taking it seriously, whereas I feel if I was playing by myself, then I might have been more receptive to some of those tones and themes. But the paradox is if I was playing by myself, then I wouldn’t have bothered finishing the game. Now A Ways Out and It Takes Two found ways to do it, those games you have to play with two people and in both my playthroughs of those games, one being with my brother, we both felt that core impact in the message the game was presenting. Thankfully at the $30 price tag, I think those themes are worth exploring and despite the dated feel, Brothers still will make you stop, question and cherish aspects of your own life and perhaps spark an appreciation for the things or people that matter most to you. Yes there are some gameplay obstacles and a paradox to navigate as both modes to play the game come with their compromises, but if you have a couple hours to spare and a little bit of patience, Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons the Remake will reward you for the time you took to listen and understand the values enshrined in this acquired taste of video game art.

_childDocuments_.review: The main draw of this remake compared to the original isn't the visuals, in my opinion. It does look gorgeous, and I think it's a genuine noticeable improvement both in terms of the graphical quality and the emotional impact of certain cutscenes, but what the original lacked in raw technology it made up for with an art style that I think holds up relatively well for what it is. To me, the new appeal of this game is in the addition of the local co-op mode. It does make the game a lot easier when you don't have to coordinate the brothers yourself (it sometimes starts to feel a bit more like a narrative game than a puzzle platformer), but I found myself surprised at how well it worked, and it reminded me more of the games Hazelight would go on to make than I realized back when I first played this. I don't think this game requires co-op in the same way that A Way Out or It Takes Two do, but it's more viable than I thought it would be.In either case, whether you play the remake or the original or singleplayer or co-op, Brothers is a fantastic game that I'm happy to return to, particularly since I think it was kind of overlooked in comparison to their later games. But I should warn that from what I'm seeing from the other reviews, the optimization here is extremely rough. I'm running a 4070 ti so I didn't have any issues, but I also averaged at around 70 fps even with DLSS, and the game in general seems heavily CPU-bound. If you don't have a considerably strong PC, it might be good to wait for updates, if they come; until then, there's no shame in sticking to the original.

_childDocuments_.review: The original  is one of my favorite games. Despite the clunky controls, the rich art and music, vibrant world, beautiful story, and one of the most brilliant marriages of mechanics and narrative I can think of made the experience extremely memorable. Was it a game that particularly needed a remake? Not really. So how does the remake measure up? Overall, fine, though I wouldn't call it a straight upgrade. The environments and the lighting look gorgeous, but in some places they've lost some of the style of the original. The soundtrack, too, sounds wonderful independently, but in some places it sounds a little too grand for the story. The biggest detractor from the remake is the new character models, which don't really suit the game or the story. The best thing the remake did is improve mouse and keyboard controls, which work much better than they did in the original. I enjoyed my time with the remake, but overall I think the original was the superior experience--minus the frustrating mouse and keyboard controls of the original.

_childDocuments_.review:
With their father suffering from a deadly illness, two brothers must bravely set out to find the "Water of Life," the one cure that can save him. With no option for failure the brothers must rely on each other using their individual skills to protect one another and overcome the obstacles ahead in this unforgettable journey.

Hailed by critics when it was originally released, Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons is back! Faithful to the gameplay and touching story from 2013, Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons Remake features rebuilt characters and landscapes based on the original and has been updated to the latest generation of graphics, performance, and gameplay. Paired with a re-recorded soundtrack with a live orchestra, prepare for an emotional experience that will take your adventure to all new heights.

detailed_description: After half a millennium of peace, a new danger hangs over Antala. Its fate depends on you, Imë, Lysfanga of the New Kingdom, protector of the realm. The ancient cities, previously locked in time, are now free again, and an old evil has escaped, threatening the peace. But you won’t be alone. Gifted with temporal powers from the Goddess of Time herself, something no other Lysfanga has had before, you have the ability to rewind time in combat to summon clones of your past-selves to help you. Master your power to become legion, and crush hordes of the escaped demons, known as the Raxes . With your army of past-selves , progress through the ancient cities to extend your arsenal of weapons and learn new spells, preparing for the much greater threat ahead... Use Imë’s godlike powers to rewind time a few seconds in the past and summon clones of yourself – remnants – to create an army and overpower your enemies. Challenge your skills and your wits to outdo yourself. Master and replay each arena to beat your high scores, and challenge yourself by changing the difficulty settings and adding combat modifiers to unlock new rewards. Each arena can be approached in countless ways. Adapt your strategy and use all the tools at your disposal to emerge victorious. Success will only depend on your combination of remnants, spells and weapons. The old time-locks are gone. The Raxes are now free to create chaos again. Explore the abandoned cities of the old continent previously locked in time and uncover the truth behind the resurgence of the Raxes.

_childDocuments_.review: I was hyped for this after seeing the reveal at last year's Gamescom but after finishing the main story I'm fairly disappointed. The game does some things well: the world-building and lore are fantastic and add a lot of life to the game, and the resulting plot of ancient rival kingdoms and the conclusion to centuries-old grudges is also quite engaging. The gameplay concept of hack and slash meets strategy with time-shifting mechanics to solve puzzles is also great on paper. Where I feel the game lacks overall is in its execution. The aforementioned plot is brought down by lifeless characters and stilted, oftentimes 'gamey', dialogue, and the gameplay falls into this awkward middle ground between its two genre inspirations, not leaning enough into either to feel particularly rewarding. Other than being able to survey the battlefield arenas before a fight there are no features to allow you to deeply strategise (things like being able to pause and zoom out to see where and what your remnants are doing as a potential example of something that would help), and because arenas are time gated and set up as puzzles the hack and slash elements are restricted. Another fault lies in how utterly repetitive the game gets. Exploring feels unrewarding due to generic collectables and linear-level design, so all that's left is arenas and combat that play out similarly each time. It's a shame too as the art style and levels look gorgeous, and when the combat deviates from its basic premise, like in the boss fights, it can be incredibly fun. Overall a lot of cool ideas, just lacking the execution for me, but worth a buy if you know you enjoy the combat as there is a good bit of depth in the game with varying levels of goals and challenges to aim for.

_childDocuments_.review: Lysfanga: The Time Shift Warrior is an . But it’s also a game that , since that’s firmly where the core of its gameplay lies.So first things first: I’m seeing lots of people compare this game to other games which I think have very little in common with Lysfanga. Some expect it to be an isometric action RPG like  or . This is not the case, as  instead of being randomised or procedurally generated. Other people compare Lysfanga to , which is perhaps even more confusing, since   (from the same developers as ). Much like , Lysfanga is all about following mostly linear paths from one combat arena to the next, and all fights are essentially handcrafted combat puzzles that task you with dispatching your enemies in the most efficient way possible. Both games are also :Fights in Lysfanga are  featuring a bunch of enemies with unique gameplay mechanics – some of them carry heavy shields which make them invulnerable from the front, others are magically connected in pairs of two so both enemies have to be killed at roughly the same time or else they’ll revive, and so on. . You can repeat this multiple times, creating more and more ‘remnants’ of yourself, until you’ve reached the maximum number (which can be further increased with collectibles). So now you can spend one loop getting the attention of the large shield-bearing enemies, and use your second incarnation to backstab that same enemy while they’re distracted by your previous self. The gameplay loop repeats for every combat encounter: .Now, normally I’m the kind of player who quickly gets tired of constant combat in games, and I usually prefer my combat to be more organic, with enemies roaming the world instead of being corralled into self-contained arenas. But Lysfanga does enough to keep me entertained and motivated throughout, by giving me lots of  to flesh out the story and setting, as well as some collectibles to hunt. Sure, , but the storytelling and easy-to-find collectibles create just about enough variety to tide me over. As should have become clear by now, however, this is very much a ‘your mileage may vary’ situation and I can absolutely see how the formulaic arena-hallway-arena-hallway structure of the game may become tedious to other players. Worst-case, you don’t even like the idea of the time loop mechanic that’s so central to the game, at which point I’d say Lysfanga is a definite ‘pass’ for you, because that’s pretty much the entire gameplay right there.But if time loop puzzle fights sound interesting to you and you don’t need much more than some collectibles and story dialogue for variety, . Having played the original Itch.io build from when the game was a humble student project (called “Lysfangha” instead of “Lysfanga: The Time Shift Warrior” – I can see the SEO and PR teams hard at work there), I’m doubly impressed by how they managed to take their already gorgeous visuals and their interesting gameplay idea, and turn them into a full-fledged game with a constant drip of story segments as well as new abilities, weapons, and enemies to keep you entertained. That alone may be enough reason to support a fledgling development studio, and let’s be honest: Many other small studios have also started by focusing on perfecting a very limited set of gameplay systems instead of going for massively complex games for their first outing ( comes to mind, since I’ve already name-dropped  and  here). Who knows where Sand Door Studios may be headed if Lysfanga sells well enough...

_childDocuments_.review: Under a hundred steam reviews on a game of this quality is really quite saddening to see. This is a good little combat puzzler with an interesting world with lots of lore to read, a pleasant, adventurous atmosphere and some solid time loop gameplay as you and your copies run around defeating enemies as fast as possible.If it suffers from anything (other than being completely overlooked), it's how it feels like a game of two halves, and they don't always complement each other in the best ways. There's the story, cutscenes and exploring the environments for upgrade spheres, bits of lore and new outfit colours. It's all pleasant and interesting enough, if maybe not the most gripping and sharply written stuff. It's got an air of a saturday morning cartoon, a kind of "we can do this, together!" tone that can be both endearing and a little on the nose in equal measures. I appreciate it avoids going for too much melodrama, and a hopeful, positive tone is definitely welcome.The other half, the thing that really makes the game special, is the combat puzzles, but if you are following the first half, the narrative, you will just bash your head against each encounter, mashing away at enemies, taking hits, dying, looping again, until you either run out of copies and have to restart the encounter, or you eventually clear it.But in order to really make the mechanics of the game sing, you need to play, and replay each encounter until you reach the presented par times. These really bring forth how carefully planned each encounter actually is, and how much depth all of your abilities and skills have. Each encounter adds a new skill or a new enemy type or some new twist to shake things up. Playing for the par times really pushes you to plan your routes carefully, requiring clever use of timing, placement and the kind of 5-dimensional chess stuff you'd only expect in the weirdest, most demanding indie puzzlers. Destroy this thing here, so that it opens a gate for your next copy to dash past to get to the exploding enemy sooner, so you can launch it against another group of enemies you will be fighting with your third copy, which will free up the crystal your fourth and fifth copy can destroy together before the fifth one can join the second one and distract the shielded enemy for the fourth copy can smash through the other crystal and-" and it's really compelling stuff. It's just that it gets really tough, and it can be exhausting after several of them back to back. And so you kind of end up with a choice: do you proceed with the story, intending to maybe replay previous fights later for the par times? Ignoring the par times and just going for normal completion means the combat encounters can start feeling repetitive and more than a little annoying interruptions when you're trying to just get on with the plot. Ignoring the par times, there is no challenge really, you just run against the wall until you clear it. OR do you grind story progress to a complete halt, embrace the robust play mechanics and really learn and route every encounter to get the most out of the gameplay and reach those par times? You risk exhausting yourself, but it's a more rewarding game to PLAY. It's just that there is a LOT of encounters.So it's hard. I don't know how to solve that problem, and neither did the team. They chose, probably very wisely, to let you take everything at your own pace, and hope you will have a good enough time to want to engage with the deeper mechanics when going for the par times later. By request the team updated the game and added online leaderboards for comparing and competing for the best times in each encounter. They even added even more optional challenges for replaying past fights, with additional modifiers, enemies and tricks. If you don't exhaust yourself, there is a wealth of stuff to play, but if you're just trying to "get on with it" a lot of that feels like it's just in the way.So it's not perfect, but it has a lot of love put into it, and I have to stress how rewarding reaching those par times is. I hope the team gets to make another game, I'd love to see what they do next.7/10

_childDocuments_.review: First and foremost the bulk of the content should be taken more as a puzzle combat game, and less as a sheer mechanical skill check. I thoroughly enjoyed routing each encounter and pushing the times below the challenge benchmarks, and hope to continue my time perfecting every encounter to reach 100% completion.There is mechanical skill, but it honestly is much of a side factor compared to the strategy and planning each encounter demands you do. The move set of each weapon is individually simple, but combined with the large quantity of different active and passive abilities to choose from it leads to many interesting approaches for each combat encounter. --  in particular is worth calling out, as once unlocked it opens up huge depth to how you can interact with the time-loop mechanic. It was my go-to active for the majority of the game.Other elements of the game are serviceable for what they are; the story gets fairly predictable, the characters are tolerable enough, and the environments look good, albeit slightly irritating to navigate at times.The largest disappointment with the game I had was the "Motes of Magic" system, which are collectible items you can pick up throughout your whole journey. They are entirely useless until around half way through the game, when you recruit a smith. -- I expected these to be another form of character upgrade to reward diligentexploring, but ultimately they ended up just being purely cosmetic. The game already had completely separate cosmetic collectibles. Why bother making two entirely separate and conflicting systems for cosmetics?Overall, I highly recommend Lysfanga.

_childDocuments_.review: At the time of reviewing I'm not too far in, but I think I'm ready to give my thoughts! Once I finish the game I might put an edit at the end if my opinion changes further in. Honestly? Pretty solid game! There's definitely some parts that are more rough around the edges, but I'd say the good absolutely outweighs the bad! I'd give about an 8 out of 10 on the whole.Incredible. A good gameplay loop is a top priority for me in games, and Lysfanga does not disappoint. I'll admit that I picked up this game primarily because its combat kinda looked like Hades and I wanted to play something Hades-like that... wasn't Hades (I play too much Hades lol—also go play Hades it's good). There's definitely some superficial similarities to Hades in Lysfanga's action elements (two different attacks, a cast, dashes, and a call) but in practice it plays completely differently—in a very good way.This is obviously due in part to the headlining time-shift mechanic. It lets you replay the same battle scenario over and over as your Remnants perfectly replicate your prior movements, allowing you to tackle other new areas while they handle the work you've already completed, which by itself would be an interesting gimmick.However, it's the hard work that the developers put into the   that elevate the time-shift mechanic out of gimmick territory into something...  I can identify 2 things in particular that contributed to this: handcrafted encounters and the timed challenges.Each and every encounter in the game is entirely built by the developers. This means that instead of enemies being placed haphazardly or procedurally,  is placed with a purpose. This, combined with the fact that each encounter has an optional time challenge (which I consider required for optimal enjoyment), means that you really have to strategize about where you go, who you hit, how you hit them, and when you do all of this. You can't really afford to just mindlessly go to the nearest enemy: you have to think about it.   is what makes the game so good. There's a kind of cerebral satisfaction that I get when I'm on the last loop of a really hard room and you see all of your Remnants go and expertly take down an entire army of monsters at once  within the time limit that I haven't gotten from another game before. This game struggles with crashing the most out of any game I've played. To be fair, the games I play are usually polished very, very well so I might not be the right person to ask, but it is enough to be bothersome. My issues usually happen while menuing—if I switch too fast between the menu and gameplay or in a specific spot, the game crashes. My rig is no slouch either, so I doubt it's a hardware issue. There are also a couple of occasional framerate issues; for example, there's an area early on where there's a wall with a few waterfalls coming out, and I went from a smooth 60 fps to chugging at 25. The environments are actually quite pretty, for the most part! I'd say that my big issue with them is the fact that they feel WAY more constrictive than I think they should. Sometimes I think "oh I want to go look over there", but then there's this convenient pile of rubble and tables blocking the stairs. It kind of breaks immersion for me because it reminds me that it's not a real game world: it's just a path from point A to point B. This isn't always the case though—occasionally the game rewards you for going off the beaten path, but then it just feels like that's the only reason you were supposed to go off the path at all. Idk, I feel weird about this, take it however you will.This is an opinion from early gameplay, but I get the feeling that the rest of the game is like this.Hit and miss here. Sometimes it's done well, sometimes not. I have gotten a couple of laughs out of the intentionally funny bits though! To be honest I'm not terribly invested in the story yet, but who knows, maybe it'll get better? This is a bit of a downer, because gameplay and story are both really big elements for me. Here's hoping hahaDefinitely recommend this from what I've seen so far! Not a perfect game, but creative and ingenuitive in ALL the right ways. With a bit of bug-fixing and optimization, I could recommend it a little more strongly.

_childDocuments_.review: This thumbs up comes with a word of warning - AMD video card users need to be wary, as there is currently an issue that can cause the game to crash in menus from time to time on 6000/7000 cards (had it crash my video card drivers over 10 times over the course of completing the game, necessitating a system reset each time) - wager this will be fixed with patches eventually (hopefully), so be sure to check any upcoming patch notes.As for the actual game, outside of that issue, and why I give it a thumbs up - it is actually a decent game, with an okay story, if you're looking for what amounts to essentially an action puzzler (aRPG combat, with more 'puzzle-like' combat arenas) - I also hope that some of the weird gremlin bugs (ie bugs that are hard to reproduce) are fixed in the future too - namely a bug with a unit called "boombats" that makes them malfunction on death (getting stuck in dying animation, rather than doing their death explosion effects - and can sometimes result in them flying weird directions), as well as the game sometimes forgetting an enemy got killed, even if you avoid interacting with it in future loops.Neither were super consistent, and I was unable to find a specific, repeatable, trigger for them, but they were there.Game will take 7-12 hours to reach the credits on a casual playthrough, but some people will sink a lot more in it to get all the achievements and extra bits and bobs for 100%. _childDocuments_.review: For the love of god let us skip Cut scenes, and stop wrestling control from me every 5 steps, also while i appreciate that you want us to look around a arena before the fight starts dont do it, it completely takes you out of the moment if we fail the time limit because we cant preview the arena thats fine, you actually did a really good thing by putting the fragments to try again either in the arena or close by so they are supper easy to get to, and we are not punished for failing the time limit so lean into the fact that those 2 parts of your design are good and just let the game flow naturally until THE player decides to slow it down and do extra stuff. _childDocuments_.review: A really nice game. The gameplay is easy to pick up and very effective. _childDocuments_.review: TL;DR Well worth your time - smart, fun, detailed, gorgeous, and makes you focus on your timing and combat execution as much as your movement and routing across multiple runs through a single encounter.I came into this from a quick brush with the trailers thinking it was Super Time Force x Hades, but left my first (short) session with it suitably impressed with what it is instead: an action puzzler where the goal is to work through each independent, hand-crafted combat puzzle in as little real-world time as possible. No randomization or rogue-lite/light elements (so far), no stacking up well-placed "remnants" to nuke a boss in record time (again, I'm barely clear of the tutorial here), but instead it has you focus on movement, combo execution, and manual rewinds to keep your total real-world time under each encounter's par. It feels almost closer to a more level-based speedrun game like Neon White in general structure and goals. The leaderboards for this will be crazy once people really get their hands on this.

_childDocuments_.review: The premise for this game is so simple, yet so brilliant, that it hooked me right from the first trailer, then the demo, and the game itself. This is a game to hone your skills, like Ghostrunner, Hollow Knight, Katana Zero, Commandos, etc.The game is very tactical. Some kind of 1-character DotA with a Commandos-like pre-game analysis phase and Katana Zero post-game analysis. It is not just one gimmick, though. New game mechanics will keep coming up, adding more and more depth till the end, so it doesn't get repetitive. If you like to repeat a boss or a challenge, you can, you can even play an 'enhanced' version of the fight if you want to practice.As the story goes, Imë, an iron-abs Eastern-looking woman who would give Krishna a run for his money, but with a very British accent, goes on an adventure. In which she can spawn multiple images of herself to do her job in parallel, perhaps a not so different dynamic compared to the modern iron-abs British lady life. She has an even more British-accented brother, who she will try to save from some dark web things, and between fights and sips of Earl Grey, they will meet ferocious magical (but very Britishly polite) beasts. She will also eat nuts which she will crack with her abs.The discoverability of this game has been very bad. My favourite game of the year so far, and hard to imagine a game along these lines coming up anytime soon. Yet I haven't seen it in any trending or top 10 of any kind, buried below the mountains of anime nonsense. I just wish this game gets the recognition it deserves.

_childDocuments_.review: Lysfanga is a rundimentary top down Action-Hack'Slay, with the typical what I would call "blink combat" fighting system. Your natural dodge is a short teleport, besides this, there is not that much going for it. You unlock 3 weapons over the course of the game with basic combo potential and one secondary attack as well unique properties. The sword & shield is the only weapon that can stun enemies for a split second, the Chakrams can be thrown and do great AoE-dmg if the the normal attack is pressed right when the charkam was catched again and the trident has a storable ranged AoE attack, that need to be charged first by quick normal attacks.Overall the weapons are well balanced and there is an justification for all of them I thought the trident you unlock last might be very strong with it's piercing attacks, but it's biggest downside is it's aim, as all attacks have auto-attraction to the closest enemy, while the spear has the lowest wide range of all weapons.This is a solid foundation albeit still quite simplistic, but that basically suffices, there is a customizable component as well, you have one additional magic attack with an cooldown that can be swapped between battles, one ultimate attack (where you have to fill up an bar) and an passive perk, that gives you one advantage like making more damage from behind and such shenanigans.I think the game pretty much nailed the right amount of simplicity, so it doesn't overload you cognitively if you try to accomplish the tasks which the premise of the game provides.You have only about 20 seconds to kill all enemies on the field. Since that doesn't suffice, you're able to go back in time. Yet your past self will remain as an clone unhindered by the present, yet able to damage the enemies, your player performance was recorded and is executed again, now it's on you to kill the remaining enemies called "Raxes".Basically this results in two interesting tasks, for one you have be wary not to distract the beaten enemies, so the past can play out unhindered and second: you have to fully utilize this abilitiy to kill the Raxes as optimized as possible, reducing the downtime to an minimum, basically at best letting all cycles end at the same time with no buffers between.With that in mind a more complex combat system would highly detract from the more puzzle/tactical orientated approach. Enemies are simple and serve to create an interesting level layout to untangle. So if you expect an combat heavy game isometrical game you will be probably disappointed, you are so under time pressure, that you're rather relieved if you kill the enemies as fast as possibe.Unfortunelately that also means you can never really adore your elegantly planned out route, since the game has no replay function or at least an end result where you can watch your temporal clones working together.The first levels are quite simple and like it should be in all games, each of the 3 worlds slowly ramps up the difficulty, new enemy types will be introduced, some of them are more sturdy and dangerous (you can still die, which just ends the current cycle and starts the next one) but most of them serve an purpose that forces you to consider the order how you kill the enemies. Like there are "Twins" who need be killed relatively close within an 3 seconds timespan or Raxes with huge shields who can be only killed efficiently if they are are distracted by a past clone or if you use up an ultimate attack. This will always force the player to carefully lay out their path and incrementally new elements will be introduced even near the end of the game.While I really like complex game mechanics it also comes with a detriment as I thought that the later levels became quite straining, there was so much to consider, that each level took me some time, it's not a game where you can just turn your brain off as well one where you most likely won't succeed the first time... well at least if you try to accomplish the "par times".Actually the game is quite easy, almost trivial if you merely play for the storyline, since you can only truly die if all your "remnants" are used up. These are the amount of clones you can create when rewinding the time, and the numbers increases steadily at the end of the game you have 15 clones, So you have to become hit 30 times at minimum until you die and then the whole screen is already crowded with clones doing 14 times the damage. I think the par times are there to make the game more interesting with actual time requirements, otherwise you can play as sloppy as you want. Though asides from achievements there are no further stipulations for the time requirments and most of the time they still felt rather benelovent. Just low enough to require you to fully utilize the level layout, but high enough that you didn't really have to optimize the right approach. This makes the early levels really underwhelmingly easy with par times beat about under 20 seconds and more, the later levels yet will be a bit harder, since they are just more complex and like I said complex to a straining level.At some point there are enemies, you have to kill twice, respawning at another place, shields you have to deactivate first, switching polarities each cycle, enemies that can be only killed if you killed other enemies, enemies only vulnerable to specific weapons, closed gates, alternating gates, yada yada yada, and each of it eventually becomes topped on another, at some point there are even vertical stages where you can't see the whole layout at once. It's quite rewarding when you figure it out, but sometimes it also feels quite exhausting considering the game doesn't have much else besides it's combat.Yes the game consists basically of almost 100 combat encounters scattered across 3 worlds, you progress linear going from one arena to another, between them there are basically just some forked paths with pretty useless collectibles strewn across (that are sometimes really hard to see depending on the color palette)No puzzles, no plattforming, only sometimes dialouges. So it's basically just one arena combat after another, with walking sequences and some story in between. (which I won't comment on I liked it for what it was, bu the character limit of reviews is pretty dense you know?)Considering this, winning one fight with a really complex layout will just lead you 1 minute later to another even more complex fight with even more intricate layout, as such I could only play the game in small bursts. People nowadays ♥♥♥♥ on "variety" in combat focused games like god of war and so on, but basically this game proves why it's important to keep some downtime between tense moments. Halfway throughout the game you will unlock the "Figments of Battle" these are basically the best part of the game. Yet part of me wished I could've done them from the get go, the game has a lot of levels, yet to fully master it, you have to redo them now on more tight specifications, measuring not just your time but also the amounts of remnants you required and the effiency. It's great because each levels comes with modifiers that make these old stages quite interesting so I understand why you have to unlock this mode first. It's only that it's just too much considering how long the base game took. I S-Ranked 30 of them for story reasons (great idea to have one last stipulation at the end to clear them) but now I feel I really need a break, considering how much I still have before me, with almost no tangible rewards.Reaching the end of the review character limit 2 remaining remarks:- The bosses were awesome, I wish there were more of them, really great design!- Some abilities still seem a little unbalanced and slightly overpowered (Goddess Blades giving you invulerability, 50% speed perk)Overall splendid Core-Gameplay, just could need more variety. Yet I love the high skill ceiling the FoB's provide. At some point I will probably return to this.

_childDocuments_.review: The game knows what it wants to do, and does it really well. First few arenas are just to help the player wrap the head around fighting within consecutive timeloops, and then the things begin to get complicated. Every 2-3 arenas a new mechanic is being introduced, making the fights more like puzzles than just hack and slash. Still you need to hack and slash and dodge fast, if you want to make it to the end of each loop and milk every second of each run on the arena count.The graphics are nice, the story is nothing very special, but it's not what the game's about. It makes you feel very, very smart at the beginning, and then incredibly stupid by the end, when you cannot figure out how to master your moves on arenas so complicated, you need to spend some serious time assessing, how you want to approach the monster / environment / variable powers scenario.Last few fights got me terribly frustrated but just because I was to tired to understand, how various mechanics introduced earlier lock with each other. The game was always fair, and the difficulty level is being increased steadily, to reach unfathomable heights by the end.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall I recommend the game, the time shift mechanic is pretty unique and fun. Took me a little over 7 hours to beat the story so I personally don't recommend getting it at full price, wait for a sale. Game is a little to easy, as long as you explore and upgrade how many clones you have its near impossible to fail levels. Biggest con is that the mouse cursor color is very similar to the environments so there will be moments where you lose track of where your mouse isThe combat puzzles don't get that complicated until the last few levels but by then you already have a lot of clones so its hard to fail.Replay ability is pretty much replaying levels to beat your old time or trying harder versions of existing levels. There isn't an upgrade system to work towards.Story is passable, I don't recommend getting this just for story.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is awesome. It is not a hack'n'Slash. It is a puzzle fighting strategy game. That'ts it. The story is OK. I can't understand why some reviews are pointing this out when it clearly shows (everywhere) that this is a PUZZLE game with combat. The only thing I think they should've added was a way to us PLAYERS to compete with our steam friends (or a dev time)  to see who did the best time. it could have been PLUS for those who wants to compare their times.Also, the game reminds me so much of LARA CROFT : guardian of light. It has a little of exploration. This game could easily be a totally different game. YET for what it is. Its a good game. But It definitely could be more. Is it fun? YES. Does it worth its price? I guess, but a discount is welcome.ART is beautiful (but nothing WOW)Environment is AMAZINGGameplay is fluid and easy ( the more you go in, the "harder" it goes)Sound effects are OKStory is below average but nothing horrible

_childDocuments_.review: In Persona 3, be it FES or Reload, you cannot say it didn't make you cry or feel sad and happy at the same time. I could talk about the game for the same amount of playtime i have on this version of it, but I'll try to keep this review relatively short. This game is beautiful has engaging turn based (1-more system) combat, cool cutscenes, improved stories and details (especially at the end). Also, it has a little different of an identity you could say, so playing FES or Portable too before or after is recommended. The game doesn't try to replace the old versions, but to bring new people, make veterans remember and play it in a new refreshing way and expand on a few concepts. It's an absolute Masterpiece that every person who has the time (and shouldn't be doing anything else) should play or at least watch the movies or read the story. Trust me. Its might change your life a bit, for the better (that is if you open your heart to what the game has to say to you). It normally does not involve religion, but some of  the same messages can be found in those. You can play the game as an Atheist and still get something useful. Overall 9.9/10 since there will never be a PERFECT game, only really good games (PERFECT games revolve around a person's point of view about his memories with it. I'm still young and i was not even born when the game first came out (2006) so i think my opinion about it is not biased. Do yourself a favor and find a way to experience the story, and if you can, buy this game. You won't regret it (on a sale).

_childDocuments_.review: I just beat it and I'm not sure if I like this as much or a bit less than P4. Quite frankly the ironing out my issues with the battle system (a bit too much honestly, the game was a bit of a cake walk) helped a lot in terms of enjoyment for me. On top of fixes, the new systems added made mounting tartarus a bit less of a drag to be honest. Also I'm not sure if the script has been rewritten significantly, cause I'm not a persona 3 expert, but the characters seem a whole lot more fleshed out this time around. I find the only one who I don't exactly find more enamoring is Akihiko. He's still the same character with the same story beats and growth, but it culminates in a character much more focused on strength and training. Which was always a part of his character, but they've shifted it to be his main characteristic. Which they've been doing since arena, BUT it's not to the point of making him annoying like it was in arena or Q2. (can't speak on q) Still a likeable and more than adequate character that appeals to the same fans but a bit less complex. If you like him, I recommend checking out the movies or his social link from Portable. Regardless, still definitely the definitive way to play 3.

_childDocuments_.review: Persona 3 Reload breathes a breath of fresh air into the classic pulling Persona 3 into Atlus's current standard and aesthetic of "Persona" games even outdoing Persona 5 in a couple small, but noticeable ways... all while maintaining a lot of smaller details that hearken to Persona 3's original identity. _childDocuments_.review: I don't care that it's not the most definitive version of P3. This game was literally all I could've asked for and more. I loved every second of it. The game so perfectly captures the dread of death... the realization, the build up, and then the release when you finally have to let go. I, of course, wish we got the more complete version of the game and I think the "Expansion Pass" is pretty scummy, but I didn't get to experience this game the first time around. This game, in its most bare bones form, is better than any game I've played that's released this decade. The combat is amazing. Never has it felt so good to hit an enemy with debilitate, grind buffs and de-buffs and go in for the kill. I'm not sure what it is, since the combat is essentially a less-advanced version of P5R's, but almost every fight was an absolute joy. While I've heard from other fans that the difficulty felt too easy, I'm honestly not quite sure what they're talking about. The combat felt very balanced for me. For the first time throughout my tenure with the series, I've actually felt like I wanted to get into fights simply for the satisfaction of defeating difficult shadows.EDIT: Sega/Atlus decided to change the terms used to market the Premium Edition of the game some time before the Expansion Pass released but some time after most people bought the game so a majority of players are now discovering they must spend an additional $35 on top of the $100 they spent on the Premium Edition in order to get all the DLC for the game, despite the game's listing clearly stating otherwise. DO NOT BUY.I want the game to win awards but I hate the publisher still.

_childDocuments_.review: Why do you live? For what reason do you live, knowing that the inevitable end will arrive upon you on a certain day? In that regard, the arrival of the certain day will differ between people. How would you confront the distinct vicissitude of life, towards the inescapable end of the people around you? Will you fall into despair, directing your way to nihilism until the fated day? Or, will you press on regardless, believing that your actions may be of positive impact towards someone's continued life, no matter how minuscule the spark may be?This game encapsulates the fragility life may be for a certain someone. For how we wished for their story to continue; For how we wished they would know the transformation the life of the people they had impacted; For how we wished that we could converse with them once more. It truly does show that to those that continue to live on after the fated end of one they hold dear- that life is truly fragile relative to the clockworks of time. The connections you make throughout your stages of life; at the end of the road, will they all be meaningless due to the knowledge of the certainty of the end? Or, will they sincerely become significant due to burning away all dread and flourishing each day of life? In each and every encounters and goodbyes, it matters not for the strength and severity of the bond built upon. Surely, they will all become the backbone of what you define "meaning" in building up the foundation of living a sincere life.20 February 2017 was a day I truly resonated with a moment of the narrative of this game. For one of the characters, it felt as if I was them. Their wavering emotions on that day. The suddenness of it all. The end to all that was once there. Disbelief. Exasperation. Contemplation. Sorrow. Prevail. For what was worth undertaking, the leftovers of those who continue to live must carry on to prosper their remaining days in sincerity. At least, that was what I had done and will continue doing after that fated day.Persona 3 (OG, P, FES, R) will remain as the best JRPG of all time to me as it has always managed to convey a chronicle that the players will eventually have to confront during their lifetime. The acceptance of losing someone. The regrets of those continuing on. For if not unto themselves, the everlasting impact will surely be felt by those around them. I believe so. Because; The arcana is the means by which all is revealed.PEAK/10.

_childDocuments_.review: Persona 3 Reload is a superb remake of the original game. You can feel it everywhere, even if you've never played the original just like myself. The pacing is terrible... seriously.... from like 1/4-1/3-rd of the game its awful grind in the worst way. However its an easy grind, its very easy if you have any understanding on the SMT core gameplay mechanics... but even with the improvements its pale shallow what you can do in the overwrold and the underworld respectively comparted to P5.... its a very good retrospective on where the series come from and what does it excels in as I strongly believe there's none better than Atlus who can make such stellar JRPGs et all.... Sure, they had a rendered cutscene, but it just isn't the same. The remixed songs have mostly been not great, which is a shame because I really enjoyed the original's soundtrack. I'm mostly fine with the art direction, however, not drawing the protagonist's clothes feels lazy. There's just a shadow over the clothes. Also, there still isn't a definitive way to play this game, which a remake should have fixed. There's no female protagonist option, no The Answer, and no Desert of Doors. Junpei doesn't sound as good or as young as he did in the original game. I'm going to continue to play the game because the frustrating thing about FES and the original was not being able to control your party members and this game gives you that, but so does Portable. _childDocuments_.review: I played this game a couple months after I experienced the loss of a friend. I was starting to feel really apathetic about life, and decided to spend my time with a new game. I was already familiar with the Persona series and knew that this one touched on themes that might feel relevant. That's how I found it. At it's core, the game is a fun action rpg social simulator with astounding music and fantastically funny and dramatic voice acting. It's characters are endearing and enjoyable to watch. The finer points of this game's narrative feature it's characters suffering the death of someone close. It is not a perfect representation of the grieving process, as the story needs to maintain a certain pace. Nevertheless, this game's story really touched me. Like any sort of character in fiction that suffers loss, the ultimate moral is to keep living despite it. To live for their sake. The message is cliche, until you're actually feeling that apathy that comes with grief. Many story beats successfully pull this message off quite a few times. Besides being a fun and enjoyable RPG, P3 reminded me of the importance of living for myself and the bonds I make with others. Some people don't get to finish their lives to completion. So for their sake we must live doing what makes our lives meaningful.

Easily ranking in the top video game soundtracks.Negatives:- Microtransactions on day one. Cosmetic, personas, and bgm packs as paid content in a $69.99 single player rpg is scummy, but at this point with Atlus it is not surprising.- Missing story content present in previous iterations of the title in what is supposed to be the definitive edition of the game. Overall, Persona 3 Reload is my favorite in the franchise and is highly recommended!
