_childDocuments_.review: Get yourself a copy of Persona 3 Reload so you can pay your proper respects to Death.The Persona series is known for a number of things, each of which come to mind when you think of any one of its entries: good story and characters, monster collecting, turn-based combat, and social simulation, with some of the most infectious musical bangers ever to grace video games. One more thing it's fair to say about Persona and the larger Shin Megami Tensei series as a whole, is that it is INCREDIBLY dense in symbolism, and most if not all regular players will agree with that. All Persona titles and the MegaTen games I've seen are extremely allegorical to Biblical and Gnostic texts and usually draw on a great deal of other world mythology as well. I believe Persona 3 is where this symbolism really hit its stride.Persona 3 is known for being the first Persona title to introduce its social sim aspects, dividing the day as a student with responsibilities and friendships to maintain from the night, where you infiltrate some rendition of human subconscious and combat hordes of Shadows. But for me, what I like to highlight about P3's contribution to the series, is the overarching theme that these systems were created to lend credit to. You've probably figured this out by now, but that theme is Death, and it is EVERYWHERE in this game.Persona 3 takes on a damn near Poe-esque level of literary totality where EVERY cinematic, nearly every piece of dialogue, and all the music reflects the game's constant rumination on Death -- dying, making the most of the time you have, facing death and uncertainty with courage, longing to connect with someone before you die, the inevitable passage of time, the coming End of Things. Every character you meet is dealing with, in some way, the possibility of death, the inevitability of death, the grieving of death, the need to be successful before death, the need to make friendships before death, the questing of what the point is if no matter what there is death, so and and so forth and so death, death, death. You are constantly bombarded with images of ticking clocks, calendars and moon phases counting down, and the reminder that you don't have time to hang out with this person AND study for that test AND go to karaoke because guess what? Death! At certain hours of the night, people turn into coffins, containers of Death. Orpheus, the protagonist's first Persona, is a Greek character who descended into the realm of DEATH. Tartarus, the tower that serves as the set piece of most of the game's combat, is the deepest part of the Greek realm of DEATH. Thanatos, one of the final Personas, is DEATH. If you stay on one of these floors of the tower too long, who comes to kill you? DEATH! In order to summon your Persona, you literally point a gun at your head and pull the trigger. Why? Because you must have the courage to face DEATH!!Someone really just sat down one day and said "I want Memento Mori, but in video game format" and Atlus figured it out.The reason I bring this up isn't to spout facts or further psuedo-intellectualize on DEATH, but to point out that if it weren't for this obsession with DEATH, Persona as it exists today would not be the same. Maybe that's why in the Tarot, Death does not represent an end of things, but instead of transformation of them... (I said I wasn't gonna intellectualize dammit). The Social Links, or Confidants as P5 calls them, exist as a reminder to develop relationships why we can, and so too does the persistent counting down of time and that limitation on what can be done in a single day. Persona 4 and 5 and, it would seem, Metaphor: Refantazio, are shaped by none other than Death.So. If you're a Persona/SMT fan, or looking to become one, Reload is a faithful adherent to the philosophy laid down by the original game: you are going to die one day, so cherish life, friendships, and enjoy as many remarkable stories as you can while still you breathe. This is one of them.

_childDocuments_.review: If you remake what is, debatably, the best video game ever made, it’s really hard for people not to be extremely critical of every single aspect of it. Even with some sloppy changes to the narrative presentation and somewhat misguided (poorly executed) attempts at fixing the battle system, a remake of Persona 3 is still “Persona 3” boasting the best cast of characters in the medium, and one of the best stories. The version you play is really up to your taste and how you view games.If you're a person with love for video games in your heart and you have the maturity and patience to realize sometimes enduring dated systems might be worth it for getting the genuine experience intended by the director and staff, you should play Persona 3 FES for PS2. If you can run this, you can run PCSX2. If you like video games but care more about a game being "fun" and "not obtuse" and want to play a JRPG with a great story play Persona 3: Reload. There’s a lot of changes in this version that come from modern sensibilities regarding cutscene presentation and gameplay elements that feel like they completely miss the mark, but it is a lot more pleasant to actually sit through due to massive quality of life changes and more content to fill in downtime, while also removing a lot of tedium. It boils down to games as art vs games as pure entertainment I guess. Just whatever you do DON’T play the god awful PSP version of the original that’s been ported to consoles/PC. That’s the worst of both worlds with terrible presentation and balance changes intended to fix the gameplay that don’t really work. Please dear god just don’t dismiss FES just because you can’t control your party members and decide to play the version missing half the cutscene graphics.

_childDocuments_.review: With the possible exception of P3 Portable, this is the best way to play this game. TL;DR I love this iteration of the game. The voice acting is great, the remixes are banging, and the additional story elements are well-done. This quality without being a reboot is exactly what I wanted--and didn't get--from the Final Fantasy VII remake. Pleased to report that they didn't overhaul my all-time favorite game for a new audience.If you've played Persona 5/Royal, P3R isn't as polished a game. Social links are more diverse, but most are not as memorable or nuanced as they are in later games. But considering the original P3, in 2004, was the first iteration of Social Links, the calendar time-management, and All-Out Attacks? Respect where it's due.Never Played a Persona before:- Half the game is dungeon crawling with turn-based combat. Half is a social sim/time manager.- You better like reading, although the new voice acting means less of it.- Punchy turn-based combat is kinda adjacent to Pokemon (in that it has a colorful character doing elemental status effects on your behalf,) but you can mix your minions together to get better minions. Very unlike Pokemon, you have party members that each fulfill an elemental role, and your fights are in groups.- More forgiving game play than other Shin Megami Tensei main-line games, if you've come here from SMT 4 or 5. Also less parable and more slice-of-life plot than most of the other SMT games.- Crank the soundtrack!- This game is about death. You are going to have some feels.Newer Persona Fans Should Know:- There is one dungeon. Rather than that dungeon being about party members (Persona 4) or malicious adults inflicting their will on party members (Persona 5), each character has different motivations to enter the dungeon. That dungeon is randomly generated and does not have the kind of puzzles you see in 5, nor the brightly-colored hallways of 4.- There are a few social links that really make the game, and many are less memorable. Hermit, Hanged Man, and Sun are some of the best outside of your party members. Magician, Chariot, and some of the others are more boring, slice of life stuff. As this game reflects the original Persona 3, there are tragically no male party member social links. (This is where Persona 3 Portable shines.)- More magical realism and off-the-wall designs. Your teachers are absolute characters, for example.  - Just keep going for All Out Attacks. I promise.- This game is about death. You are going to have some feels.Persona 3 Fan:- No Femc- No male party social links- Removed the first hours of slogging through a town you weren't allowed to interact with- Significantly easier combat for several reasons, from button economy to status effects to vastly improved navigation.- I have never seen in-game characters resemble the original design and marketing work this well, and it is gloriousIn conclusion:Not everyone is going to appreciate a slower, plot-heavy anime game about death. But this is probably the best slower, plot-heavy anime game about death ever made.

_childDocuments_.review: Persona 3 has been an all time classic and this remake truly manages not only to make this game more accessible to new players who want to experience it without having to struggle with old-school mechanics, but also heightens the experience for old fans who wished to relive the story with newer graphics, a better combat system and a few additional content here and there.For new players, this game is potentially now the best introduction to the persona series, as it has the same structure as persona 5, but is less overwhelming with the amount of content and hours required in order to finish it. Story:P3's story immerses you by both its themes and structure, slowly building upon itself event after event. It has a slow start, sure, but once the plot starts moving, it is bound to keep your interest. The characters are constantly moving forward, each of them gradually developing throughout the entire story. Needless to say, with Reload that experience was heightened. Linked episodes with your party members manage to give you a better understanding of the story, get you more emotionally invested, and the additional scenes with Strega were brilliant. The voice actors did an amazing job at expressing each characters emotions, and along with the music made for a highly immersive experience.Gameplay: Tartarus, the main dungeon, is made a lot better in Reload. Each block was designed beautifully and made exploring through it feel way more enjoyable, whereas in the older versions it became quickly repetitive. Combat wise it is also a hundred times better, now similar to p5's style (though I must admit, persona 5 still remains better in that aspect). Theurgy, every characters own special move, was done beautifully and the variety of team combinations based on who you pick is fun to play around with.Social Links:Now this part is tricky, as persona 3 has both some of the best social links the series has to offer, and some of the most boring ones. You might not find yourself liking every single one of them, but surely a few are bound to resonate with you. Still, with the additional voice overs Reload has to offer, each social link feels more alive than before. Unlocking pre-requirements and reverse social links are still there, which is also a nice touch as they don't exist on later games.Graphics:The color-scheme is as close to the original while offering a more fresh and bright look. The art style is, obviously, closest to Persona 5's, which took some getting used to but is by no means bad. The animated scenes were also pretty good, CG included. Graphic-wise it is as any other atlus game, personally didn't notice frames dropping.Overall, Persona 3 Reload manages to keep the essence and vibe of the original game, simply enhancing the experience in a newer format. Without a doubt this remake does the game justice. 10/10

_childDocuments_.review: Just finished today! I thoroughly enjoyed this game; highlights include the OST (baby baby, dada da daaa da da da daaa) and the story, both of which packed a serious punch. However, I felt like the game was poorly paced, especially during December/January where you're left with nothing to do during evening segments. Another criticism I have is that there are no social links for the male members of the S.E.E.S. and there is thus little character development for, for example, Ken and Akihiko outside of the main storyline's exploration of their relationship with . I'd also like to mention in passing this game's continuation of the Persona series-wide problem with tasteless tropes that undermine the themes of the games—if you know, you know. I know it's somewhat trite at this point to compare this game to Persona 5, but I think that despite the excellent restyling of the UI, updated graphics, and addition of new mechanics like , this game seems to only on the surface level possess the polish that I felt even the base version of Persona 5 did. The Shift mechanic feels inferior to the Baton Pass system not only because Baton Pass is more potent (one might argue, in Royal, game-breakingly so) but also because it feels less fluid and satisfying in a way that I'm not able to fully put my finger on. One more gripe I have with combat is that, unlike in Persona 5, when selecting a Shadow to target with an attack it doesn't say if the Shadow resists that attack type. Lastly, people who are used to Persona 5's heavily curated Palace experiences might be disappointed to find that in Reload fighting takes place exclusively in randomly generated spaces analogous to Mementos. This wasn't an issue for me but may prove to be for others. Overall, though, I would recommend this game to players if it goes on sale for 50, maybe 40 dollars. Despite a heart-wrenching yet inspiring story, one agidyne tracklist, and a cast chock-full of believable characters that you'll love to root for, I can't help but feel like this JRPG is seriously, seriously hindered by its pacing (I don't know if I emphasized this enough, it's REALLY bad).

_childDocuments_.review: I wanna preface this by saying that I've only played through the portable remaster and exclusively the female route, so don't look for too many comparisons between this and the original male route. With that said, this game is like a solid 9/10 for me. I've played through Persona 4 Golden, Persona 5, Persona 5 Royal. Unlike those games, it runs on an entirely new engine, the Unreal Engine. As a first attempt for Atlus, the game looks beautiful visually - at least in the sense of still retaining that Persona artstyle while looking new and fancy. This is probably the strongest game in the series when it comes to its theme. Otherwise, it's a little lacking in multiple areas - but well-rounded enough that it bounces back. Storywise, the game has a great focus on the theme of death, which can always go wrong in a variety of ways. For the most part, if you have played the original Persona 3, there is absolutely no big story changes. This a one-to-one faithful remake of the original, with recreated visuals and added flair. There may be some added scenes here and there to elaborate on certain story points. Atlus also added plenty of character moments to help the team you're apart of feel more cohesive. If you're new here, the game will do plenty to keep your intrigue - but don't expect some god-tier writing from Baldur's Gate 3 or something. This time around, the characters feel less like they're there to rub your ego and more like their own individuals that will even clash with your decisions. There are new link episodes for primarily the male party members that vastly improve upon their lacking presence in the original games. These add plenty of character building and more emotional weight to the story for those characters specifically. For gameplay, this is the same formula used in most Persona games. You summon demons in all sorts of mythology from different aspects of your personality called "Persona" to kill shadows. It plays somewhat like a dungeon crawling pokemon game, but it's a lot more complex than that. When you're not fighting the enemy shadows, you're living your daily life and making friends. More friends is good, since it'll boost your personas' abilities while even letting you unlock higher tiered ones. If you're worried that all of previous games' QoL are gone and nowhere to be seen, have no fear, since almost every single mechanic from the newer games have made the transition. You can actually reject and turn down romantic interests without breaking their social link now. All characters have a new ultimate mechanic called "Theurgy", speeding up battles immensely. You can pass on turns to other teammates when you hit enemies' weaknesses, there's a somewhat convoluted autosave mechanic, there's plenty of different ways to boost your social stats for some of those requirements later on, and everything in the game is quick and abbreviated. It knows that it's a pretty long game and won't make you sit through hours of animations to get to the action. Even the infamous railroading at the start of Persona games is pretty absent here. You get into the freetime around the hour and a half mark. The voicework and OST are amazing. If you play in Japanese dub, the voices suit all of the characters. If you play in English dub, some of the voices may sounds a little grating at times - but to be honest Persona dubs are always relatively decent, this one especially. I swapped between the two to keep dungeon-grinding a little fresh. Between this and AI Somnium Files, the English dubs in both are pretty decent enough to consider if you have the option between Japanese and English. The OST got a whole makeover, whilst still retaining the important key parts of their original counterparts. The new vocalist does an amazing job, but in my opinion - she does far better vocals on the newer songs. While listening to some of the tracks play out in-game, it sounded like some of them lacked the impact and tenacity that the original tracks did. That's not to say she did a bad job, even then, the songs still sound great. However, the new vocalist has a more soothing voice that's suited to the more somber songs in-game.The UI is something to die for. Although, it was a little disappointing that they decided not to go with some of their original concepts (since those would be more thematically appropriate), the game has so much flair and style that it doesn't matter. This is best UI from any persona game ever, with Persona 5 Royal's being in close second. All said, some gripes or things I didn't like about the game:1. No way to turn of motion blur in-game. (I know there's a workaround on PC, but this should've just been added in regardless)2. Personal gripe - Tartarus (Main in-game dungeon) gets super dull after a while - with samey environments for 20-30 floors at a time. 3. Some of the Theurgies (Specifically MC's) feel very underwhelming and experimental - rather than polished.4. Social Links are the EXACT same, so some of them are very...controversial to say the least. If you didn't like the social links in the original, you will not like them anymore here. (Same just with FULL voicework). 5. There are not many in-game engine cutscenes, which is a HUGE shame in my opinion. These look way better than the anime cutscene style that they tend to shoe-horn into the games, but that is ESPECIALLY the case here. The new in-game engine looks so nice that it's a waste that they decided not to animate more scenes with it.All in all, this game is worth the price point if you're a longtime persona fan. 70$ is a little steep if you're a newcomer. You might not like a lot of the game's themes and topics. If you can't buy into the anime wackiness and tropes, this isn't the game for you. If you hate JRPG grinding, this ALSO isn't the game for you. I would nab the game on a sale of 50-60$ if any of the above apply to you. As much as I love Persona games, I have to admit, ALOT of the writing is pretty poor and struggles when compared to modern writing in videogames. I've loved these games for decades, but at the end of the day it's just an anime power fantasy with an overdone highschool setting.

_childDocuments_.review: When judging the overall quality of a remake it is important to question the fundamental basis of its existence. The question is: does this remake justify its existence? In other words, were there any major issues with the original game, and is the remake an objective improvement on those aspects? A remake that passes this test with flying colors is the Dead Space Remake, which stays entirely true to the original game's level design and overall aesthetic while improving upon the aspects that needed it(weapon balancing, etc). Unfortunately, Persona 3 Reload does not live up to this standard. To preface this review, let me first say that Persona 3 FES is my favorite game of all time, and I am willing to argue that it is the greatest game ever made. Persona 3 Reload is a misguided and poorly crafted recreation of P3 FES that loses most if not all of the aspects that made the original game so fantastic. There are three major aspects I want to cover: story, gameplay, and overall aesthetic.Story:The core story of Persona 3 goes pretty much unchanged in Reload, which is great. The new cast of voice actors ranges from good(Junpei) to really bad(Akihiko, Ken, Shinji), and the removal of animated cutscenes in favor of in-engine ones makes many scenes come off as lackluster and removes the artistic cinematography of FES. The social links are the strongest part of the game, as they remain mostly unchanged with a few additions that improve upon the original iteration. The casting for all of the social links is also very good. Overall, the core story is the best aspect of this game as it stays true to the original and makes improvements where necessary. This is the end of any merits that Reload has. Gameplay:The combat gameplay from P3 FES has been completely gutted in Reload, replaced by a tedious gameplay loop. In FES, exploring Tartarus was a well-designed balance of combat and resource management. You clear randomly generated floors by finding the stairway leading to the next floor while managing your health and sp. Every party member has a hidden fatigue meter which causes them to become “tired” after a certain amount of battles. When “tired”, party members do less damage and take more damage. As you level up, their fatigue meter increases. This mechanic is designed to force you into spacing your trips to Tartarus out over multiple in-game days. It also works hand in hand with the exp system. Enemies will be sized based on how much exp each encounter will give you, meaning you need to choose if you think fighting a smaller enemy is worth the exp when it may cause your party members to become tired. The floors are procedurally generated, so it's pretty easy to run past an enemy and find the exit quickly. Once you have completed a certain amount of floors you will come to a mini-boss floor with a teleporter that brings you back to the ground floor, restoring your party’s hp and sp and acting as a checkpoint. However, if your party members are tired, they will automatically leave when you return to the ground floor. This creates another decision between fighting the mini-boss while tired and possibly saving some in-game time, or playing it safe and coming back the next day. These mechanics, along with the standard persona fusion system made P3 FES have an amazing, engaging combat loop. All of this goes out the window when it comes to Reload. The tired mechanic is gone, meaning there is no reason to ever leave Tartarus. You can obtain so many HP and SP items that leaving and coming back the next day will never happen. Along with this, there is now also no reason to not fight every single enemy. Unless you want to be woefully underleveled, this is almost a necessity. These two facts alone draw out Tartarus visits quite a bit compared to P3 FES. These combat encounters are even more grating now that the tactics system has been removed in favor of direct party control. Now instead of managing the behavior of your party members and adapting to possibly unexpected combat situations like in FES, you just spam the same moves over and over again depending on the situation and what party members you have. The new Theurgy mechanic is also terrible, it only exists to make the game incredibly easy with literally no downside. You can drop four atomic bombs on a boss numerous times during 1 fight if you haven’t already instakilled your opponents. Exploring Tartarus has also been needlessly complicated, with irritating gimmick floors that simply exist to pad out the playtime. The introduction of skill cards damages the gameplay quite a bit as well. Being able to buy and then duplicate extremely broken abilities and then slot them into any persona you want is nothing short of gamebreaking. The fusion system is also much worse. The addition of being able to choose which skills personas inherit when fused makes the meta extremely boring, with the only viable strategy being to keep the same 5 support skills on every persona you fuse for the entire game. In FES, the fact that skill selection was random and that personas had very strict skills that they could and could not inherit meant that you had to think about your build and what you were using to fuse rather than just mindlessly selecting what you wanted from a massive list of skills. The time management gameplay is not much better. The “late night” period is now gone, meaning it's infinitely harder to level up academics. The addition of part-time jobs that are free to work at and payout with money and 2 social status points makes time management extremely one-dimensional. There is no space between social link unlocks like in FES, so you will always have to coin-flip between 4-5 characters every day. Social links are also, for the most part, available much more often. Not to mention the onslaught of useless mechanics that are introduced during the time management sections. In FES, there were very simple uses for each social stat and very simple ways to level them up. At max, there were 2-3 ways to level each one up. Reload clutters your screen and your schedule with way too many available social links and options to gain items/social stats, to the point that it is overwhelming and bloated. Overall Aesthetic:This category is easily the most offensive of the three. The subdued, bleak aesthetic of the original game has been destroyed, and replaced with Persona 5 Blue Edition. Everything is bright, colorful, and inviting. The town is alive and bustling with people. Everything looks all pretty and done up in the terrible Unreal 4 graphics style. You can fast-travel to any location in the game. All of these changes completely ruin the point of the original game. The oppressively bleak atmosphere of the original greatly contributes to the themes of death and loss of purpose that are present throughout all of FES’s facets. In Reload, the “stylish” presentation betrays the content of the stories and social links, creating a very polarizing environment and severely damaging the overall quality and impact of the game’s message.Conclusion:There are a bunch of other smaller things that I hate about this game, like the remixed music, but I can’t find a good place to put them. Since this is a review of the Steam version, if you haven’t played P3 FES before I implore that you try emulating it on PCSX2 before playing this vastly inferior version. To all of you who have played the original game, enjoy this mess if you can I guess. Ultimately, this game is not worth anyone’s time or money as it completely ruins all of the aspects that made the original game so great. _childDocuments_.review: I really liked this remake when it came out about 7 months ago. I had not played the original (which I will call FES from now on) in 7 years so it was a great refresher for me. The only things I did not like were most of the rearranged osts (why did they make the guitars so thin with the literally smallest amount of distortion required to be considered distorted? why did they also remove the booming distortion of the drums? it was awesome!), how easy the game was made (like ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ physical builds are stuuuupidly strong in this game, not to mention ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ theurgys oh my lord) and the focus on modernizing the graphics and art style, causing a loss to a majority of the vibe of FES. Basically, it lost a lot of it's 2000's edgy and gloomy vibe which I was not a fan of. But at the time, in the grand scheme of things, I felt like it didn't matter all that much, because of all of the quality of life improvements made to the game. Then I rewatched footage from FES, played about ~15 hours of FES on my ps2 CRT combo, and watched a video showcasing the differences between this remake and FES. The destruction of the original overall vibe/aesthetic/art direction is truly something to study. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Even majority of the in game cutscenes are directed worse, and the subtlety removed from many moments in the game. The original felt so much artsy-er... arty? You get what I mean. Just watch the original Intro movie (not the FES intro) and compare it to this game's. Yes they are both good, but Burn My Dread the song AND the visuals have just got way more sauce! FES feels more like an arthouse film, and this feels like the big hollywood blockbuster remake of that arthouse film. This all, in my opinion, is in favor of a more heavy focus on making the game more appealing to mainstream audiences, instead of keeping true to FES's style. Also for some reason this game looks WAY worse than persona 5??? I expected it to be at the bare minimum on par with a nearly EIGHT year old game! I'm very saddened by this, because I still enjoyed the game and would recommend it to people. Y'know the only thing that keeps me from recommending FES is that it is MUCH more of a grindfest, which I know would put a lot of people off. But that's okay. I still recommend this version. It is good. It keeps the story beats and themes of FES quite intact so I still enjoy all of that a super big bunch. I just STRONGLY prefer FES.This is the most conflicted I have ever felt giving a game a9/10

_childDocuments_.review: UPDATE: nominated P3R for Best Soundtrack, Best Game on Steam Deck, and Most Outstanding Story-Rich Game in this year's Steam Awards.This is one of those games where words really can't do it justice. It was like I didn't realize just how special of an experience this was until it was almost too late.For context, I've only played Persona 5 Royal. I cannot speak for other Persona games, or previous releases of Persona 3, but this game reaches the same high bar Atlus set for themselves.This game really snuck-up on me. The pacing and storytelling are different from P5R, but in a refreshing way. The characters grew on me overtime, for example, compared to P5R where I felt attached to many of them almost right away. The dungeon crawling aspect works quite different from P5R as well, but it's broken up as you progress with some really nice designs for the various areas (except one in particular that hurt my eyes). The introduction of new characters and new abilities also keeps the dungeon crawling fresh.Do yourself a favor and spend time with your team members! Not just the ones with social links; there are other side activities and time-sensitive optional hangouts too. I think P5R does a better job of getting you to bond with the characters through the main story, but here I think you'll really miss out if you don't go out of your way to hangout with them.I did miss a really important detail in the ending, so the full weight of what happened didn't occur to me until I found a comment online. At first, I thought that the ending was more open to interpretation. But boy was I wrong. Anyway, even if you miss it, Episode Aigis explains things (the DLC, I think also called "The Answer.")I have not played the DLC yet, and I'll leave a separate review for that.Altogether another 9/10. Besides what I said about spending time with the characters, do yourself a favor and just enjoy the main story. I'm a perfectionistic completionist, which I think ruined the experience a little bit for myself because I was looking certain things up and trying to optimize my playthrough. That's what ng+ is for. A hard way to learn, but despite all that I can recognize that this is a truly special game, one that will leave a lasting, positive impression on you.

_childDocuments_.review: I love Persona 3 and it is currently my favorite Persona game out of all. I started with Persona 3 Portable, then Persona 3 FES for "The Answer". Then I bought the P3P port on my Switch. That's how passionate I am with this game.Now, with that out of the way, here's my honest review, humor me for a bit:I've seen many trailers of this game since last year, found out a lot of things like new and arranged music, the content compared to the original games, etc. I was kind of disappointed that we won't get "The Answer" from FES in Reload, nor we get to play as FeMC from Portable. I was also neutral in terms of the new singer Azumi Takahashi replacing Yumi Kawamura. I've heard some sample music from YouTube and there are some parts that she's good and there are also some that is quite out of place for my taste. Despite that, I want to try this game without my nostalgia blinding me to what Atlus has cooked for this remake.What can I say, the graphics is good compared to the originals, even compared to Persona 5 Royal. The soundtrack is  on its own right. It has its own identity. It was never meant to be a "Yumi Kawamura" style, and I am fine with that. Lotus Juice spitting fire as always with the rap. "Color Your Night" and "Changing Seasons -Reload-" also slaps.  A welcome mechanic. It is like a "Limit Break" for playable characters that can turn the tide of battles. You can only use it when your gauge is full though, and every characters have different ways to charge it fast based on their personality. It's neat and I like it. The rest still plays like neo-Persona. There's 1 more when you hit weakness or land critical hits, and there's "Shift" that works the same as "Baton Pass" first introduced in Persona 5.They also added some stuff during the exploration of Tartarus:- There are some "petrified" shadows with shiny things that they're holding. Players can destroy it and get valuable materials for selling or get "Twilight Fragments" that are very important, which I will explain further down.- "Twilight Fragments" are valuable items because you will need this to unlock special treasure chests and use the clock in Tartarus (Yep, you can't use your money anymore). You can find these fragments while exploring Tartarus, exploring the areas of the map, or by progressing your Social Links then talking to Elizabeth.- . These special shadows are addition to the existing "Hands" shadows. They will sometimes appear when you first step on a floor, and they swipe all the chests available in that current floor. The only way you can reclaim the treasures is by correctly traversing which direction the shadow went. (Yes it is random and there is no way you can know for sure as far as perception is concerned). I kinda hate this new mini-game but after I unlock the navigator's "Tartarus Scan", which skips the mini-game entirely and proceeds to fighting, I am no longer bothered by it.- Monad Gates. There are two types of it, the first one is the type of gate that appears randomly on a floor the moment you arrive. When you go through it, you will fight a mini-boss that blocks your way to the treasures. But once you defeat it, claim the treasures, and go outside, you will have full map of the current floor you are in and the next floor, which is neat. The second type of Monad Gates are the fixed gates stationed in some of the floors with a two-way teleporter on it. Similar to the random gates, you have to defeat mini-boss to proceed, but this time, there are multiples of it, like 2-3 mini-bosses. The treasures you get here contains tarot cards, some lore documents, costumes, etc, so it's definitely worth doing.-  is back, but without the actual shuffling like the original games. It's kinda like in Persona 4 where you just pick the cards you want. There's also an Arcana Burst mechanic wherein when you maxed out of Arcana cards to pick, you can never pick another Arcana card for that night, but the usual "Sword", "Coin", "Cup" and "Leaves" cards will be upgraded 1 level up. I personally like this change because I'm not fond of the cards shuffling in the original games, it makes me dizzy.- Ambush. You will need to progress to the game before you unlock this but once you unlock this, it will guarantee a preemptive strike or "SEES Advantage" during battles whether you attack the shadows in the front or back. You can also upgrade your ambush by buying URLs in the Net Shop or the guy in the club. A neat addition in my opinion. It makes preemptive strikes easier to do.They also made changes to how Social Link works with people that the protagonist can romance. You are not forced to enter a romantic relationship with them in order to max their Social Link anymore. Also, technically not a Social Link, but you can now hangout with your team members at the dorm. You can cook, tend plants, watch TV, and read books with them. They also award you with social stat increase and some useful items. I personally like this addition as it adds more character depth and development between the SEES members.I might have missed some other new gameplay mechanics but this is what I remembered on top of my head. Overall, Story is pretty much the same as the original, but they added some scenes that added more context and character depth like . I'll not expound further in this as it is spoiler territory, but I personally love these scenes.As stated by Atlus themselves, the game doesn't include "The Answer" part of the story, first introduced in FES. It also doesn't include FeMC and her unique Social Link characters. If you don't want that, then avoid playing this game. But personally, I don't mind and I still like that they made it faithful to the original Persona 3. There is a New Game Plus available on this game, meaning your clear save data can carry over to your next new game. This is useful for people who want to try the game again to experience new dialogue options normally not accessible due to lack of social stat points, try to romance a different Social Link, or to just complete the achievements that they missed on their first playthrough. But story-wise, there is not much worth replaying the game as it has only two endings that I know off. One is the good ending and one is the bad ending where you  and the game will end prematurely. Man, overall I love this game and Atlus made a good remake to satisfy this Persona 3 fan. If you're a fan of Persona especially Persona 3 and don't mind the missing "The Answer" or FeMC, or if you're new to Persona in general and a JRPG fan, I highly recommend playing this game.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're new to RPG's then I think the Persona franchise, and Specifically Persona 3 Reload, is one of the perfect ways to introduce someone to the genre. In an ideal world where you're not spoiled for the Main Story and the DLC, Persona 3R has an enthralling and unique plot with lovable characters and many emotional moments. Although there are many highs, it has a slow and steady start which can be a turn away for some. The gameplay loop is also likely unique to most and may take time exploring and getting used to before understanding and enjoying it. Even still, there are many downsides as well such as the long wait in between major story moments, as well tedious and sometimes obnoxious game design. However if you're able to overlook or work around these lows, Persona 3 Reload is an extensive and in depth game about the concept of Living and Dying. It's very worth your time if you're willing to invest it, and likely you will leave the game with a slightly altered view on life, that wasn't there before.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a complicated placeholder until I've completed the game, but I would not recommend it unless it is on sale. I do not believe it makes sense to pay 70 for the base game, or nearly 100 for the premium version, especially as the DLC it contains is not in fact the full DLC. Regrettably, I will have to pay the extra 30 for the expansion pass later this year. This is a sad trend Sega also did earlier with Yakuza Like A Dragon, where I had to pay 100 for DLC and new game plus.Context for the review - I have played Persona 3 FES quite a while ago on PS2 and maybe about a decade ago via emulation. I have played Portable on the PSP quite a while ago, and I have tried to play the Portable remake but stopped as I don't like the lack of navigation and cutscenes from that version. I think the only aspect of the game I haven't completed is the female protagonist in FES, but I can't remember. I will try to play it later, maybe after finishing this.I'll briefly cover audio and some visual aspects next. The songs were rerecorded for this remake, and as a result, some music sounds worse to me. I wish there was an option for original and new versions like the Super Mario RPG remake for Switch. I personally prefer the original theme, and some of the other songs from cutscenes. I think I even had the soundtrack after buying FES years ago. Some songs are better, but to me a few were made worse. There are new songs which are also nice though. On a related note, the digital soundtrack and artbook are launched as an option when loading the game, but I wish they were files we got access to. Regarding visuals, as others have said in previous critiques online, some cutscenes are not as impactful rendered the way they are in this remake. The first scene where someone is in dark hour and transforms or dies while others around him are coffins looked better in the PS2 version as the man didn't simply collapse. Likewise, the intro cinematic, while sharper and modern like Persona 5, does not have the same impact or edge as it did in the PS2 version. I would prefer the other.While I have only played a few hours so far, I am not able to comment on other areas that may be great or not so great yet, and I have not listened to the English dub which may not be something I like, but I am please that there is an option for original Japanese audio. I also noticed that questions seem to be redone for the school life portion. I wonder if the translation/localization was also redone. If so, I really hope we have an option of choosing a translation and not localization to avoid issues with not lining up with the intended meaning. As a linguist, I know a lot can be lost in localizing, and it's great if you can just contextualize a translation. An example would be the most recent Yakuza Like a Dragon, where many portions of the game are not translated appropriately in the English subtitled or dubbed version, and the game even admits that other language subtitles will follow Japanese, but English follows the dub instead which is sad.

_childDocuments_.review: I have cherished (parts of) Persona 3 as a story and as a work of art in the eight years since I first played it. I never replayed it in all that time until P3R came out, and I finished my P3R playthrough this morning.I have so much I want to say, but in a nutshell:If you are willing to accept/do without the inclusion of the female protagonist from Persona 3 Portable, and if you can stomach the inclusion of some misogynistic tropes (sexual harassment of female cast members played for laughs, optional cosmetic bikini armor), Except for the aforementioned caveats, P3R in my eyes is a perfect remake. It keeps the things that gave Persona 3 its unique soul and character, compared to both past and future Shin Megami Tensei games, and what it adds always fits well. Theurgy, for example, is an immensely satisfying and helpful combat mechanic that helps tie character development into gameplay changes without rewriting or harming the original Persona 3's attempts at the same thing. The music is all redone but all recognizable, familiar enough to kindle nostalgia but fresh enough to not be defined by it. It's a pleasure to both recognize and not recognize a song, and these joys often happen simultaneously in Persona 3 Reload's soundtrack. They also changed an overtly transphobic scene from P3 FES/Portable and made it actually funny instead. In what I would call a bold decision, P3 Reload also keeps the generic Shadows and the procedurally generated structure of Tartarus from earlier iterations. This won't be popular with people who were introduced to the series with Persona 5's demon negotiation mechanics or handmade Palaces, but I found (to my great surprise) that I did not miss these innovations. In ways I cannot adequately discuss in a spoiler-free review, something about the expressionless masks of P3's Shadow enemies and the tedium of Tartarus... actually works with P3's atmosphere, to me.However, while I cherish what Reload brings to the table, I also want to take a moment to thank Persona 3 itself. A game with this many tonal shifts - from casual school life sim to an emotional main story to a delightfully camp and self-indulgently emo aesthetic in turn-based battle - has no right to feel this earnest in its central thesis, but Persona 3 manages to be sincere despite the frequently fantastic and dramatic turns of its battles and plotlines. I do not want to expound at length on what the game is trying to say, find out for yourself- but I am in a part of my life where I needed to hear Persona 3's message again, and I will always cherish Persona 3 Reload for letting me do that, if nothing else.By way of a small comparison, I actively dislike Persona 4 and 5. I used to adore these games, but I have soured fully on them as I believe they have terrible writing for their female characters and make light of the topics they try to tackle. P3R proved to me (subjectively, of course) that Persona 3's story and cast are not merely the best writing in modern Persona by a country mile, but also one of the most poignant stories about finding one's purpose in the entire medium in my eyes.

The more vibrant visuals in Persona 4 is what drew me in to give the series another chance and it was a fantastic game. Then Persona 5 came and provided one of the best RPG experiences I've ever had with a tremendous sense of style and flair seldom seen in gaming. The reason I provided that history was because I view Persona 3 Reload as a game that received the Persona 5 treatment and it is better for it as a result. Because I never played through the original Persona 3 or its alternate version, I can't speak for whatever differences there may be when comparing the older versions with this new one. What I do know is Persona 3 Reload looks, plays, and sounds fantastic. The makeover Persona 3 has received has given new life and renewed vibrance to the source material in a way that Final Fantasy VII Remake did for the original Final Fantasy VII. In the four hours I played of Persona 3 Reload, I'm finally ready to appreciate and dive into what Persona 3 has to offer. I want to play more and I will play more. In short, this was an impressive remake and one of the best that I've seen in my 40 years of gaming. If you are a Persona series fan, I highly recommend it. _childDocuments_.review: Persona 3 Reload is Atlus's move to modernize P3 for a current audience. One that is familiar with Persona 5, and while it doesn't render any of the previous versions obsolete, it modernizes it wonderfully. Even if it might not go above and beyond or reach the same heights as P5R. One of the biggest contentions about Persona 3 as a whole was the story. While it was a story that was amazing on paper. Many thought that it had a lot of pacing issues, especially with its cut scenes. Regardless of how you feel about the original, Reload makes a lot of attempts to remedy this and to good measure. A lot of characters are alluded to early on to give them enough screen time but also not alienate the player. Sure some parts can go on for a while, but considering the story being told, I think its worth it. One of the new selling points of P3R is the amount of voice acting used in the game, this is the first game in the series to have fully voiced dialogue. I think this is a great move for the series as it helps keep confidants engaging and some of these moments are made that much funnier as well. Speaking of, the English dub sees a mostly new cast. Now I got the privilege to meet the members of SEES at a convention, (where they all signed my PS5) and I can tell a lot of them are really happy to be apart of this project. Some of the new voices I think are leaps and bounds better such as Aigis and Junpei. Though others not so much, like Akihiko and Ken. Overall I am happy with the voice cast and I don't mind the recast, especially considering a lot of the original cast got cameo roles ala the Mario Movie which is really cool to see! Obviously this is not a thing with the JP cast where most of them reprise their roles with a couple of exceptions. Gameplay is very similar to the original though with some new improvements such as balancing, menu navigation, world exploration and mechanics such as shifting or theurgy attacks that are based off of Persona 5. While it might feel a little derivative, its also important to know that if it ain't broke, don't fix it so I don't mind this. One important change made was being able to control your party members, which also changes both the dynamic and balancing of battles since now you have a lot more strategies to down enemies and take them out instead of having an AI decide based on your options. It goes a long way to keeping the flow of battles up while still feeling like enough of a challenge (at least for me). Music is good as well, rapper Lotus juice from the original and he does not mess around, especially with the new verse of Mass Destruction or Its Going Down Now. Although the vocalist can be very hit or miss. New songs like Color Your Night work well for her, and even some old ones such as the credits or Master of Tartarus, but then you have When Moon's Reaching Out where she just sounds like a peanuts character simply put. However overall I like a lot of the remixes and the new songs so its a net win, even if there are some stinkers. One point of contention among Persona fans is the lack of The Answer or Femc from FES or Portable. While it is indeed a missed opportunity, it doesn't weigh down the package overall so its loss doesn't feel as noticeable as some might make it seem. With that said, there are rumors about the Answer being a DLC campaign and Portable is on Steam and other platforms so there are still options. Personally I think this does enough to stand on its own, maybe even surpass both versions. I had a really good time with this game, Its no secret that I am a big Persona fan, but this is the kind of game I will recommend to everyone. Although I think Persona 5 is still the better starting point. While I got my moneys worth at $70, when P5R is $60 (and goes on sale a lot physically and digitally) plus is just a newer game all around, I think that works better overall. But still if you like Persona in general or RPGs such as Like a Dragon, you honestly have no reason to skip this one.

_childDocuments_.review: Like "Of Mice and Men", this game was real slow for a while, and then the ending ♥♥♥♥♥♥ me up. If you're a JRPG fan who's never touched a Persona game before, wondering if you should pick up P3R to try, the answer is a resounding yes! Just generally, the Persona franchise is a strong performer in story-driven games and P3R is no different. A beautifully designed story is packaged nicely with gorgeous new graphics and enthralling gameplay which has been enhanced with quality of life upgrades introduced to this revamped copy of the title. It makes it easy for anyone to pick up and roll, even if you've never touched a JRPG before. The nature of Persona games as thick packages of unique branching stories also means that no two runs of the game are the same. You can always come back to this title for a fresh and enchanting experience. The Good: Characters - Like P4 and P5, the cast of characters is heart-warming and easy to attach yourself to. Your main party is made up of an incredibly strong core that never feels stale, especially with how closely tied to the story they are. Junpei's entire character arc is probably my favourite in the series, beating out my previous favourite of P4's Kanji. Yukari's entire character is a powerful story of overcoming the pain of loss. The dynamic between Shinjiro, Mitsuru and Akihiko is really second to none, with how well the characters build off of each other within the narrative. And of course, Koromaru is the best mascot character in the entire series. Teddy and Morgana cannot compete. The weakest of the cast is certainly Ken, with how awkwardly he is shoe-horned into the story. But Ken still has a lot of powerful moments that makes his involvement a worthy investment of your time. Combat - P3R's combat system has quickly become my favourite in the series. Although I was definitely missing the Psy and Nuclear elements from P5, the inclusion of three separate Physical attributes was a nice compensation. P3R's combat is largely a better version of P5R's. The Shift system occupies the same role as Baton Passes, although it lacks a cool sequence of Persona protagonists giving each other high-fives. Guns have been dropped from P3R, with attacks that shared the Gun-Type from P5 changing to the Pierce-Type physical skill. All-Out Attacks and One Mores make a return, allowing for a quick dusting of your usual rank-and-file enemies. All-Out Attacks have been improved in P3R, as not only can their damage be buffed from Shuffle Times, but they can also be used when untargetable enemies are present on the field. The presence of Theurgy skills further enhances the combat experience, allowing for devastating opening attacks against bosses, or a powerful final push to finish off a particularly nasty foe. Overall, if you're a fan of turn-based combat from other JRPGs like Dragon Quest, P3R's combat will really scratch that itch. Music - Persona titles always have stellar music. Every time another franchise brings good music to their games, Persona comes out and moves the goal posts to the next galaxy, as if to taunt the rest industry. P3R is no different. If you believed P5R to have the best music of the franchise, P3R hands Royal its own ass on a silver platter. Lotus Juice has returned with this title, bringing out a group of new tracks that build off of P3's J-Pop base to narrate a beautiful story. There are few games where you're inclined to listen to their soundtracks on repeat while level grinding. There are even fewer where you're inclined to download their soundtrack on Spotify and listen to it while grinding on other games. Persona 3 Reload joins Persona 5 Royal on that vaunted pedestal. The Story - Persona 3 Reload has a story that was originally crafted in 2006, so sometimes you have to meet the narrative where it's at. Certainly there are moments in it where it can be a little cringe-worthy. But the game constructs an amazing tale about coming to terms with loss, and the personal struggles involved. Each character brought in enhances that story, all dealing with some sort of personal loss that is for you to explore and root out. The game does a great job of casting a sharp contrast with your character through their social links; if you chose to be apathetic and uncaring about the people around you, you end up powerless and alone. But if you invest in those people, you're rewarded with beautiful stories, tear-jerking moments, and an incredibly powerful array of Personas. The main story has amazing payoff down the line, and once it sinks its claws into you it can be really hard to have it let go. HOWEVER, be aware that this game can take a little bit to get going. A lot of its best narrative moments are locked behind the second-half of the game. Remember to give yourself breaks so that you don't burn out on some of the monotony of the first-half of the game. And ALWAYS make sure you go back to the flower shop to buy Junpei white flowers. The Bad: Social Links - Clarifying, this is not to say that all the social links are bad. Rather, the social links are a mixed bag that can feel like a drag to complete if you're not fully invested in a character. Because P3R tries to be a faithful remake of the original P3, the bonuses that Confidants had in P5 are nowhere to be seen, meaning that the only benefit of maxing out a social link is the persona at the end of the link. While that's not necessarily a bad prize, it can make some social links feel grating, as you're not gaining anything from interacting with particularly annoying characters until the very end of the social link. What further frustrates social links in the game is that most of the better social links, including your teammates, can only be advanced while school is in session. This means that if you don't map out your social link plans, you can end up on a school vacation and not be able to interact with anybody. Night Time - Again a flaw of P3R trying to be a faithful remake of its original copy, the activities that can be done at night are incredibly restricted. Much of the map gets closed off at night, with only two social links being made available at night. While the introduction of the hacker's relationship website certainly helps in the second half of the game, the fact remains that nighttime in P3R is largely a waste of time once you've maxed out your nighttime social links. Although you can just jump into Tartarus straight away, the simplification of the navigation of Tartarus means that only 2 - 3 trips into Tartarus are really required between the major story beats; 1 - 2 to scale to the levels and 1 to serve as an extra exp grind. Lack of FEMC: Persona 3 Portable introduced a female lead option for Persona with unique social links, story beats, and other cool features. Unfortunately, Atlus decided not to pursue bringing the FEMC option up to P3R. It's a disappointing development, especially given how beautiful P3R is on the whole, but a dedicated modding community is working to make this feature a reality. Hopefully one day soon you'll be able to stand awkwardly between Akihiko and Ken as they bicker about whether or not you should be wearing battle panties in Tartarus.  The Ugly: Your face after finishing Akinara's Social Link. Overall P3R is an amazing addition to the Persona franchise. It is another solid JRPG that brings the stellar P3 experience into the modern age with incredible quality of life updates, superb music, and bonus story moments with party members that helps to flesh them out. It is the best edition of Persona 3 out there, and definitely deserves a place in the library of all who consider themselves JRPG fans.

_childDocuments_.review: Welcome back.Like for many others, Persona 3 was my first foray into the Persona series, having played through FES back in 2011, and will always hold a special place in my heart. I have also been wanting for a Persona 3 remake since at least 2020, so I’ve been extremely excited to play through Persona 3 Reload ever since the rumours were confirmed to be real. And yet, with years of lofty expectations weighing down on it, I absolutely loved Persona 3 Reload.Story-wise Persona 3 has always remained as my favourite one in the series. Granted, some of that might be nostalgia for my first Persona story, but it’s a feeling that’s stayed with me after Persona 4 and Persona 5. I just really enjoy the theme and overall feeling of the story. And now that I have experienced it again, I think I can still confidently claim it to be the superior of the three. Thankfully Reload manages to not alter the story even though it does ever-so-slightly expand it here and there. Not changing the story is also to its benefit since ATLUS’ efforts to add new story content for re-releases have often had very mixed results. And despite knowing the story, although fuzzy with some details after 13 years, the emotional highs still bit hard.The gameplay side of things has a lot more changes, but it still very much feels like Persona 3. I was actually quite surprised that they didn’t relax the social link calendar to make it more like Persona 5 Royal. Getting all of my bonds maxed out in a single playthrough was definitely challenging with few days to spare. Granted, the social links are still considerably easier than in the original, but not to the point of feeling like the other games. The overall package does feel like a very good balance of the old experience and new quality of life.The new Rewind system is excellent. I imagine it’s going to become a new staple feature in every single Persona game going forwards and reduce some of the save overwrite anxiety. Would’ve definitely saved me some time in prior titles. It’s also nice to see that despite trying to be faithful to the original game, they’re not beyond innovating when they have good new ideas, especially when they’re ones that do not dilute the original experience.The combat side of things has definitely been Persona 5-ified – but actually less so than I imagined. I fully expected them to just clone the Royal combat system and call it a day, but they actually made a system unique to Reload. Familiar, but unique. And much like Persona 5’s combat system, it very much works. It’s fluid and fun. I always remembered Tartarus being the worst part of the original game, but somehow it doesn’t actually even as bad as I remembered in Reload. Either I am completely misremembering the experience or Reload has just improved it that much. Of course, it is still very repetitive labyrinth of procedural generation, but still a decent climb. The visual update also does help to make it less bleak and boring. The background music is however very faithful to the original, as in, not very inspiring. Might’ve listened to a couple of podcasts while I was at it.The new visuals do look and feel excellent. It’s not exactly the sharpest edge of graphics technology and not all of the art assets are polished to the highest degree, but the style does make up for a lot of it. Especially when the only available versions of Persona 3 have been extremely low fidelity, Reload just feels extremely pretty in comparison. And I just absolutely love all of the character models. I wanted them to remake Persona 3 with the character models from Dancing in Moonlight when that came out, but Reload’s models are even better. And in a series first, there’s ray-traced reflections, which do look really nice.The biggest downside might be the performance though – there’s some definite Unreal stutter happening even on powerful hardware. Maybe they’ll patch that out in due time, although I wouldn’t count on it. There’s definitely room for improvement on that department.There’s still 2D-animated cutscenes, although some cutscenes that I remember being 2D animation in the original are now 3D live-rendered cutscenes. While the quality of the 2D animation has never been the highest, both in the original and Reload, I’m of two minds about this. The cutscenes in Reload are definitely good, but there’s just something irresistible about 2D cutscenes.The voice acting in Persona 3 Reload is immaculate. First of all, almost all of the original cast from Persona 3 returns to redo their lines and they all sound exactly how I remember them sounding over a decade ago. The only exception that I am aware is Tanonaka, who passed away in 2010, and they got a fairly alright soundalike to voice Igor in his stead. And to make things even better, they got a bunch of voice actors for all of the social links, with every single rank of every single social link (bar the obvious silent one) being fully voiced! I really hope that we can expect all new Persona games to keep up this level of quality and quantity when it comes to voice acting.The music side initially feels rather uncanny. Everything sounds so familiar to the songs I’ve had in my music library for the past ten years and yet are strikingly different. However, that feeling of uncanniness did wear off as I kept playing, and the music does feel like Persona 3 – even if served with the whiff of a bootleg recording. The couple of pivotal songs during critical parts of the game are also kept and sound very similar to the originals despite Kawamura Yumi being replaced with a new face in Takahashi Azumi. There are also a couple of original bangers, so I’ll definitely be adding Reload’s soundtrack to my usual music rotation in the future.Yet I unfortunately can’t fully shake the feeling that maybe a small bit of Persona 3’s identity has been lost in the Persona 5-ification of the game. Not to a degree where I’d want to not play this or not recommend it to others, but just enough to make me think that there’s still a place in the universe for the original. I know that there’s definitely still a place for Portable, since the alternative perspective story for the female protagonist is not part of a Persona 3 remake. A lot of people were very vocal about this omission, but I don’t consider it critical: Portable always made it very clear that the female protagonist route was an alternative one. A new perspective, if you will. And who knows, maybe ATLUS will find the strength and courage to take our money again in the form of DLC for new perspectives.Remakes are always a contentious topic; if it’s okay to replace part of the history with the new and shiny. However, I do think that Persona 3 Reload is a product of exquisite quality and that it’s definitely a great version of Persona 3 and more accessible for fans both new and old who’ve gotten used to the new way of things. However, that is what I think it should be considered as: a new and different version of Persona 3, and not as the new Persona 3 to replace the old. A great way to experience the original story, even if wrapped in a remixed experience. It’s not like hordes of people were going to dust off their PlayStation 2 to experience Persona 3, especially when the games are often going for what they retailed for originally – or possibly even more.As an old fan of the series, I do highly recommend Persona 3 Reload. Whatever annoyance I felt before for the increased 70€ price tag has been replaced by the sheer joy that I got from my 100-hour journey into an old friend. I also imagine that people completely unfamiliar with Persona 3 will also enjoy it, as it is definitely a great game.PS: Don't pay extra for the digital soundtrack. You'll hate yourself if you do. Just wait for a real soundtrack release.

Compared to P5, this game is a lot of fun but the age is still evident in some ways.The art direction and menus are phenomenal. I love how blue this game is, and all of the menus feel satisfying to click through. The ability to Rewind is actually really cool, it makes it much easier to optimize if you are going for achievements, or if you want to go back and see what other dialogue options you might have gotten. I didn't use it so much on my first play through, but found it useful on my second run. The Social Links and Episodes are pretty sweet - I found them a bit easier to keep track of than in P5R. While you don't gain abilities in combat or exploration like in Persona 5, they are still useful for Persona Fusions. The stories are a lot of fun too, I particularly liked the Tower and Star Social Links. It is neat that you don't have to romance everyone, though there is seemingly no consequence for doing so.The combat is good enough, though gets repetitive. _childDocuments_.review: An absolute 10/10 JRPG experience from Atlus with the Persona series. For someone who has played the original, the entire P3RE journey from start to finish was 100% a love letter from them to us; from the character's voices, to the remixed soundtracks, all of it were a familiar experience, yet different, in a fresh and exciting manner that grows on you all over again.For those new to the Persona series, this is an easy recommend to get into the series due to the ease of the game's pacing and flow, seamlessly balancing the story and the dungeon crawling aspect of the game. But bear in mind, like any of the other Persona series, the early beginnings of the game is quite story heavy before it slowly eases you into allowing you to manage your own day to day schedules.

_childDocuments_.review: This is not the right way to experience a PS2 Classic.Right from the start we're greeted by a shockingly pathetic warning that this game has VIOLENCE in it. Wow, you mean like every game in existence? Oh wait.. it has BULLYING too. If you can steel yourself enough to progress past this warning you'll be greeted with the new opening. It serves to remind us that whoever they got to sing for this game is unable to perform. Her monotone voice and lack of energy persists in every song throughout the game. You'll hate it so much, you'll want to die. Once we get into the game proper we find that our beloved characters have been replaced with souless American voice actors. The setting we remember is now grossly oversaturated and if you keep playing you'll find the worst awakening cutscene in a Persona game. Gone is the cool anime cutscene with proper pacing, cinematography and cool factor. Instead we get a lame in game cutscene.. 70 dollars worth indeed. Honestly i don't have anything else to say. To me this is like going out to eat a 5 course meal and the first dish they bring you is a piss broth soup with bits of chicken. Maybe the next course will be better but I ain't sticking around to find out.FInal Score : Trigger warning ( it's gonna be negative)

_childDocuments_.review: Persona 3 FES is one of my favorite games of all time, so when I heard that a remake was on the way, I was elated. Over time, doubt started to set it before the game's launch, remaking a title that a lot of people hold in high regard is no easy feat. As someone who loved Persona 3 and holds it's themes, characters, gameplay, and everything else in between in high regard, this remake completely delivered. Gameplay enhancements go a long way, and while yes, Reload is the easier game, it's combat feels like a dream to go through, fast, snappy, and oh so stylish, it never feels truly boring. Soundtrack is another strong aspect of the original Persona 3, and while some may argue that Reload "butchers" Meguro's arrangements, I strongly disagree. I'm of the mind that Reload's ost is at worst, a sidegrade, and at best, is an upgrade. Everything that made the original soundtrack great is here, and then some. The story received minimal changes, only adding scenes for Strega, these scenes, while admittedly small in number, go a long way in establishing the individuals of Strega as actual characters. Who hold their own goals and motivations. A far cry from how they were handled in the original.Persona 3 Reload is a triumph for anyone who loves JRPGS, and an even bigger triumph for huge fans of the persona/megaten series. It's only competition this year are games from the same publisher, a testament to the overall quality that they put out. Easy 10/10. PLAY IT NOW

_childDocuments_.review: Overall I'd say this is a solid remake, I do have a lot of issues with it however. For one a lot of the English dialogue is just completely different from what the JP text is. But there's also issues with the mediocre English voice work, the original was amateurish but the fact that most of the OGs returned as side characters makes it even worse. _childDocuments_.review: My first glimpse into the world of Persona was with Persona 5 (PS4 version available to play with PSN after buying a PS5). It was the JRPG I never knew I wanted. I knew there was a fanbase for Persona 4 Golden but after playing Persona 5, got sidetracked away from the series. Jump to this year when I saw that Persona 3 Reload as part of the summer sale and I had to get a copy. I'm glad I did. The play style feels like an extension of Persona 5 with fantastic visuals. It looks and plays well on the Steam Deck and if you're a Mac user with an Apple M2, using the Wine + Apple Game Porting Toolkit app 'Whiskey', it plays at 4K with max settings *very* well. Having never played the original, I don't have a comparison but can only say that it has been great getting back into a really solid Persona title after not playing one in about 3 years or so. Stop reading this and go download it already.

_childDocuments_.review: I have mixed feelings about P3 Reload.First off, I did really enjoy playing this game very much, especially around the middle and its absolute legendary climax... But some things just felt "off".On the one hand, its Persona 3, arguably the best Persona game narratively and thematically, and on the other, its a remake that fails to capture aspects of what made the original great to begin with.As of writing this, I have not played the original release of P3. Its hard to find so I won't act like a longtime fan, but enough comparisons exist for these things.Reload loses a lot of the original's stylistic/thematic direction in favour of a more condensed experience. So much so that it feels like its contesting with itself at points.Gameplay also feels quite condensed. This game is REAL easy, a bit unbalanced (therugys...) and too many restrictions were cut.(Also mad that MC can't use all the weapons in this one).All this is to say, I recommend because its Persona 3, but not for much else.I feel like I missed out on something with the remake but I still appreciate the work that was put into it.Hopefully be able to play the original at some point...

_childDocuments_.review: Persona 3 Reload takes us back to the iconic world of Shadows, Personas, and the enigmatic Dark Hour, bringing with it a wave of nostalgia that effortlessly intertwines with modern gaming sensibilities. As a devoted fan of the original Persona 3 FES, I couldn't help but appreciate the dedication ATLUS has shown in preserving the essence of the classic while injecting fresh elements that breathe new life into the experience.One of the game's standout features is the retention of the vast majority of Persona 3 FES, including the beloved fusion spells that add depth and strategy to the already engaging battle system. This fidelity to the original not only pays homage to the roots of the series but also ensures that longtime fans will find comfort in the familiar mechanics that made Persona 3 a timeless classic.The cast of characters, who have become beloved fixtures in the Persona universe, seamlessly transition into a modern setting. ATLUS' careful consideration in hand-picking new voice actors shines through, as they manage to encapsulate the essence of each character flawlessly. The chemistry among the cast feels as authentic as ever, making it easy to invest emotionally in their individual stories and the overarching narrative.Undoubtedly, the standout element of Persona 3 Reload is its phenomenal soundtrack. The iconic tunes that accompanied us through the Dark Hour are back, but with a refreshing twist. The addition of the newest singer, Azumi Takahashi, injects new life into the music, offering her own interpretation while staying true to the originals. The result is a soundtrack that manages to be both nostalgic and innovative, enhancing the overall gaming experience.As the narrative unfolds, the bittersweet ending of Persona 3 Reload hit me with a powerful emotional resonance, leaving me in tears. The game's message lingered in my thoughts long after the final credits rolled, a testament to the storytelling prowess of ATLUS. The ability to evoke such strong emotions is a hallmark of an exceptional gaming experience.In conclusion, Persona 3 Reload is a masterful blend of old and new, offering a captivating journey through the familiar while introducing fresh elements that enhance the overall experience. With a stellar cast, a phenomenal soundtrack, and an emotionally resonant narrative, this release cements itself as a must-play for both longtime fans and newcomers alike.

_childDocuments_.review: Persona 3 Reload: A Journey Worth RelivingPersona 3 Reload is a nostalgic hug that welcomes you back to a world full of mystery, friendship, and self-discovery. As someone who has fond memories of the original game, I was eager to see how this remake would reimagine one of the most beloved games for me in the Persona series. Atlus did not disappoint. They’ve taken everything that made the original game special and enhanced it, making it a perfect blend of old and new.From the very beginning, stepping into the shoes of the protagonist feels like reuniting with an old friend. The familiar setting of Gekkoukan High School and the enigmatic Dark Hour have been beautifully reimagined. Whether it's the eerie glow of the midnight world or the bustling life of Iwatodai, the game’s environments feel alive and immersive.One of the most heartwarming aspects of the game is the deep connection you feel with your team,Each character, from the ever-  optimistic Junpei to the determined Yukari, has their own story and struggles. The enhanced voice acting and character animations breathe new life into these relationships. Conversations feel more genuine, and the emotional moments hit even harder. It’s like catching up with friends you haven’t seen in years, only to find your bond is just as strong, if not stronger.Music has always been a big part of Persona’s charm, and Reload excels here too. The soundtrack, with its mix of energetic and hauntingly beautiful tracks, has been remastered to perfection.  Shoji Meguro’s work remains iconic, and the new arrangements add depth to an already powerful score. It’s the kind of music that stays with you, long after you’ve put the game down. Sadly there's no option to switch it to the classic tunes from FES. Playing Reload is like going on a nostalgic journey while discovering something entirely new. Balancing school life, forging friendships, and battling through the Tartarus, you find yourself immersed in a story that is both heartfelt and thought-provoking. The social links, which delve into the personal lives of your friends and acquaintances, are more engaging than ever, offering insights that make the game’s themes of life, death, and human connection resonate deeply in your heart.As the story builds to its climax, the emotional stakes become even higher, making the resolution hit hard. It's a reminder of the transient nature of life and the enduring impact of the connections we make. The ending stays with you, prompting reflection long after the final credits roll.Ultimately, Persona 3 Reload is a beautiful love letter to both fans of the original and those experiencing it for the first time. It captures the essence of what made the original so beloved while enhancing it with modern touches that make the journey feel fresh and exciting. Whether you're a long-time fan or a newcomer, this remake is a testament to the enduring magic of the Persona series and a reminder of the powerful stories that games can tell.Persona 3 Reload isn't just a game; it’s an emotional journey that invites you to reflect, grow, and cherish the bonds you form along the way. It’s a reminder that, no matter how much time passes, some stories are timeless.
