_childDocuments_.review: I was VERY skeptical about the game and this is coming from someone who is a 40K fan AND also played Pathfinder: Kingmaker on day one. To give a bit of context, as I mentioned, I played Pathfinder: Kingmaker on release and fell in love with the game in the first few hours but that changed gradually to a complete 180 degrees turn the more I advanced in the game. The game was FULL of bugs on release to the point that I did not managed to finish it due to game breaking bugs and the worst was that these bugs only appeared later on from Chapter 3 in that game. It ended up hating Kingmaker with a passion due to that experience, that's something that never occurred to me before so with that in mind I was wary of Rogue Trader and held off on buying it right away. The experience was so bad that it ruined it for me and I never got to trying it again after they fixed all the bugs, it simply destroyed any desire to give it another shot. Something I did not wish to repeat with Rogue Trader.At the moment I am currently in Chapter 4 and I have noticed only 1-2 animation bugs where NPCs are sitting in mid air and perhaps a dialogue reference where I ask an NPC where is one of my chars even though the said char was on my ship and not on some weird planet that the other NPC claimed them to be on. A bit strange but so far nothing game breaking and I hope it will stay as such. I'll post more about this subject once I finish the game but so no game breaking bugs so yay!Now for the game itself, I must say they managed to capture the essence of 40K perfectly. The character and level designs are spot on, the dialogue fits, music is awesome and I love the level of choice I have in the game. It might get a bit overwhelming with all the info dump, especially for those who are not familiar with 40K lore, but take it slow and you'll adjust with time.The companions are what you would expect from a 40K setting although I would of liked a bit more cutscene 1 on 1 interactions with them besides the initial cutscenes after you bring them on the ship for the first time. I also found the romancing a bit... strange, to be exact I had no plans on romancing anyone simply because imo it's 40k I have no time or interest in romance since my duty is towards the EMPEROR so you can imagine my surprise when I try to pacify the Eldar in my party when some human insults her only to get the achievement of "Start a romance" while I was trying to mediate the situation. Emperor protect me, I don't wanna be hit on by some elf ginger that keeps calling me mon-keigh, even her darker cousin has more respect towards me. So yeah, jokes aside companions are nice and the romance was a bit ...interesting. (I friend-zoned the eldar before the Lord Inquisitor double tapped me in the back of the head just to be safe)Combat is pretty good but you'll get a bit overwhelmed at first with all the abilities, traits and gear that you can find. What I found fun is the fact that gears don't offer only passive stat increase but also conditions where it adds new effects to existing abilities. For example boots that give the wearer a free attack whenever they parry a blow, combine that with a char that has high parry and abilities that make enemies attack them and you have a killer duelist that counters the ♥♥♥♥ out of everything. Overall the combat is fun and has a lot of options for creating builds based on backgrounds, arch-types, traits, gear and maybe some traits received from quests, buildings etc.Speaking of buildings, the planet managing system and ship system are pretty good. Managing your planets is very straight forward; you build structures based on what resources and previous buildings you have available, and get rewarded with more resources, items or unique traits. Do take note that some buildings lock you out from building other structures so choose wisely.The ship system proved more fun than I thought, despite only having one ship they managed to make it enjoyable although it feels fairly simplistic despite all of the abilities you get down the line. It's not bad, I actually like it just feels like it pales a bit when compared to normal combat and all of the build combinations you can pull off there. Overall still enjoyable since it never overstayed its welcome, although it might not be everyone's cup of tea.Story is interesting both main and secondary quests and I really enjoyed how they managed to offer a lot of variety and tell even side quest stories in a way that was interesting and made me wanna discover just what the hell happened here? I don't want to enter into too much details but it does seem like they managed to grasp the feel of what it is to be a rogue trader. Although I think one of my main gripes might be that one of the main baddies makes an appearance at the end of Chapter 1 and hardly hear about them later on, and I'm already in Chapter 4. Feels like they just disappeared and I got side tracked by other things. It feels a bit odd but not a major complain.Currency is treated differently in this game, unlike in other games where you need to go to a store to buy or sell stuff, you're a Rogue Trader, you have servants to deal with that. So instead of gold you instead have a resource similar to profit points which show how much you are worth. This combined with what reputations you have with other factions dictate what you can 'acquire' from them. Basically reputation dictates what items they are willing to sell to you while profit dictates if you can afford the said items. If you can afford an item? Great! You just get it and you don't lose ANY profit points from the purchase BUT you can lose profit points due to other reasons like building structures and dialogue choices. It's a system that walks away from the standard RPG ones of old but it is fitting given the setting and the status of your character. I mean, you're a Rogue Trader, not some plebeian that walks around with pocket change in their pants. Oh and there's no encumbrance system like in previous games, I guess you have servants to carry your stuff for you which makes sense!Overall, I've really enjoyed my time with Rogue Trader so far and I hope it stays the same or gets better, it's probably one of the most immersive 40K games out there and if they managed to stomp out all the bugs then I would highly recommend this to all 40k fans and anyone who wishes to get immersed into this setting.I'll try and post an update once I finish the game and offer my final thoughts along with whether I discovered any game breaking bugs since that would be my main issue with this game.

_childDocuments_.review: One of if not the best 40k game since Dawn Of War. I was getting really tired of the Warhammer money grab games that were all the same. Tactical turn based combat with a loose narrative written around it. Not engrossing or immersive at all. But then they got Owlcat to do one for them. And to true Owlcat fashion, the wrote an engaging and immersive story which makes the 40k universe feel massive but tangible all at once which I think is important for how large and complex the 40k universe is. This is the game the Warhammer folks needed to make to get people back interested.This game definitely does have bugs. Like using some abilities do all the animations and such but don’t make virtually guaranteed hits. Like Cassia’s “breath weapon”. And there’s one early companion quest that is broken which locks it out completely. There are also some fights that feel more like slogs rather than something I’m engaged in. Non-sniper ranged combat gets very underpowered in the mid game I feel and the weapon drops don’t scale well against enemies. This game also really needs a jump or leap mechanic in combat.I’m sure many of these things will be addressed, but there is a surprising lack of early updates so I’m guesssing they’re planning on doing one big patch in the next few weeks or early next year after the holidays. I recommend buying this game because I believe it’ll encourage Games Workshop to focus on narrative driven, quality games over huge numbers of money grabs.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a bit mixed on this one, but first, the positives. The game absolutely nails its setting. Dialogue, descriptions, art, and sound are all excellent and all utterly Warhammer. There is a diverse cast to interact with and always something new to discover. On the downside, the game is quite buggy at release. I managed to miss the big game-breaking bugs and the devs have been releasing a constant stream of patches, so I'm sure this will get better over time. But there were quests I couldn't finish, character moments I couldn't see, and sections I had to replay due to bugs. More fundamentally, I don't know that the combat system here works. And, if it does, it's not much fun. The problem is buffs. You get a number of action points each turn, and most of those are spent applying buffs to maximize the effect of your one or two attacks. Most buffs either last only a turn or stack, so you generally need to apply the same ones each turn. And each application is accompanied by an animation and maybe a voice line. This isn't that interesting and you tend to do the same thing every turn so it gets old quick. Then, once you win a few fights and level up your faced with giant list of dozens of talents to select from, most of which modify those buffs in some subtle way. You'll likely reach around level 50 by the end of the game and have around a dozen party members who each need to be leveled manually, so expect to spend a lot of time reading tooltips to determine which 2% increase to some effect you really need right now. If you dropped the animations and cut a third of the nonsense from the combat system this game would be half as long and likely better for it.Combat also just doesn't feel particularly balanced, at least on normal difficulty. Your characters are fragile and outnumbered relative to your opponents. To counter this, your characters tend to have quite good defenses (parry and dodge). Perhaps too good? With solid tactics, a lot of combats feel trivial as the enemy struggles to even do damage. The last boss, as an example, managed to push through only 1-2 pips of damage on my characters in the whole fight. Splash damage from my own area attacks was the bigger threat. But then you hit a fight where the math is against you and suddenly half your party is down without warning. I haven't tried other difficulties. Maybe things are better higher up, or maybe the spikes just get worse.Overall, if you're looking for a good Warhammer 40000 game, buy this. It's worth your time. If you're looking for a good tactical RPG, maybe try something else or wait for a year of balance patches.

_childDocuments_.review: Have you ever wanted to play an RPG as an evil ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ but always hated being hated for that? Never fear! _childDocuments_.review: (I actually have many more hours than logged in Steam)The most fun I had in an RPG in a long time. Many times better than Baldurs Gate 3 in my opinion. It feels overall more mature and less than a kind of random, generic fantasy story.As I am not a Warhammer fan and this is my first real contact with the setting and universe I can wholeheartedly recommend it to anyone who just wants to play a very good RPG.This game is very story and text heavy from beginning to end. While it had some minor bugs I didn't run into anything gamebreaking.In the trailer and screenshots the UI looks worse than it is. They actually did a very decent job UI wise. There is minor annoyances like in most games, but I found it a lot better than the BG3 one.I like how this game actually takes things and decisions into account and doesn't wait till the end for any outcomes or effects.There are many paths. For example there is a fight that many people complain about being too hard/not possible to beat, and I also failed many times only to then wonder off and notice I can skip that fight completely through exploring. The game has many non-obvious parts, even things like hidden companions. So if you like to explore and just role play your character this game does an amazing job.I also love things like the concept of a veil value filling up when "magic" is used and another dimension starts to break through. I love both the gameplay part of this and how it is done effects wise. Even the words your characters speak, even sounds from attacks, etc. are distorted and have echos. There is many surprises in this game.It goes new ways, also with how trading works. You are a rogue trader, have riches by definition and so you are not trading with some gold/credits, but with "whether you can afford it" (Profit Factor) which you don't lose by trading items. Every items also doubles as cargo that has multiple uses, though the biggest being building colonies and getting favor from factions. But that favor isn't just sitting as a stand alone thing for buying items, but also has effect on the story. Sure, if you don't care you can probably ignore it, but it's always nice to see role playing decisions having story effects.Another thing I really enjoy is that the story, the pieces of texts, conversations are interesting, sometimes even thought provoking. Sadly I've played quite a few games where there might be a lot of stuff to read, but it's all rather dull and boring. That's not how most things in this game are. Sure some stuff is more interesting than other, but nothing feels like it's forced in just as filler.Every character is pretty thought through and while some of them are cliche they don't feel empty. There is a lot of situations where you are surprised, but those are genuine twists and not a character suddenly acting out of place.The characters also all fit into the world. They have opinions they might or might want to have romances. That's a gripe I had with BG3. It feels like every characters is generic, the companions party feel like an out of place bunch of hipsters. Don't get me wrong, it's fine to be a hipster, but if somehow every companion is a bi-sexual hipster ready to be seduced the characters start to feel generic. It also makes it feel like a bit of a dating sim. Not so in this game. The characters feel like they actually have, well... character.I just played through the game and I am already looking forward to have a play-through with a completely different character.EDIT: Now also seeing that in the context of Pathfinder. Wrath of the Righteous. I think this game is a huge step up. There are quite a few annoyances, parts of unsatisfying gameplay, things causing confusing, lore that goes nowhere, things that don't make sense. Roguetrader in comparison is really great. Don't get me wrong, I really like Path Wrath of the Rightous, especially with that war mechanic disable (great idea, but boring/annoying/barebones feeling).  So if you thought Wrath of the rightous was intersting, but annoying (weight mechanic) then get this game!

_childDocuments_.review: Despite some bugs and other criticisms this game has been the best experience of existing in 40k I've ever seen. While other games might capture the battles perfectly, they rarely delve into the interesting locales or grim mysteries of the universe itself. The game gave me a sense of wonder that only the books have ever really even tapped into. Mind you it's a terrifying one but the game itself feels like existing in this universe, horror and all. That being said, there are valid criticisms.-Bugs. Not the Terminid/Tyranid kind either. These are getting patched and for the most part, other than a floating character screen, I've been pretty lucky to avoid any game breakers-Character leveling/skill system. It's pretty on the surface, but the sheer volume of skills and effects is mind boggling. Almost every other level you get a trait/skill/ability and instead of having say, 5-10 for each class, you get a wall of about 60(not exaggerating) different ones to choose from. And while some are easy as buffing an attribute by a few points, others are dense walls of text telling you how something effects something else by x% if you hit y range. Needless, it can be very hard on the brain. -Battles. I don't fully fall into the battles are tedious. THey are fun challenges at best, and terribly annoying slogs at worst. I think so far though the balance of them hasn't been too brutal(plus you can mod this away). You will have to slow down to do fights since they are turn based and each fight is pretty big. You don't have quick one offs here. It's either a gang of 12 baddies or like 5 baddies and a super boss and until late game you won't really walk through any of them.Now to the positives:-Vibes. So many 40k vibes here and they are perfect. Walking your ship feels like your on one. Your crew and teammates are wildly different and well written. There is even courting of characters. Nowhere near the best of the genre but still actually fun and at least on my run has been quite accurate to the character.-Fighting feels brutal. Tearing off limbs. Exploding groups with grenades, meltaing off people's faces. It's all here.-Terrifying side quests. These are small one off text adventures, but the flavor here is perfect 40k horror. Be careful what you pick up in this game cause it's rarely ever good-Fun ship fighting. The ship figfhting is just a cherry on top for those who like turn based strats in space. Hello Battlefleet Gothic.Overall I highly recommmend the game. It's a fun time once you look past the normal blemishes and already many big patches have come out to fix and smooth it over. Good luck!

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic application of the Owlcat formula for CRPGs to the Warhammer 40k franchise, I can't get enough of this. The writing and quest structures are good, character designs are great as well. I love the interesting mechanics (the officer class is more fun than I would have expected a support class to be).That being said, It needs better optimization on Mac. I'm playing this after Baldur's Gate 3, in that game, my machine (Macbook Pro with 6-core Intel i7 proc with 32GB ram and AMD Radeon Pro 5600M 8 GB) didn't start to bog down until act 3 (when a load more people start showing up onscreen at any given time), and even then, the most I had to do was turn my graphics settings from 'High' to 'Medium' to fix it; yet, even with crowd density turned down & quality set to medium (and film grain turned off), RT still seems to regress to slideshow levels of stutter (was especially bad during the post-triumph cutscene in act 1). This is especially evident in battles with a large number of characters... sometimes, the game will hang for a bit when taking enemy/npc turns, and characters may blink out while a movement/attack animation is meant to be playing. Please keep in mind that these graphical issues are not necessarily game-breaking, and honestly, I'm supremely grateful to Owlcat for putting out a Mac version of this game at all. It's a fantastic addition to the 40k franchise. I just purchased the DLC that came out yesterday, and can't wait to tear into it.

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't given this game the time it needs for a fair review, but so far, it's truly astounding.The soundtrack is incredible, the graphics are good, and the scene detail and immersion are top-notch. The voice acting is great, but, maybe could've had more.. that said, I can count on one hand the amount of games where I've sat and read the text rather than skipping through it. The writing is just that good.It definitely has that XCOM feel, as expected. However, the plot is shaping up to be one of the best I've played in this genre. This is coming from someone with little to no exposure to 40k lore.Everything is well-documented in-game without being overwhelming. Character motivations and how their backgrounds influence them make for a great experience. I'm learning the lore thanks to the incredible storytelling and immersive environments.Regarding the builds, talents, and so on, even at this early stage, I’ve found a lot of great synergies, which bodes well for replayability, especially in terms of team composition and experimentation, not to mention the choice between Dogmatic, Iconoclast & Heretical, all which offer significantly different encounters throughout a playthrough, based on the reviews I read before making this purchase.The pacing of the game is better compared to even great games like BG3, very little time spend running back to camp for regen, or spending large amounts of time performing inventory management.I have to mention the bugs, they are plain to see (Strange flickering shadows in some scenes, character animation stutters on both Steam Deck and a Well specced machines). I would argue it's because I am running it with Linux/Proton on both systems.. but I have seen matching complaints from windows users. They are very minor however - not gamebreaking & respect is due for supporting Steam Deck (And Linux by extension) compatibility.It's got all the makings of something I'll enjoy. At €50 its fair, but on offer at €35, its kind of a steal, considering there's more proposed updates and some DLC coming up. Hopefully hundreds of hours of gameplay to be had in here.

_childDocuments_.review: +++ Warhammer: Rogue Trader - A Love-Hate Odyssey in the Koronus Expanse+++After 100+ hours and a rollercoaster of emotions, I've finally beaten the story of "Warhammer: Rogue Trader," and I'm left with conflicting thoughts that could spiral me in the clutches of the changer of ways with ease. Only faith in the emperor of the most dogmatic approach can let me recommend this game. But recommend it, I shall.This game is a paradox, offering a deep dive into the life of a Rogue Trader, ready to chart your own way. this review is a tale of both adoration and frustration.+++ The Highs ++++ Narrative Brilliance +The campaign and its conclusion are nothing short of perfection. The story captivates from start to finish, with a richness that beckons for another playthrough. Despite broken quests and clunky UI, there is a gem of a narrative to play through.+  Grandiose Systems +The game nails the feeling of being a true Rogue Trader, where wealth is more about influence and power than coin. It's a fresh take that I greatly appreciated and the sprawling scale of it is something to compliment. You go from bashing the heads of lowly rebels to negotiating and making diplomatic deals to commanding your starship into space battles and managing your colonies all in the same game, and they are all meaningful experiences that add to the aforementioned grandiose feeling. Well done.+ Stunning Visuals and Environments +Each of the hundreds of unique locations is a visual treat, brimming with detail and atmosphere. I wish I could go down to eye level on this game, the fixed camera doesn’t do it justice.+ Engaging Combat and Strategy + Once you crack the combat system, it's incredibly satisfying to dominate battles through tactical genius.+ Meaningful Connections + The relationships you build with your crew and the systems you interact with add a compelling depth to the game.+ Varied Quests and Playthroughs + The quests are thematic and engaging, offering distinct experiences based on your choices. Whether you're playing it safe or going full heretical, the game feels different each time.+++ The Lows ++++ Difficulty Spikes From Hell + The game's difficulty can be as unpredictable as the Warp, forcing me to adjust settings just to keep my sanity intact.(My rule of thumb was 3 unfair reloads = “story” difficulty for the first round of combat)+ Overwhelming Complexity + Between leveling, gear selection, and inventory management, the game sometimes felt more like a chore than an adventure. The cheap non-existent icons and confusing (or just lacking) skill descriptions don’t help.+ Clunky User Experience + Navigating the game's interfaces often felt like battling an ancient tech-priest's worst design, detracting from the overall experience.+ Loot Logic That Breaks Immersion + For a game that excellently captures the essence of being above mere monetary concerns, having to sift through trash for loot felt disappointingly out of place.+ Lack of Seamless Transitions + The jarring shifts between scenes, like going from planet to ship, unnecessarily broke the immersion.+ Broken everything + The quest bugs are the worst because you never truly know if it is a legitimate quest state and you just lack context or if it's truly broken. It didn’t stop me from enjoying my 100+ hours with it, but I just had to get into a “war is hell” mentality and let go of my desire to have my beautiful quest log clean and finished.+++ Final Verdict +++"Warhammer: Rogue Trader" is a game of contrasts and grandiose ambition. It masterfully captures the essence of the Warhammer 40k universe, offering an immersive experience of life as a Rogue Trader with a narrative depth that's rare in the gaming world. However, it's a journey marred by frustrating gameplay mechanics and design choices that can test your patience.For fans of the 40k lore who dream of navigating the complex life of a Rogue Trader, this game offers a rich, thematic experience that's hard to find elsewhere. Be warned, though: for every moment of awe and victory, there's a potential frustration waiting around the corner. Despite its flaws, I recommend "Warhammer: Rogue Trader" to those willing to embrace its chaotic blend of brilliance and bafflement. It's a love-hate relationship, but for a 40k enthusiast, it's an odyssey worth undertaking and echoes the complex bureaucracy of the verse, it feels like this would be a game made by the administratum itself!

Simply put, there are times you need to manually fly to a planet to resolve specific conflicts, wasting even more of your time.- Maps+Inventory management is buggy. _childDocuments_.review: Highly recommended to play if you already like Warhammer 40k, in case of being new to the universe and want to play an CRPG, then I would recommend Pathfinder or BG3 Why I say that ? Gameplay is something that doesn't stay too far from any previous CRPG, but with the Wh40k universe, things can't be that simple. The extermination of civilians, attacking innocent alien species or killing a companion which sounds bad on paper, actually are good things in the Warhammer universe, which makes the game really interesting since, you know the consequences of keeping alive civilians that got in contact with heretic materials, and exterminating them is the right thing to do. This is what makes Rogue Trader so interesting, the constant fight on what in the real world would be something bad compared to what would happen in lore In the other hand, there is a in depth build of the universe in which we have to travel, explore, conquer and even administrate since we can have our own planetS that will give us resources for our trips Long story short, and quoting the beginning, if you like Warhammer40k, this game is HIGHLY recommended. Play it the most blind you can and enjoy the trip, is going to be long and you will need the most interesting companions possible

_childDocuments_.review: If you’re looking for some screenshots  to view all the ones I took for this game.Your position as a Rogue Trader, one of the Emperor’s most important Chosen, will allow you to traverse the Koronus Expanse; no text is spared in outlining its lore, characters, factions and events in detail. Hundreds of well-written and sometimes voiced pages of dialogue will be the joy of avid readers. The characters part of your retinue or surrounding most major events are competently-written, while the variety of reactions and changes based on your action is impressive, although half of them feel out of place or pure nonsense, like an Astartes saying nothing after seeing you commit heresy.Visually, RT doesn’t impress; aside from the beautifully drawn comic panels and portraits, the graphics are modest for 2024 standards. Even with that, it still manages to have FPS issues in several locations. The world is built with solid care and attention to detail: even side locations have their own atmosphere and identity, although the keener eye will spot a large number of half-assed or borked elements, since the devs clearly preferred quantity over quality. The grimdark feel of 40K is there, but you’ll never feel fully immersed in such a setting. Exploration is divided between planetside and space. On the ground, you’ll lead your retinue of up to six members through a variety of locations, from Imperial cities to forgotten bunkers and even dimensional anomalies. There’s always a huge amount of secrets to find, with the help of your Awareness stat, which house unique items or secret level sections. Traps might be hidden anywhere; you can disarm them, or run through without a care since you’ll always have healing items far in excess.In space, your ship can jump between systems through the Warp, which may trigger enemy encounters or debuffs unless you make the routes safe using your Navigator’s limited Psyker powers; you’ll have to choose which paths to use the most in advance. Planets can be scanned, vessels hailed, pirates battled, which leads to a number of dialogues and text-based roleplaying panels that will put your party’s stats to the test.Fights play out in a turn-based fashion, with separate points for actions and movement, a high/low cover system, attacks of opportunity, but no overwatch mechanic. The system is vast and factors calculations to determine the outcome of every single shot, dodge or action—everything, from equipment to stats to perks, will be factored in at all times to the finest degree. Enemies are varied and have an enormous amount of unique abilities, weapons, perks and AI diversity based on the faction you’ll be facing, while bosses, at least early on, feel like decisive challenges. Having a synergistic party composition is paramount for victory, as usual you’ll be put against overwhelming numbers; the consequences of your fights, such as wounds, will weigh you down for the level, unless you heal them. The “Momentum” mechanic, based on enemy kills, rewards aggression and allows you to unleash a character’s “Ultimate” skill once charged, different for each class, raining destruction on your foes or buffing your team tremendously.This is all good and exciting, except from about halfway through, your party will become so OP that none of it will matter anymore. You’ll steamroll everything once you figure out what perks and items to stack together and create absurd combinations of statistics. Bosses and enemies that in the 40K lore could slay entire Astartes companies are demolished in a few turns.Space combat works in the same way, but in a simpler fashion, having your ship usually put against many foes, with a shield then health separating you from the void. A number of skills and maneuvers, depending on which character is assigned to what station on the vessel, will prove critical to succeed against foes. The balance is, again, screwed majorly except for late-game enemy ships, which are OP, forcing you to resort to kiting strategies to emerge victorious, even with the best gear money can buy.All your characters can choose various specializations that will define their role on the field, with the possibility to respec and even create custom mercenaries from scratch to build the ultimate party that suits your strategy best. Leveling up will have you access the next tier of your current class, which may unlock stat bonuses, new abilities and more. They can also acquire proficiencies to use new types of weapons or armor, and their moral inclination will allow them to use specific items that are restricted, such as some only being usable by a Heretic character. You’ll also be able to upgrade and customize your ship with better guns, engines and so forth, other than upgrading the vessel to have more armor and HP, if you have enough resources.As a Rogue Trader, a number of colonies are under your command, and not only you’ll have to order them to execute research projects that consume the resources gained from planetary scans and space battles, but also react to the events happening on them and decide wisely on your next move. Such random events can majorly alter how a colony functions, and often lead to situations you’ll have to personally deal with, and result in unique skills or items should you manage them in the right way.

_childDocuments_.review: Title: Navigating the Grim Universe - A Rogue Trader's Take on Warhammer 40,000Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader, the latest venture from Owlcat Games, throws gamers headfirst into the brutal expanse of the 41st Millennium. Despite a few glitches and hiccups along the way, the game's standout features—mind-blowing art, a killer soundtrack, and an engaging story—make it a worthwhile journey for any Warhammer 40K enthusiast.Art (5/5):Rogue Trader knocks it out of the park with its visuals. The attention to detail is insane, capturing the gritty, war-torn feel of the Warhammer 40K universe perfectly. The game's art direction is a love letter to every fan of the franchise. It's like stepping into a grimdark masterpiece.Music (5/5):The soundtrack is a force to be reckoned with. Blending orchestral elements with a touch of electronica, it complements the dark and intense atmosphere of Warhammer 40K flawlessly. Whether you're knee-deep in a battle frenzy or unraveling the game's darker secrets, the music nails the mood every time.Narrative (5/5):Rogue Trader takes the lore-hungry gamer on a wild ride through the 40K universe. The story, following the exploits of the Rogue Trader, delves deep into the complexities of this grim and dystopian future. The characters are well fleshed out, each with their own motives and struggles, and the narrative hits all the right notes for Warhammer 40K enthusiasts. It's a captivating journey through a universe rife with political intrigue and cosmic horrors.Some bugs frustrating, no doubt. But here's the silver lining—Owlcat Games is on it. They're pushing out patches and updates, showing a commitment to making things right. So, while it's a hiccup now, there's hope that it's a temporary setback.Conclusion:Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader is a best cRPG in the 41st Millennium. The visuals, music, and narrative offer a solid experience for any Warhammer 40K fan. Yeah, the bugs are a downer, but the devs seem hell-bent on fixing them. If you can weather the storm, there's a promising journey awaiting you in the grim darkness of the far future.

That said, I am very disappointed that even several months after release and a fairly steady stream of patches, there are so....so many bugs still in the game. All of what I've experienced are very minor and don't impact gameplay so far, but are very immersion breaking or just plain annoying. I've seen everything from stretched out meshes on models, T posing of corpses hanging around, to outdated info on the expanse map like telling you there are hostile ships present that aren't there anymore. I can only imagine what this game must have been like on release if there are this many minor bugs still so prevalent and they haven't had time to fix them. edit: just after writing this review I encountered 2 more bugs: one where someone who died earlier in the game was magically alive again and another where a quest marker appeared on a map where there was no quest at all. They just keep coming, lolIf it weren't for the regularity of little bugs like these I'd happily rate this game a 8-9/10 for what I've experienced so far. As is it's around a 7-8/10

_childDocuments_.review: Positives:Good writing. Texts are fun and exciting to read. Very important in CRPG and devs delivered here. Characters don't feel like teenagers in adult bodies.Atmosphere. They nailed 40k vibes. Grimdark is strong here.Music. Another one for the collection, alongside Darktide and Mechanicus OST.Negatives:-Combat is lacking "oomph". Heavy attacks or crits are exactly the same as normal attacks. And animations in general aren't varied, nor have cool visual effects.-Archetypes aren't unique enough. They don't define gameplay of the character much.-Sparse voice acting. The voice actors they hired sound amazing and strongly enhance the characters at those rare moments they speak. As of now, only Prologue has full voice. After that, only general conversations on the ship deck, some of the romance-related events (not all) and very few other plot-related conversations have voice over. The choice which character-related event is voiced is inconsistent: some less important have it, and more important not. Two of the major antagonists has no voice whatsoever. -Speaking of combat again. Balance is meh. I played on Daring difficulty for my first playthrough, which is the most balanced one, with no bonuses for player nor debuffs on for the enemies,  and it was very easy outside two encounters. One of the two wasn't even difficult in a proper sense, but heavily reliant on RNG - boss is always going first, let's see if he knocks out several members of my party and makes the fight unwinnable from the get go forcing me to reload, or I get a chance to fight.-Leveling takes too long, which is, as I read, a common issue across Owlcat games.-Space battles.Putting the balance and system issues aside, lacking in regards to VA and animation stems from Owlcat not being a money-rich, triple A developer. It's sad, as should Owlcat get 100+ million $ budgets, they have high potential of making a CRPG game that would rival Baldur's Gate 3. Nevertheless, unfairness or lacking budget aside, combat in Rogue Trader is lacking and I can't just ignore it. Same for Voice Acting. Wish they were utilised more, for how damn good they are. Space battles... well, they're underwhelming, to say the least. But again, credits where they're due. I had very few moments where I were bored tons of unvoiced text. And music does add SIGNIFICANTLY to the enjoyment. It's phenomenal.All in all, I think Rogue Trader is a fantastic Warhammer 40000 game and would recommend playing it for both old and new fans alike. I dumped about 170h into my first walkthrough and will do another with the DLC release that's due in about an hour from posting this review.

_childDocuments_.review: I think overall Rogue Trader is a game worth trying at least once. It's a game that is very ambitious but overall gets in its own way too much. I have been a fan of Owlcats and player both Kingmaker and Wrath of the Righteous many times. This game is rougher than both of them, but it was a good introduction for me into the world of Warhammer 40K, which I always heard about but never bothered explore (being a longtime D&D fan). The game's number one flaw is that it's trying to do too much. If you are familiar with Owlcats games then you have seen this in Kingmaker where the management of the kingdom kind of got in your way too much, they improved this in WOTR where you could delegate some of it, and it did not get in your way too much while you were adventuring, but here, they regressed to a very poor state. Basically, to move around the universe of the game, you have to "warp jump" from start system to star system (so you cannot go from system A to system D, you have to jump A to B, B to C, C to D) and almost every jump there's something going on (an invasion of your ship and a mini-fight, a skill check event, a companion wants to talk to you, a colony event needs your attention, the ship has taken damage, ..., etc). Every jump. So, by the time you get to system D you forget what you even wanted to do there. It's incredibly distracting and provides little entertainment or thinking value. Feels like getting advertisers calls at home when you are trying to enjoy a movie. The game also lacks polish. Several quests are bugged (only one companion quest was fatally broken for me), many skill checks are bugged (instead of using anyone in the party, they use the main character), you'll find yourself save-scumming if you care about learning and understanding the full plot of what's happening in the story. The arch-types (classes), talents leveling up and combat were interesting and a cool change of pace. Space combat is a fun distraction. But overall, the game is just bogged down by all these minute, meaningless events. I hope they improve that in future updates. I usually get a lot of value from Owlcats game by playing the games again and trying different moral alignments... This game is so tedious, I have no intention of doing that.

_childDocuments_.review: Heavy Bolter go BRRRThis game is excellent - good writing that pulls you into the 40k universe, interesting characters, tense decisions, and a good balance between combat & dialogue/exploration. The combat itself is also a lot of fun, giving you lots of opportunity to figure out how to use your characters abilities most effectively & adapt to the situation- this is supported by character progression and gear choices which give you a lot of different ways to optimize you characters and combine their strengths.There are, apparently, still a fair number of bugs at time of writing- I have not encountered any that had any serious impact on the story (softlocking quests etc) that some players have reported, only minor ones of specific gear/talents etc not working exactly like they're supposed to. I haven't found it intrusive, but the devs also seem to be releasing bug fix patches pretty rapidly, so hopefully the more critical ones will be dealt with shortly anyway. I am 56 hours in and just about to finish Act 2, so if there are bugs later on in the story they will probably be fixed by the time you get there :)Edit: I have now completed the game, nearly 100 hours in- I think it is extremely good, but the highlight definitely becomes the writing. I played on normal/default difficulty, and for the later acts found that combining solider/arch militant with few officers meant that I could pump out truly absurd damage, and many fights were effectively or literally over before the enemy could do anything to me. I still found it fun to execute the combo & figure out the most efficient ways to do things, but combat was not particularly tense at any point after acts 2-3.However, the writing is very engaging, and they stick the landing with some really excellent conclusions to companion questlines.  and  are personal favorites, the former for being a really cool way to build on existing 40k lore & some fun metatextual symbolism/jokes, and the latter for just being extremely fun execution of a straightforward concept. The central plot also has some really high notes and ends with a flourish, with (at least for me) a great balance of foreshadowing and sudden reveal of how things interconnect. I think the core stories & the overall tone and attention to detail in the writing make this game very fun for both 40k lore buffs and newcomers alike.I ran into exactly one "important" bug, which did lock me out of completing one of my companions quests, though I didn't mind too much (I had been increasingly apprehensive regarding the character & where I thought there story was going, so I decided my rogue trader simply decided not to help them out), but I didn't encounter this until I was ~ 80 hours in, so given how fast they are putting out patches it will probably be addressed before new players can encounter it. The other bugs I ran into were random abilities or items not working as intended, and I never found it particularly impacted my experience, but be aware there are still plenty of those if that will bother you.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, Rogue Trader is a great deep dive into the lore and world of 40K, and it realizes the world, characters, factions, and dynamics excellently. This was my first Owlcat game, and my first non-Larian CRPG, and the experience was impressive to say the least. My criticisms for the game largely stem from narrative bloat, a few annoying mechanics, the leveling system, and a lack of continuity with some of the companions' quests.Starting with the setting and world, Owlcat nailed it. This game could not look or feel more 40K, from the way the characters talk and interact from different factions, to the setting on the worlds you explore, the highlights for me being the Mechanicus areas. Those in particular were excellent. I think if you're looking for a deep dive, narrative rich 40K game it does not get better than this.The main story itself isn't terribly complex, you're re-establishing your protectorate as a Rogue Trader in the Koronus Expanse, so fairly simple in that regard. What frustrated me somewhat with the story is the fact that every act is rather isolated, instead of tying together well. A few things stretch across several acts, but for the most part every chapter has its main focus, leading to less of a feeling that there's a developing story stretching across the game. In my opinion chapters 2 and 3 were among the strongest, but act 4 had a few shining spots as well.I did not like that certain companions quests were short and were resolved within like 30 minutes. Maybe it's the effect of having played games like DOS2 and Baldur's Gate 3 where the companions story stretches across the acts and builds up to a great finale for their stories, but that is by far a huge missed beat from Owlcat in my opinion. It's kinda like a side chore you have to do, and then you're back on your way. I would've liked more to do with my companions in their quests throughout the story.Addressing the final chapter, it is by far the weakest of them. Introducing the finale and setting it up in the final 5-10 hours of the game meant that, for me at least, the finale was totally unsatisfying. Most of the major threads of the story that you've already likely spent around or more than 100 hours building up have already been wrapped up, so the "ending" of the game if you can call it that feels like more of an epilogue than an actual ending. I was extremely disappointed.Concerning the actual gameplay, it's a XCOM ish game where cover does play a significant role. I thought the combat was a particular high point of the game, and I give a lot of credit to the variety and builds that are possible within the Rogue Trader system. I thought the archetypes were interesting and varied enough as well. Plus, Argenta's heavy bolter spray and pray build just annihilated anything and everything, she's the real MVP of my campaign.Sadly, some of the side content that you could do was a straight up chore. Space combat also wasn't the best. Owlcat apparently does this in other games, but there's just one mechanic in this game that I find outright frustrating and it's Navigator's Insight. It's totally unclear how to get more and it can softlock you into having to fight the same chaos enemies every time you want to jump to another system, which can be time consuming.The roleplaying in the game was superb, and frankly that's where Rogue Trader gets almost everything right. Being able to choose between convictions of Dogmatic, Iconoclast (basically objective moral good, merciful), and Heretical, and actually leveling up those convictions, unlocking different dialogue options and even equipment, felt great. I was annoyed a little bit with some of the random checks you have to pass, because it'd only go through my personal Rogue Trader's stats rather than my companion who had a much higher stat. A minor gripe. The writing is superb, and the characters all feel really well realized. The way you interact with them, the way they talk, the way they react to your choices, all feels very authentic. You can influence them in their thinking as well, which I also liked. Concerning the technical state of the game, I didn't really have any issues, mostly minor stuff that a quick reboot of the game fixed, and occasional camera glitching.Overall I think Rogue Trader is a great CRPG, a fantastic 40K game, and a really great adventure. It is extremely long campaign, and you really do have to do the side content to be at a decent level so you're not suffering against some of the later game enemies. I give Rogue Trader a 8/10, a solid game.

_childDocuments_.review: Treat this as a promising, highly enjoyable, but ultimately still flawed and incomplete early access game. It's technically playable from start to finish, yes, but the amount of gamebreaking bugs and performance issues involved in a rushed release quickly sour the experience of what is, at its core, an amazing exploration into the perspective of a player in one of the classic Warhammer FFG tabletop games. The reason I am giving my recommendation is because the game is easily worth multiple playthroughs (although I have some reason to voice objections over some of the decisions that make it impossible to get everything in one game, as they stink of artificial replayability) and the story is mind-blowing if you're a fan of 40k. They got the atmosphere of Rogue Trader down to a T. My final verdict, buy it and play up to Act 1 to get a feel for things. Explore what you can do. Then wait a couple of months and really play the game.

I can safely say that they didn't change anything about their game design since Kingmaker.Act 1 starts off strong and then the Owlcatness occurs so allow me to place everything in bullet point form so I can show my dissapointment of this game and Owlcat in generalPros - it's warhammer- the actual system that was taken from the TTRPG is presented well- that's itCons!!!- constant combat for every scene. I can count on one hand how many times I could influence combat through my stats - the ship combat is utter slow garbage. Ships move at a snail's pace and even when you clear the board of ships you still have to wait 1 more round until enemy torpedoes explode!- exploration post Act1 is a chore. If you get an event on the other side of the map and you don't have navigator points, you have to click on each individual system until you get there and God forbid you run out of navigator points and have to go through Dangerous warp paths because you will have to do combat on each individual jump- everything moves slow. Ships, companions, text, all of these move ungodly slow even with the anymation speeds cranked up to max.- SO MUCH TEXT! Owlcat is known for it's purple prose and this is no different. Mind numbing pointless text on 80% of events.- Most quests don't go anywhere. If you go to random events on planets for some extra xp and exploration, you would be shocked to see that the lore behind them is basically non-existent. Why is this here ? what happened ? ♥♥♥♥ if I know! and i read the 2 little entries and wall scratching in those places - companions are not detailed. Apart from the default introductory text that you get, they have almost no interaction with the outside world, no input on pretty much all of the quests and generally a lack of point. The party banter is relegated 100% to this format: "statement" -> "Response". That's it, all of them are relegated to 1 line of dialogue each and done.In short, I'm done with these guys. They're mediocre developers that are stuck 20 years in the past, have mediocre writers that ♥♥♥♥ the bed usually after Act 2 in every game and have no idea that while you can make a 100 hour game, if you fill it with pointless fighting and opening 1000 chests of junk this doesn't equate to good game design. I wanted to slog it and finish it like I did WoTR (another dissapointment) but I can't. It's too much of a mind-numbing chore!

_childDocuments_.review: PC Gamer is simply wrong about this game.   It could use a little more polish.  And a little more voice acting to alleviate the heavy screen reading for this old man's tired eyes.  I am not a 40K nerd like our true Gaming Emperor Henry Cavill, First of His Name, Defender of the awesome Franchises.  However, the game does a fantastic job of being both incredibly deep from a lore perspective and also accessible.  It also has the added bonus of having companions that I don't want to space out the nearest airlock as soon as possible (BG3, Starfield).  The whole thing is a little weird and ridiculous, but then again so was the Flash Gordon movie.  It has that fun factor as well.      While I've had my issues with Owlcat's last two titles with their questionable balance and terrible add on sequences (Crusade battles) nothing in Rogue Trader has derailed the story yet.  I am very early on however.  But the more I learn about this dark universe the more I want to know.  I really enjoy that when your psionic baddass uses her powers a bit too much dark void spirits start to mill around the party from the ether.  Now we're talking!  Character gen is about as complex as Pathfinder was, although for someone with an understanding of a D20 system or even the old Marvel Superheroes D100 system it is fairly easy to pick up.  Anyways.  I was skeptical.  I am very impressed with what I have gotten.  I paid Steam full price for it and I haven't regretted my decision.  This is a good one which will slow down my completion of BG3 and Cyberpunk Stringer  Bell.  If you are on the fence-  Did you like X-Com 2?  Dune?  And... a touch of Fallout 2 actually.  If so you don't have to be a 40k nerd (All Hail Lord Cavill!) to enjoy this.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't understand how this game isn't a bigger deal in the WH40K video game community.  Maybe it's because it doesn't center on Space Marines? This game, for me, blows Chaos Gate: Daemonhunters straight out of the water.There's a lot more conversation and role-play going on here, this is much more of an RPG than Chaos Gate, which was basically a purely tactical game with some light overlaid supply mechanics.  It did have a good story though, as does this game.I'm a good bit into Act 2 and really having fun with this one.One thing I will say is that for a new player, the level up options are staggering and almost demoralizing. _childDocuments_.review: First allow me to say in its current state, with random bugs, it is a 3 out of 5, after those bugs are fixed and the devs are fixing them, it will be a 4 out of 5. Maybe higher if the Expanse game proves interesting. I have only just got in to the expanse so I may have to update this review based on what I find.First, im a huge 40k fan and I also read the books, the writing style in this game is not the same as the books, it lacks that dark forbidding universe feel that I have come to expect from all things 40k. Its a little nice basically. But that is the worst element of the game, by worst I mean its only Okay. Not bad, not good, just Okay. This is a character RPG, heavily reliant on turn based combat. You get to recruit several characters and make them part of your squad. All are interesting and diverse. For example I have an Admech character that favours working with machines in the name of the machine god, a Navigator with her third eye, an inquisitor and a number of other characters. Also not all lines are voice acted, a vast majority are not in fact, so you really have to like reading to understand whats going on. The Journals are basically titles of quests you have to finish, not very useful and the quests them selves are written in such a way you can often and all too easily miss doing something such as destroying an ancient anti aircraft battery, that you have to return too later and finish the job if you miss it whilst doing your sweep. There are a few issues like this. As a quest maker in my own right, the first thing you learn is to think "how will the player bugger up my quest" and then make sure he cannot do it. But even when thinking that way, its all to easy to miss one or two things. So im not holding this against the dev team. It is an easy fix and im sure they will be attentive and fix these annoying issues over time. Difficult levels take a very sharp turn upwards at the end of the first chapter, even turning down the difficulty to story does not help much. Those who tried it before release reported it was easy, I think the devs have over compensated and made a game for those who are prone to exaggerate in their reports. After Chapter 1, I would call Story Mode Hard and go from there. Tactical combat is basic compared to games like UFO and other similar games, with cover only counting as cover if it has a cover symbol next to it and you are stood beside it. This means statues, large objects etc can be shot through as if they are not there. Cover literally is only applied if you are stood on a cover symbol.The idea of first learning to control your squad, then learning about your Rogue Trader ship, before heading out in to the universe and fighting space battles and battles on planets against xeno, heretics, chaos and other things is a really cool one and it works really well as a game. The expanse element that comes later is a mix of short simple missions you randomly get whilst scanning planets and resource gathering. Or missions involving chaos, elder, pirate or imperial space ships. With a fair number of unexplained events along the way and spacehulks. You can build up a picture of the 40k universe from these smaller missions which are closer to the actual 40k than the longer missions have been so far. Truly dark and foreboding. The trading and resource games mystify me right now, you might expect it to be easy to understand being a well established element of most games but not this time. It seems to be a way to increase reputation, there is nothing straight forward about it. I am looking forward to a Rogue Trader 2 if they ever make one, where they will take this formula even further. The game is fun right now and so far I have not found a bug that could not be worked around by reloading a save, adjusting difficulty levels etc. But it is my hope that the devs address all of these over the coming year.

You can follow an heretic path, dogmatic one and an iconoclast one. the game has content for 100h if you rush to the end in one go and much more if you do other stuff.the game include:deep storyPathfinder 40k style charactersReputation system with some imperium factionsspace battlesromancehuge amount of encounter be it trough exploration or warp travel companions that dont like other companionsresources and planet managementno item limitation. you can take every thing in your inventory, if it is on the map, you should take itI will divide this review into pros and consPros:+ Lot of character options+ Re playable+ 40k universe+ the hub design is neat+ the soundtrack can do a lot for immersion +the gear variety, example: you can have a laz gun, laz pistol, hotshot laz gun, hotshot laz pistol assault laz gun and many, many more only for laz gun, the other types are doing the same+great enemy variety, you can face a lot of one faction during one chapter, but enemies always seemed diverse and non redundant.Cons:-Lots of texture bugs: characters in purple due to missing textures, arms stretch glitch during animations and rag doll, character being invisible except floating gear.  -the terrain you visit have static characters that stay there even if the said character got executed, abducted or declared traitor-some skills often don't act as said or are just plainly not functional sometimes-The Corpus Valencius... is a lexicon where all mechanics are explained like a dictionary. I expect a only a low amount of player will read it, all myself included, and I realized only in the end game that i missed some key functionality in the game-your character options are as vast as a normal human can be in 40k: except your origin planet, you are no tecpriest, adepta sororita, space marine and etc yourself.-not balanced-you can soft lock your exploration*-*spoiler* the game premise give you a lot of dialog choices but in my play trough I realized that if you play a pure dogmatic character that always attack xenos, you cannot beat chapter 3. You gain 1 point for every sector that you chart and you can chart them only once, you can have more trough story event and if you have some chance, you can generate 2 with warp travel but it happened to me twice in 160h of play. you can spend these points to make paths easier to navigate and make new path to navigate. _childDocuments_.review: An enjoyable and solid game with the usual Owlcat quirks. It got me genuinely interested in Warhammer 40K and did well to introduce the player to the world and the factions involved. I would welcome another game set in this world, seeing that there are two Pathfinder games. Single-player playthrough, no DLCs. Abelard, write me a review!Pros:Excellent atmosphere for the Warhammer universe, great writing, and companions, but that does fall off towards the end. I really enjoyed a few companions, and they are very memorable if you stick with the ones you like. The OST matches the scenarios well. Voice acting is really good for characters that are voiced. I would have liked the important events to be voiced. RPG elements and your decisions are tangible throughout the game. You can influence events, the path of your own character, and that of a few companions through your actions.  Great character build options. The turn-based approach was implemented really well, and rewards proper skill usage for your character builds. Ship combat was a fun addition to the game, but ship movement in combat was weird until you unlocked skills to help you with manoeuvrability.  Cons:I am used to Owlcat games and played this game way after release to ensure I did not have to deal with bugs. Hopefully, Owlcat will release more polished games going forward. I had no major bugs besides running out of a certain resource needed for space exploration. I used the Toybox mod to fix this, and it’s a great tool to fix any other bugs experienced. The quest log was poorly implemented, and there are no maps or quest markers, which can help or hinder your enjoyment, especially if you take breaks between sessions. There should be an option to toggle this option on or off. Skill check percentage success is very unreliable, and the same can be said for some ranged attack hit success; it almost felt like XCOM at times. The skill ‘Expose Weakness’ seems to be broken. Some explanations of skills/abilities can be a bit much, and I feel it can be explained better in terms of the direct change it would have on your characters. There are quite a few loading screens for actions, and it gets noticeable the longer you play. It can also be slightly annoying when exploring space. The reputation paths and character paths are quite hard to max out, and this can lock you out of dialogue, gear, and colony projects. The space map is very large but, at the same time, feels empty and under-utilized, especially towards the end of the game. There was no actual use of your ship in quests or visiting locations on board, and I feel that it was a missed opportunity. Acts 1-3 were really well done, but the story gets rushed from that point onwards and feels incomplete as you near the end of the game. The game needed more time before being released to explore the latter story fully. After you have completed the game and reviewed the outcome of your journey, you will find a lot of contradicting information regarding your choices, and this needs to be fixed. I recommend this game to any Warhammer or CRPG fans. It is an enjoyable experience and another great game in this genre. This is probably the best Owlcat game. There are plenty of guides and the Toybox mod that can assist with issues. Looking forward to the next game in the series!

_childDocuments_.review: I've been waiting for a game like WH40K Rogue Trader for almost 30 years and I still have no idea why it has taken so so long for a game like this to be made in one of the greatest Sci-Fi settings of the last 50 years. I mean 40K has such a large and rich base of lore that you can pretty much make or do whatever you can imagine. Owlcat Games has understood that and definitely used the deep lore to make Rogue Trader. Sure the game has some bugs but what game doesn't these days and, unlike the beta, there doesn't seem to be any game breaking bugs in the release version which is great. I am so thrilled that new people can come and play this game set in the universe that I have loved for many decades. The lore of 40K is amazing and I recommend to anyone who enjoys the story or the setting or anything about this game to go and read as many Black Library books as you can get your hands on.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very well written game with meaningful choices, well acted and voiced characters, and enjoyable story.Like most of the releases from this dev/publisher your tolerance for nuisance and game breaking bugs should dictate when you buy the game.  In 6 months or so there will be a GOTY version that includes all DLC, has decent guides for builds (more on this later), and eliminates the bugs which range from nuisance to showstopping. Combat is good and sensible.Story, writing and acting are all enjoyableRomances are non-cringy (this is looking at you starfield)Core game systems are solidGame is stable and has crashed on me once (but there were clear warning signs)Setting is fiction adherentShip combat is crisp and enjoyableCan make custom squadmates just after the prologueAlternate ships are locked away behind overpriced deluxe versionsSome chaos/freewill/neutral choices are conceitedly forcedSome equipment has less-sensible alignment requirements (a gun that requires you to be evil)archetype imbalances (some archetypes are enormously effective, others are immaterial)Overly contrived trick fights (to be fair, some are enjoyable and others are just not)Several of the archetypes are relatively pointless, compared to the combat contribution of others.Some of the archetypes are overly complex and rely on turn-wasting buildup without any meaningful output.As it sits right now, so long as you avoid the stinker archetypes you are golden and the game stacks up pretty well all things considered.Excellent RPG in the vein of fallout tactics/baldur's gate/etc.  Some design stinkers but the game rates an extra star if you go in knowing not to make an agent, bounty hunter  or grand strategist.Many of the fights that seem too hard, are really about player strategies and tactics.  My first play through I chose a crime lord officer which seemed good for game and RP purposes but turned out to be awkward.  Officers excel at boosting others.  While I recommend having 2 in your party, I do not recommend playing one.I hate spoilers, and if you hate spoilers too then be prepared to play 20-30 hours of the game to really learn the game mechanics and then start over and be amazed at how well you do now that you know how to play.I give this game a solid 3/5 stars, and a recommendation that if you don't love great RPGs just wait for the GOTY,  If you're like me and have poor impulse control then it's a 4/5 and just avoid the character archetypes I listed and have a great time.

_childDocuments_.review: Yes, there are bugs. Yes it's a complex game with a daunting amount of powers, talents, and rules. Yes, there's a lot of text to read. Yes it deviated from the tabletop rules. Yes it's demanding for your PC, etc.But it's a great game. It portrays the universe well, offers great depth of progression and character building, and it's a rare non medieval crpg. Devs are not a big shop, they didn't promise the world, the didn't hype the product with 3 years of early access on an Act1 which was 10x better than the rest of the game, etc. There's also no overt political and social proselytizing, which is great to see.It's a WH40K CRPG and it's well designed.  Some things are new and need to be learned (profit factor), but it's very modern in it's design choices: auto-heal after fights without consumables (only 'injuries' need medkit), consumable for when you fail skill checks (picklocks etc) instead of wasting before hand, etc. The story is good so far and it drips with classic 40k theme. The Rogue Trader fantasy is there, and tons of systems support it (ship combat, setting up colonies, wrap travel, commerce and reputation, contracts, etc.)It's also priced cheaper than big releases and I don't regret giving them my money.  Like many games these days, this will probably be much better in a year with tons of bugs fixed. But it's here, it's playable and we are lucky to get a WH40k crpg of that caliber.

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game so far. It does have some bugs, but none have been game-breaking for me, just a little frustrating. Less bugs than the WOTR release which required me to install a mod to get past a certain point during release week. Combat seems to be divisive for people but I think it's excellent, far more depth than games like Xcom or Wasteland 2/3 (all great games). My only issue so far is that I have found it to be far too easy on normal. I feel like maybe this is because im playing a very melee heavy team as I have heard a lot of people say the game is quite difficult, and all I can think is that my ranged characters seems much less effective than my melee. But the combat just FEELS great. The weapon sound effects and death animations are all perfect with a ton of weight to them. It's exactly as brutal as 40k should be.It doesn't quite have the insane character diversity of the Pathfinder games, but that's difficult to achieve in the setting and without a system that has had decades of development behind it already.The lack of full voice acting is a complaint I have heard as well, but I grew up on games like Planescape Torment so while it would be nice, I really don't mind that much.Overall it's been a great game so far. I would put it on the same level as WOTR. With slightly less in the way of RPG mechanics (specifically options for character progression), but a setting that for me I like more.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're not already a 40k fan, you probably shouldn't pay full price for this.  The writing, characters, and setting are what takes this game from a strong 6 to a 9 from me.While much of the mechanics will be an easy translation for anyone familiar with D20 systems (this one is D100, but they basically just multiplied all the numbers by 5) there are some fun novel ideas in here, one of which is a neat inversion of the concept of mana.  Typically, each spellcaster has their own pool, and they can't cast anymore when it runs out.  In Rogue Trader, the whole map has one mana pool (shared by all allies, but also by all enemies!) and when it runs out, you can keep casting, but there's a significant chance of something really bad happening, like summoning a hostile demon, inflicting a status debuff, or taking damage.)Every character is required to multiclass partway through the game, so you'll want to pick classes that synergize, both within the character that has them, and with other party members.Don't sleep on Cassia.  She seems pretty underwhelming at first, but when you get used to her abilities, she's arguably your most powerful party member.It's 40k, so it's extremely grimdark.  Your alignment options include chaotic good (Iconoclast), lawful neutral (Dogmatic), and chaotic evil (Heretic).  Most of your team is lawful neutral, and they'll tolerate chaotic good well enough, but will eventually abandon you if you go Heretic, greatly limiting your endgame party selection if you choose that path.All in all, I find the combat engaging, I think the novel aspects work really well, and the writing and artwork are excellent.  If you're a 40k fan, this is a can't-miss title.  If you're not, but you like X-COM-style combat with a story tying the battles together, grab it on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Rogue Trader is not without its flaws (mostly: bugs, incomplete voice acting, short final acts) but it's quite a fun journey from beginning to end. I particularly enjoyed how nearly all of my choices had an impact on the epilogue, which is rare to see. If you enjoy Warhammer 40K or CRPGs (or both) - Rogue Trader is fantastic.

_childDocuments_.review: So I'll give this game a thumbs up. It's got decent graphics, decent stability, and overall decent gameplay.it's turn based combat. LOTS of loading screens. _childDocuments_.review: I’ve played until 6 am, got just over 6 hours in and apparently I’ve not finished the prologue yet. It feels like I’m close though as I’ve just got quests to travel to different parts of the galaxy on a ship plus some side quests. You immediately get sucked into the story. It’s well written and not predictable. It’s dark, proper grimdark dark. I had 40k fanboy moments (“♥♥♥♥ yeah, for the emperor!!” “Omg they included it in this game, that’s so sick”), I laughed out loud ( tried putting an item in a wrong slot and this female character goes “That is not the Emperor’s will!”), but also mechanic wise I was pleased (omg simple things like you loot all the corpses in the area and not one by one etc). I play on “Daring” difficulty which is one above normal, the ones above are hard and unfair where unfair really seems unfair. You can also customise the difficulty. I’ve not played Rogue Trader system before and looking at the stats even though I enjoy Ironman/hardcore difficulties, WoW included, I was like “nope”. Feel like I’ve made the right choice when it comes to that. First boss fight took me 3 tries with totally different strategies, character positioning and weapon choices for each one. I currently have 2 psykers in my team, using psychic powers at start without nullifying talents will get you closer to tearing “the veil” and opening your reality to daemons and other really nasty ♥♥♥♥ meaning you have to be careful and can’t go full blown Sith Lord casting thunder AoE at the enemies. The environment skill checks are fun and make sense. You can open the door by restoring power at the cogitor or just straight up blowing it up with charges. The choices matter and the decisions can be tough and I mean really tough. You can go three ways. Dogmatic, Heretic or Iconoclast. I’m doing a full Imperialis run so that’s a dogmatic trait. 5 crewmen burned alive because of me for me to prove I can walk through fire because well… Emperor Protects. Loot is nice but not over complicated. I find a lot of similarities to Pillars of Eternity. What else? I think I need to play more but I’m loving it. Oh and the music is sick.

_childDocuments_.review: I've enjoyed the game but I feel like it's mostly because I'm a Warhammer nerd.TL;DR - it's a good Warhammer game and a meh game if you are not into the grimdark stuff.The good:- World building is great - the environment, lighting, sound and all the fluff is just spot on with the grimdark feeling. It's very immersive with how not-streamlined it is - you often have to do the leg work to be able to progress your crew or the ship. All the banter between the crew and variety of characters you meet really keeps you invested.- The game is huge so you always feel like there is something more to do - plenty of items, places, quests and skills to explore. It provides your characters with a lot of choices and as the game progresses you sometimes change the playstyle to utilize the newly acquired items.- The combat system is a lot of fun and the learning curve feels very natural. The gameplay loop is well designed and winning some of the combats was very rewarding.- The characters - they are quite cool and not one-dimensional, very well voice-acted and written (despite the cringe "romance" dialogue options).The meh:- Story. It fits well within the setting but every single time you end up in an obvious ambush. It often feels like the choices made have no impact on the game, especially with the tedious random issues you have to solve while traveling. Despite that there are some great loyalist/iconoclast/heretic choices that are interesting to explore. - Progression system of the characters. It seems overcomplicated, but you don't have to fully understand it to play the game. Each characters has some kind of stacks, statuses, modifiers, buffs and most of the time you don't even know which ones are applied when - the UI is not very clear with that. Also when making leveling up decisions you don't even see what the character stats are so you have to kinda remember who is supposed to improve which way.- The variety of the enemies - sadly, there's only 2 races. Within those races there is plenty of different flavours - the good guys, the bad guys and the questionable guys. There is a bit of extra monsters and even a couple space marines (in my playthrough I've only fought against 3 of them though...). Feels rather underwhelming given how rich 40k universe is. It's a huge shame there is no more xenos, or at least some recognizable guard regiments. To be fair though, the factions included in the game are portrayed with great detail and a lot of variety.- Difficulty - I've played on normal and the combats were either too easy or barely beatable.The bad:- So. Many. Loading. Screens. Managing the party takes a couple loading screens to even buy and use new equipment. Whatever you want to do in the game you have to plow through a couple loading screens... Say you've finished a mission and got some reputation so you can buy new stuff. You're in the boss arena, loading screen, previous area, loading screen, previous area, loading screen, starting area, loading screen, map view, loading screen, ship view, somebody wants to talk, loading screen, you are in your chambers, loading screen, ship bridge, FINALLY YOU CAN BUY STUFF...- The game interrupts you all the time with "hey this place needs your help" and if you go with "scram, I've got no time for you!" option you end up with some bad outcomes. If you click through the dialogue you end up with nothing or a bit of experience. It feels like the game is just tedious - There is SO MUCH TEXT TO READ if I was to read all of it the game would take twice as much.

Some ship encounters even in acts 1-2 are mathematically impossible (start your first turn with 2 HP on your ship since the enemies act first against 6 xeno ships). Beyond act 2 the encounters could be . If I need to adjust the difficulty for each encounter, I'm doing the balancing they should've done. It's a constant vacillation between being way too easy and impossible when playing on a constant difficulty (Daring).- way too easy = I steam roll encounter and get a boring experience with no incentive to go back and replay the encounter on a higher difficulty- way too hard = I get steam rolled and need to spend way too long before either lowering the difficulty or toy-boxing my way out of itBeing able to change difficulty mid-game is just a band-aid for their garbage balancing. Additionally, frequently changing the difficulty destroys the immersion of having an objective power level.
