_childDocuments_.review: Neutral but closer to Do Not Recommend.Bleak Sword DX is a game that is trying to be more than it should be. It's a basic top-down 2D minimalist game that has been extruded into a pointless 3D presentation, and has an array of poor and baffling design decisions.You have Dodge, Parry, Attack and Strong Attack. The basic gist of the game is to bait/wait for an opponent to attack, then you parry or dodge and counterattack until it is dead. It is largely about being patient and timing your inputs, then watching your stamina bar regen for your next series of moves.You slowly build XP and can level up either your Attack, Defense or HP stats. The major problem is apparent IMMEDIATELY with these tacked-on RPG elements: There is literally no reason EVER to upgrade your Defense or HP - is it your PLAN to tank blows and hit back with the power of a frozen wet string??? If you don't upgrade Attack, enemies can take up to several more hits before they die, and this extra timing gap gives other foes time to spawn and overwhelm. If you can't finish-off a foe with your full Stamina bar and you'll have to Dodge away and regenerate, it gives time for new enemies to spawn leading to impossible situations. Pointless upgrade mechanic.I beat the game on Normal difficulty and wanted to start again on the Doom difficulty (Hard) and the above complaint completely solidified. In my Doom run my first 5 Level-Ups only gave me the Defense/Health options and it made it unplayable, requiring me to either restart or grind the earlier levels again. It's literally a punishment to Level Up if you aren't given the AT upgrade option. Yes you can grind for more XP but now it's not fun!!! Let's face it, once you beat a map (level arrangement) doing it over and again isn't fun, it's just ROTE REPETITION.There's another major design flaw with the Inventory system. RNG gives you a chance for an item after each fight which could be a consumable or gear with stat boosts. Seems innocent enough but it can quickly lead to unpleasant feedback loops. If you do well you'll keep your items which give you a good advantage; if you aren't performing well your punishment is losing the items that gave you a chance and now you're back to grinding. This mechanic is so fundamentally broken I actually can't believe it's still a thing in 2024. This game doesn't even need the Inventory Mechanics, much like the Stats mechanic it's just tacked-on and detracts from the game.Bottom line: It's a 2D top-down parry/counter game that has layers of BS presentation and pointless game mechanics heaped on top. It would have been a much more sound design decision to leave out the Stats and Inventory systems and just have a series of carefully designed level-arrangements. The game lets you grind for gear and XP if you'd like, but it's a pointless activity that only serves to force the player into tedium.My final grievance has to do with the Parry mechanic. The game slowly phases it out as you advance, and the gameplay devolves into a dodge/mash/dodge/mash affair.I did enjoy the game to a reasonable degree. The dodge/parry was fun enough but grows wearisome. This product is nearly all window-dressing and distractions, and very little core game. If you need to know what its like, wait this one out for an 80% sale but don't feel a sense of loss if you never play it - there's not much here.Positives are music, sound and animations.
_childDocuments_.name: Bleak Sword DX

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not recommending this game because frankly, it just irritated me to no end playing it.Controls are simple and fluid, but really all you do is attack and dodge/roll. Not much point in parrying when it's difficult to execute/doesn't feel quite right and also can't even be executed on a wide variety of enemies.So speaking of enemies, they are basically what the whole game is made up of. They have to be good, and there have to be a lot of them. There are a lot of different types, but many of them are just annoying to fight, and the game loves to just re-use most of them 50 times before the game is over. There are instances where an enemy will dodge your attack on basically the exact frame that you execute it, which feels pretty unfair. Oh but wait I'm not finished, some of them actually 'dodge' your attacks A F T E R you have already executed them. That should not happen in any video game, ever.So there are tons of enemy types, but a lot of the humanoid enemies are a tad difficult to distinguish because of the art style. Not a huge deal, but yet another minor annoyance. Later on, the game just throws more and more piles of enemies at you to fight in a row, and most deaths are just due to attrition. "Oh, you can beat a knight. can you beat two knights? how about three? bet you can't beat four. How about two sets of two knights. how about 5 at once. How about two sets of 3. how about 6? Let's add a rat or two, and take it from the top." Then later on, early enemies reappear and just get health/damage buffs to keep them from being obsolete, adding even more repetition.The arenas are basically just squares with few meaningful configurations. whenever a stage is anything but an open square, it basically just means something is needlessly blocking your vision or you're looking down a hallway that's so long that walking to the end means you can barely see what's happening because the characters are tiny. It's almost comical that the art style (despite being just gorgeous) manages to capture the worst of both 2d and 3d worlds. the depth that 3D adds really only gets in the way of the experience. the game is basically a side scroller with no scrolling, so the world, despite being pretty, lacks something. The game's just a beat em up, and the distant parts of the arena are basically no-go zones because the sprites are so small. why not just make this a classic left-to-right beat 'em up with less depth? Instead there's just a painfully small amount of real estate to play with, making it all the more unacceptable to have parts of the arena obscured by pillars, fences, whatever.I will say this, the game has a pretty good foundation and a killer asthetic, some people will like it a lot and that's fine. props to the horseback riding level. It's early in the experience, and made me feel like the game would continue to experiment, like i was on an adventure. Nope, just a one off and the rest is the same. The game starts strong but just fails to keep things interesting after about 1/3 of the way through. music is great, though.The rpg mechanics are just utterly pointless. lvl up with 3 stats to pick is fine (Zelda II does it with great success) but the souls-like "lose your xp" only detracts from the game in this format. Just an artificial way to add more tension to recycled content. And the item system is baffling in how worthless it is. why give me an item that permanently buffs a stat... if i die, i lose the item, so i'm just going to use the stat buff imediately once i realize that. so... that's not even an item, really.Whatever, I've ranted long enough. I beat the game and won't play it again, mostly I remember how irritating it was, even though I did genuinely enjoy it early on. There's a lot of better stuff out there.
_childDocuments_.name: Bleak Sword DX

_childDocuments_.review: This game is amazing overall. I love what it has to offer in terms of combat and simple yet effective artstyle, plus the stage progression that dictates how the game moves forward like a retro console game.It's not too complicated in its mechanics and it feels so good to jump right into a stage, parry enemies, and counterattack them afterwards to wipe the floor with the whole stage. It offers a significant challenge at certain points, so if you're not careful, you can find yourself stuck on one stage and not be able to progress due to a loss of extra items and EXP upon death, but the game allows you one chance to get them back, kinda like Dark Souls. Speaking of Dark Souls, the dodging feels great, especially right after you've hit an enemy and need to avoid its next attack. Some enemies cannot be parried and must be dodged in order to avoid its attacks. Some enemies are more effectively killed if you block/parry its attacks (That's how I was able to clear the swamp and catacombs). One enemy in particular (the ghost) requires you to charge up an attack in order to kill. The variety in the game's bestiary allows for a varied combat experience and keeps the gameplay really engaging. If you need to learn the controls, the game offers a tutorial for beginners, which is great.The item and EXP system relies on clearing a stage to obtain experience for leveling up your character and a random chance at finding an item, which can be put in one of two inventory slots available. Some items are consumable and the stat boosts they offer will last one stage, or they can heal you for some much-needed health, but if you level up or go to the next stage, you get healed anyways. If you die on a stage, you lose all items and EXP you currently have and must retry the stage in order to get them back, otherwise you lose them for good, but at least you can still keep your stage progress within the world.For every world, there is a boss at the end, which offers a significant challenge and is themed after the world it is in, and many of them play differently. One world in particular centers around horseback combat with Wargs and Centaurs chasing after you and ends in a big fight against a giant Warg. Different worlds will offer unique hazards for you to deal with, such as the swinging axes found in the dungeon or the billowing flames found all over the Aryndale Village, but thankfully many of these hazards can also hurt enemies, so use them to your advantage.If you're a fan of Dark Souls and old-fashioned arcade games or old console games, this title is certainly for you. I hope this kind of game gets expanded upon, such as continuous levels to traverse and explore instead of one stationary stage where all the enemies come in from the sides, maybe an expanded inventory to pick and choose items from instead of only having two slots, or perhaps an expanded arsenal of weapons to shake up the combat even further. This game is great on its own, but a sequel has the potential to make the formula even better.

_childDocuments_.review: If you pick it up just know you're going to hear the same 4 notes being plucked on a harp ad ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ nauseum throughout the menu screens and many of the levels, which is unfortunate, as the sound design otherwise is pretty bang-on.  The roll function is a bit OP in that you can often just spam roll to escape enemies and then roll back toward them to do the roll attack -so in that sense it certainly is Souls-esque combat. A parry / counterattack make combat more engaging, as well as the various patterns of enemies and timing their attacks to hit one another due to friendly fire. Altogether a fun experience with a perfect cost of admission, plenty of content over the course of 12 varied levels but if I hear a harp again I'm going to pull a double Van Gogh and chop both of my ears off.It's cool. It's unique. The harp sucks.

_childDocuments_.review: As a fun diversion for a few hours, Bleak Sword DX delivers on a simple but well-tuned combat system and a unique aesthetic. I appreciated the progression as it introduced new enemies, with many of the levels ending in a climatic sword fight against stronger enemies. Occasionally new areas add new mechanics like mine carts to avoid or wind that blows you, but most of the time you're just fighting in a room with pretty window dressing. If the game was longer, I'd expect more, but for its length the combat carried me to the end.Check this game out if you like 2d soulslike combat boiled down to its basics and the 3d pixel style. Just know there's not much more under the hood.

_childDocuments_.review: Way too hard of a game. Playing this is punishment. The wiping out of progress + any weapons you might find is like starting an RPG from scratch every time you play it, but the enemies just keep getting harder.With 540 deaths and 20 hours, completing this game became a slow, frustrating grind, with little to no reward. Brutal, millisecond-reaction button mashing, playing the same level over and over again, and no re-spec system made me regret not investing all my rare level-up points in damage. All in all, there is nothing wrong with Bleak Sword, it is just too damn hard.

_childDocuments_.review: Bleak Sword DX is a well done retro souls like that is a bit more punishing than it should be. You lose all your current XP progress towards the next level up AND all your items if you die twice in a row. You can reclaim your XP and items if you beat the level the second try, but for that second try, your items are already not active, so you are weaker than in the first try. Leveling up is rather quick in the beginning, but takes multiple levels (4-10) later in the game. Losing the xp shortly before you would have leveled up is really frustrating. Fighting feels good in this game. It is mandatory to learn how to handle each type of enemy. There are a lot of different enemies and I disliked only one or two because they annoyed me. I finished the game in basically one session and would recommend playing it that way.

_childDocuments_.review: I Thought this would be a skill game but I couldn't shake the feeling that it creates new challenge by changing established rules. It was easy but the mechanics changing felt like a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ way at artificially increasing difficulty. It's a shame playing this and wanting to return it. Truthfully the demo on the hardest setting was super super fun. unfortunately the pivot from the demo to full game was too heavy. Between you and me this is one of the big reasons I wouldn't recommend and open demo as a dev or publisher. Application only and a larger demo to span more of the mechanics. Some of the real problems that where inexcusable are as follow:Incredibly inconsistent hit-boxes, Constant changes to players ability to navigate the map confidently which may temporarily increase difficulty it is only for a brief instance (If learned skills of navigation was reused later on it would be an issue) The gray scale is unique and it makes for more popping pixel art but when it comes to needing precise timing against small enemy's it creates an unintentionally loud screen. All together this game had some real potential and with the backing of a name like Devolver Digital I am sad that it fell through. You guys had such a good running start the art the level design everything was amazing for 1-1 - 1-12 that demo was so much fun. But that fun ultimately vanishes as you hit 2-1 and 3-1 and 4-1 as you slam through the game it gets more and more frustrating from a design standpoint. If you make a simple game it has to respond it has to have polish the sloppy hit-boxes is inexcusable  as my biggest complaint. Devolver if this gets more polish let the people know it's not without hope in its current state

_childDocuments_.review: I'm just gonna say this before I get to the nitty-gritty, ever since I saw this before it even came out I was immediately hooked on it. Literally! Like, for example, not only was this originally a game you could get through Apple Arcade, this is also literally one of the greatest Dark Souls-like experiences you can have.From the locations perspective of their own little areas and layouts to the variety of monsters and beasties you can hack, slash, bash, block, and just carve your way through. Speaking of which. I should mention; I love the usage of both typical and atypical kinds of enemies that I feel are very seldomly used in any other game, be it your run-of-the-mill RPG to whatever. I mean, honestly, as a man who loves his monsters, I personally like that sort of thing. Though the names of some leave a lot to be desired for me, I suppose they work just as is.The movement is pretty simple, you exactly have a total of 3 buttons you would need to use when you're in a fight, whilst the others, being the arrow keys, are obviously to move (go figure, I guess). The actions you have while on the field are Blocking, allowing you to counterattack any enemies as long as they don't a have red exclamation over their heads. Attack, which if charged enough can deal a ton of damage to something, and finally, the most vital of them all: Dodging. Dodging, unlike when you swing your sword, does not take stamina to use but can temporarily impede it as it recharge, meaning you must do it wisely as you try not to land yourself into a world of hurt.Apart from that, it's a pretty standard control scheme that one can easily get behind and grow adjusted to. But even then, in one of the chapters, you mostly riding on horseback, which means your blocking ability is replaced with a jump until the end of that chapter's boss. So be prepared for that, potential readers.Bosses, while on the topic, are a real treat. If the true, near-pureblooded-ness of the Souls-theme wasn't enough, then the end of the world fights are surely something. Tall, lumbering monstrosities that dwarf you in sheer size and strength in which you must do battle with them as a means to progress with the game and the story. Every boss bearing it's own pattern, moves, and specials. In one instance, you might fight some tentacled bug dude while the next is when you're fighting a giant floating head that pukes lasers. Also worth noting is that when you die during a level you lose any given amount XP you had on you as well as your items, effectively raising the stakes as you're also given a second chance to get them back. But in truth, that's it. Simply put. But even after you finish the story, you have the chance to explore some of the other things you can do, like changing the kind of campaign or difficulty level you want, duking it out in Boss Rush, or taking the time to test your skills in the arena and see how long you'll live. The option is yours.But as to whether or not you should decide you buy this game, I would, without a doubt, say yes. Yes, in the sense that you should indeed buy it, play it, and beat it. It's a fantastic game that offers an enveloping experience that, although simple, is delightful nonetheless. Everything you see, from some of the most fluid of animation you can get just out of any pixel-based game, to the haunting yet whimsical tunes you hear while you play. It is, without the doubt, one of the best things you can spending your money right now. And it's a steal just by the pricetag alone, so you'll at least you don't have to worry about spending money on something incredibly expensive from some big company.If anything, treat yourself to getting this game, and just have fun with. Although it can make you ragey, just remember, if at first you don't succeed try, try again. Besides, it IS a game for those acquainted with the original or those more memorable of all the attack patterns of each individual enemy/boss, so just be prepared for when the difficulty gets going. Other than that, just have fun!

_childDocuments_.review: I'm about halfway through the classic game mode, and I'm having a wonderful time.  The combat is simple, responsive, and challenging. The HD2D art style, monochrome color scheme, and diorama-esque layouts for each level are charming.  The music is immersive, the monsters sound great, and the battle sounds are satisfyingly impactful.  There are a few extra game modes including The Arena (essentially a survival mode where you keep fighting waves of enemies), Boss Rush (you only have one health bar to fight each boss consecutively), and there's a campaign randomizer which will mix up the order of the enemies and bosses you fight as well as the items you find.  This is a pretty sweet package for the price.  If you enjoy simple fast-paced combat with new and old school flavors, this one is for you.  I highly recommend!

_childDocuments_.review: This game is fun. It's an arcade action game. Something about it feels off. I had to turn off the annoying bright glow everything has. After that it feels and looks much more playable. Overall I think it's missing something, but the difficulty, concept and satisfying collision make it a fun playthrough.One complaint I have is that the difficulty doesn't scale. So there are some bosses toward the beginning of the game that are more difficult than the ones later in the game. There are also some levels that are more challenging than others randomly placed throughout the journey, which is good, I think, it keeps you guessing. This game would have benefited from some kind of stripped down magic system, or different weapon, like a firebolt or a black jack option.Regardless I think this is a solid 7/10 and great if you want to pick it up and play a few levels at a time.
_childDocuments_.name: Bleak Sword DX

_childDocuments_.review: Exhilarating gameplay and an awesome soundtrack. New enemies and traps introduce enough variety that the game feels fresh with each new area. I would really love to see a sequel in the future with more story, because this world interests me. I will say, there are parts of the game that feel a little too easy on normal difficulty, but that's all the more reason for me to replay on a harder mode.
_childDocuments_.name: Bleak Sword DX

_childDocuments_.review: I'm just beyond the first world but so far so good!  It's a pick and and play Dark Souls.  Count me in for that! _childDocuments_.name: Bleak Sword DX

_childDocuments_.review: It's okay so far 6/10Played on Doom difficulty (hard) and it was a decent challenge, but- Square fighting arenas for every encounter gets stale quick- No single enemy feels difficult, it's only packs that give you issue so I never really feel scared or beaten; only overwhelmed- There's some levels where rangers can attack you freely without being attacked back- I would call this clever level design if they made you use the rangers to solve the level, but it's only an inconvenience that you can't reach them- Horse levels badI don't feel particularly pressed to continue with this game, but likely I'll pick it up for a play sometime in the future-
_childDocuments_.name: Bleak Sword DX

_childDocuments_.review: Not a bad game, but also not one that held my attention in a world with so many games, shows, etc, competing for my attention. This is basically pixelated, simplified Dark Souls played on miniature, diorama-like levels. You dodge roll past attacks and enemies, punish during openings, and if you die you get one chance to recover your corpse before losing all accumulated items and experience. The design influences are obvious.However, this game has a couple of fairly glaring flaws. First, the default key bindings are absurd and reek of a lazy console port. They should have used WASD for movement, left/right mouse for attack/dodge roll, and bound items to two logical keys. Instead, we have arrow keys for movement (really, in 2023? In a game released on PC by a serious publisher?), and a bunch of nonsensical bindings for everything else. The game is also brutally inconsistent with which enemies you can roll through. After 10 stages where you can roll through any enemy, the boss has an attack that deals damage if you try to roll through it. A lot of damage. And yet you can roll through the boss's attacks (and model) for every move up to that point. Same thing with the undead knight enemy in the swamp. Sometimes you cannot roll through him. No, don't ask why. It's just like that. Perhaps there is a telegraph, but the overly-pixelated graphics mean I couldn't see it.The basic question you want to ask yourself before buying this game is do you want mini-Dark Souls? If yes, then consider picking it up, as long as you rebind the keys to be closer to the control layout for the real Dark Souls (not sure why they didn't steal the key bindings when they lifted so many other features). If not, give it a pass. Maybe pickup Monolith instead if you want a great action rogue-like with a retro art style.
_childDocuments_.name: Bleak Sword DX

_childDocuments_.review: I was fully and immediately addicted to the gameplay loop up until it was derailed by the horseback section (Chapter 3).  I was thrilled by the change up, but the buttery smooth gameplay is thwarted by reduced movement, reduced defense, clunky attacks, reaction based obstacles, and projectile enemies that it became an unfun mess.This was all in Doom mode, so I tried again in the standard mode and it's just not as gratifying to solve the scenarios as when not on horseback. Edit: Play the demo first. I like this game, but it's a 49% for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Bleak Sword DX

_childDocuments_.review: This is an action game that demands fast reflexes - so far so good.However, the devs somehow saw fit to include a lightning mechanic in the game which either makes the screen fully black or fully white your for a couple seconds at a time, every 30/40 seconds or so, and during those seconds you have no idea whats going on. Considering this is a game with tiny arenas and fast enemies, you'll get damaged for sure.There are several ways of increasing difficulty without making something frustrating. This is definitely not one of them.
_childDocuments_.name: Bleak Sword DX

_childDocuments_.name: Bleak Sword DX

_childDocuments_.review: While I was intrigued when I saw Bleak Sword DX's reviews on Steam and Metacritic, it is no more than an action rogue-lite dungeon crawler with uninteresting upgrades and simple items to obtain. Many of the positive comments addressed the game's graphics; and while the art-style simplistic, it becomes repetitive shortly after running the game for the first time. Listening to it's music and sound effects is like listening to iron being scraped by a knife: its music is just a few notes in a loop, it becomes annoying after some time. While it may be interesting to other players, but for me the game-play loop is not fun. It has no potential and even if it will be developed further, they will not be able to fix this mess-of-a-game; the core system of fighting baddies is not innovative in any way, this concept is repeated over and over again in this game and will be repeated in further ones. This game will be a mesmerizing experience if you like bad controls and over-simplisticgame design.My verdict is that this game is a 4/10 slop game.
_childDocuments_.name: Bleak Sword DX

_childDocuments_.review: Not a fan of the Souls series (I got sold purely by the game's aesthetics). If you are a Dark Souls fan - go for it! If not - you'll understand me. The window to parry is too brief and not evident at all. Most of the time, I managed to do it by luck. While the gameplay can be enjoyable and the art is fantastic, sadly, I still have to refund it because I don't think I'll have a good time playing it. I felt blood boiling in my veins as I got stuck in the second area. There are around ten more areas, and I just can't bring myself to continue torturing myself and being frustrated because I really want to like it.
_childDocuments_.name: Bleak Sword DX

_childDocuments_.review: Game feels okayish and swing between neutral to not recommended, but steam don't have neutral so here we are.Cheap, especially if it's on sale.Gameplay is okay, basically darksoul in low polygon.Dodge, parry, attack, these are all you have and it's all you need.Not too long, can be finish in an afternoon.Enemy variety is bad, every stage add 1 or 2 new mob and a boss, but game feels dull after first half.Visual is so bad you can't see anything in certain stage. Games go low poly but the grass, lighting and the RED COLOUR of stage 9 are abysmal when you need to time your dodge and parry. There's random thunderstrike in background that can blind you for a whole second.Gear matters too much, and Leveling stat are poorly balanced. When player die twice in a row, you lost all your items and exp while keeping the level gained. Every level you get to choose between 1 point of defense, attack or 5 point of hp, and you have two item slot that can be gear or consumable.  that gives +1-6 stats. That means if you miss twice in a row and lost all items, you're losing around 4-12 level of stat bonus, which matter quite a lot, and you cannot get them back quickly cause it's ALL RANDOM DROP. Around level 25 the xp required to level up are scaling extremely high that takes 5-10 stage of grind, which means you can't gain stat through leveling easily. Game punishes dying so hard even Soul series are not this bad.After stage 9, the rest of the 3 stage are DX version stage, and it only worsen the game imo. Mob spawn with invulnerability time with no visual indicator, making you waste a hit and open for counter attack. Dev made mob from previous stage attack motion go faster and harder to react for no reason, plus all the HP are bloated badly boss fight is easier than mob fight.Game's still fun for a while and challenging, give it a try if it's on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Bleak Sword DX

_childDocuments_.review: While I find the game's art style, enemies, and most bosses great, I find the concept of losing both all of your XP and items after dying twice to the same level inherently flawed. This incentivizes players to "get good" but due to difficulty spikes and walls, it makes it so that carrying items will only result in the player losing said items. A system like this that is integral to gameplay cannot be this punishing without negatively impacting the players experience. Also the unique perspective the game provides the player with is flawed in that it can end up blocking certain enemies behind  other enemies or bosses, and there should be a top down mode for those that wish for it. And having enemies or bosses without parryable attacks is just bad game design, as it makes the player both rarely attack the boss, and forces the player to spam roll to dodge the attacks. If that brings into question game balance then maybe the boss timings would be tighter, or you would have to parry multiple attacks in a cycle to stun the enemy. The arena mode is poorly fleshed out, offers nothing new, is badly designed, and is very repetitive. The same thing can be said about the boss rush
_childDocuments_.name: Bleak Sword DX

_childDocuments_.review: is an Action Roguelike, with a 1 bit (kinda) graphical style. It might look simple, but it works so well.But even better than the visual choice, it's the combat system. It's a hack and slash with very responsive and precise mechanics; it's unforgiven but fair; it's easy to understand but difficult to master.But it's not a perfect game. One thing that disappointed me is that the game has a parry mechanic, but unfortunately you are likely to use it more at the beginning of the game; after you progress, a lot of enemies will begin to deliver attacks that you must dodge because you can't parry them, and there are about 70% of enemies who deliver such attacks in the game.But I was able to overlook this nuisance because the game is so good at what it does, the atmosphere of the desolated, dangerous world is spectacular, and the soundtrack complements it with ease. Combining that with the visuals and top-notch combat is what makes this game so good.Overall,  is a very compelling game; it's hard but satisfying to play, and there is a lot of replayability in it. My score, given all that, is:
_childDocuments_.name: Bleak Sword DX

_childDocuments_.review: This is a really great, bite-sized arena-style fighter that emphasizes the best parts of soulslike combat. The combat strikes a good balance of demanding patience and punishing button-mashing with pushing you to dispatch enemies quickly before more spawn in to crowd you out. The level-up system is also quite good, as you don't lose levels (and upgrades) when you die, just how much progression you've made since last level up and any items you've collected. The items are pretty rare but are quite good as they're either consumable health potions or give you passive buffs to your attack and defense. You will randomly pick them up after completing a stage. Very solid game, I enjoyed myself quite a bit, and after you beat the Mario world 1-1 style story mode, you unlock endless mode, boss rush, etc which gives it some more life as post-game. Def pick this one up
_childDocuments_.name: Bleak Sword DX

The lofi look and pixelated graphics creates an amazing atmosphere to an already addicting gameplay. Im not that much into games without a good excuse to play and this game has an interesting story of course nothing to go crazy about but at least it gives me some purpose to see what is next. Gameplay is simple but fun, but i wish i could change the parry button to the trigger instead of the bumber but still doesnt ruin the game at all. Now please sell some keychains or promos because i love the graphics and wish i could carry them on my keys.
_childDocuments_.name: Bleak Sword DX

_childDocuments_.review: is a bite-sized hack 'n' slash wrapped up in a dark fantasy aesthetic painted in blood and shrouded in darkness. It's most definitely, a mobile game, everything at its core suggests being made for pick up play and ease of access. The basic controls and simplistic graphics, though not always to its detriment, keep the game limited to a measly scale and often repetitive nature. An issue exacerbated by the games general lack of depth in both combat complexity and 'build' potential. But, despite this, if you expect little, you receive a lot, as this ends up being a title suited perfectly to something like the Steam Deck. Or even as an experience peripheral to another big game you might be playing, one that doesn't exactly de-stress but adds some much needed spice to your gaming life. It's stylish, it feels good to play but it's also hollow, short and lacks any personal replayability by way of it's lacklustre mechanics. Flaws aside, I'm glad I played through this little adventure and happy it was rescued from the depths of Apple Arcade where it can be appreciated by people who actually play video games.
_childDocuments_.name: Bleak Sword DX

_childDocuments_.review: Really cool looking game with a neat art style. Gameplay is very skill based and focused on reading your opponents to dodge and parry. You progress through worlds with their own set of levels and each level is a small box arena with small terrain variations. There are moments where you're steamrolling everything and enemies are helpless to your parry. But, enemies telegraph their attacks pretty clearly so it's not always super gratifying. Of course, this is a challenging game so there are also moments where you're dying repeatedly until you manage to barely succeed on a level with a challenging mix of enemies. It's subtle but there's a lot of depth to this combat that probably comes into play later on.
_childDocuments_.name: Bleak Sword DX

_childDocuments_.review: Great little game that gets a ton of fun and complexity out of faux-4 bit (faux-2 bit?) style, some well-done but extreme tightening of modern game mechanics/aesthetics. My only complaint was the reward system seems inverted: you get better stuff the better you do, but when you're having trouble, you lose your stuff and therefore have a worse chance for the next attempt than the time you just died. That forced some backtracking to farm for levels, items a couple times, which was annoying. Still, very much worth a few hours.
_childDocuments_.name: Bleak Sword DX

_childDocuments_.review: Nice, stylistically minimalistic game with soulslike combat mechanics on a micro-scale. One of those games (akin to  and ) in which the music of Jim Guthrie makes everything several orders of magnitude better.The Good:- Strong minimalistic art style and atmosphere, complemented by the music.- Simply fun, nicely fine-tuned combat mechanics.The Bad:- Some occasional issues/bugs/glitches with pad controls at times.

_childDocuments_.review: SPOILERS!!!!!!So I bought this game because I love hack and slash and the entire look of this game caught my full attention and interest. I had to give it a try because of its low price and uniqueness. Upon playing it, I soon began to enjoy the style of game, how it played, and most of all probably, how it looks. You almost can't argue that this game is just "beautiful." It has such a unique style and look to it. I haven't done incredibly vast research into other similar games that are pixelated, but this game really stands out and I have no regrets in purchasing it to explore just what the game had to offer. The game already pulled me in with the design and I had to play it out. The game is short-ish depending on your "skill." I beat the game, going into it completely blind, in 3 hours and 39 minutes from start to finish (only including the main game and no extras) I would say I am satisfied with it and its' entirety for what it is. It is a game that can be challenging, but really unique and enjoyable. Definitely worth at least giving it a shot. I am fairly sure the developer worked really hard on this game and it is just awesome for a cool little game of its type. If you think you enjoy smaller games, "indie" style, 2d, pixelated stuff like that, I fully recommend giving this game a try. There really aren't any negative things that come to mind when I think about my play through. There are a good variety of enemies, the level design is really interesting and unique. The only thing my brain can muster that is "negative" is that the white light on the title screen is a little blinding, but no complaints really because my eyesight is already bad so maybe it's just a me thing lol.

INCREDIBLY boring.I love Devolver Digital, one of my favorite publishers!!! But *this*? A disappointment.

_childDocuments_.review: A distilled Souls-like that is all around really solid and fun to play, except for the endgame where it just gets a little unbalanced. This is basically all you need to know. Also the final boss is a pushover, which just added to a pretty unsatisfying ending. But, nonetheless, the mechanics are really fun, the graphics are super unique, the sound design is punchy and crunchy and i think it is absolutely worth buying.

_childDocuments_.review: This was a very enjoyable arcade game. Game play is your basic mix of attack, power attack, dodge, and parry, with a strong emphasis on memorizing enemy attack patterns (which are well-telegraphed - I should mention that this game tends to have the fairest bosses I have encountered and most of them can be bested on the first encounter if you play well). If you get stuck on a particular level, you can revisit earlier levels to grind up your stats and some amount of this will probably be necessary to beat the game.Took me about 5 hours to complete the base campaign, which seemed reasonable for the price. Once you beat the core campaign, you have a few other options available if you wish to revisit it.The pixel art is strong and well done and the music fits the somber mood (with a nice sting with the victory screen that never got old).My one complaint is you only regain about 15 HP after completing a level, so there are times to progress in the game you have to go back and grind a few easier levels to recharge your HP (level 5-6 is a particularly good choice as there are only four worms to kill and it should take you under 10 seconds once you are properly leveled). This can get a little old when you're in the later stages of the game but recognizing and making use of the exploit will make it much easier to progress in worlds 10-12.
_childDocuments_.name: Bleak Sword DX

_childDocuments_.review: It's fantastic, improves upon the apple arcade version in so many ways. The sound effects are melancholic, the levels look like beautiful miniatures, and the retro styling is great. Combat is more finely tuned, you can actually walk around now, and there are some good attack variations. Enemies are simple on their own, once you learn their pattern they're easy enough, but the game pairs enemies together in a way that really adds to the challenge. Some bosses could benefit from a lil more variation, but enough have several phases or smaller enemies to keep you on your toes.Now for the gripes. The depth of field takes some getting used to, and it can mess with enemies that are in the back. It can feel like they appear out of nowhere if you're not close enough, especially if they have ranged attacks. Shame, because the depth of field makes the levels look so incredible.A more in depth bestiary would be nice. Health and attack stats, combat previews, the works.The loss of xp and items after dying twice returns from the og game, and I'm still not sure if I like this system. It feels punishing to force worse players to continue the game with lower stats, whereas better players get to keep excelling. There is the second chance you get after the first death, but its not always enough. I can't really think of a better system without tanking the challenge tho, and at least you're able to replay older levels.Controls. Fine with a controller, mediocre on pc. Firstly, menu navigation. I think more options than the enter key should be usable when using the arrow keys. Secondly, combat. It WORKS, but not very well when locked into 8 way. I think the game would benefit from a mouse aiming option, or a targeting system when there are several enemies.Lastly, weaponry. The sword works fine, blocking, dodging, and swinging has enough depth. But I think it could be nice to upgrade the weapon itself. Come across a blacksmith occasionally who can upgrade your block time, sword reach, add a spin attack. Or maybe even new weapons, either for a full game or for individual levels. Pick a crossbow for an aerial boss, or play through the game with a slow but strong hammer.I wholeheartedly recommend this game for this price, but I do think that it could still use a little something more.
_childDocuments_.name: Bleak Sword DX

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game. It is brutal at times, but if you like the grind of a challenging game, it's definitely worth the price. I like the system of getting one chance to retrieve dropped experience and items by beating the level you died on. I also don't mind backtracking to previous sections and leveling up a bit if I'm having trouble with a room. Most enemies have multiple attacks and parrying / dodging is satisfying. Some rooms will gank-squad you, but memorizing when and where enemies spawn helps. The game forces you to learn how to dispatch enemies quickly before you're overwhelmed.Criticisms: - I wish you could level up stamina to increase the bar and/or recovery speed. - The parry timing could be more responsive. It feels delayed compared to dodging.- I wish you could retrieve items from a bloodstain without having to clear a room. The item drops are really the only rogue-like feature in the game and if you're lucky enough to get good drops on a run, it sucks that those buffs are taken away when you need them the most.
_childDocuments_.name: Bleak Sword DX

_childDocuments_.review: Bleak Sword DX is a pretty simple game with clear pros and cons. Your character progresses through individual, hand crafted levels which offer various stage hazards and enemies to deal with.The game's a treat to look at and listen to. The simple story and quick cutscenes help create an atmosphere of generic but epic fantasy that i really enjoyed. Sounds effects are meaty and satisfying and the combat overall felt snappy and responsive. There are plenty of different enemies and while they share a lot of moves (melee combos, gap closers, ranged attacks and AOE attacks), some of them have quirks that make them more unique than they otherwise would've been.However, i felt like the game tests your endurance more than your skill most of the time; what i mean by that is the way enemies spawn rarely puts you in a situation where you have to deal with threats in an interesting way. The game will spawn one enemy, then another once you kill the first, rinse and repeat... There are moments where different enemies spawn together at once, which leads to more interesting battles, but it happens way less often than i would've liked.Bleak Sword DX is a fun and quick affair; it's not a must play but those looking for a quick, accessible actiion game to play will undoubtedly like it.I'll update the review once i've tried the arena and boss rush game modes as well as the harder difficulties.
_childDocuments_.name: Bleak Sword DX

_childDocuments_.review: I suspect I'll never actually finish Bleak Sword DX, since it is brutally difficult, and I have a social life. I don't know if I have enough free time to sit and force myself to 'git gud' at this. That said, so far I have to say it's a well-made and stylish arcade-style experience. I love the blocky red/white/black visuals, the soundtrack and the general feel of the combat, but it also regularly gets on my nerves with some cheap deaths and a block/parry animation that feels a bit too unresponsive to be completely reliable. I'm quite early in the game - and maybe everything will 'click' eventually - but honestly my interest is already waning a bit, since every time I boot this up I feel like I'm just slamming my head against a wall repeatedly. Consider this a recommendation for masochists only. It's well put together and has a strong aesthetic - I definitely wouldn't call it a 'bad' game. I just find my personal difficulty threshold being tested too much to call it a fun one either. If you're the sort of person who prides themselves on laboriously mastering extremely tough games then you'll probably be into this. For sword and sorcery fans just looking for a fun way to blow off some steam, be warned - this may exhaust your patience very quickly.

_childDocuments_.review: 8/10Only 8 because the difficulty scales way to high in the last world, I got to the last level before the boss fight at like level 27 or something like that, but to beat the game I had to then go back and grind levels to get to level 40 with items and then I beat that second to last level and boss of the game my first try. _childDocuments_.name: Bleak Sword DX

_childDocuments_.review: Game is simple and a lot of fun. I don't understand the Dark Souls comparison. If that becomes widespread it will mislead people into what kind of game they're buying. There is no exploration or dungeon crawling like in a soulsbourne game. Game has a linear level based system and each level is a square arena in which your goal is simply to defeat all enemies. You move on to the next level and rinse repeat for the entire game. There is also no character progression, another feature prevalent in souls games. You are a sword and shield wielding hero, and cannot customize past that. You level up but have three stats to choose from: health, defense and attack. Each level shows two of these three options randomly and you choose between the two. I level up attack every chance I get because I've played a lot of Binding of Isaac and learned that tankiness is useless if you don't deal damage.It's also hardly a roguelike or a roguelite as described. Roguelites have player agency. You control where to go and what to do when you want to. These arenas set in a completely linear order, are the antithesis of that. I'm not saying any of this is a bad thing. The game is a lot of fun. Enemy variety is surprisingly robust and interesting, the graphics and atmosphere are top tier, and the simple controls feel amazing to use (if you use a controller). I'm three quarters of the way through the game at the moment with 3 hours on record as of writing. There's a couple other modes I need to unlock after beating, not sure how much mileage they'll add to the game, but I'm recommending in any case, not based on price to hours played. Just a fun game that should be tried by anyone into this kind of game.
_childDocuments_.name: Bleak Sword DX

_childDocuments_.review:
Pure, thrilling, and wonderfully cruel, Bleak Sword DX is a dark fantasy action game challenging warriors to fight their way through compact, cursed diorama battlefields.

Through twelve tense and deeply atmospheric chapters, you must lift the curse of the legendary Bleak Sword by striking down all manner of horrifying creatures across an oppressive world wielding fierce weaponry and powerful magic.

Newly updated for PC, Bleak Sword DX expands on the critically acclaimed Apple Arcade version with elegant controls, three new game modes, and multiple gameplay and graphical improvements.
_childDocuments_.name: Bleak Sword DX

name: Volgarr the Viking II
detailed_description: The Return of the (Vi)king More than a decade after Volgarr the Viking’s chaotic, challenging debut, the barbarian king’s story continues in an uncompromising new form. Volgarr the Viking II is a hardcore, 2D action-platformer where precision is everything and one false move can spell a brutal death. Players of the original game will feel right at home on this relentless voyage, even with the addition of new power-ups, new forms of magic, new enemy types, and a chest-thumping new soundtrack. While the sequel delivers the same unforgiving 1980s-arcade level of difficulty as the original, Volgarr the Viking II also (mercifully, begrudgingly) offers modern quality-of-life options such as checkpoints, save states, and an undead mode. You decide how punishing your quest should be – but now anyone can be a viking! With new and larger worlds inspired by Norse mythology, multiple endings, and a variety of ruthless bosses to conquer, Volgarr the Viking II expands and improves on the original in every way. Draw your sword, don your helmet, and chop your way through this violent viking adventure!

_childDocuments_.review: Revised review after Undead Mode patch:I originally gave this game thumbs down despite being a big fan of the first game because of what I felt were some very questionable design choices that really harmed the experience. The most glaring of those has been addressed in a patch but overall I still find the game very disappointing. I am giving a thumbs up now because it's not a bad game, just not nearly as good as the original. Honestly I would rate it neutral if I could but I do want to acknowledge the developers admirable ability to incorporate player feedback. I have quite a lot to say about this game but if you want the short and sweet:TLDR: An unworthy sequel to an all time classic that's not bad, it's just okay. I can only recommend if you've played the first one to death and absolutely NEED more Volgarr. Volgarr II is a very confused game that lacks the tight cohesive design and imagination of the first game. It feels like the devs were told that they had to make a sequel to Volgarr despite not having any new ideas or a clear vision of what a followup to the original should look like. The core game play of the first carries over and is still phenomenal, but nearly every change or new addition either feels pointless or actively worsens the experience. It seems like the devs couldn't decide if they wanted to make the game easier or not. The first Volgarr, being very old school, had a reputation for difficulty and perhaps the devs worried that would keep a mainstream audiences away. To remedy this they added checkpoints to the levels that work like the checkpoints in Shovel Knight where you can destroy them for extra gold. However I guess they thought this made things too easy as they also added limited lives, something that was pleasantly absent from the original game despite it's classic inspirations. They also made the levels significantly longer which simultaneously pressures the player to make use of the checkpoints while also making game overs all the more annoying. I consider lives to be a very outdated concept that stopped making sense as soon as games left the arcade and only serve to add frustration rather than genuine difficulty. It's increasingly rare to find a modern game that includes lives, even among hardcore old school style experiences like the aforementioned Shovel Knight or even the original Volgarr. In my mind the simple removal of lives was already an elegant compromise between the old school and the modern. If you want to go even further then go ahead and add the optional checkpoints, maybe just use less of them if you're worried it's too easy. But adding in lives is a complete step backwards. I recall a minor controversy when the first game came out and people were angry that the game "didn't have a save system" forcing you to complete the game in a single sitting or have to start all over in the next session. This wasn't actually true as the game had a way to skip over levels you had previously beaten but this feature was cryptic and poorly explained. A lot of this games presentation and design seems like an overreaction to the first game's rocky initial reception. If their intent was to "modernize" the game to avoid another PR misstep at launch, they unfortunately failed spectacularly. I'm referring to the new central mechanic that is "Undead Mode" which has to do with the newly implemented lives and checkpoint systems. After 6 game overs you are immediately locked into the worst ending and turn into a zombie. At launch this made you immune to all damage other than bottomless pits and could not be turned off without completely erasing your save file. At the risk of offending the devs, I don't know how anyone thought this was a good idea. Fortunately the game has been patched to allow you to continue to play the game normally as a zombie, although you're still locked to the worst ending. Unfortunately lives and continues are still central to the way the games endings worked and can't just be patched out without majorly redesigning huge chunks of the game. The brilliant treasure chest system from the first game is back but has been significantly devalued as it is no longer required to get special items from them to get the best ending. You also always have the metal shield and charged spear which is another thing that makes the game easier but also makes the chests less important. Now your ending is almost solely dependent on how many continues you use. If you reach the end of the game without using too many continues you just automatically get to go to the secret final level. This is again,  a huge step backwards from the first game where opening enough chests without getting hit got you the souls which unlock the alternative harder levels where you can get the keys to the final level. The new system is so much less interesting and involved. On paper both systems require to go through the game without dying but the new system feels so arbitrary and lazy compared to the original which really felt like you were earning  those extra endings by going out of your way to achieve special objectives. Not to mention this makes the game have significantly less content than the original because there are no alternate hard versions of any of the levels. The best way I can think to say it is, Volgarr II is a game that punishes you for doing poorly rather than rewarding you for doing well like the first game did.Those are the biggest design issues but overall the game just feels less quality than the original. None of the new powerups are interesting or introduce any useful or meaningful utilities. The levels are long and repetitive and many of the new enemies are annoying to fight. The bosses feel smaller and less complex.I could go on but the bottom line is that Volgarr II is by no means a bad game, it's just okay. But when the first game was such an amazing experience, being just okay is still pretty disappointing.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm LOVING Volgarr II. It's like the ideal version of so many of those hardcore games I played as a kid, but without making me cry (as much). Beautiful pixel art, simple but great mechanics, feels refined and solid.If you're skilled enough, you can ramp up your survivability and lives. If you just want to get comfortable with the game, you'll get into 'Undead Mode' after six continues or so. I see some complaints about this. It would probably be better if the undead mode was a toggle, I agree. It's also essentially just a hardcore mechanic; you have six continues before you 'have to restart' (which, of course, isn't technically true since that just triggers the undead mode, but if you hate the undead mode, git gud and don't die so much so you don't have to continue six times).A couple relevant notes here. By default, you have three lives per continue. You can increase that number up to six lives, and apply items to protect your lives (taking more damage before dying). There are also checkpoints, which are also optional since you can destroy them for more money.Personally, I'm playing through in Undead Mode and loving it. I'm learning the levels, finding secrets, improving my skills, getting an understanding of enemy moves, and so on. In turn, I'm really excited to restart after I finish and try it without ever hitting Undead Mode. And it's still going to be an exceptional challenge. That's my kind of replayability.

_childDocuments_.review: I highly recommend this game to those who love a challenge - think Castlevania, Ghosts 'n Goblins, Rastan. The game is masterfully crafted, paying high reverence to classic arcade game design and building on it.At first, Volgarr may seem restricted in his abilities, but once you experiment with movement and attack cancelling animations, you will find many techniques and nuances that slowly build you into an unstoppable badass - bending and breaking the rules of the game. The level design is tight with varied enemies, creating new and interesting challenges throughout. It's important to note that this game is deeply rooted in arcade game design, which means it encourages players to complete the game with a total of 6 continues. If you go through all 6 continues, you have the option to continue playing as an invincible undead Volgarr. However as some players have pointed out - playing the game in this way is not very fun. This is 100% intentional. Volgarr is a game that is fun when the player overcomes its challenges by mastering them, not by brute-forcing their way through them. Becoming an invincible undead after 6 continues is the game's way of telling the player that while they can keep playing by brute-forcing their way through the game, it's not a very fun way to play. At that point, the game is suggesting that you should restart by deleting your save file and try again - something which admittedly is not effectively communicated to the players (specially those with no arcade gaming experience). The intended way to play is to learn by methodically approaching each challenge presented, and then blasting through them all in one go once mastered!

_childDocuments_.review: I adore the Volgarr the Viking 1. Volgarr the Viking 2 is fun enough to recommend but I was really hoping I would like it more.2 plays nearly identically to 1 but its stages are significantly longer, now have shovel knight style breakable checkpoints, and are designed to be noticeably more difficult. If you run out of lives, all checkpoint progress wipes and you go back to the start or halfway point of the map. It is similar to the original in that way but the longer stages make this feel infinitely more frustrating even with the checkpoint system trying to help you out.I actually replayed Volgarr 1 for the first time in years right after beating 2 to see if my warm, fuzzy memory holds up and it absolutely does. 2 isn't a bad game, I just enjoy 1 significantly more.

Tying it in to the multiple endings is a wise move too!Changes to the powerup system are also welcome, allowing for more agency even when the player is getting slowly beaten down trying to progress.A well thought out and made sequel!

_childDocuments_.review: This will be one of the few time I flip my review, but I want to comment about it. My old review will stay under the dotted line.I was wrong about the checkpoints. There are checkpoints in the game, but they are actually destructible for gold. When I encountered the first one, I thought it was an enemy that was going to spring up, so when I attacked it and did damage...I kept going. That made it seem more like possible checkpoints but instead more treasure. I don't think this is explained well in the game...so you can either destroy them for gold or use them as a checkpoint.And that little change makes this a lot more recommendable. I still don't think it will be for everyone. But if you are into hard games, this one wouldn't be a bad choice. Like I mentioned below...I didn't dislike the game, but the way I was playing didn't leave me room to recommend it to anyone. So don't play how I did and it will be a lot more fun.-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------Ok...I need to point something very important out about the question that Steam asks when it comes to reviews. The reason why is this review is bound to get jesters from fanboys that fail to read reviews and just jester anything that disagrees with their outlook in life. i am not being specific in saying "Volgarr fanboys", but just fanboys in general.Steam asks one thing. It is not "Do you like this game?" It is this:Do you recommend this game?So to really answer this lets talk a bit more about Volgarr. I picked up the first one a while back somewhere. I actually enjoyed it even with its challenge even knowing it was a game I would never complete. I was used to games like it in the arcades growing up....especially Rastan. Even thought it was hard, it still had a good balance to it, and learning to overcome obstacles wasn't overly difficult. It came down to a lot of mastering the timing.Now here comes part 2. Everything is ramped up to brutally unfair, which isn't bad if that is what you are looking for in a game. i don't mind brutally hard, but Volgarr 2 does something that is not good: levels have to be done perfect and are excruciatingly long with no checkpoints in them. A level can be like 20 minutes of having to run perfect...or starting over from the beginning. I mean...Super Mario Bros even had halfway points. In addition, there are parts that can be downright unfair...like having to blind jump to a rope that might just happen to be swinging the other way. Then guess what...you are dead and start all over from the very beginning of the level.I got so frustrated with one specific part of the 1st level, I forced undead mode, just because I still have no idea how to pass it without getting hit. Now with saying that, I still did enjoy it...but I have to answer the question how it is asked. I have a few friends that will rage quit by the first continue. I have a couple others that are swamped with other games to even consider devoting time to this. Then i have some that just won't want to sit down and run the same level over to get it perfect, and probably say "well that was fun, whats next?" after the first death. So, in short...I have no one I would or could recommend this game too.....except hard core "I want impossible games" type of people....which is probably less that 1% of the gamers out there these days.I mean, I enjoyed it for what it was...but even on undead mode I don't see my self ever finishing it or even rushing back to it anytime soon. I grew up playing NES games and with work I was able to get my way through them. Volgarr 2 is different, but more of a cheap way.  So without anyone that I could or would want to recommend this to. I can only enjoy it for myself.. But I am in no rush to get back to it, so who knows when that will be.

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT: Undead Mode is patched! The review is reposted to reflect these changes. Check "Undead Mode" below for details.I highly recommend purchasing the bundle with Volgarr I and II on the store page.The original Volgarr the Viking is a bit underrated and one of the few Kickstarter success stories. It boasted that it would be a modern take for a retro-inspired game: no handholding, just pure classic difficulty with a tough but fair challenge. While games that boast high difficulty are a dime a dozen nowadays, Volgarr is an early example of a modern Indie title that figured 16-bit-inspired platforming down to a science. Crazy Viking did not frontload your character with a ton of mechanics like most other modern platformers: they purposefully limit your mechanics in a very specific manner in order to give you a challenge.It is over 10 years old: there isn't very many accessibility options or an easy path for newer players, but it's still revered by fans of the Mega Drive (and other similar games like Ghouls n Ghosts, Zelda II, and Rastan) for being a tough and fair take on the genre. It is still a classic and worth playing even now. I'd give it a shot, since it's only $10.It's excellent. There are easier options if you don't like the challenge, but don't expect a cakewalk.Volgarr II takes the difficulty up a notch from the first game and allows for longer levels and more melee and close-quarters combat. You begin with a sword and shield, then find upgrades along the path allowing you to take extra hits as well as dish out more damage. Getting hit loses an upgrade you've collected. Get hit at the lowest level (or fall down a pit) and you die. Lose all your lives, you'll have to spend a Continue.Yes, there are now Continues in this game. It's similar to Cursed Castilla and how they handle Continues, which allow players to experience the majority of the game even while still giving experienced players rewards for beating the game without dying. Losing your lives will force you to the last crystal checkpoint (pretty far away). However, your Continue supply is INFINITE, and you will have the option to gain invincibility if you lose 6 of them (see Undead Mode). You don't get a good ending if you use this mode, so veterans have an incentive to attempt runs in a legit fashion. Since levels are longer, there are now more checkpoints between each level. Similar to Shovel Knight and many other games, you can choose to destroy them for a big point bonus, but doing so will force you to start from a previous checkpoint if you end up dying. Checkpoints in Volgarr 1 are incredibly far apart, so I'm VERY glad they've added an option to keep checkpoints and reward players for destroying them if they want more points.If you are familiar with the first game, this one is much more fast-paced. You will be fighting enemies constantly and have to make more split-second decisions. If you are familiar with the Tower during Ending C, it is very similar to that throughout. Everything feels a lot more constrained and close together, from the lack of/minimalistic background parallax scrolling to the constant placement of enemies everywhere. I feel that this is where Volgarr shines, as getting to the action quicker and taking on hordes of enemies at once is super satisfying.You also no longer lose your metal shield, as well as the ability to carry 4 upgrades instead of 3. Oddly enough, this makes the game much harder to play. Levels are now focused around blocking as well as getting to your sword upgrade quicker. The game now expects you to block more things and to kill enemies faster. That means more people to fight and more enemies who know how to handle a weapon. This is one of the biggest strengths to this game. It really does make you feel like a master viking who has overcome so much and is now being put to the ultimate test once more.I guess my biggest issue with the sequel is that levels seem to go on a bit too long. You might think that's a problem with the first game, but the original Volgarr's worlds are definitely a lot shorter. Breezing through both World 1s from Volgarr I & II (without dying or getting hit), Volgarr I takes me 5 minutes and II takes me 12-15 minutes. It's not that it makes it any easier or harder, it just ends up being monotonous when I am not in the mood to play. If there was a break in the action (like maybe a miniboss or some guy you meet or something), I feel like it would work a lot better. However, this is a minor complaint and the way the game functions is, for the most part, just fine.Undead Mode has been patched! In the game's initial release during 1.0, the following would happen once you lose 6 continues:-You respawn as a zombie. You flinch when take hits, but you don't take damage except when you lose a life during pits.-You can only finish with a bad ending and have to start a new save if you want another crack at a good ending.-The game does not tell you this at all.Thankfully, the developer has listened to these complaints and has patched how Zombie Mode works. Kris is not a stranger to listening to feedback: he has patched the original Volgarr with a toggleable camera option and hints about loading saves despite his hardcore design philosophy. In my experience, he has a very good track record of taking negative feedback on the chin and patching highly-requested ease-of-access things.Now a piece of text comes up when you lose 6 continues:"You have used 6 continues and succumb to the forces of the Undead! You have a choice to make. Do you wish to continue your journey in the current setting or embrace the Power of Evil? (Toggle this option in Modifiers)"You now have two options: a Standard Mode or Easy Mode. Easy Mode is just as it works previously: you do not take damage from hits. Standard Mode works as it normally does: no invincibility. However, in either case, you are still a zombie and cannot unlock the good ending. You can even switch between Standard and Easy Mode via the Modifiers menu. You also have the option to start with Easy Mode right away on any world after unlocking this state, though you cannot progress to a normal ending on that save file.This is a fantastic change. No more confusion once you hit that state: you are told right away that you have entered an easy state. My only minor complaint is that the prompt that appears does not tell you that you cannot unlock the best ending, but that is easy to figure out once you realize that your color palette has changed. This, in addition to saving your last armor/weapon during the last undestroyed checkpoint, is the best of both worlds: providing an easier solution for players while still rewarding veterans for finishing the game.I have already seen complaints from a few people that they should not be stuck with the worst ending if they choose the standard mode after 6 continues. My question at that point is why should you expect to be rewarded with a good ending if you are not willing to try on the game's terms? You are still experiencing most of the game with infinite continues, so all you're really and truly missing out on is closure. That is rewarded to players who overcome what this game has to offer, not for people who want to take a shortcut. It's not exactly uncommon: Cursed Castilla and even Spelunky does the exact same thing.Overall, this game is definitely the perfect sequel to Volgarr. It features a lot more action without having to sacrifice difficulty. Having a Continue system MULTIPLIES the brutality of this game, but since you can experience a large majority of the game after losing 6 Continues, I see it as a good thing. You are still encouraged to play the game by its own rules despite becoming a dirty, filthy zombie.

name: Songs of Silence
detailed_description: Explore, Expand, and Dominate in a World torn by War Songs of Silence is the next-generation of turn-based 4X strategy games. Explore hand-crafted maps, build powerful armies, and crush your rivals in fast-paced, real-time battles where every decision is strategic. Unique Factions & Cunning Tactics Lead one of three unique factions, carve out your place in a ravaged land. From dense forests perfect for ambush to towering strongholds ripe for siege, every map presents new challenges and opportunities. Manage resources, rebuild shattered kingdoms, and stake your claim in this living, breathing world! Unleash Fast-Paced Tactical Chaos Skip the slow build-up and jump straight into the action! Battles are intense and decisive. Optimize army formations, and tip the scale of power with your heroes' abilities. Reinforcements, divine interventions, or devastating maneuvers make every clash dynamic and unpredictable. Steer your Strategy with the Cards of Fate No decks to build - these cards are earned as your hero levels up. Play them at key moments to turn the tide of battle, as you summon mighty creatures, or wreak havoc on your enemies with fire and fury. Every card is its own tool in your strategic arsenal. A Feast for the Eyes & Ears Step into a world brought to life with stunning Art Nouveau-inspired visuals that set it apart. _childDocuments_.review: I think I've played turn-based games for over 15,000 hours by now. I started with Heroes of Might and Magic 1 when I was around 5 or 6 years old, and now I’m in my 30s. So, I’m very picky when it comes to turn-based games. I’ve played almost every strategy game on the market before writing this review. Just bought the game and spent 11 hours with it so far. Here’s my first impression:Art: The game has fantastic art, being the first turn-based game I've seen with an Art Nouveau style. The art team really carries this game—both the monster and human designs are incredibly unique, unlike anything you’ll see in other games. They’re weird, yet beautiful.Music: The soundtrack is composed by the same artist behind Final Fantasy Tactics and Final Fantasy XII, which perfectly suits the game’s warlike atmosphere.Gameplay: There are three distinct factions, each with a unique play style. The game includes eight campaign maps, offering around 20 hours of gameplay. Plus, the skirmish mode generates random maps, so there’s endless replayability. In skirmish mode, completing quests unlocks new classes and subclasses for your factions. For instance, winning a map with the Thousand Kingdoms unlocks the Paladin class, which has three sub-classes, each offering different playstyles. Each faction has multiple classes, adding plenty of depth and replayability.Combat: Battles are auto-resolved with your minions clashing automatically. However, you have ability cards that allow you to influence the battle. For example, a "Charge" card lets your cavalry rush a single point to trample the backline, while a "Fly" card helps you escape dangerous units. The system is simple yet very deep because knowing which units can counter each other is key. For instance, cavalry can break through most formations, except units with the "Hold Ground" ability. There are over 120 different units in total, with each faction having 18-20 unique units. The rest are wild life units that can be recruit inside the outposts. Some units are only recruitable with specific classes (e.g., only the Lord class can upgrade regular spearmen to honor guards). Some bosses battle are pretty challenging on hardest difficulty.Map Movement: Map movement is similar to Heroes of Might and Magic, but with an ambush mechanic—if you use more than 50% of your movement points, your army is vulnerable to ambush. Certain classes can build camps or use scouting abilities to prevent ambushes. You can also hide in forests, becoming invisible and waiting to ambush enemies.Overall, this game has the potential for 100+ hours of gameplay, especially with future updates, like new factions and neutral units, if it does well. (Right now I gave this a 8/10). It has some bugs, but there are no game breaking bugs. If this game have a 4th faction, I will give it a 9/10. But its understandable, the game were made by a small indie team, with a budget around a few hundreds thousand USD, so its good if you can support them to create new contents for this great game.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is made with love and this is noticeable in the details from the first minutes of getting to know the game. Gorgeous icons, rich artwork, delightful music, and high-quality voice acting create a seamless experience. It’s hard to ignore all of this, but I will try to mention the most ambiguous aspects (), leastways according to my opinion and preferences. In terms of mechanics, you control a hero who leads a detachment of specific troops. Your task, considering the enemy’s analysis, is to assemble an appropriate set of troops and position them correctly on the battlefield. Ideally, you should inspect the detachment you plan to attack or that is about to attack you beforehand. During battles, you lack direct control, because units just automatically target nearby opponents. Occasionally, you can use your characters’ ultimate abilities ()I still haven’t got a personal impression of whether the game is easy () or hard (). On one hand, you can relax and let the units handle the work. On the other hand, , the game won’t forgive planning errors before battles. Additionally, characters take a really long time to recover after battles, and only under specific conditions.In my opinion, the game beautifully uses card elements. But also, conceptually, this is the same as the usual icons, for example. In order to add a military force to the hero, you click on the card of a certain type of force/unit (having a corresponding set of resources for this and mainly just being in the place where the corresponding cards available) and "Voilà" you have troops (). In battle you have only a few cards and their have cooldown time, a kind of "charging/cooling down" of an ult, which you must use in a timely manner to gain some advantage. I've played quite a wide range of card board games and, in my opinion, this is a far cry from that experience. However, I still like the aesthetics of this idia more than standard icons or macros.Most importantly, still, that the game has just launched in early access, and the potential in it seems promising (). It will be interesting to see what happens next. ~ Go Chimera!
