_childDocuments_.review: So This is going to be my 1st steam review but i really have to put my thoughts out here because this is getting ridiculous. 1) Original Owners of the Game HAVE to buy the game again to continue playing with all their progress resetwhich makes no sence since the changes of the definitive edition could've just been added to a small dlc pack 2) While new portraits are nice and all there isn't an option to use the old ones from the settings menu.3) Balance changes and QOL improvements are basically non-existent (except for the "Open hero Menu" before a battle which is pretty nice but thats pretty much it)4) Exact Same Story , Dialog , Battles , everything , nothing new added in singleplayer which removes the freshness and originality (If it had any to begin with) of this re-release and makes it boring to replay the entire story so you can get items and characters for MP 5) Very short duration for each singleplayer faction (took about ~ 2.5 hours to complete sylvan faction and even less for fortress which is good for MP players since they will do it once and thats it but removes any replayability for the classic slow-paced players and the new players who enjoy SP more than MP) 6) No new singleplayer trinkets , units , bounties , map areas , more interesting fights (like the one in the tree in the sylvan story or the inn fight in the fortress one) or generally new content , its basically the exact same as the base game. 7) MP Changes include 1 new hero....and thats basically it.So What are you paying for exactly? well , you are getting new portraits (that you are forced to use since there isnt a change portrait option so this might not even be a plus) , 1 new hero and the Villain DLC (both of these are MP only) , some promised QoL improvements that i havent found yet (except for the hero menu one) and some balance changes who are doing absolutely nothing and have zero impact on the game. in my honest opinion they shouldve either made this a "new" game so people who had the original wouldnt be forced to buy the new one to keep playing or they shouldve just simply made it a dlc which is an optional thing that you dont have to get.Edit : Forgot to Mention the Frame Rate problems , sound problems (including the fact that songs get cut randomly or sometimes have very bad transitions) and also the fact that you can only have up to 4 saves for the Singleplayer campaign which isn't enough to save the start of each faction since there are 5 factions in the game.

_childDocuments_.review: This review is a strange one for me. I bought this game for myself, and two extra copies for a community raffle. I loved the original CoH, and I intend to keep and play this game. But I am very disappointed with this release. My main gripes with this release are that the developers changed very little, communicated poorly with the community, and have made this version essentially a forced buy for anyone interested in continuing to play CoH online.Let's address these points. The developers have changed very little. To summarise the known changes: -New character portraits (no option to toggle between original) for upwards of 15 characters. -New Menu assets. -Very slight changes to two non-impactful units from one of five factions -Very slight nerf to one special ability (down to 30% from 50%) -One new special ability to round out the only faction that only had 2 instead of 3. -One new sound effect.I love CoH, but I won't pretend that it's balance was perfect, and there were plenty of interesting directions rebalancing could have been taken, some of which the community has been speculating about for years. Additionally, the game is notoriously a little unstable, with hangs, freezes, and disconnects a plenty. There seem to have been no changes to the stability of the game, but we can't be sure, because... The developers have communicated very poorly with the community. -There is no change list. -The hype building announcements before release often contained grammatical errors, reflecting a lack of care.-Those same announcements had some information regarding in game stats that were completely incorrect. -The developers would pick and choose which topics they would reply to the community about. They still completely refused to comment on cross-play and rebalancing.I would be fine with this game as an optional, slight update to an old game for old players, and a nicely packaged deal for less than the old price for new players, however...The multiplayer, which is a huge component of this game, is not compatible with the old version. So, anyone wanting to keep playing CoH with new players must purchase this version. To be fair to the developers, they did implement a larger discount for people who own the original version. However, ~$11 aud that I have to spend to keep doing something I love, with minimal effort and poor communication on the developers part, still feels bad. Quite frankly, this leaves me in an odd place. The developers reached out to me and gave the discord community 5 free copies to put into a raffle, which was really lovely, and I actively defended the developers when they had an issue with the conditional refund on steam's end, and players were being impatient.I want to like this release. I really do. But it seems so low effort that I find that hard. I'm going to keep the game and play it. Make of that what you will.EDIT: With some time passed, we have discovered that two of the most powerful artefacts, Tome of War and Celerity Ring, have been heavily nerfed, Celerity Ring being outright banned in multiplayer and Tome of War (by far the worse of the two) only preserving one leftover move per turn instead of unlimited. This is appreciated, but not a significant enough change to sway my overall opinion, especially with the online troubles seemingly still present, including instability and level resetting.

_childDocuments_.review: UPDATE: As expected, Ubisoft and DotEmu provided no further post-launch support - no patches, no additional content, nothing. Literally just "drop it and forget it". Beyond shameful.----------------With over 450 hours played in the original version, I'm deeply torn over Clash of Heroes' "Definitive" Edition - on one hand porting the game to a new generation of consoles, including Nintendo Switch, is a very good move, and the new edition would not only renew interest in this underappreciated title, but also bring a fresh wave of players to its (frankly dead even before the 2021 shutdown) multiplayer servers. On the other, from the perspective of a PC player it's a rather barebones and at times simply inferior re-release of the previous version with only a handful of new features, coupled with the removal of the original game from Steam.There are precious few balancing changes - two artefacts were removed from multiplayer, but others were directly carried over from the OG PC version, even after several of the other outliers got rebalanced in the Android/iOS port. Hero abilities are pretty much unchanged. Unit statlines saw next to no changes, either. There are no new units, items or events in the campaign - you're effectively replaying the same game all over again, and replay it you will because, as mentioned before, you can't import your previous campaign progress.New additions worth praise boil down to adding one new multiplayer hero and integrating four multiplayer DLC characters into the base game, revising character artwork in dialogues and implementing a couple of QoL UI features such as skippable dialogue windows (not the entire dialogue sections though) or access to hero menu from pre-battle screen - and this came with a number of minor downsides and small, but irksome changes.The revised artwork is a mixed bag - some NPCs look better, and the portrait graphics are overall more impressive on a technical level (with finer linework, smoother detail and more complex light rendering), but some of the heroes (like Anwen, Aidan or Nadia) and bosses (Azexes) look rather offputting or stray too far from the sprite design. Unit sprites were completely unchanged, leaving them in low resolution and with persistent minor graphical artifacts on many frames, and the only changes to animations include a small QoL update to the Ghost (she no longer swipes on every single unit in her path) - the Druids still awkwardly revert to a single frame of idle animation after performing their attack. The pre-rendered cutscenes were not only left as-is from the original release, but now also suffer from minor compression artifacts.The UI (and UX) was actually downgraded in some ways, like with subtle but offputting changes to the game fonts (they look thinner and more spaced out, making them less readable on a glance), mouse wheel click no longer working as a shortcut for battle grid view (it was replaced entirely by Alt key, coupled with a rather ugly prompt permanently glued to the corner of the screen), odd changes to the Campaign progression screen (the time/percentage box in the map's corner feels almost like a placeholder), untouched map layouts (ahoy, getting awkwardly stuck on your first playthrough because you need to click the movement node you're standing on and the game doesn't highlight this in any way) and weird lack of feedback in the Options menu leaving you guessing if your changes were even saved. Also, the game still requires a reset to switch resolution or enter/exit windowed mode, and completely lacks any kind of animation speed setting or, more importantly, colorblind mode despite relying almost entirely on color-matching units - all those things were jarring for a game from early 2010s, and are downright baffling in a 2023 "definitive" re-release.Sound design is lackluster on the technical side, too - the music often doesn't fade out properly on loading screens or during screen transitions, leading to abrupt cuts. The main menu theme pauses when entering a different game mode, then abruptly unpauses mid-tune rather than resetting to the start. Some tracks are more or less blatantly mis-assigned, playing in areas that used to be devoid of music or that played a completely different, more fitting track. The altered grid clicking sound is too loud and turns into a grating screech when moving your cursor quickly over the battlefield, and some of the ambience and battle effects are mixed incorrectly resulting in audible volume spikes (if I can hear Inferno walls merging sound being much louder than anything else with both music and SFX turned down while playing without headphones or in a Discord call with three other people, something is wrong) or constant jarring noise in the background (like with crickets on the nighttime Sylvan arena). There are also no separate volume sliders for battle/unit SFX and general ambience.A lot of my grievances may be just complaints of someone who spent over four hundred hours with the previous version of this game, and developed an eye (or ear) for certain details - but that's where the devil is. The supposedly revised port is either on the same level or technically inferior to the original game, lacks truly notable upgrades, is still missing a crucial accessibility feature, is a paid upgrade for the owners of the original version and replaced it entirely on Steam's storefront. Given Ubisoft's poor history of post-release support not only for this game (both on PC and with the utterly abysmal mobile port), but for the entire Might & Magic franchise, and DotEmu's role as a "quick and cheap" freelancing port studio, I'm not expecting any kind of further patches, updates or DLCs for this game.What should be a source of joy and celebration for me as a fan, instead leaves me worried and disappointed. Clash of Heroes is still a deeply playable and enjoyable experience in 2023 - yet it deserves better. We as customers - old players and newcomers alike - deserve better. And even if the not-so-Definitive Edition isn't outright broken in its current state, I still can't recommend it over the original version. Capybara Games clearly put a lot of effort and love into recreating a DS game for PC and X360/PS3 back in 2011 - I wish DotEmu would be allowed to at the very least match it 1:1.

_childDocuments_.review: A great little game that mixes strategy and 3 in a row genres in a surprisingly fun and engaging way that nobody has really done better ever since, despite its age. While simplistic, story is not without its charm, and the world, despite being roughly linear, still has enough freedom between key story battles to explore for loot, secrets and sidequests. If the formula described on storepage even remotely interests you, this game will be worth your time.The negative reviews have mostly nothing to do with CoH's faults as a game; instead, its a reaction to this "Definitive edition" being a rerelease with minimal changes, most notable of which is fixed multiplayer (which is very welcome) and redone portrait art (which about nobody asked for), while the original version is taken off the stores. Make of it what you will; knowing ubisoft and its absolute lack of ♥♥♥♥♥ given about this franchise, theres probably some IP tomfoolery involved. Despite the sour taste, this is still the best treatment  Might & Magic has gotten in recent years, and ill gladly take it over another soulless mobile microtransaction client.EDIT: after looking into things further, turns out that Ubisoft pulled the plug on multiplayer among many of its older properties without warning last year, so what happened is most likely that Capybara/Dotemu chose to re-release the game to run off their own servers; and since servers cost a pretty penny, yeah, no qualms about this not being free.

_childDocuments_.review: This screams of a cash grab and I’m sad about it.CoH is hands down my favourite puzzle game of all time, it also ranks up there as a favourite across all genres. The game play is very unique, I have never found anything else quite like it. It is relaxing, while also having a decent degree of difficulty. There is also a tonne of replay value with the quick matches and multiplayer.My original version on Steam stopped working over a year ago. It is too laggy to play, sometimes the game won’t even make it to launch (some recent reviews on the game page for the old version stated the same issue). I also own the game on mobile, which has not worked for multiple years. It stopped being supported by the developer. I had resigned myself to the fact that I would never be able to play it again, so seeing a definitive edition coming out was a pleasant surprise.However, I can’t help but feel extremely disappointed by this release. Of all the things that could have been added or improved, the focus seems to have been on the artwork (which arguably is the LAST thing that needed changing, if at all). Would have been amazing to get some new factions/units or a little story expansion. I appreciate the interface changes and new multiplayer character, but that really isn’t enough to justify a whole new game. It really does feel like an overpriced patch. I can only hope that more may be added in future.As much as I love CoH it leaves a bad taste in my mouth to think that my prior versions were forced into obsolescence in order to make this low effort re-release viable. If you have a working version of the original game, you do not need this unless online play is important to you. If either of my older versions still worked, I would be getting this refunded in its current state.

If you click the hero menu button but under it is a movement node, the game will open the menu AND move you on the map.Other improvements sorely needed include things like:* Ability to click anywhere to move conversation forward, instead of having to click the skip or next button.* Autosaving (with options to turn it on/off and use an autosave slot).* Load screens... why? Try loading back into a campaign as fast as you can and you'll find about 5 to 10 seconds where you're just waiting for the UI to load or transition.* Better UI displays, it's obvious they took old code, and ported it and that's all. Shame they didn't fix things for a PC or current-gen release.

_childDocuments_.review: Let’s get straight to the point, this definitive edition doesn’t add a lot to the game. The art of the characters got changed (some characters look much better), same for some of the UI and you can edit your party before starting battles. I might be missing some other minor things but this is what you can expect for the most part. The game itself is a mix of puzzle and RPG, the fights are the puzzles and the rest is a light RPG. Your party members and the hero level up individually, you find artifacts to equip on the hero, level up increases a few stats, you have currency to re-buy some party members, you run through areas, talk to NPC and you can do some side quests. There are 5 mini campaigns with a different hero each with unique moves, party members and artifacts.  The campaigns are unlocked one after another because the stories are connected. The game perfectly balances many elements. While it’s not a full fledged RPG in terms volume and options, what’s there has a purpose and is well designed. The game has a kind of simplicity that makes it easy to get into but it’s also complex enough in the right way. The puzzles are very addictive. The story, while nothing original nor the best, is engaging enough to follow. The entire game has a good pacing with no real filler. It took me around 31 hours to 100% the achievements. It looks and sounds nice, you can save anywhere and the game seems to generally respect your time even with the most grindy achievement. That said, the game seems to have many loading screens that take longer than I’d like. The loading times themselves are not too bad but I’m surprised how many times the game needs to load. There are some multiplayer exclusive achievements with at least one requiring 3 other players. They’re not bad if you can find others to work with but you’re basically on a timer to get this done. I got lucky when I checked steam forum. Lastly, this definitive edition could have added more to the game. The text on the game’s steam page is misleading when it mentions many new quality of life additions. It feels like it was released with the bare minimum effort to cash in on the game. I bought it when it got released with a discount for owners of the original game (I paid around €8). The normal price is way higher than the game’s original price. Even with all of this in mind, M&M CoH is a game not to be missed if you haven’t had the chance to play it. It’s a beloved game that is timeless. It doesn’t feel old despite the age. I’m an RPG and puzzle fan. The game offers the best of both worlds without the bad stuff like bloat or dragging out the experience. I wish we had more games like it.

_childDocuments_.review: Pieced together by Dotemu, Clash of Heroes: Definitive Edition provides redrawn artwork, quality of life improvements, a retooled Online mode, and all the previous DLC slapped together into one package.  Full disclosure: this is my foray not only into the Clash of Heroes title, but Might and Magic in itself, so if there are any inconsistencies within the plot, I will probably miss them and am judging the entire game upon fresh, green eyes.Battles are smashed together in the art of turn-based RPG, and Puyo-centric, Match-3-esque Puzzle Fighter.  Characters go into battle with 3 slots of small units, which can be mixed and matched to suit playstyles, and up to two special units, which I’ll call Double Units and Quad Units for ease of understanding going forward.  Damage is dealt by matching three small units in a vertical line followed by a set turn amount before they march into battle to fight whatever is in front of them.  Defending your territory is done by matching three or more small units in a horizontal line that’ll build walls that will mitigate incoming enemy attacks.  Walls can be built to higher levels with additional units made into walls behind it.  The basics of this system is vertical-offensive, horizontal-defensive.This also leans into your special units.  Remember the Double and Quad Units?  Stacking two small units behind a Double Unit will activate them, while stacking 4 small units in a 2-by-2 square behind a Quad Unit will activate those.  These units carry bigger health and attack points as well as powerful passive and lasting effects after attack.  It’s worth defending these to allow a devastating attack after their cooldown time finishes, as well as shifting the battle to your opponent having to deal with the gigantic issue now in front of them.Each faction in campaign and multiplayer have their specific units that all carry different styles of play (use one style of unit 3 times to stack the same attack or spread out evenly to diversify your violence portfolio) and each character comes with an Ultimate move, powered up by MP that’s gained by taking and dealing damage, that plays to each faction’s strengths.  Some feel more powerful than others, but all Ultimates carry a significant change in momentum once used, except at times for the dice-rolling luck-based Lightning Strike.Clash of Heroes boasts a massive 20+ hour story (it took me about 22 hours to complete) spanning 5 main areas.  Each chapter follows a different character within a different part of Ashan, starting each character and their units at Level 1.  You progress the story through meeting main NPCs, learning more of the mysterious Demon King and his nefarious plot, as well as engaging with various side quests sprawled about the boardgame-like setup.Side quests are marked with a Silver-based icon (with main quests wearing Gold), and are there with the sole intention of providing you EXP to level up, and resources like Iron, Gold, and Crystals.  These resources are used to buy Double and Quad Units once you’ve unlocked them in their respective areas within the campaign world.  Side quests boil down to three styles: Puzzle Quests, Bounties, and One-Offs.  Puzzle Quests are pre-set boards that are won by defeating every enemy unit in one turn, using combos to refresh turns and allow extra moves to proc every unit.  Bounties have you sent off to find various NPCs of advancing difficulty and battle them for whichever reason the Bountyman provides you.  One-Offs are exactly that, random NPCs providing you some reason to battle, and your job is to oblige.These side quests may be side quests, but you would need to do these.  Shoot to do nearly all of them.  Why?  Because the campaign pulls no punches and does not play nice after the first area, which is used primarily to give you a rundown of how the game’s mechanics work and what strategies to look into.  Enemies will be a higher level, and you’re consistently expected to be punching upwards at your opponents.  The issue with this is some main and side quest enemies are just too high of a level to even compete against, so areas then boil down to walking around aimlessly for the random battles to pop up (which those can even be over your level), or banging your head against the wall until you get a favorable drop of units.But be warned, the AI will get some absolute filth for their “random” drops.  I don’t want to sound overly salty, but enemies will get gift-wrapped drops of units that allow them some extensive combos to naturally “increase” the difficulty.  This is already done by most opponents being over-leveled to your own, but getting bombarded by perfect combos whilst activating their Double and Quad units that are more powerful than yours will deal with multiple Game Overs, and it won’t feel like a skillful defeat.  To circumvent some of this hill-climbing, some areas will implement objectives outside of draining HP bars to achieve victory, but most of these had me wishing I could just slog through a HP bar instead.The inspiration to the puzzles are a neat idea, but each puzzle presented supplies a small issue that makes it unbearable to play.  Need to hit two buttons behind walls?  You must hit them within 2 turns or they revert.  Need to hit those units running around the map?  They do not telegraph their moves and can jump upwards of two lanes each turn.  With vertical attack patterns taking upwards of 3 turns, most puzzles turn into a game of pure luck that the enemy you need to hit is within firing range, or wasting 15 minutes not knowing a prime piece of knowledge for the objective because Clash of Heroes just didn’t tell you ahead of time.Completing these side quests, puzzles areas, and everything in between will need you Artifacts, which are passive buffs specific to your character.  Each character has 10 artifacts that can provide substantial upgrades to specific units to better bolster a specific playstyle, to giving buffs to specific actions like deleting walls to gain MP for your Ultimate, to giving you a second life if your HP hits 0.  You’ll also unlock special Double or Quad Units for use in campaign and multiplayer as well as extra characters when you complete an area.  Running through the campaign is your only way of unlocking them for use in multiplayer, so get ready for the long haul if you want to use the interesting things with your buddies.With Capybara Games’ intention to provide unlockables through the campaign only (you are granted 1 artifact per 5 levels gained in multiplayer, but there being over 50 artifacts, good luck with that), you are purposely guided to run through the story and everything it has stuffed in these five areas.  But the spoiled AI, teeth-grating puzzles, and the fact the campaign is just way, way too long make going through this quasi-mandatory experience a dreadful slog.  Which is a shame considering how ridiculously fun the battle system is.Which is why most of my time has been spent within the multiplayer.  1v1 battles play out as the battles did in the campaign, and it’s incredible how fun this game can really be.  Add in a couple friends and play the 2v2 for a mind-bending but intensely satisfying experience as each player on each team controls a preset amount of units and must work together to create devastating combos.I’ve put around 33 hours into Clash of Heroes and after this I will certainly be back to put more in.  The Match-3 style breeds a satisfyingly high skill ceiling with a pick-up-and-play moniker that will gladly greet anyone that finds its way into its world.  But having to tackle an overly stuffed campaign poisoned with artificially high difficulty and most of the game locked behind every stuffed nook and cranny of poorly executed objectives almost soils the entire experience.

_childDocuments_.review: While I have never played the original Nintendo DS version of Might & Magic: Clash of Heroes from 2009, I have played and greatly enjoyed the “HD” version of the game released in 2011 on PC, PSN and XBLA. It was a unique and highly enjoyable attempt to mix the turn-based strategy of the Heroes of Might & Magic games with very simple match 3 gameplay reminiscent of Puzzle Quest. It had frustrating aspects to it, of course, but I remember liking it a lot 12 years ago. And I have been considering revisiting the title for a while, but those plans had to be put on hold because I didn’t want to deal with the technical issues. Sadly, the original PC release became quite problematic to run in recent years and on top of that fans of the multiplayer aspect of the game (which I have never been interested in and have not played) were disappointed when a few years ago Ubisoft disabled the online functionality entirely.The announcement of Might & Magic: Clash of Heroes – Definitive Edition was a very pleasant surprise and I dove into it as soon as I had time. Unfortunately, I have to say that the game hasn’t aged as well as I have remembered and this new release does nothing to the biggest frustrations the original game had as well.But to quickly recap – Might & Magic: Clash of Heroes is a match 3 turn-based strategy that serves as a prequel to Heroes of Might & Magic V. It was one of the first entries in the series under the ownership of Ubisoft and, just like the preceding Heroes V and Dark Messiah of Might & Magic they were set in the new world setting that was completely separate from the previous Heroes games by New World Computing. As in a proper Heroes game, you have several separate campaigns, each of which has its Hero character and a unique army. Although, unlike Heroes, you do not get a Castle to revisit and upgrade and you get or buy your troops from other parts of the map (more similarly to King’s Bounty, in a way).Each Hero gets three infinite common troop types and five limited and more powerful special troop types. And the way the match 3 comes into play during the battle is in the fact that all of the troops are colour coded. Matching 3 horizontally will create a wall that will absorb damage. Matching 3 vertically will set the troops into a charging state where after a set amount of turns they will launch an attack. While special troop types require 2 or 4 common troops to be matched to it vertically to start charging. Each Hero also gets one spell to use to their advantage and both the Hero and the troops get experience after combat and can level up. You get a limited amount of moves per each turn but doing chains of matches can give you a move back or even add more than you had, while matching via deletion does not use a move. It’s all very simple to grasp and nicely combines the tactical nature of Heroes with casual fun of match 3.At least, for the most part it’s a good mix. One thing that has been annoying in the original release and remains exactly as such in the new edition is the fact, that when completing the story campaign you will occasionally stumble upon story battles, success of which will far greatly depend on the random nature of match 3 than any kind of tactical skill. For 80% of the game it doesn’t matter much, but when it does (and most of the final campaign is exactly this) it becomes infuriating.Especially since while there is usually no punishment for loosing, your actual punishment is sitting through several loading screens. The overabundance of “Loading” after each tiny little thing was unpleasant in 2011 but in 2023 it feels especially not fun, especially when the game looks this simple. There’s also no autosave either and manual saves take about as long as said loading screens. This, along with minor bugs, dumb lack of quality of life for some aspects of the game and later campaign designs slowly erodes any fun you might be having with the game. So by the time you notice that some smaller bugs that you remember seeing 12 years ago are still here, any kind of goodwill evaporates.Fans of the original DS version might also be sad to hear that there is still no way to switch to the original visual style or the soundtrack of that version. And while the “HD” sound and visuals are very good (and seem to have been further retouched for the Definitive Edition), the original release had a certain charm to it that will now be lost unless you have a DS/3DS and the original version. The story in the game is very bland and the fact that it occasionally tries to be funny and cute feels odd. Not that it needed to be serious, but something about the Saturday-morning cartoon aesthetic feels at odds with the setting of Might & Magic and the plot this game in particular tries to tell. Oh and also it seems that the cutscenes of the game were not reencoded or upscaled since the older release so by today’s standards they look especially blocky.I still had fun with most of my Might & Magic: Clash of Heroes – Definitive Edition playthrough, for how horrible the final campaign is, and it still is a very unique and entertaining experience. And I am glad that the game, with this new edition, is properly playable again instead of becoming lost to time. But at the same time, it’s hard to be excited about this “Definitive Edition” when it does not address any of the biggest issues of the original release and feels more like a “It’s working again Edition” of the exact same game but now sold as a new title. It’s quite likely that the budget for this release was extremely low and the way it was published has more to do with the legal aspects of the game. But as a player I cannot help but be disappointed. Still, this is the way to play the game, which is still quite nice, even if not as fun as it was for 2011. And there’s still nothing quite like this.

_childDocuments_.review: Might & Magic: Clash of Heroes - Definitive Edition is an absolute delight that masterfully blends elements of puzzle and strategy RPG games. As a long-time fan of the Might & Magic series, I can confidently say that this remastered version has taken an already fantastic game to new heights, making it a must-play for both newcomers and veterans alike.The first thing that struck me was the beautifully updated graphics and artwork. The developers have breathed new life into the game, making it visually stunning while retaining the charm and essence of the original. The vibrant colors, detailed characters, and imaginative landscapes make every moment a pleasure to behold.The gameplay is where Might & Magic: Clash of Heroes truly shines. The game cleverly combines match-three puzzle mechanics with turn-based strategy, creating an addictive and engaging experience. The puzzle battles demand both quick thinking and strategic planning, challenging players to outwit their opponents in a unique and satisfying way. Each faction offers a distinct playstyle, and the array of units and abilities at your disposal ensure that battles always feel fresh and exciting.One of the game's strengths is its rich and immersive story. The narrative unfolds across five different campaigns, each with its own set of memorable characters and intriguing plotlines. The way the story intertwines with the gameplay keeps you invested in the world of Might & Magic and leaves you eager to uncover what happens next.The Definitive Edition has also addressed some of the minor issues present in the original release. The improved user interface and streamlined controls make navigating the game a breeze, and the addition of various quality-of-life improvements enhances the overall experience.Multiplayer mode is an absolute blast. Competing against friends or other players online adds a whole new dimension to the game, and the strategic depth becomes even more apparent when you face off against human opponents. The online community is still active and welcoming, creating a friendly atmosphere for new players to jump in and enjoy competitive battles.The audio design deserves special mention as well. The music perfectly complements the game's fantastical setting, setting the right mood for every situation, while the sound effects add an extra layer of immersion to the battles.In conclusion, Might & Magic: Clash of Heroes - Definitive Edition is an exceptional title that effortlessly marries puzzle mechanics and strategy RPG elements. Its stunning visuals, captivating story, and addictive gameplay make it stand out as one of the best games in its genre. Whether you're a fan of the series or a newcomer, this game is an absolute must-play that guarantees hours of enjoyment and challenges your tactical prowess. Grab your sword, muster your troops, and prepare for an epic adventure that will leave you wanting more.

_childDocuments_.review: NOTE: I never got around to playing the original edition of this game, so this review is strictly for the definitive edition. To my knowledge, many veterans of the original were disappointed with the change of art style (from what I can see, it has been Anime-ed up somewhat)  and the lack of gameplay/balancing changes.I've basically only ever played the single player mode; tried out the online multiplayer once just for completeness.The good:- The puzzle battles are somewhat tactical and mostly fun. Boss battles and puzzle challenges provide a good amount of variation to the basic formula.- Gameplay is well tutorialized and easy to pick up. - Pacing is good; the difficulty builds up evenly with some (surmountable) cliffs. Only the last chapter can become a bit of a slog.- The token RPG elements allow for some nonlinearity; allowing you to back off a challenge that you find too difficult and try some other opponent first instead. The story is broken down into five chapters, with each having its own mini campaign map; there is no mentionable amount of backtracking. - The art and the worldbuilding evoke a high-magic, goofy fantasy world reminiscent of the 2D Might and Magic (and HoMM) games. - Surprisingly involved and complex fantasy lore and storyline that ties into Ubisoft's other MM games; takes about 25 hours to complete. The characters are a bunch of kids, but mostly likeable. It's a bit quirky that the story seems too serious for the bright anime-style art. (There is even some light body horror, which I found a bit jarring.)- To my experience, the game is bug-free (as one should expect), but see below.The bad:- I wish there was some way to speed up the computer opponent's turns. It is a pointless wait.- Side quests are not really optional; you need to complete at least most of them (apparently I missed one) to gather items and XP.- Units seem somewhat unbalanced; Items are extremely unbalanced. In several chapters, there is a single best item, and all you gather after it are useless by comparison.The ugly:- There are two points on the story map in which you have to click on your own space to interact with a challenge instead of the opponent's. At first I thought it was a bug and I would have to restart the game. - While I don't generally mind the artwork, the portrait for one of the protagonists (Aidan) seems a bit off. Verdict: Recommended for people who like Match-3 puzzles and high fantasy. Also highly recommended for veterans (such as myself) of earlier Might & Magic and HoMM games. Even as a pure single player experience, you get your money's worth

Might & Magic: Clash of Heroes is a unique mix of puzzle, strategy and RPG: Plan your every move and combine your attacks to defeat your enemies in matching puzzle inspired battle scenarios, upgrade your heroes and creatures to unleash increasingly devastating attacks onto your opponents, and let the strategic thinker in you lead your troops to victory.

STORY

Taking place 40 years before the Heroes of Might & Magic V saga, Might & Magic: Clash of Heroes tells the tale of five heroes scattered across five different regions of Ashan. Each must travel their own dangerous paths to grow in strength, unravel a demonic plot, and ultimately save their world from devastation.

MASTER UNIQUE AND DYNAMIC COMBAT MECHANICS!

The unique puzzle/strategy battle gameplay of Clash of Heroes will put your tactical skills to the test in the 20+ hour-long story mode and against players in offline and online PvP. Adopt the perfect strategy, let the leader in you guide your troops to victory!

Be creative, find the perfect combination of units, artifacts and spells. Piece together crazy combos and break the enemy lines. Every additional combo can be decisive!

Gain XP after each battle, level up your hero and units in order to get an unbeatable team. Find artifacts and hire mercenaries, it will help you on your quest to save the world from devastation.

name: Top Racer Collection
detailed_description: The thrill of 16-bit racing from the 90s is back! Play the complete Top Racer series with Top Racer, Top Racer 2, Top Racer 3000 and Top Racer Crossroads, a brand new game with new cars and exclusive content made especially for this unmissable edition. Go back in time and travel to the future for the pure nostalgia of racing at breakneck speeds. Arcade gameplay where it's all about floor it and quick reflexes! 4 games combined in a single title! Over 140 tracks around the world and beyond! 4 new incredible and exclusive cars in Top Racer Crossroads! Manage your time, nitro and fuel just like in the original Top Racer, but this time with exclusive cars! There are 4 cars for you to experience for the first time! Reminisce about the old split-screen days and play games to see who's king of the track! 2 players in Top Racer, Top Racer 2 and Top Racer Crossroads Up to 4 simultaneous players in Top Racer 3000 Challenge racers anywhere on the planet in online mode to enter the world rankings! Get in the mood for 90s games by using filters reminiscent of images from old TV sets! Relive the experience with colorful and vibrant pixel graphics just like in the original games! Race in campaign mode on the 140 tracks available! Race against the clock in time attack mode! Have fun without compromise in quick race mode! In Custom Cup mode you're the king of the show and you can choose 4 tracks in any of the games to set the challenge for everyone. Play again or experience for the first time the series of racing games from the 90s that many old-school racers miss. Play the original TOP RACER with exclusive new cars that make reference to vehicles that are symbols of other great racing games and even popular Brazilian car culture. The first game in the series was released in 1992 for the SNES and left a legion of fans, especially in Brazil and Latin America. In the best arcade style, choose between 4 different cars inspired by real sports cars and race on 32 tracks, opting for manual or automatic gear changes and using nitro boosts for those times when you're in a pinch. The second game in the series, released in 1993, also for the SNES, considered by many players to be an even more incredible sequel to the first game. This time, with a more realistic feel, you have to control the damage to your car, collect resources, make upgrades for greater performance and keep an eye on the weather to change the tires! There are 64 tracks to show off your skill and strategy. Released in 1995, Top Gear 3000 brings a different and completely mind-blowing experience at unthinkable and challenging speeds. A thousand years in the future, you'll race on 47 tracks on different planets in an interplanetary competition! You can count on hyper-technological upgrades such as nuclear fusion engines and titanium-cobalt armor. You can also use weapons to improve your strategy, such as jumping over your opponents or using a magnet to slow down the cars in front of you!

_childDocuments_.review: Top Racer Collection, (known as Top Gear outside of Japan), excels as a fantastic compilation of the original SNES trilogy, Top Gear (1992), Top Gear 2 (1993) and Top Gear 3000 (1995), including in collaboration with Horizon Chase an exclusive Top Gear 1 modification which features new cars from Horizon saga.In addition, Top Racer Collection offers a ton of extra content. This includes high quality scans of the original Japanese box art and manuals for each game, a wide variety of arcade and online modes, improved ingame visuals with various filters, screen types, and background images. The audio quality is excellent, complemented by a sound test option, and there's a great selection of achievements for an enhanced quality of life.What sets it apart is the great gameplay; the emulation runs perfectly on every game without frame drops, bugs, crashes, or any issues. The controls feel highly responsive, ensuring a truly enjoyable gaming experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Top Racer Collection

_childDocuments_.review: Haven't heard of Top Racer?  The Top Racer Collection consists of four awesome racing titles in one glorious package.  With great music and almost 150 racing tracks throughout, what makes the Top Racer titles stand out is the amount of depth found in each title.  Sure you can pickup and play for a great arcade racing experience however to succeed you'll need to understand the in depth mechanics that encompasses each title.  With split screen and added online multiplayer and a huge amount of content the Top Racer Collection is a great add to everyone's library.- Happy Thanksgiving 2024 :)
_childDocuments_.name: Top Racer Collection

_childDocuments_.review: A great compilation of the classic Top Racer (over here called "Top Gear", but due to license issues this name was dropped) games, including a new version of the OG game with new vehicles.The games are the SNES versions, but this is not an issue since those were arguably the best versions.I had some issues with the sound, but it seems if you don't ALT-TAB, it doesn't get out of sync as easily.But I certainly recommend this compilation, to every retro game fan out there, especially those who love classic arcade racers like OutRun, Lotus Racing, F-Zero, etc.
_childDocuments_.name: Top Racer Collection

_childDocuments_.review: I was hyped for this game. BlueTag (for those of you who know who that is) made a review for it and I figured "sure, why not? I grew up with the first two games and never got to play the third. This is going to be excellent!"Issue started on one of the first splash pages. "bleem!" That's a name I haven't heard in forever. bleem! has its own history and story, being one of the first, if only, boxed emulators. Meaning around the same place you could pick up "Bioshock" and "Norton Anti-Virus", you could pick up a copy of bleem!....but then it dawned on me. The UI, the way it just snaps to the original music when you play the game, the way the multiplayer doesn't work and wasn't able to connect me to a single match.I just bought an emulator. Multiplayer is just netplay on bleem! There's nothing about this game that suggests it's a port, it's just an emulation. Despite the whole "Made in Unity" splash screen, it's nothing more than to tie UI elements together and get you to the emulation.It's not worth it. It really isn't. I'm gonna boot up SNES9x and go back to what I've been doing for a while. Save your money, don't give into bleem!.

_childDocuments_.review: I am a huge fan of the original Top Gear for SNES. It is probably one of my most played games. When I saw that this was coming I was very excited. I immediately purchased this collection. However the "Very Positive" rating is extremely misleading if you care at all about this game. This is a garbage way to play these games. I cannot believe the developer dropped the ball this hard.There are multiple long legal agreements before you can play the game. Two more to play multiplayer (I was never able to find a match).Replacing the original menu music with this generic guitar music is also CRIMINAL.There was ZERO reason to change the original menu to this weird Xbox Live Arcade looking monstrosity. I don't know why they did it. They just removed the menu from the original game. WHY?The "new" Crossroads game might as well be a rushed rom hack. I only noticed they modified the sprites for the cars, nothing else was changed. Same tracks. The new cars look bad.I'm so upset this license went to this developer/publisher. At least there's a sound test with the actual original soundtrack. (But you cannot hear it if you turn off the terrible menu music so they still messed that up.)I immediately refunded. This game has ZERO reason to be rated this high.

_childDocuments_.review: A Blast from the Past!Top Racer is one of the most underrated arcade racing game franchise from the 90s that holds a very cult following in Brazil. If it wasn't for them, we wouldn't have the spiritual successor series, Horizon Chase, AND this collection.Yes, the graphics are dated and the gameplay can be tedious to newcomers, but the game is very addictive and takes more than just trying to avoid bumping on your opponents. It's very simple and backed up by their soundtrack to enjoy throughout each race.Yes, there is online to play with friends or the world, but unfortunately, it doesn't have crossplay, so the playerbase is divided. Not sure which system will have the most players in, so pick a version carefully.Overall, it's a collection of one of the most beloved racing games. Would recommend it for those who want to relive that childhood, but this may not grab attention to new players wanting to play another racing game, Top Racer 2 would have some RPG elements into the game if that peeks your interests, but don't expect too much.

_childDocuments_.review: I love Top Racer 1, easily one of my all time favorite racing games. But this "emulator" is missing frames, the games run very poorly and hurt the eyes. Right now i cannot recommend it as it's just better to grab an emulator online.They also made "another game" but it's just a rom hack with the car sprites replaced, it doesn't have its place here... And it should never be called a "new game", pretty wrong to do this.

_childDocuments_.review: Dove right into Top Gear 3000, one of my favorite editions of the series. It runs quite well on PC. I think the new modes and features are a really nice touch, i haven't had the chance to dive into everything yet, but wanted to leave a positive review. Grew up with this series and have many, many hours across each of the games. Top Racer 2 and Top Racer 3000 being my most replayed. I hope new players will find this series and enjoy it as we all did back in the day! Back then, the 4 player split screen modes were a lot of fun while hanging out with your friends or vs AI, etc. Thank you to QUByte Interactive for giving us this surprise, nice to see this on steam!

_childDocuments_.review: TOP RACER is the  original JAPANESE NAME of the game. TOP GEAR was the name given to in the US due to legal reason (at the time(in the 90's)); also today there is now a show named also topgear. Yeah it is very confusing.That said, its a port of the SNES games that you ever wanted on PC.The UI is changed for modern systems but the games are there, just like the original.I used to rent these games when we (my family) had spare money when i was younger.New and young players won't like this game tho, it has a snesish flavour only 80&90's kids can taste.Snes cartridges were so expensive i never had any game besides the one that came with the console.To be honest i bought this gem pack because of my sentimental value to my childhood.Obrigado pelo port senhores.

_childDocuments_.review: Although a bit unknown worldwide, these games are basically patrimony of a brazilian' gaming history, truly one of the most memorable SNES racing classics, and I am SO GLAD it has seen the light of day again... If you know Top Gear/Top Racer then what are you waiting to buy? And if you don't, what are you waiting to discover one of the best ever racing classics?Summing up all Top Racer games, they're arcade racers with very simplistic gameplay and functionality, and even for very old games they still hold up well in fluid gameplay, but yeah do remember that you're still playing old games. The main core of all games' is going through career mode and ranking well in the leaderboards so you can advance to the next cup, pretty straightforward. TR 2 and 3000 got upgrade mechanics, the better you finish the better you're paid to upgrade your car and keep up with the competition. As for Top Racer Crossroads, in a nutshell it's essentially Top Racer 1 reskinned with cars from the game Horizon Chase and with some different stats from original TR, apart from that nothing much changes.All the games are pretty much original and untouched, devs made it clear many times that they do not have the games' codes, only the license, so there's not really much they can do super deep into the core besides what they already did with some new game modes and such, so yeah do bear that in mind before you buy please that you're not buying a remaster or anything of the sort. There's autosave whenever you advance a cup so you don't need to note passwords, and three save state slots you can use for that extra edge.I'm personally very happy with this package, for the purpose of having the games running untouched it's well delivered, and offers good modern resources for convenience, that plus the possibility of playing these games online, even with Remote Play Together. Nostalgia is speaking volumes in me right now, I highly recommend you give this a shot if you never heard about this series before.

_childDocuments_.review: Faithful collection of three games with welcome modern additions and old-school frustrations.This is a collection of Top Racer's three first-generation titles. Depending on where you live, the series is also known as Top Gear, which is unrelated to the British show. If you never owned a console in the past, you might be unfamiliar with the series. Although there were a lot of similar racing games, Top Racer was never available on home computers. As an added bonus, there’s a fourth title that’s just a modified version of the first game. Everything remains the same; the only difference is that cars are replaced with new ones.Because the games are authentic to the originals, screen edges are not used. You can stretch the game to fit the screen, but it does not look good. It is much better to use one of the four generic backgrounds to fill out that empty space. While the choices aren't generous, it will not detract from the gameplay.Unfortunately, the extras aren't really intriguing. The best feature is the addition of achievements, which provides a compelling motive to play and beat the games. While the music player is pleasant but unremarkable, the gallery will be useless to most people. It only features a game manual in Japanese for all three games, which cannot be zoomed in. However, the extras menu is really deceiving. When you choose one of the games, you'll discover a lot more interesting content. First, there is a manual with a brief history of the game, controls, and a list of all the cars and mechanics in the game. Then there are a variety of other modes, like quick race, time attack, and custom cup. Each game has its own set of screens, and each selection (cars, tracks, and options) is custom-made for this game and does not take place in the game itself. The only thing that remains original is the driving.The ability to save at any time, even while racing, is a significant quality-of-life feature. While it may cheapen the experience, it is a nice inclusion because you will not have the time or patience to complete everything in one session. The campaign is the main mode, and it plays similarly in all games. You have throttle, brake, nitro, and steering. Nitro is replaced by weapons in the third title. There are minor variations between the games. The first one is basic. You choose one of four cars and drive the tracks in order. The campaign takes you around the world to eight different countries. Each country includes four tracks, and the goal is to finish with the most points so you can move on to the next country. Tracks are circular, you have three nitros, and you have to worry about fuel, which may be refilled by entering a pit lane. It's fair to point out that the game is not fun today. Most of the blame falls on frustration when you bump into obstacles on the road or other racers. This slows down your car and even a single bump can ruin all your chances of winning. But the worst thing is that, with the exception of your rival, none of the other cars need to refuel. This makes winning impossible because the best you can be is second. Although you can select difficulty, this apparently doesn’t do anything because you’ll be left eating dust even on amateur.The second game improves a lot. There’s only one car, but it adds a lot more tracks, more nitros, and more chances to win. Although it still has fuel, it drops pit lanes. This means you need to use your earning to upgrade your car to be able to win. And the third title adds a simple story, a lot more upgrades, lines on the track to refill fuel and repair damage, and weapons.

_childDocuments_.review: I can’t recommend this game, as it falls short when compared to playing the originals on emulators. I paid around R$50 ($9), and it didn’t feel worth it. A more reasonable price would be R$28 ($5).The game suffers in terms of performance, and key features, especially for Top Gear 2 and Top Gear 3000, are missing. For example, in Top Gear 3000, you could use passwords to start with a fully upgraded car or unlock an "alien car," which is both overpowered and colorful. These options are unavailable because passwords aren’t supported. Worse still, it seems like the developers didn’t even play Top Gear 3000 themselves. When you finish the game, cheats are unlocked, but you can’t actually start with a fully upgraded car due to how the upgrades are handled. Cheats also don’t provide unlimited gadgets, which is the core mechanic of the game.Other minor issues:* Online play is dead and irrelevant.* The UI is clunky, requiring too many clicks to start a race.* Only one save slot per game (single and multiplayer), making the save system more of a limitation than a helpful feature.* Top Gear Crossroads is just Top Gear 1 with reskinned, overpowered cars. One of them is even a Brazilian joke car. People talk about “balance,” but there’s clearly an overpowered car that beats the rest.* The music in the UI is terrible; they should have just used the main game themes.Instead of keeping the original game menus, they wrapped everything in a worse UI. Features like save states, custom cups, and online multiplayer could have been added without altering the main game menu.* The achievements are uninspiring and generic. They missed the opportunity to add interesting challenges through Steam achievements.This purchase is only worth considering for people who want to play these classic games online without setting up emulators and LAN parties, which isn’t difficult but can be a hassle. Another potential reason to buy it is for Steam achievements. For most players, it's better to stick to emulators. It’s not even a good platform for speedrunning.
_childDocuments_.name: Top Racer Collection

_childDocuments_.review: Some might say, "Don't buy this game, just play it on an emulator," but let’s be real—the legality of that route is murky at best, especially since there don’t seem to be any official options to purchase the ROMs in this collection as of now.So, what does this collection bring to the table beyond the classic SNES Top Gear games? Quite a bit, actually. It includes modern enhancements like leaderboards for competitive bragging rights, network multiplayer for racing friends online, and a solo race mode with selectable tracks—perfect for practice sessions or casual play. There’s even a mirror mode for each track, which adds a fun twist, though it’s worth noting that the mirrored UI might feel a bit disorienting at first.Overall, this collection does justice to the golden age of ‘90s arcade-style racers, giving both veterans and newcomers a chance to relive (or discover) the magic of Top Gear. It’s a well-crafted package, and I’d wholeheartedly recommend it to anyone with a love for retro racing games.

_childDocuments_.review: As a big fan of the original SNES games growing up, i highly recommend this remastered collection to anyone looking to replay the originals or to fans of retro 16-bit racing games in general. Here's hoping that if enough people buy it the developers will be able to get the rights to re-release the N64 games as well.

_childDocuments_.review: Worth the full price, to me and imo :steamthumbsup:.For starters the keys can be rebinded and I can use reshade, which is very important to me.  I played the Top Gear games as a young teen in the 90's and while I loved the games back then, I can say that I appreciate and enjoy the games a whole lot more as a adult.  Definitely a timeless classic imo.  Even to this day, I especially can't say that there's a better racing theme than the Top Gear / Top Racer 3000 theme, and that's along with the mechanics and gameplay of the game; definitely way ahead of it's time imo.  Having all of the Top Racer games remastered in a single collection is awesome, but Top Racer / Top Gear 3000 was definitely what convinced me to immediately buy this collection.I highly recommend this collection if you like the series, but I also highly recommend it if you're looking for a low priced arcade racer to enjoy :steamthumbsup:.edit:Fair warning, these games aren't easy by any stretch of the imagination.  You will struggle a lot, but hang in there and focus on the mastery of each course.
_childDocuments_.name: Top Racer Collection

_childDocuments_.review: Makes me nauseated, unlike the original versions. I can do VR for hours on end but this makes me sick relatively quickly.I'm not positive what the issue is, but it seems to be some choppiness or framerate issues that differ from the original SNES version or the ROM versions. It sucks because I truly love the game, but being nauseated before even finishing a set of countries in Top Gear 1 (4 races) and then spending the next 12 hours ill (I repeated it the following night and the same effect of getting sick so it was 100% the game and not another factor) is just...yeah...not fun and as much as it pains me (Top Gear 2 is my most played SNES game of all time thanks to weekends with friends all deciding to play it instead of going to the bars), I can't give a thumbs up to a game that makes me sick when thousands of other games I've played do NOT have that effect.In the end, I sadly had to refund. I have noticed several posts on the forums talking about the framerate issues (though it may be something else, like, missing animations or something since apparently Steam shows it running at 60fps or above). Whatever the issue ends up being, I hope that the devs figure it out for those that have issues with it and I hope no one suffers the ill effects I have from it.
_childDocuments_.name: Top Racer Collection

_childDocuments_.review: Decent enough port but I experienced some audio issues (music tracks sometimes would skip notes). These problems are not present in the SNES versions if you're wondering.I gotta say though, the "new" game Crossroads is a bit lazy as it's just Top Gear 1 with slightly altered cars. So it's not worth buying just for Crossroads. (Maybe it is if you REALLY, REALLY love Top Gear 1.)I already owned Top Gear for the SNES but without this collection I would never have discovered that Top Gear 2 was such an awesome game - it actually inspired me to buy the original cartridge.Anyway - my rating for this collection is 7/10. It has some issues but the included games range from good to excellent so it's still worth it if you're looking for classic racing games and don't own a SNES. And even if you do, this package is far more affordable than buying the original games.

_childDocuments_.review: As a Kid, Top Racer was one of my favorite games, and it was something that helped me in my upbriging.it teached me 4 passions i have up to this day: Math, Geography, Astronomy and Videogames.yes, you heard that right. it was Top Racer 1 and 2 that made me a Nerd on Geography, wanting to know more about the cities and places depicted in the game, its climates, when it rains there and everything.it was also Top Racer 1 in particular that did teach me about Math: calculating time and fuel strategy is essential, to win, since the CPU is always breathing on your neck. and to this day i know that if you're using the Sidewinder in the original game, San Francisco, Chichen Itza and Hiroshima are tracks you don't need to stop to fuel up if you're fast enough (Black forest and Bordeaux are another ones but you gotta be extremely fast and lucky not to hit anything on the road). also, it teached me a lot of efficient strategies on how and where to pit, usually piting early to open a good gap and undercuting the CPU taking advantage of the fact there isn't many backmarkers on the first laps of the race, and that the computer named CPU tends to slow down to follow your pace. with the passage of time, the strategy became second nature to me, calculating fuel times to the second to maximize each strip of juice and be stoped as little and as early as strategically viable.and 3000 teached me all about Astronomy... many people may not know this, but the system stars all do exist in real life as white-blue stars in the milky way, altough some are miswritten by one or two letters like Toygeta (in real life Taygeta) or Vega 5 (wich is only Vega, but there is a planet called Vega too on the game so i think on this one they did that to differentiate). it made me look to the sky, even if i couldn't see the stars themselves anymore due to the light pollution the city of recife, where i live, got over the years. and made my imagination run wild with what alien civilizations might be there or what kind of Sci-fi buildings and societies we might find when we get there....and then this collection launches... i could not believe in my eyes that those games, maybe lost to history were being revived and re-sold, by some compatriots of mine that got the license from Kemco and Gremlin Graphics. i thought they were just found memories i got to relieve here and there in an emulator... that i never could own 3000 again, even if only digitally... so i had to get them for myself, even if they would end up only as a collector's piece on my steam library... for old times sake...so i thought that i would just touch them once... little did i know that after 18 hours of pure gameplay later i would be writing a review praising these games and a lot more...the graphics are all there, the nuances, the little glitches, even the old pit strategies were all there... it hadn't changed one iota from what i remembered. and it offered me more... i... couldn't be more happier... to be that 7 year old kid with that top racer 3000 cartridge on my hands again gifted to me by my now late mother...and there was even crossroads, that made me LOVE the Twilight car and learn new strategies all over again since its fuel consuption is different. it accelerates fast, runs fast, and is a pure bliss to drive... to experience all the circuits i know again from a total new perspective...i simply couldn't be more happier... so i played... and played and played untill platinum it. and for me... there is little if anything i can say to criticize it other than super minor nitpicks: of course the dificulty on the last cup and especially the last track on 3000 could be toned down a bit. that track felt like a Kaizo hack... but it made me sweat, breath heavily, to say: "you are not beating me, not after 25 years of experience. the true champion is ME, and i'm here to claim my trophy again, EVERY TROPHY on EVERY TRACK IS MINE!!!". i spent some hours there praticing, geting every corner right, every nuance, every curved ball that planet called Mechan could trow at me, to triumph (albeit using modern tools) in the end on the champion dificulty. it's... a frustrating but ultimately unforgetable experience.other thing was the upgrades on 3000 unlocking earlier than i remember... i thought my eyes were playing tricks on me, but later i did discover that yes, there was this boost by the new devs to prioritize more urgent tech you need on earlier races. and on the Champion dificulty, it made everything much better and smoother.another small nitpick is the minimaps on TR3000, their road bifurcations not always are there for you to read out, and it is something they could've touched up. but hey, it wasn't in the original either, so can't blame them for it.\and one last nitpick on Top Racer 2, the last dry tire, it isn't slick, but "bald", if you know what i mean. zero grip. maybe that's again my instincts playing tricks on me... but this one i have more concrete doubts if it isn't a true bug.you see, little gremlins and bugs like this, since no one is perfect. but that didn't subtract one iota from my experience. maybe i have an overpowered PC (I7 8th Gen, 48GB ram, 2070 RTX), but this ran so flawlessly and in 60 FPS on all 3 games, it even bugged my brain on how smooth it was on the first top _childDocuments_.review: If like me you're old enough to remember these 1990s Super NES games (American & European gamers might know them better as Top Gear, Top Gear 2 and Top Gear 3000), these are those games with a few modern day tweaks and a new compilation game added. The games are simple but fun and challenging, in particular the first Top Gear because it added dialogue bubbles where players would randomly taunt others or make relevant comments, and they had good multiplayer too. I in particular liked Top Gear 3000 for it's space theme and extensive car building. These games also inspired the excellent PC/mobile game "Horizon Chase". They also added 4 new cars for the "Crossroads" game, one which looks exactly like it came from "OutRun".Yes they are simple, but also challenging (Top Racer 2 in particular) and they are also fun and now you can play multiplayer with up to 4 people too. If you liked the original games on SNES this is a must-buy, but it's also worth picking up if you want simple yet deep racing with some good multiplayer.

_childDocuments_.review: The thrill of 16-bit racing from the 90s is back! Play the complete Top Racer series with Top Racer, Top Racer 2, Top Racer 3000 and Top Racer Crossroads, a brand new game with new cars and exclusive content made especially for this unmissable edition.

name: Europa
detailed_description: Features An emotive story-driven adventure, with around 3-4 hours of playtime. A breathtaking world of lakes, meadows and mountains to explore, scattered within the remains of a fallen civilisation. Free-flowing movement that empowers you to glide serenely from boost to boost, building power and momentum over time. Uncover secrets, solve puzzles, and navigate hidden dangers in the ruins. An intimate story about growing up and humanity’s relationship with nature. About the game On the moon Europa, a lush terraformed paradise in Jupiter’s shadow, an android named Zee sets out in search of answers. Run, glide and fly across the landscape, solve mysteries in the ruins of a fallen utopia, and discover the story of the last human alive. Europa is a peaceful game of adventure, exploration and meditation. As you travel you’ll gradually upgrade the capabilities of your Zephyr jetpack, boosting yourself further through the air until you can flow freely into the sky. “Come to the Island if you ever get lonely. Come here, and think of me.”

_childDocuments_.review: I should preface this by saying that I would prefer to give a neutral review, neither recommending or not. I really wanted to like this game. There's so much to recommend here, but the end result is not as great as it should be. And I don't mean in a "I got hyped by Peter Molyneux before release and nothing can live up to my expectations" kind of way, I mean that the dev's vision is so simple and clear, but the delivery falls flat. What could go wrong with a stunningly beautiful Ghibli-esque setting with movement and puzzling like Journey, and a lovely story behind it all? Well, a lot I'm afraid.Firstly I never thought that I'd complain about a game that's all about floating for being too floaty, but here we are. I don't mean the levitation though. It's just that there's no sense of weight to your movements. To make matter worse, the controls are clunky too, and the world pushes back on you both literally and figuratively all the time. That's not even mentioning how you're given a vast beautiful landscape to explore, then gated off from almost all of it.As an example, very early on you're walking through a gorgeous canyon when a series of wide flat ledges come into view that set off your spidey senses--there must be something up there! A nice view at least, surely?--but you really shouldn't bother trying to reach it. Not only can I guarantee you there is nothing there, but you might spend a minute devising a way up only to hit an invisible wall in midair, or have the wind at the edge of the map blow you back off the cliff, or worse, blow you into a crevice that you could escape from if only the wind would stop blowing, but it won't stop until it has blown you far enough away from the edge of the map, which it can't because of the crevice, so have fun reloading. It's like this absolutely everywhere--every hill, every mysterious stone machine/creature, every sunken building--you can get stuck, or bounce off of things, or slide uncontrollably past your landing zone, or stop to "climb" a ledge the character should have stepped up without stopping, or stop and not climb at all when you reach a ledge that looks the same size as all those other things you climbed automatically, and you lose your flow. And that's the crux of my complaint--there's no flow to Europa.Again and again the game will stop you to pan the camera around when you should be moving, put a levitation recharge point awkwardly low to the ground or out of your path, or put a "boost pad" in your path when you have just arrived in a new area and want to stop and explore. There's no way to keep your flow going when you just want to zip around. Similarly, the buildings that you can enter mostly look identical to the buildings that you can't, and the same goes for landscape features--a lot of the time a promising hill is just a bump on the map with no reason to go there. All of your instincts from years of playing games will be frustrated.So what about the beautiful vistas? In a game this pretty, can't I accept that sometimes a cliffside ledge is just a ledge, and enjoy the view from up there without any other reward? I would love to, believe me I've spent hours enjoying the view in less pretty games than this, but sadly the camera in Europa doesn't cooperate. It won't spin around to let you, the player, actually see the view. The camera has a strangely large "personal bubble" and won't go near any solid object, so you're stuck looking at Zephyr's disturbing little face as he takes in the view that you are denied.All told, this is a game that should be about the fun and beauty of exploring that actively punishes your efforts to explore, and that's just sad.

_childDocuments_.review: If you value gameplay over aesthetics, you best steer away. But if you enjoy relaxed exploratory gameplay set in stunning environments, head to Europa.First, the soft spots.The controls, as others have noted, are a bit dodgy. The jumping control operates more or less exactly backwards from every game since Mario. Normally when you hit a jump button you instantly jump, with the height of the jump determined by how long you then hold the button down.In Europa you don't jump until you  the jump button, so you can 'charge' a longer jump. If you push and hold the jump button again while in midair you will 'glide'. Over time I coped with this mechanic, but it never felt natural, it doesn't flow well, and occasionally when leaping to a floating crate I would instead bunny-hop into the abyss.Combine this odd jump behavior with the competing floating mechanic of the 'Zephyr' (the cylindrical device you wear on your back) and hilarity ensues. The Zephyr lets you fly and float--but only if it is charged. If you intend to 'jump and glide' but instead 'jump and float' with a depleted Zephyr, well, enjoy your plummet to the ground.In any case, the eccentric controls are acceptable because the game doesn't require tight, precise maneuvering. Even my fumbling fingers got the job done. The margins for error are generous, and failure is rarely punished. Europa's heart is closer to 'walking simulator' than '3D action platformer.' Do I wish the controls were better? Yes. Is it a fatal flaw? No, far from it.Likewise, the story is a mixed bag. Early promise that this might be an interesting tale, with faint allusions to Genesis and Milton and Shelley (probably only in my mind), sadly gives way to banality. And as often happens when developers attempt to have a narrator wax profound, the results are sophomoric. For roughly half of the game, the story falters to ensure the player gets 'the message,' forgetting the cardinal rule of storytelling: 'show, don't tell.'I also found the protagonist almost a non-entity. Except for the wilted little grunt he emits every time he jumps, he doesn't speak or emote or reflect. His character development is a huge missed opportunity: there is none.But enough criticism. While the story is lacking, the journey itself is compelling. The environments are grand and glorious. The music is excellent. The in-game cutscenes are fabulous. As a game of exploration and discovery it delivers the goods. I goggled at the sights and sounds, which changed from scene to scene and stayed fresh and interesting from beginning to end. The world is alive with intriguing creatures, both friendly and hostile. The hostile creatures add some needed conflict to the gameplay without overwhelming it; dodging their ranged attacks is simple fun (there are no melee attacks).The visual navigation cues are well done. I found where I needed to go easily enough without getting lost, and I can get lost in the time it takes me to put on my socks. Puzzles are intuitive and add a pleasant change to the pacing. You won't be stumped.As a game world, Europa is well realized and a delight to explore, making its strengths far outweigh its defects.
_childDocuments_.name: Europa

_childDocuments_.review: This is a lovely experience... I just wish I felt satisfied with it.I feel like this is trying to be like Journey, but missed on what made Journey such a great title and is instead bogged down by controls that want to feel fluid, but instead feel clunky at times.Pros: Gorgeous atmospheric scenery, with moments of flying around and through it.Cons: -Invisible walls/ceilings: I wish these were telegraphed better than just wasting your flight energy running into them, getting blown back, and turned around. I found it tedious to the point that I didn't want to explore too much to avoid running into them and stalling me for a few seconds each time. I probably missed a few collectibles partially due to just going to the obvious telegraphed way forward and trying to just avoid running into the boundaries. -Getting your joy of momentum stolen by unavoidable swarms that only exist to do just that. I feel like these things only exist to clip your wings, rather than lend themselves to any particular challenge or "fun", vs the land mines or turrets  This title sets much of itself up to be this wonderful free-flying exploration adventure, and there's so much that just robs you of that experience.-Controls: I think with a little tweaking, things could "move" better. The platforming feels stiff, and when you're not able to fly, you're forced to slowly move through the terrain. Even the flying could be better, but it's still a smoother experience that makes the walking feel horribly bogged down and torturous by comparison.-Story: It's serviceable, but nothing that grabs me or makes me endeared to the characters. I feel like it's more background to the game than anything.Overall it's not an awful or bad game by any measure, and maybe this is best as an 'entry to gaming' title for kids. I wish I could give it a middle rating, but when I found myself near the end, trudging to get through for the sake of completion and not desiring to replay it any time soon (if ever), I think that was the turning point from a thumbs up to a thumbs down for me.
