_childDocuments_.review: Halls of Torment is a Survivors-style "Bullet Heaven" title, of which there are now many on Steam. It goes for a slower and more methodical pace then most games of this type, especially Vampire Survivors, lacking a dash mechanic, and uses a Diablo 1-esque visual style with prerendered sprites that I quite enjoy. HoT stands out from the pack and I would put it on par with Army of Ruin and 20 Minutes Until Dawn in terms of quality and addictive gameplay. It can be a bit opaque with how some of its mechanics and stats interact however, and available guides reflect this issue.As mentioned, combat in HoT is somewhat less frantic then other Bullet Heavens, though it can be no less tense at times. Enemies move towards you in specific patterns and you can learn to direct your movements to avoid tighter massed groups if you don't have the damage to clear your way through them. You will likely not win your first couple of runs, but this is typical of the genre. There are seven available characters in total so far, each with a unique primary attack and stats and play fairly differently from one another, thanks in part to some level-up upgrades, or "Trait" trees that are character specific, in addition to general upgrades that grant attack damage, move speed, pickup radius and so on. You begin with only the humble shirtless Swordsman, deceptively powerful when compared to a number of the flashier characters you can unlock- especially if you spec into attack range and cone/area. My personal favorite is the Exterminator, a flamethrower-equipped plague doctor with high attack speed that excels in applying on-hit effects.HoT features a sort of hub area where you can choose your character class, purchase upgrades, review your achievements unlocked and yet to unlock and interact with some helpful NPCs, though they must first be rescued from the dungeons. In addition to the requisite roguelike upgrades you earn in-game, HoT has persistent upgrades purchased using gold (Referred to as "Blessings"), but also a few unique mechanics that really add to the long-term gameplay. There are two NPCs in HoT currently, the Wellkeeper and the Cupbearer. Once they're at the camp, the Wellkeeper allows you to set equipment loadouts- a mechanic I've only seen in one other Survivors game so far, Death Must Die, while the Cupbearer provides potions that let you reroll Trait options, "banish" a Trait from that run (as in remove it from the options pool, as in other Survivors games), and, unique to this game, potions that make your next Trait count for double, and one that freezes an option in the pool until you take it later, useful if you get multiple good options in a roll. When in the dungeons, certain boss monsters may drop treasure chests containing new equipment and bottles. Once per run, you can place one of these items in a bucket of a well leading back to the surface. Once this is done, the item can be purchased from the Wellkeeper, permanently adding it to your available equipment options or potion uses. Any gear not yet purchased this way and not sent up in the well will be lost at the end of a run.In addition the game has internal achievement tracking (called "Quests" in-game) and each achievement completed confers a small but additive in-game percent XP bonus, making almost every subsequent run just a little bit easier. Between this bonus and the various upgrade systems, it's easy enough to become quite powerful, though it never reaches the hands-off auto-shooter level of say, playing as Queen Sigma in Vampire Survivors.At my current point in the game I don't have many quests left to go and I've enjoyed nearly every minute of my time with the game. I look forward to future content updates. Any fans of roguelites with persistent progression and of Bullet Heaven games in particular should give Halls of Torment a look.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is really good to cure that vampire survivors itch you might be having. The oldschool diablo-esque visuals look great and the amount of Characters and Itemization currently available should give you more than 50hrs of gameplay for a completely fair price of 5$. Give it a try, you won't regret it!
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game. Even though it doesn't play like Diablo 2, it's art & sound design and power curve will give you some of the same dopamine hits. The various classes provide enough variation in play to keep it interesting. I really appreciate the array of configuration options that let you configure movement and attacking to suit your playstyle.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: It would be a yet another vampire survivors clone, but this one I like. It has nostalgic old school diablo 1-esque graphics.  There are several forms of metaprogression: you can spend money on perks, unlock and purchase equipment, unlock and purchase level up manipulation tools (rerolls, banishes and buffs). There are milestones/feats. which the game calls quests, and they unlock additional content and/or move metaprogression forward. There's a substantial variety between different characters. Bosses telegraph their ranged attacks. There's a substantial variety among mobs and bosses, their movement and attack patterns. Definitely and improvement on VS formula.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: This game was a pleasant surprise. i don't normally venture out of my comfort zone in gaming, but i'm glad i did this time. i highly recommend Halls of Torment. I wish every developer would put this much thought and effort into their endgame. This game will provide you with hundreds of hours of fun, and for the asking price, I feel like its a steal.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: The game play is simple at its face, but underneath it can be pretty complex. Don't let the simple graphics fool you. As you progress you unlock more passives to level up as well as characters (9 so far and the devs plan to release more). Progress unlocks passive bonuses that affects everything. Unlocks future equipment and traits you can see when leveling up. Each character feels unique and entirely different. One negative thing about the game and it is minor, is the lack of explanation with certain interactions and abilities/traits so you have to go to steam community for the answer. Sound is generic, but gets the job done. Or how to unlock certain quests. The game play is what you are here for anyway and wow this developer delivers.This game is only 5 dollars which honestly seems like robbery for what you get. Support an actual indie developer and buy this outstanding game so you can avoid sleep by playing it on the Steam Deck instead of supporting Blizzard that heavily monetizes their games and all you end up with is a middle finger.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: After diving in to the Halls of Torment, I can say it is an absolute blast! The art style is beautiful with its 2.5 D styling.  There are a nice selection of characters, each with their own type of combat (i.e. warlock that uses summons to damage). I enjoy how you upgrade your character by using the well system to retrieve pieces of gear as you progress the stages. The abilities are tons of fun to use, and they each have their place in the progression.  The music is great, I felt myself becoming entranced as I was playing because the musical score fits very well in to the stages.  The only downside, and it is not really that bad at all, is when there is a lot going on in the stage, the audio tends to get choppy due to all the skills being used. Overall, Halls of Torment has managed to suck me in with its art, music and ability combos! I would recommend this game to fellow gamers who enjoy the auto battler style games! Enjoy.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: while some people might get something out of the diablo1 nostalgia and lose their mind over some items, i'd rather focus on more basic gameplay mechanics. which are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. this game is basically just a stat-check timeline. on map x a boss y spawns that has f.e. movement speed z. if you haven't picked movement speed z+1 until then, you die. he'll run you down, you have no chance of survival. same goes for dps-checks, defense checks, etc.memorize the maps, when which bosses spawn and pray to god you have been randomly offered the required stats up until this point or your run ends.i get nostalgia but i had hoped we as a global society had decided to leave those mechanics in the 90s where they belong. pass on this one, there's a plethora of much better vs clones.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: I will not recommend this game until they add a weapon slot. Imagine playing WoW and you can never change or upgrade your weapon but only your armor. Talk about losing the ball.I think the class identity sucks because as a warrior, you'd think your main weapon would be the sword, but it's not. It's just a random lightning strike for example that you end up upgrading instead of your weapon. What is the point of the warrior then? Add weapon slots and make upgrades stem from your class' main type of weapon. The class system is too meaningless and generic.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: What if Vampire Survivors got a Diablo I skin and sound... Which is actually... fantastically executed!Artistically, this game is top tier and it definitely outweighs the lack of originality (95% weapons/abilities/mechanics are Vampire Survivors clones). The graphics, the sound, the character movement, it's all perfect.I loved playing it, but I can't continue until some serious gameplay issues are fixed.- Too many freezes. The last one surprised me after 29 minutes into the session... It was heart breaking.- Single run is too long, i.e. this game will destroy your eyesight. It's requiring you to stare at center point of the screen for 30 minutes straight. Your eyeballs will dry out like prunes and your eye muscles will sore from the constant strain.- The slowness of character and enemy movement in first 10 minutes of each run is unbearable.Content wise, this game is 90% there. Add one more map and bang, you have it all.Quality wise, it really needs more stability. Autosaving would kill the gameplay, so it needs to be stable AF. Vampire Survivors didn't crush on me once in the same play time (~50 h), while HoT crushed on average once an hour, with some better and worse timings.Also, please think about introducing a hurry mode or something similar. Brotato, Vampire Survivors, 20 Minuttes Till Dawn, they all play shorter and for that they're much more enjoyable from well-being perspectiveI feel bad for giving HoT a thumbs-down, as I had a lot of fun with it, BUT the above mentioned issues make me think there's better alternatives to play if I want to have a casual fun..
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game at noon today. Aside from a small break this afternoon, I spent the entire day playing. Seriously addictive gameplay, despite its simplicity, the old school graphics are a throwback to the PC games I played as a kid, and I find myself planning out my gear builds for each class. For the price, you're honestly getting way more than you bargained for. Drop the $5, and play this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: Good game for good price. Its nothing new, its the same formula as Vampire Survivors and the many games like it, but it is done well and it has an old school style too it - the npc talking heads specifically are oozing in old school charm and their voice acting (as well as the narrator's) is excellent. A 2x / 15 minute mode would be great.I don't understand the wellkeeper mechanic. If you find gear in a level, the only way to use that gear again is to send it up and then pay thousands of gold for that item? It makes sense that if you die you lose the items you found that run, but if I survive the full 30 minutes I should be able to keep all of my items. The gear the player finds in a run belongs to them, they shouldn't lose it unless they die. Having to grind for 1-2 hours to get enough gold to purchase ONE of the items you find in a run removes all the enjoyment from finding gear. Getting loot is supposed to be fun but in this game its a nuisance.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: With only a handful of hours logged so far, I obviously can't give a fully balanced review, but so far...It's like the beautiful lovechild of Diablo II and Vampire Survivors that scratches an itch that Diablo III and IV just haven't for me so far.I like the progression system a lot, and the graphics and sound give me that Diablo II nostalgia without being too basic.One minor feature I'm missing is a map on the pause screen, but perhaps I just haven't unlocked that yet.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely phenomenal game iterating meaningfully on this emerging genre of "horde survivor".I really can't praise this game highly enough for really examining and understanding what makes the genre fun and where it can be improved. The systems are all crafted with the utmost care and work flawlessly together. The progression is smooth and fun - every run feels meaningful and different because pushing through focusing on different skills or stats is the way to progress fastest.There are subtle signs that show that immense thought and care have gone into crafting the player experience: there's no intro and minimal help but it's easy to get started and play. It's very easy to understand every decision that you need to make (no need for a wiki here) and it's easy to understand what you need to do next in order to hasten progression or unlock new content. Little details (like how the well only works once per run means that you may agonise over sacrificing your first piece of gear but you know for sure that you can keep your second piece without even thinking about it) may seem like limitations but they smooth out the progression and keep the runs enjoyable, even when they're being done largely for the grind.Even the way that some systems work in the background and add to the experience without even being noticed or understood (e.g., I didn't discover until several runs in that each unlocked achievement boosts XP gain by 0.5% but I was feeling the effects of it through longer, more powerful runs).This game knocks it out of the park as both a rougelite and a horde survivor. I would happily have paid $30 for this game and I really hope the devs get all the success that they deserve.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: I don't get the high reviews. The only difference between the characters is the weapon and stats. Any upgrades are marginal at best. The fighter is god-awful. The characters get the same 3 skills that are random targeting and do nothing to progress you deeper into the level. It's just a walking simulator at best.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: This game is AMAZING, if you like survivor-like games, this is the pinnacle. Run capped out at 30 minutes you you don't have to keep pushing and pushing and get overly long games. A ton of different unlockable characters that you get just from playing and completing more stages. A good amount of unique bosses and mini-bosses on each different stage. Really smart loot system. The list goes on and on of reasons I love this game, just buy it. The fact it's only 5 dollars is insane to me, they could put it out for 20 easily but they just care about developing and making something people love.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: Best of this genre if you enjoy survivors-type games with a slow (grindy) roguelite progression for characters, mechanics, upgrades, items etc.To unlock everything you'll have to use every character & upgrade, but they're all fun to use. Enemies have varied movement & attack patterns which keep stages & waves feeling fresh and different. The overall aesthetic is well crafted, consistent & charming.In short: Highly recommend the game, especially at this cheap price point.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: I purchased this game thinking to myself that, hey, where's the harm in spending 5 € for a little indie game that I'll play for a handful of hours and then forget about? Well, I'm now 200+ hours in, and loving every bit of it!Halls of Torment is crafted with passion, and you can feel how much the development team loves the aesthetic and the overall feeling of 1990s games. The progression is quite challenging at first, as it should be; but once you've unlocked a few upgrades and understood how to build up your character, it gets more and more interesting. Until you reach the late game, where you get the satisfaction of destroying the mobs and bosses that previously made your life hell!It is worth every penny.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: Probably one of the most fun games and time wasters. Up there for me with Left 4 Dead.This game takes the classic DIABLO style experience in a more compact "survival" style double stick RPG mode.Where with your mouse or one stick, you control where your character aims and with the other you move the character around.The game features plenty of enemies that attack or move in waves.The game also a bunch of maps and various classes.Not to mention it also has mini missions inside each main mission.So yes, I recommend it.Check my gameplay video here:
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: This is the best bullet hell game. period. With toggleable controls that allow fully manual and directional combat, or if you're feeling lazy, you can toggle auto attack and aim (like Vampire Survivors). What really sells me is the identity of your character's build for that particular playthrough, with the ability to dynamically chose builds and make certain abilities substantially stronger with the potion system, as well as (retrieving) and choosing gear from the camp before venturing into the depths (with a chance at getting an upgraded piece of loot from each chest while in Agony).Can't recommend this enough for bullet hell genre and devs have been killing it with consistent updates and patches to keep the game balanced and entertaining.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: Good base for a game, took like 40 hours to 100% the game and I enjoyed it a lot. Hope it continues in the same direction that it already has, the only feedback I currently have is the following: The biggest issues with the game right now is the lack of clarity. Visual clarity is bad in the sense of grey slimes on grey level, red enemies on red level. Some abilities obscure your character completely, so even if the bosses having mechanics to dodge is a positive for the game, it feels annoying in a bad way when you cannot see your character for like 5 seconds. Having some of the exp crystals be in a gold color is also confusing not only to me but I have seen many people thinking that it is money you are picking up. Statistical clarity needs to be better too, unlocking a new character and going into a map in crit gear only to learn that that specific character cannot crit. Or having a character have a quest to not regenerate health but that character having 0.5 regen rate and having to go in with all the other characters to learn which ones have and which ones font have regen rates is an annoying decision. If you don't want it to clutter the selection screen so it looks more like D2 at least put up an obelisk or something for the characters and powers so you can see what they do. You'd think the magical orbs spinning around you are doing magical damage but they are physical as they got damage up from damage up (physical) but having to experiment inside of the game with different power ups not knowing what is best for your character without a bunch of trial and error is also annoying obscuring that is just a time waste and doesn't add anything. It would also be nice to have a mode that adds more and harder monsters to the maps, and a mode that shortens the time you have to play.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: The game is pretty fun but unfortunately it just plays so slow. If the moment to moment gameplay mattered it  would be fine but once you get a couple levels the game borderline plays itself for 20-30 mins until it might get hard at the end of the run. Vampire survivors knew this was a problem and instead of insisting on wasting everyones time they added a "turbo mode" that made it so the runs were a lot tighter and more fun.Unfortunately halls of torment wants that slowness as part of it's asthetic and the game quickly wears out it's welcome when you realize that you are doing what is the equivalent of a 30 minute side scroller.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: Dont even remember the price or when i bought it. But been playing it for sometime. So gameplay wise very addicting. Scratches the RPG gearing itch and the gameplay loop is actually challenging but very fun. And the D2 art style is a plus for me. What i want is more depth in the RPG aspects of the game. Maybe more items. Or sets (small sets 2-3 items max) Or talent trees based on the abilities and not the characters. Anyway i totally recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: Not the first in the series to pioneer the genre, however, it was the game that introduced me to the reverse bullet hell genre. Halls of Torment is a masterpiece in my honest opinion. 1. Fantastic OST.2. Incredible progression system.3. Each class feels unique with fun / rewarding level up choices.4. The graphics of the game hit the mark perfectly. 5. No performance issues. Game runs flawlessly on 21:9 with no additional support.6. Maps are gorgeous and well designed. In this day and age where AAA games cost 80+ bucks and release in a buggy - halfbaked mess; you owe yourself to support developers who actually care about their product, listen to player feedback, and release incredible content patches. This game is a 11/10 recommendation from me at any price.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: This game is RAW entertainment! It has the feel of Diablo 1, and Vampire Surviors. The Key difference is the fighting mechanics. In Vampire Survivors, there is skilled play only in the movement. In this game you aim where you want the attacks and move skillfully. It is Challenging and rewarding, with interesting boss mechanics and a great game feel. Trust me spend your lunch money on this and get a great game!
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: I like this game, the artstyle is so amazing, gameplay is fun too. The only thing archaic about it in a bad way is the gender lock... this shouldn't be a thing! I'm missing the ice witch archetype in this game so far, freezing and shattering packs of mobs would feel awesome. But overall it's a good game.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: I love Vampire Survivors, and I love the idea of a different take on the sub-genre that Vampire Survivors created...But the similarities are too great and the differences are too few... This comes off as more of a rip-off. To me at least.So uhh, yeah, if you wanna get into this type of game, Vampire Survivors is further along in development and seemingly essentially the same. And if you wanna play more Vampire Survivors-ish games, this is not different enough to warrant a new game.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: Somehow I forgot to leave my review for this when I covered it last year. Better late than never I suppose!Things have changed a bunch for this game since I played it last year, the biggest is it went full release.I liked the game's more gritty style and less visual noise than the previous games of this genre (like the seizure-inducing visual noise of Vampire Survivors).The characters are mostly fun to play, although some require more work than others (looking at you Sage....) to truly be worth using. The abilities are all decent and the upgrade paths aren't too complicated (you can expect to complete all the trees by about level 90-110 on average).However, I do recommend play this game on low graphical settings and turning down transparency as it becomes really difficult towards the end-game to see through your own attacks (like the meteors). I can't say much for the music as I have it turned on but never seem to hear it so that's a null point for me (I remember it being rather ambient though).There is also the matter of the developer refusing to modernize the screen size (they have stated multiple times in their discord their refusal to fix this): the game starts in such a small window you have to spend a few seconds manually dragging it out to a larger size, assuming you don't just force full screen. Would really be useful if they added a few common screen size options (like 1920x1080) as choices. Probably my only real complaint for this game, but it is truly annoying.At the cost of $4.99 USD you are getting more than a bargain for the game and I've sunk 270+ hours into it by this point and will probably sink a few hundred more into it (they do have 500 achievements to conquer after all). The more recent updates give it even more replayability so I do suggest picking it up.While my original VOD for this is dated now, this is an example of the earlier game and is a good comparison for the game in the current state. So why not check it out :D
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

But every time I play I feel like I know whether I've won the run 10 minutes in, and then there's 20 more minutes to go. I've found myself nodding off at my computer playing this game more than once.

_childDocuments_.review: Latest patch did a number on the game, and thanks to the massive ramping of the difficulty, it turned the game that used to be the reverse bullet hell (like Vampire Survivors) into more of an actual bullet hell game, except with all the problems that come with games such as Vampire Survivors. I don't know what the developers are doing here, but I didn't but the game to suffer, and if I was thinking about buying the game now, I would've refunded it, because I can't beat the game with fully upgraded character (while basically previously doing so with my eyes closed), and I can't imagine how much more painful it has to be to start from nothing now.I understand that the previous iteration of the game was too easy, but this is an extreme change. You can't make a change where enemies deal like 3 times more damage and think people will be OK with that.

You'll spend a lot of time trying out different builds and trying to get all the achievements (some of which open up new skills for the different classes). This is not.Your one game will take about 40 mins (30 mins + around 10 while you are trait-choosing or fighting end boss)Satisfaction? Just pure fun. Graphic style is in late 90's, its like back in D1 days .... nostalgia hits hard man.100% must buy. Dev is not greedy, value that you get for few bucks is even more than you get by buying most of AAA games. The only thing I am missing in this masterpiece is crafting. _childDocuments_.review: Honestly, I already got my money's worth. If you're reading this, you can see I've played around 8 hours of this game. Those 8 hours I've played feel like 3 or 4, in other words: the game's good. This game feels like vampire survivors and if you enjoyed that you'll enjoy this too. There are different characters with different weapons and upgrades, doing different achievements and progressing in the game gives you access to new items and upgrades across any character, as you naturally progress through just playing for fun you'll unlock a lot of these at a steady and good pace. According to achievements i'm around 20% of the way to full completion, again, in 8 hours, which considering the game only cost me around £3 I think it's safe to say I'll be recommending the game even more than I am now by the time I'm done. What's especially nice about me recommending this game is that I started playing once 1.0 was released and so none of my thoughts or opinions should be any different to by the time you get to playing it yourself. I'd honestly recommend skipping out on a coffee or something and buying this instead, so worth it!

_childDocuments_.review: Great aesthetic and builds at first, but after a certain playtime every run feels incredibly identical to the last. This suffers the same plague of other games in the genre where new content is constantly added, making the pool wider and wider and the content gets increasingly shallower. The content problem aside one other main issue is that if you want to experience everything a class has to offer you have to pull up the wiki and really plan out your build. If you just intuitively pick out upgrades that sound good to you, you unintentionally lock away some game changing synergies, just by how the draw pool works. This is a great example of where hiding away information from the user actually makes for a worse experience, because choosing the wrong card is a permanently destructive action on the rest of the run. There was a sweet spot where this game was great and the aesthetic alone was enough of a selling point, but it's kinda just too far past the point where I can recommend it anymore.

_childDocuments_.review: Among the Children of Vampire Survivors, Halls of Torment certainly has a good claim to the throne. A solid visual and auditory presentation inspired by diablo 2 (and actually manages to imitate the look! many games that do this fall short in my mind), with mechanics of a similar inspiration make for a meaningful difference to Vampire Survivors, something that in my mind automatically beats out many of the other contenders.Character differentiation is quite solid as well, with characters having a base attack that forms the basis of their class. The swordsman swings a sword in a forward cone, the archer shoots arrows, etc. Later classes have more nuance to their abilities, such as the exterminator doing fire damage and the priest (I think?) having a base attack that does more damage on fewer enemies, with its unusually high damage being split between all of the enemies being hit, creating neat little mechanical differences from other classes, solving what is probably one of my biggest problems with vampire survivors and vampire survivors likes, character not being particularly differentiated from one another. Additionally, upgrades are not simply more weapons, but statistic upgrades that boost your base attack. Building on the class difference discussion, classes have different strengths of these base upgrades; the shieldmaiden gets (strong) defensive upgrades, making them slightly better then other classes, and pushing you towards certain build paths for certain characters. As you level, more tiers of these upgrades unlock, as well as other upgrades themselves. An upgrade that applies fragile to enemies that are hit by your basic attack unlocks around level 25, for instance, something that naturally has more benefit on characters with larger hit areas. All in all the character differentiation is fantastic, and I wish more survivors-likes took a hint on it.But it is a survivors-like and there are still weapons, called abilities. You come across scrolls that unlock them, varying from thrown sawblades to a wide flame shot. They're quite powerful, and when obtained, unlock their own upgrade trees, tending to be more efficient per level then your basic upgrades. They always felt a smidge bland, but they are statistically significant and make for yet another meaningful choice while working through a stage. Taking a fire weapon while using the exterminator whose basic weapon benefits from fire affinity upgrades, for instance, makes for some satisfying synergy. Other such synergies are not quite as obvious, but they do exist, and do strongly effect how you're going to carry out a run.Between all these things, I'd argue the game has already more then proved itself, but there is additionally an equipment system, ala D2. You unlock various armor pieces, ranging from simple multipliers on defensive stats, to pairs of shoes that lay fire when you walk, rings that give you summons, so on and so forth. There's truly an absurd amount of items in the game and they only add more variables for you to play with.FInally, there's potions, which are simple stat pick modifiers. The standard skip/banish options are here, as well as others, including a potion that doubles the effect of an upgrade taken, one that locks an upgrade in place until you take it, and so on. Not an exceptionally exciting part of the game, but yet another well made one.Serving as the vector for all this is the unlock system which is quite standard. You'll unlock a lot of the content just by playing the game without thinking about it, but there are yet more unlocks for those interested in chasing high damage values, or kill counts, or whatever.Among all this I have some minor complaints. There is your standard "pay gold to get stat upgrades" system, and in my mind it really crowds out the equipment system for something that is quite bland and not particularly interesting. I'm often torn between spending my gold on permenant upgrades, or spending my gold on equipment unlocks. You can find the equipment during runs (this is how you unlock them for purchase, in fact) but you'll often get something that either isn't particularly relevant, or maybe even worse, is quite boring. The gold = stats system always sort've stuck out like a sore thumb in vampire survivors and frankly the sooner it gets lopped off the genre the better, I say. I'll also make the fairly petty complaint that the first boss in the game being what is probably the hardest one is a bit of an oddity. A bit more gentle of a curve couldn't hurt, though it's not like you have to beat the guy to unlock more stages, so I suppose it's fine.All in all a Fantastic survivors-like, and certainly worth a look if you're still dipping your toes into the genre.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

Well, after playing the demo for a few hours I felt like stealing from de developers and purchased the full version (to show up my support). What a game should be about, entertaining and fun, and no micro transactions.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: Basic summery:The art style (personal preference)Quests  Interesting and diverse levelsElaboration:The art style; throw back to classic 90’s RPG’s. I understand this is a personal preference in art style that doesn't work for every game, but with this game. It works, and well. I love it, its nostalgic, with out being old and dated.  Taking modern concepts like slimes and making them 90s style! Quests: says enough really, do quests get gold and rewards, fun, traditional, and adds some extra flavour to the game. Levels; so far I have only unlocked 2 locations, but both are distinctly different. Over all, I love the game, it feels like a nice mix of nostalgia and modern game concepts. 20’s meets the 90’s!!
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: I've only played this a few hours today but I can already see that it deserves a positive review. I played Vampire Survivors and really enjoyed it and I like this better. It's more like a Rogue Diablo to me.Positives:1) It's super cheap, especially on sale. (cheapest game that I can remember buying even)2) It's a great break from more serious game.3) Graphics, skills, gear seems well thought out and it isn't over done. Gear seems to be very rare so has to be chosen carefully.Negatives - none that I've seen for early access and review!Obviously I don't know how long the game is, how many characters there are (I have 2 to choose from so far), how many different mobs, etc. etc. I paid $4 for this today and I've enjoyed it for 3 hours so far +/- and I know that I'll play it at least 10 or so more minimum to finish some unlocks that I already started. To me that's a great deal. It's not my best game or my favorite but it's fun and a deal so I recommend it based on that. I've bought a ton of games in the $15-$60 range that I can't stand and will never play again so it's a nice change to find an inexpensive one that's enjoyable.Cheers.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: Awesome game. Absolutely chill, no commitment needed. Either you play 20-30 min or few hours. 500 quests/achievements at the moment giving a purpose to play. 200 hours of fun for less than 4 eur is insane. I play it together with Vampire Survivors. It's not one or the other, it's both. Same concept, 2 awesome different approaches. Active development, haven't met any bugs stopping me to achieve 100% completion.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: Truly one of the best games in this genre, but it still has a ton of room to grow.As the game develops, I would love to see:- an endless mode- higher difficulties than agony- more iconic/unique/memorable bosses- better gold scaling- more ability diversity and upgrades- new enemy types- additional maps- new stage objectives unique to each map (like the blood trail)- hidden goodies/easter eggs- an expanded hub- character trees (or some kind of character expansions)- cosmetics- a co-op mode of some kind- true end game content- more graphical settings and adjustments to make visibility better (some maps are impossible to see on after a while)As for what's already there, but could be better:- Some upgrades are confusing. Clarifying or simplifying their text and making wording more consistent would go a long way.   > ex. Why do some say "+10% Crit Chance" while others say "+0.10 base Crit" when it's the same buff? What does "At 200x on." even mean? Etc.- Better balance for abilities. Some of them are total doodoo and never worth picking.- More balanced characters. Some are terrible, while others always over perform.- Merchants are in a strange place (feature wise). Buying retrieved items from them feels awkward. Not sure how to improve this experience, but we saved their lives and this is how they repay us?? Feels forced and weird and retrieved items cost way too much.I'm sure some of this will be addressed as time goes on, but these are my thoughts on some additions/changes that could make the game God tier as of right now. I'm still giving it a HUGE thumbs up because it's already really, really good and if none of these things ever get added or fixed, it would still be a solid purchase. I'll continue to keep playing though and keeping my eye out for new patches and content. Very impressed so far!
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: This would be more a middle with a slight leaning to no.Good time killer but lost interest trying to 100% everything. Not enough variation. The abilities you get on the map aren't really all that interesting. Its a nice nod to Diablo though.Id say get it for a flight or something but its really kind of a sideways thumbs up.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: A rather interesting, but not unique game in the overly popular nowadays genre of "Zoomer Survivors" - a genre invented, or some say discovered, by a game called Vampire Survivors, which was created by a casino game developer, who had a deliciously devilish idea to apply all his vile human psychology knowledge and gambler observation experience to design a game aimed at frying your dopamine receptors. Some say Vampire Survivors did not invent a genre, but lets face it, who ever cared about mobile games? Halls of Torment does not do much to deviate from the basis of the genre gameplay-wise. You kill, collect exp, kill, level up, kill, customize your build, kill, complete side tasks like defending an area or collecting specific things scattered around infinite and barren map, kill, and then kill the final boss of the stage to receive rewards in form of currency or items that make future runs easier and kill potential higher. All is well and good, you wont find anything as entertaining in a real world. Meta progression includes unlocking new heroes, spells/abilities and various specialized items that can make or break your desired build. A wide possibility of choice and theory-crafting that can make your journey to the highest damage number more engaging. Unlockable heroes have drastically different gameplay, at least until the very end game, which is deservedly called "Agony Mode" - a hardcore difficulty where even reaching the baseline requires specific ability or item builds. It completely feeds into the expectations of a longtime digital entertainment enjoyer, with meta progression buffing your stats and level up choices that *work* with your desired build engineered to engage your reward system in an extremely exhilarating, and yet vicious, abnormal way. There are many industries that only exist because of how well human psyche can be taken advantage of by these abnormal stimuli - casino and gambling, narcotics manufacturing, advertising and marketing, and we simply don't know any better. Higher number - more dopamine, higher survival record - more satisfaction, more and more and more as we move deeper and deeper into hyper engaging digital spaces graciously (or mercilessly) provided by videogame industry.   The game's graphics is one of its strongest points. It has a pleasant color palette and a pixelated, clay model look that really resembles old isometric RPG games (mostly the diablo series) and alludes to nostalgia, making us remember the good times of yore, when games were better, online gaming felt engaging and had actual, real socializing, grass was greener, and sun's shine was more golden, felt the brightest. Halls of Torment feels like a Gem, comparing to many videogames on the market, especially if you have been an avid player for a decade at least. It feels enjoyable to unlock achievements, level up during stages, spend meta currency on increasing your base stats and feel skeletons pop up from that crit chain lighting.This game still has an appeal, even though most games getting released nowadays simply aren't enjoyable. Is it the simply state of the industry? Is it the fault of the new generation? Is it the power hungry executives? Or did we, perhaps, change? Habituated, empty, fried from incessant stimulation? Having your videogame *hits* on schedule and having those *hits* provide less and less relief than they used to? Resorting to playing videogames that try their best to copy practices literally used by casinos to strip people of their money? Perhaps the solution is to somehow break this despair spiral and stop using videogames as a space  that you can absent-mindedly retreat to, before its too late and you sink deeper and deeper into the halls of torment, that, to think of it, is of your own making.Essentially, now that the game has fully released and has a wide variety of content and even more achievements to grind for, i highly recommend it to everyone and consider it the high point of the genre. It has pleasant graphics, good build variety and simply *clicks*. Hopefully the developers will continue expanding the game, as it happened with Vampire Survivors.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: Is the game good? Yeah, it's pretty fun. Does it measure up to other games in the genre? Not really. Content is on the short side, and the mechanics are a bit underbaked. At this point in development, while I would not recommend the game to others, it's worth keeping an eye on.There is no "neutral" option on steam, so I gotta go with down fingahs.

_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: I love the overall style of this game but currently I can't really recommend it. But in the end the few hours ive spent so far have just felt excruciatingly slow, and it seems as though there's still a huge grind ahead of me before it starts getting more interesting. _childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: I am a fan of the genre but with every genre that becomes the new in thing, on top of how good it is you have to ask what does it bring to the table. Vampire survivors was the breakout game, and it's still worth it's price and getting better. 20 minutes to dawn let you take control of the aim of one weapon and still eventually have a massive slaying arsenal working in auto. I haven't gotten as deep in this one as I have those, but I was killing the whole screen in no time. I am sure massive power ups are available deeper in, but if not, the ones they have are pretty awesome because you can put them to good use, but they are not as mindless and wide ranging. Which you have to do, because out of the survival style bullet hells I have played, this one has the most gonna get you AI. Like there are formations more than just enclosing swarms and this is one of the few times that I have seen true value in movement speed upgrades. Bosses hide just out of range behind minions on some levels so you can't just kite them into oblivion. But for everything I have seen, the game is fair. Yes it wants you to fail, but it offers you chances to bring up items to unlock and to improve your stats. Also there is always a way through the horde if you are looking closely. The addition of story goals makes it different too because it feels like working toward something. So if you like VS, 20 minutes to dawn, Boneraiser Minions, or Brotato but you also like old school Diablo, there is something here for you.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty good survivors game.To make yourself stronger permanently you can bring items from missions, invest gold in blessings and craft potions by collecting ingredients.You can complete ~300 goals to get new unlocks and gold rewards. There are a lot of characters and several maps with unique enemies to play.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: I can easily recommend this game as one of the better entries in the current canon of survivor/bullet-heaven games. So far it's one of my favorites next to (the excellent) Nomad Survivors, Soulstone Survivors and of course the big bat in the belfry, Vampire Survivors.Halls of Torment separates itself from the pack by cribbing it's aesthetic from the ARPG  genre, and more specifically (and obviously) from the first two Diablo games. The devs here have nailed that aesthetic, btw, and it plays a large part in making HoT a blast to play. Other factors include tight gameplay, player-controlled directional aim (with the option to set things to auto if the player likes), a fun roster of characters to unlock and choose from, loot and custom gear loadouts, and a whole bevy of achievements which are also tied to in-game unlocks. The game is still in Early Access but is receiving regular updates and I'm sure will have a lot more content to keep players busy by the time it's in finished, and it already has a good amount to do in it's current state.So yeah, hats off to this game and the devs. Lots of fun and an extremely great value at just five dollars.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best bullet-hell roguelikes out there! Cool Diablo-like visuals, the sounds when you hit an enemy are really satisfying, characters have a quite unique playstyle, many options to toggle (auto aim on/off, auto shoot on/off, etc.), and there is loot!Things that could be improved upon: Some spells are really boring or weak and the music's hit and miss.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: deceptively fun20 hours in, and I've had a blast. I bought the game because it was on sale, and decided to try it out as my first real introduction to this style of game, and because I was looking for a retreat from the slog I had been having in Diablo 4. In the last 20 hours of gameplay I have had more fun than my last 20 hours in Diablo 4.The core gameplay loop is very satisfying, you feel rewarded for building your character well and positioning yourself well. There is a great aesthetic style to the game, and the sound design allows for having fun without being annoyed by the constant and consistent effects. Do no hesitate to purchase this title.

_childDocuments_.review: The graphics reminiscent of Diablo 1 with the RPG mechanics adapted for this genre was brilliant, and this time we didn't die at the end of the game and faced bosses and a lot of quests to conquer, but they could change the animation of the sorcerer's standard attack to remember that he is in fact a wizard

_childDocuments_.review: Simply one of the best games I have played for a long time. the simplicity of graphics really appeals to me since you dont have to buy a monster gaming rig to play it, and it still looks amazingly (retro) and really nails that feel so many games has lost in the race for hyper stylistic graphics. The music is wonderfully dark and spreads that Old school feel of larger than life adventure. The gameplay is the best aspect, from the easy going controls, to the no learning curve, to end-game nerding it up. it can be played by everyone, old young, ablebodied or not. this game is through and through a win-win. 5stars and a Michelin recommendation.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: bought this after a dissappoiment of recent ARPG with sorry excuse of a dungeon & boring 10-20 hours story content before the real game is the endgame begin, survivor like on the other hand is fast since enemies keep coming after you & bad build instantly punished by dead, had a lot of fun with this one
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT: After last two patches I change my review to positive! Game is getting better and now it's much more balanced. I can't wait for more!Devs really listened to the feedback and delivered, fixing many things and balancing game out the way that it's more friendly for everyone, I am very positive to see what comes next! :] ...initial negative review: I can't recommend the game in the current state, for a current price, especially after last patch (I play BETA, but I think that both converged with this patch).This game costs ~75% of what I just paid for Vampire Survivors with both DLCs, but the difference in the amount of content and possible builds is ENORMOUS.I get that it's Early Access, but after so much of feedback from the players, the last live patch feels like DEVs are kinda detached or not sure what they're doing. New version feels like a literal downgrade for the game, killing much of fun while introducing many new bugs (enemies spawning on top of you, bullets freezing and hanging in the air, game doesn't even start for multiple people etc.)But most importantly, with new unbalancing patch and unnecessary nerfs, there is even less incentive to try out different builds, which for the game with such low amount of content is just straight bad :-(Last forum response from DEVs to some complains that I saw was suggesting that someone in their discord got almost lvl 130 blah, blah, blah, with some broken OP build to munchkin the game, even though majority of people that just want to enjoy it can't even reach lvl 100. Is the game kept being crafted for that 1%-5% of people that are out there for only hardcore experience? Because even if it's playable for me, it starts pushing away new players, especially with unreasonable bump in difficulty from the last patch.I would advice to observe the game, hopefully things will get better and I will be able to change this review into a positive one! <3
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: An incredible amount of fun. The very beginning can be considered hard, but as you progress, you'll unlock distinguishable characters, equipment, abilities and upgrades, traits, potions, blessings, a lot of quests, difficulty 'Agony' (which comes with extra bosses and better item versions) and, by the time i'm writing this, over 250 achievements and 4 stages.The community is mostly positive and helpful and developers seem to care about their product.I'm scoring this:- great replayability- very large variety of builds- healthy amount of characters- mixing classes by using class marks- option to reset progress- price- item design- visuals, sounds and music are overall good, but not very coherent- runs last 30-35 minutes depending on your playstyle (some like 'em shorter, some longer)- challenging start, easy endgame- explanation of stats can sometimes be confusing- balancing is off in some cases- missing gold sinks for endgame
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: Played the prelude for hours and hours and loved it!  Very happy to see the changes and additions with the early access launch.  The old-school diablo-esque look and theme just hits like a home-run in this genre.  Looking forward to more content in the future updates but there is more than enough game to keep you coming back and slaying skeletons and demons for hours on end, Keep up the great work devs!
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: It's one of those games that's really far up its own ass about not explaining any mechanics to you in a game where there's a lot that's very ambiguous so you can't figure it out yourself (stats damage types, defense vs. block, etc.). The worst sin of all is the final boss of the first hall. It has an attack that puts some sort of mark of death on you that's very hard to avoid, and when the counter hits 0 you die. There is absolutely no hint as to how to avoid this or if you can get rid of the mark some how. You need the revive blessing...that you get from defeating the boss.That's not good game design, that's completely disrespecting your users and wasting their time.The difficulty feels completely artificial: instead of having interesting enemies that requires different footwork or abilities to tackle effectively, the game floods your screen with as many enemies as possible to the point where it's hard to tell where exactly you are, where your cursor, and to tell your abilities from enemies. It gets very muddled. This ruins the fights with minibosses because instead of having memorable  fight with them you're too busy focusing on the 100s of mobs flooding the screen. This isn't a skill issue, I've gotten to the final boss many times. The game is also a massive grind. In order to have viable builds you're going to have to grind for gold to unlock good gear and base stats. That's fine, but this level of grind is there to hide the fact that the game has very little in the way of content so far.A game like this has to ride a fine line between rewarding and frustrating, and currently it's more frustrating than it is fun with the way it's balanced.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: I read a review that said this game was more fun than Diablo 4. Kinda have to agree. It's also more fun and more nuanced than Vampire Survivors, which is to be expected, I suppose. TBF, I haven't played Vampire Survivors in a while so take that as you will. I CAN say that, for me at least, this game is more difficult. I'm 8 hours in and only just now made it through 30 minutes.Anyway, it's got that dopamine flow for sure. I'm having fun. Absolutely worth the price of admission and then some. Enjoy.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: A very fun and addictive addition to the Vampire Surviors-like genre. The combination of old school Diablo aesthetics and the horde destroying gameplay of bullet heavens is a very effective match and results in something that feels both nostalgic and new at the same time. Halls of Torment switches things up with the addition of gear, a pretty sophisticated system for leveling up that has many possibilities for synergies, and the ability to set your character up with a load out before each run. This extra layer of complexity is certainly welcome and encourages a lot of replayability as you test and run different builds for characters. While I have only scratched the surface, I am already hooked and looking forward to playing more. Highly recommended, especially for fans of the genre.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: Not nearly as good as Soulstone or Vampire Survivors.Characters are uninteresting, abilities incredibly uninspired, bland and probably the worst I have ever seen in a survivor game. The soundtrack is complete ♥♥♥♥ as well as the audio feedback. Feels like toothpicks falling the whole time. I liked the bosses but I can't see how this is so well received, just having items doesn't make it any good.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: This is the first "survivors-type" game that truly stands alongside Vampire Survivors due to map goals, clearly defined power upgrades and evolutions that don't require looking it up on Google, quest goals, gear drops, end-timer bosses, and Diablo II aesthetics. _childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: Its a good game starts off hard as hell but as with all rog.... nah just kidding even when u have unlocked a lot of stuff it will still kick your ass if you are not careful its why i recommend it, its nice to have a rogue like/garlic like with a degree of difficulty its kinda refreshing unlock the well that's my advice
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: This game is great. however there is some balancing problems. The viaduct is very unbalanced compared to haunted caverns and even frozen depths (the level after viaduct) but the enemies in viaduct are WAY too beefy, move way too fast, and hit fairly hard. and especially the imps or flying ones. they are ALWAYS right next to me even with a 7ms movement speed. that being said, this game is amazing regardless.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: The last update kills the game for me. Everything about the latest patch is mediocre, the new characters and the new skills are just underwhelming even the new map is not very fun to play. And instead of nerfing, better buffing those underused equipment or skills. This is the example that the devs simply just do not play their game. You can't expect us to pick those underused items and skills when the current state of those is simply trash tier. Only the agony system to make the game harder is the right direction.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: It was far too similar to Vampire Survivor. I was looking for something that would take it and make it better. Their "Quest" system isn't anything you have to think about it will just happen naturally as you play. The permanent lvl ups offered for coins after a run make it so the the run is tough when you first start playing but will make it very easy after you grind enough. Which mean the challenge you first faced was artificially placed (nothing to do with skill or knowledge). You're limited to 1 character, but quickly get two and are stuck with that for a while. They both do almost the same thing (ranged AOE) even though one is supposed to be melee. Yes the graphics are "better" but instead of cartoonish they are 90s or early 2000s. Which some people really like but if you're going to upgrade graphics then get them up to this decade. I didn't get to their top tier boss fights so there might be something different there. It just seemed too much of a clone that the original did better or at least not different enough to justify any more money. Play time is short, didn't want to go over return policy. So get it on sell try it out (wish there was a demo) and decide before the return limit hits for yourself.    If you've never played Vampire Survivor then perhaps try this one first.Edit: They are heading in the right direction though, so will give them another chance when it's fully developed.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: Tbh I tried to like this game. I think it has potential to be very fun, but as it stands, things are way unbalanced for new saves. Enemies have ridiculous movement patterns and lots of them just move twice as fast as you do, a lot of the options for level-ups are mediocre, and the weapons are all very underwhelming. If the game were to make the main weapons at least a little more interesting/less clunky then I'd probably be willing to change my review. However I also have had two major crashes to desktop 20min into a run and I can't say I will be playing anymore after that.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: There is still a lot to be added to this game for it to be as fleshed out as vampire survivor, but the aesthetic is awesome and the gameplay is good. The characters all feel unique. There are some balancing issues and the more you play, the more you learn which skills are pretty much a must take every time. I am going to take a break on this one until it gets some new content. But for 5 bucks this is an EASY recommend!
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: First few hours are a lot of fun. Once you get some items and upgrades, the game becomes a snoozefest even in Agony mode / hard difficulty.Then you get to the so-called "endgame", where they expect you to grind those hideously boring easy levels to get items to upgrade your dudes for the "final" stage, which is impossibly hard for the same characters you just wiped the "main game" hard mode with.Good luck if you like grinding hours of 20-minute runs while half asleep, just to be able to get a +5% damage boost for your character for the final level, then do it again and again, but I'll pass.
_childDocuments_.name: Halls of Torment

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: I play this game on Steam Deck to fall asleep and I'm not even joking.It's incredibly slow paced and it does not captivate due to it's very shallow difficulty.----The game loop in itself is nice and 'akin' to Vampire Survivors. Lots of enemies to slay that walk towards you and pose a threat or are just meat. Gold drops which you collect. There's some 'puzzles' scattered in the maps that you may be able to solve if you can bother.What I like what this game does is the challenges that reveal over time like a skill tree - but this should be displayed more prominently when entering a dungeon so you know what task is at hand.My biggest con with this game, and that's also the reason why I play it to fall asleep, is that it's slow. It's so slow. It doesn't engage you as you walk around the map hearing the gold jingle and kill sounds, the only thing that makes my sleepy eyes open is when I hear myself getting hit. That's also when I look at the timer "6 minutes left..." so I doze off halfway while walking in a circle and wait for the boss to appear so I can put the Steam Deck away and go sleep.There's no way (that I know of, besides Cheat Engine on PC) to speed up the game. The only enemies that pose a threat are those that shoot or leave puddles on the floor (if you're half or completely asleep).I would much rather have this game be significantly harder. Brutally hard so that it's hardly possible to reach the end of the timer for the boss to appear, so that it captivates and you need to stay on edge to not make the wrong call. I dunno. I just personally find this the most boring game I've played and I've played quite a few. But it's a good sleep aid at least

_childDocuments_.review: I have been playing this genre of 2D horde survival shooters most of my life, with games like Crimsonland and Alien Shooter. I have experimented with roguelike hybrids like Swarm Grinder and Brotato but I never really found one I could fall in love with until I played Halls of Torment. The Diablo or Age of Empires-esque pixelated graphics are phenomenal, and the gameplay is incredibly intense and chaotic. Choose your hero (you unlock more by playing), survive the horde, defeat minibosses, and upgrade your character by collected xp dropped by enemies. My favorite thing about the game is the fact that there is a time limit. Once 30 minutes have elapsed, the horde clears and a final boss fight begins. This gives you a clear goal to work towards rather than just endlessly slaughtering hordes until you die. Also, this is a very good game for stat ♥♥♥♥♥♥ like myself. Lots of numbers and percentages to look at. Furthermore, there are 254 achievements and I got 28 of them in 1.4 hours play. Very good choice for anyone that enjoys Risk of Rain or any of the other games I mentioned in this review. Absolutely incredible bargain at $4.99 (I got it on sale for $3.99), I would gladly pay $20 for this.

_childDocuments_.review: Halls of Torment, while still in early access currently, modifies and heavily improves upon the survivor formula, to the point where it feels like it’s the next evolution of the genre as a whole. While it may be lacking in amount of content due to its early access status, the already existing content has such a level of depth that other survivor-likes don't really have.The first and most prevalent change is wholly unique survivors, called heroes. Unlike other survivor-likes with each new character only having stat changes and a different starting weapon, Halls of Torment’s heroes have their own personal weapon that only they can use, which fundamentally makes each hero play very differently from one another. In addition to this, the trait system employed by the game gives each hero different paths to take and ways to experience runs. All heroes have universal traits they can upgrade upon level up (example: speed or health), but some heroes have different values for the same traits (a character focused on speed will have an innate upgrade to all speed traits and downgrade to health traits.) Not only that, but heroes themselves also have personalized traits, such as a hero having the trait choice to get their weapon reach farther or have more damage in a smaller area. Keep in mind that this is only a very bare bones explanation, as I think experiencing all the options yourself for the first time is a true joy to figure out.Now onto the actual damage dealing options one has. As far as weapons go, there are none. You have your hero’s unique weapon to upgrade and that’s it. So unlike other similar games, you can’t stack weapons upon weapons or create combinations. Halls of Torment instead has Abilities you can obtain from golden scrolls. There are always a few scrolls scattered around the map at the start of a run and sometimes they’ll drop from elite enemies. All heroes have the same pool of abilities that can be chosen from, meaning you can experiment in various ways. Depending on the synergy of your main weapon or desired play style, though, you’ll probably want certain abilities over others.There are a few other mechanics unique to Halls of Torment, however I think I’ll let you discover those on your own. Halls of Torment is an ever growing game that’s just waiting to take survivor-likes by storm. I’ve already dumped a number of hours into this game and I intend to keep up with it as we get more content. I’m very much looking forward to the game finally emerging from its early access title, good luck and have fun surviving the Halls.

_childDocuments_.review: Update: the new update mostly fixes the compendium and understandably nerfs the broken amulet into oblivion. the strong recommend is even stronger now.Update after 100%: Game was enjoyable all the way through. The achievements were mostly interesting. You can cheese a good number of them, but the character-specific ones are often tricky to figure out (looking at you, "reach level 150"). There's clearly some things that could still use work. Clicking 100+ times on the compendium to allocate points is tedious. There's an amulet that straight-up breaks the game and is a free win unless you throw a billion artifacts on. But overall, I had a lot of fun with it. It captures the essence of what makes ARPGs fun and packages it in a tidy and much shorter format. Definitely recommend at full price.Just finished the game in a night after putting a good amount of time into the early access build. I'm happy to report that v1.0 fixes nearly every issue I had with the game. The artifacts make the endgame much more interesting and include some QoL ones like a quicker 20 minute mode. The well system still doesn't really make sense to me--you should just be able to bring new items back through the portal with you--but adding a way to bring back multiple items in one run alleviates most of the annoyance.This has definitely secured its place as my favorite survivor game, and I'm eager to play around with the rest of the artifacts and try to break things.

_childDocuments_.review: A perfectly competent and enjoyable "Vampire Survivors"-like game that doesn't really do anything unique or surprising enough to set it apart from many other games in the genre, but is still quite fun to play and recreates the visceral thrill that is so important to these games.There are a handful of playable archetypes which can appeal to particular personal playstyles (I'm a fan of the flamethrower guy and the electricity lady), but in the late game when you're fully powered-up and have unlocked plenty of equippable items that can boost stats or add abilities, I found myself playing nearly all types the same way. I suppose repetitiveness is a given in such games, but I find it worth mentioning.The achievements were mostly fun to get, although I'm never a fan of "kill X amount of Y enemies" achievements that require me to grind the same level until I reach my quota. I did appreciate that the achievements have in-game purposes too, as each one either grants you money or unlocks a character or upgradeable stat or item or secondary attack.While I'm sure opinions vary on this, I found Halls of Torment to be the ugliest of all the games I've played in this genre. There is very little color, and each level uses drab palettes and boring environments. The characters and enemies look generic and while I get that the intention was to create a Diablo-esque aesthetic, I would have liked a little more visual pizazz.Still, I liked the basic mechanics enough to stick with it for the achievements, and I'll likely come back for more once more content gets added.

_childDocuments_.review: This game's name is not pronounced "Halls of Torment."  You have to use a gravelly voice like you're choking on something "Khhhhkhkhkalls of Tkkkhhhorment".  At least that's how I try to pronounce it.This is juicy.  I enjoy it most when I'm exercising and using a controller, as I completely forget about time and how long I've been working out!There are several "bullet hell" offerings out there ranging from "can't stop playing" to "mildly interesting".  I'd put this one deeply in the earlier category.  For example, compared to Vampire Survivors, this feels much more intense even while I'm still in the early game (and I love Vampire Survivors too).What makes it work?  I think the combination of barely being able to stay alive - the enemies move just fast enough and I have enough difficulty getting kills at a certain point - combined with better than awful graphics, which lends to some immersion, makes this game sticky.It doesn't have any voice acting, nor a story.  But what it does have it makes the most of, which is a good progression and a feeling of dancing my way around the floor trying to stay alive while dealing with all the baddies swarming in to kill me.The game works both with keyboard/mouse or with a controller - wonderful!And the game is dirt cheap.  I bought it at a 20% discount, but it was already under $4 so who cares?  It's already more than made up for the price.

_childDocuments_.review: I dunno, I don't get it. It doesn't scratch that V.Surv. itch at all. I don't see why it has such glowing reviews. I mean, it isn't bad really, it's just... so basic. I feel like I could have coded this on my C64 back in the 1980s. 96% positive atm, I dunno man.There are no real evolutions that I can find so, there are no choices that matter in that regard which removes that entire aspect of the strategy. There are very limited 'secondary' weapons and they don't really synergize in any meaningful way so, less strategy again. It's really just your primary weapon and the few rare second ones. The upgrades are ambiguous, 'Force' actually has the description that it "usually upgrades duration, pushback etc." Usually?? I mean, why have a description that ambiguous? What about when it's doing what it doesn't 'usually' do? Can it do something unusual? Either it does 'a' or 'b' or it does not. Or is it random? I dunno. Also, you cannot skip upgrades so, if you get bad RNG, too bad, your whole run is blown. There is gear in the game so, that's a nice different twist, great idea, but, the gear is just boring base stat upgrades mostly. The graphics I am unclear about as well. It's pixel art but, pixel art doesn't have to look grainy. You can change a setting so the UI looks crisp... how about the game looking a bit more crisp and defined? Pixels can have sharp edges that are defined, the UI has it... why does the floor in the game look so blurry?Look, maybe it's me. Nothing against the dev, I do wish them well and I'm glad this game is working out for them. I had no intentions of returning this, even if I didn't like it, I do like to support small dev projects and I'm not sorry I did. But, I just don't find it interesting, compelling or fun. It really isn't even challenging. Not to me anyway.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been playing video games for close to 25 years now, so I've been around the block and enjoyed games from many different genres. Like a lot of people, I got introduced to the Survivor Roguelike genre with Vampire Survivors and I'm a big fan of that game. I think Halls of Torment blows it out of the water and I consider it one of my favorite games of all time, enjoying it enough to be one of the 0.6% of players to get all the achievements. Deep customization options, cheap price for the amount of content (200 hours to 100%), addictive and fun gameplay loop, solid incremental progression, and a strong endgame that keeps me coming back for more. I can't recommend this game enough, especially if you are a Steam Deck enthusiast. Don't think, just buy!

_childDocuments_.review: I never really understood the craze behind Vampire Survivors and the dozens of cheap chyneze clones of it that were created later. Untilone day  I saw a bald incel play Halls of Torment on YouTube. I got immediately intrigued by the unique art style, making me nostalgic for the bygone era of the end of the last century, when 3D graphics became advanced enough to create assets, but not efficient enough to always render them in real time. HoT looks like many of the games released back then - a collage of 2D sprites pre-baked from 3D models rotated in a variety of angles and animation states. It is pure art in how it imitates old jank while remaining functional in a modern way. The animations and effects are fluid and everything looks and feels exactly as it should. It has some Diablo in it's DNA, including awesome sound design, but it also reminds me a lot of the very early DOS & Windows 95 action / arcade and indie games, the ones that you'd try to break to see how much entities you can spawn into the game until your processor starts to give up. The game screen often looks like nuts.WAD or that silly RTS custom map you made in the editor just to reach the absolute unit capacity.I haven't played many Survivors games since then, but nothing seems as good as HoT on the surface - there are tons of content to discover and unlock, dozens of mechanics to play around, endless variety in the combination of upgrades that you select during a run. It has an extremely engaging roguelite meta-progression, where each Quest, of which there are literally hundreds, requires you to perform a specific feat in exchange for a reward. Sometimes it's just gold to buy items and boost stats with and a reveal of the requirements of further Quests, but it might be a new ability, a new upgrade path, a new character or something else. Whether you fail a run or succeed, this makes you immediately think of the next one - planning on what you might want to try to achieve and what strategy you'll assume.The moment to moment gameplay mainly consists of movement - keeping the right distance between you and the enemies, picking up the experience that they drop, going after faraway ability scrolls and other pickups, avoiding attacks. I play it with auto-aim on a Steam Deck (docked to a TV), which means that, unless I am pausing the game or making an upgrade selection or something, I literally play it with one finger most of the time. There's rarely a need to manually aim at a specific enemy (depending on your builds) and even then 99% of the time you can get away without it. This makes HoT a very accessible game for people with manual disabilities. At any rate, playing with a controller seems to be much better than being limited to 8 directions.I think everyone should just buy it and try it, it costs next to nothing and provides dozens of hours of fun. It is brutally difficult at times, keeping you on your toes, and at the beginning it might not be very obvious how to progress or even if you're playing it right. But be warned - once it clicks for you, this game is extremely addicting and hard to put down. I bought it months ago in Early Access, but it didn't seem like it at all, I think even back then most developers wouldn't mind releasing it as a feature complete game in the state that it was in. And now there's even more content and QoL improvements.
